             Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds:
   cotangent torsion, vanishing criteria and deformation stability
                                        Companion Paper II
            AI-produced by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, ChatGPT Pro mode, effort Pro),
                                    17 November 2026

                                               Abstract
           We identify the torsion term omitted in the singular-fibre endpoint argument of Campana,
       Demailly and Peternell and prove the exact connecting-map criterion that replaces that
       inference. Proper nodal and compact examples show why the endpoint vanishings alone do
       not suffice. We determine the inverse-Jacobian and conductor maps, retain multiplicities in
       fibre cohomology, and construct compact torus fibrations with the specified normalization
       and component classes. Integral specialization and coherent restriction calculations give
       the correct component counts and Picard conditions. We prove stability of rank-two torus
       fibrations, compute the deformations of the comb and two-parameter families, and distinguish
       the remaining bundle-splitting question from the established deformation results.


Main statements, status, credit and proof map
For a reduced Cartier hypersurface S ⊂ Y , let N ∗ = OY (−S)|S , V = Ω1Y |S , T = tors Ω1S and
Q = Ω1S /T . The canonical kernel K = ker(V → Q) fits into

                  0 −→ N ∗ −→ K −→ T −→ 0,              0 −→ K −→ V −→ Q −→ 0.

When H 0 (N ∗ ⊗A) = H 0 (Q⊗A) = 0, the ambient section space is exactly the kernel of δA : H 0 (T ⊗
A) → H 1 (N ∗ ⊗ A), as proved in proposition 5.1. The proper nodal example in proposition 5.8
has a nonzero ambient section despite both endpoint vanishings. The replacement global criteria
are propositions 13.2, 13.4 and 13.7. The rank-two stability theorem is proposition 15.2; its
statement includes nonreduced deformation bases.
    The contradiction between the standard complex six-sphere family and Campana et al.
(2020a, Corollary 2.3) is due to Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Section 1.2 and Theorem 10.5).
Paper I contains the marked family, periods, discrete parameters and standard cohomology. The
present paper concerns the exact failure of the general inference and the hypotheses under which
replacement conclusions hold. The local nodal example has precisely the hypotheses printed in
its statement; its role is not enlarged to a different global theorem.

Proof map
The tangent index and Picard components isolate the global cohomological question. Local
inverse-Jacobian and conductor calculations supply the missing fibre term. The explicit quotient,
root, blowup and resolution charts establish compact occurrence with the claimed multiplicities;
the restriction maps determine the full integral and coherent invariants. The logarithmic Kodaira–
Spencer calculation and relative graph space give deformation stability. Root-bundle direct
images then give the comb and two-parameter deformation calculations. Complete foundational
derivations, source concordance and program instructions appear in the appendices.

2    Index, Picard components and endpoint cohomology
Proposition 2.1. Let Y be a connected compact complex threefold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0.
Every holomorphic line bundle L on Y satisfies
                                           Z
                                         1                    b3 (Y )
                         χ(Y, TY ⊗ L) =        c3 (TY ) = 1 −         .
                                         2 Y                     2

The orientation in the integral is the complex orientation. The group Pic(Y ) has finitely many
connected components, each a torsor for the complex vector group H 1 (Y, OY ), and π0 Pic(Y ) ≃
H 2 (Y ; Z) through the first Chern class.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The universal coefficient theorem gives H 1 (Y ; Z) = Hom(H1 (Y ; Z), Z) = 0 from b1 (Y ) = 0.
The group H 2 (Y ; Z) is finite because Y has a finite CW model and b2 (Y ) = 0. In the exponential
sequence, normalized by exp(2πi ·), the relevant maps are
                                                        exp
                     0 = H 1 (Y ; Z) −→ H 1 (Y, OY ) −−→ Pic(Y ) −→
                                                                    c
                                                                  1
                                                                    H 2 (Y ; Z).

They are group homomorphisms; the middle map is holomorphic on the Picard group.
Consequently its image Pic0 (Y ) is isomorphic to the complex vector space H 1 (Y, OY ). The next
map in the exponential sequence is H 2 (Y ; Z) → H 2 (Y, OY ); it is zero because its source is finite
and its target is a complex vector space. Thus c1 is surjective, and the component group is
exactly H 2 (Y ; Z).
   Poincaré duality gives H 4 (Y ; Q) = 0. Thus c1 (TY ), c2 (TY ) and c1 (L) vanish in rational
cohomology. The degree-six component of ch(TY ) exp(c1 (L)) td(TY ) is then c3 (TY )/2. The

divisor enters in the endpoint vanishing, and a positive multiple of its actual Cartier divisor
enters the Picard family. These statements supply an index obstruction; they make no assertion
that the failed degree-two vanishing holds.
Proposition 2.3 (Vertical divisors and the field of meromorphic functions). Let Y be a connected
compact complex manifold of dimension n ≥ 2 with H 2 (Y, R) = 0. Let g : Y → C be a surjective
holomorphic map to a connected compact Riemann surface, with connected fibres. Suppose that
its smooth fibres over a nonempty open subset of C are Kähler. Every effective divisor of Y is
supported on finitely many fibres, and pullback induces an isomorphism of fields
                                                      ∼
                                       g ∗ : M(C) −−→ M(Y ).

In particular a(Y ) = 1. Reducedness of the other fibres is unnecessary.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. For a prime divisor D, the image g(D) is analytic by properness. It is a point or all of C.
In the latter case choose a regular value c in the stated open subset for which F = g −1 (c) is not
contained in D. The canonical section of OY (D) restricts to a nonzero section with nonempty
effective zero divisor DF on F . For a Kähler form ω on F , the divisor class formula gives
                              Z                            Z
                                                     n−2
                          0=      c1 (OY (D)|F ) ∧ ω     =    ω n−2 > 0.
                                 F                           DF

The first equality follows from the restriction homomorphism H 2 (Y, R) → H 2 (F, R); the last
follows from positivity on every component with its positive multiplicity. Thus g(D) is a point.
A divisor has finitely many prime components, proving the first assertion.

                                                  4
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


    For h ∈ M(Y ) remove from C the finitely many values supporting its polar divisor. On
the inverse image of the complement, h is holomorphic: a meromorphic function on a manifold
having no codimension-one pole extends across its codimension-two indeterminacy set by the
local normality of the structure sheaf. Its restriction to each compact connected fibre is constant.
The identity g∗ OY = OC , supplied by Stein factorization and the normality of C, therefore gives
a holomorphic descended function there. To check meromorphic extension at the removed values,
take the closure of the graph of h in Y × P1 and apply the proper map g × 1. Its image is a
one-dimensional analytic subset of C × P1 , generically the graph of the descended function. Its
component dominating C has generic degree one, and hence is the graph of a meromorphic
function on C. Pullback equals h on a dense open subset and therefore in the meromorphic
function field. Pullback is injective because g is surjective. This proves the field isomorphism
and its asserted transcendence degree.

Proposition 3.1. Let f : Y → C be a proper holomorphic surjection from a connected compact
complex threefold to a compact Riemann surface, with connected fibres. Let ∆ be a nonempty
finite set containing the critical values, s = |∆|, g = g(C), D = f −1 (∆)red , and let r be the
number of irreducible components of D. Write F for a smooth fibre and

                       t0 = dimQ H1 (F ; Q)π1 (C\∆) = dimQ H 1 (F ; Q)π1 (C\∆) .

For b2 (Y ) = 0 the exact component count is

                                     r = 2g + s − 1 + t0 − b1 (Y ).

Under CDP20’s integral assumptions H 1 (Y ; Z) = H 2 (Y ; Z) = 0, the base is P1 and

                        r = s − 1 + t0 ,     H1 (F ; Z)π1 (C\∆) is free abelian.

The last assertion concerns the indicated quotient of H1 (F ; Z); it does not assert that H1 (F ; Z)
itself is torsion-free.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition A.1; equation (D1).
    The rational component-count formula is the correction in Claude and Alpöge (2026a,
Section 10.5, p. 91). The integral torsion-free conclusion under the displayed integral hypotheses
is an additional clause; its full argument is included here.

Proof. Put U = Y \ D and C ◦ = C \ ∆. The map U → C ◦ is a differentiable fibre bundle. Since
π2 (C ◦ ) = 0, its homotopy sequence is

                             1 −→ π1 (F ) −→ π1 (U ) −→ π1 (C ◦ ) −→ 1.

The last group is free of rank 2g + s − 1. Lifting its free generators gives a section of this extension.
Proposition A.1 therefore gives

                               H1 (U ; Z) ≃ Z2g+s−1 ⊕ H1 (F ; Z)π1 (C ◦ ) .                        (D1)

The second equality defining t0 follows by duality: the dual of the coinvariant quotient is precisely
the space of invariant linear functionals on H1 (F ; Q).
   The cohomology sequence with compact supports for the open inclusion U ⊂ Y contains

            H 4 (Y ; Q) −→ H 4 (D; Q) −→ Hc5 (U ; Q) −→ H 5 (Y ; Q) −→ H 5 (D; Q) = 0.

The top-degree cohomology of the compact pure complex surface D is Qr . One can see this by
deleting the singular and intersection loci, whose real dimensions are at most two, and taking
compactly supported top cohomology of its r oriented smooth components. Poincaré duality
identifies Hc5 (U ; Q) with H1 (U ; Q) and H 5 (Y ; Q) with H1 (Y ; Q). Since H 4 (Y ; Q) = 0, taking
dimensions and using (D1) proves the formula.
    For the integral refinement, the universal coefficient theorem shows first that H1 (Y ; Z) is finite,
using H 1 (Y ; Z) = 0, and then that it is zero, using Ext1 (H1 (Y ; Z), Z) ⊂ H 2 (Y ; Z) = 0. The
group H 4 (Y ; Z) can be finite and nonzero. Its homomorphism to H 4 (D; Z) = Zr is nevertheless
zero. The same sequence now gives H1 (U ; Z) ≃ Zr , since H 5 (Y ; Z) = H1 (Y ; Z) = 0. Equation
(D1) then proves that the coinvariant summand is free. Finally H 1 (C; Q) ,→ H 1 (Y ; Q) by the
Leray edge map, so g = 0.

whereas the uncorrected direct-sum argument has free rank s + 5. This is an explicit compact
complex realization of the faulty group-theoretic step, independent of the retained six-sphere.
   Let η be the nontrivial order-two degree-zero line bundle on C associated to the double cover
E0 → C. Finite-cover descent of fibre cohomology gives
                                R1 f∗ OY = η ⊕ OC ,       R2 f∗ OY = η.
The invariant part of the exterior algebra on the three antiholomorphic one-form directions,
with signs (1, −1, 1), gives hq (Y, OY ) = (1, 2, 1, 0). The restriction from H 1 (Y, OY ) to the two-

homomorphisms are induced by the displayed finite étale quotient and projection. This example
has b1 (Y ) = 4; it is a counterexample to the unchecked restriction argument, not a second example
satisfying the integral CDP20 hypotheses.

Proposition 3.4. For a connected compact complex space S, including a nonreduced one, the
coefficient map
                                H 1 (S; R) −→ H 1 (S, OS )
is injective as a map of real vector spaces.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. First take S reduced. Represent a real cohomology class by a locally constant real Čech
cocycle aij . If its image is zero, after refining the open cover there are holomorphic functions ui
with aij = ui − uj . The imaginary parts of the ui agree on overlaps and give a global continuous
pluriharmonic function. Pull it back to a compact resolution of each irreducible component.
The maximum principle makes each such pullback constant; intersection of components and
connectedness of S make the constants equal. Thus, after subtracting one imaginary constant
from all ui , each ui is real-valued and holomorphic, hence locally constant. They form a real
coboundary for aij . For nonreduced S, a class zero in H 1 (S, OS ) also becomes zero after applying
OS → OSred . The underlying topological space and its real cohomology do not change under
reduction, so the reduced assertion proves the result.

Proposition 3.5. Let f : Y → C be as in 3.1, and let j : C ◦ ,→ C be the smooth-fibre locus.
The natural generization homomorphism

                              R1 f∗ ZY −→ j∗ (R1 f∗ ZY )|C ◦
                                                             

is injective. Every nonzero global section of R1 f∗ ZY is nonzero in H 1 (f −1 (c); Z) at every c ∈ C.

                                                  7
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.1.

Proof. It suffices to check a critical value c. Represent a stalk class by a ∈ H 1 (V ; Z) for
V = f −1 (∆c ) and a sufficiently small disc ∆c . Put V ∗ = f −1 (∆c \ {c}). Assume that the
restriction of a to a smooth fibre is zero. The homotopy sequence for V ∗ → ∆∗c shows that a|V ∗
is the pullback of an integer multiple k of the positive meridian class of the punctured disc.
    Choose a smooth point of one irreducible component of the central divisor, away from all
its other components. There the map has the form t = z m u with m > 0 and u a holomorphic
unit. A small positive normal circle has base winding m and bounds its normal disc in V .
Evaluating a on that circle gives km = 0, whence k = 0. The inclusion V ∗ ,→ V induces a
surjection of fundamental groups: a loop can be perturbed off a complex divisor, including its
higher-codimension singular strata. Therefore a|V ∗ = 0 implies a = 0. Taking the direct limit
over the discs proves the asserted stalk injection; proper topological base change identifies its
source with H 1 (f −1 (c); Z).
    If a global section vanished at one point, it would vanish on a neighbourhood of that
point. Its restriction to the connected smooth locus is a section of a local system, so it would
vanish everywhere on that locus. The just-proved injection then makes it zero everywhere, as
required.

Proposition 3.6. Let Y be a connected compact complex manifold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0,
and let f : Y → P1 be a proper holomorphic surjection with connected fibres. There is a class
β ∈ H 1 (Y, OY ) such that, for every irrational real number r, the line bundle

                                          Lr = exp(2πi rβ)

has infinite order on every scheme-theoretic fibre of f . Every connected component of Pic(Y )
likewise contains a real one-parameter family with this property at every irrational real parameter.
No local-freeness assumption on R1 f∗ OY or constant-dimension assumption on fibre cohomology
is required.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (D5); proposition 3.5;
proposition 3.4.

Proof. The low-degree integral Leray sequence and connectedness of the fibres give an injection
with finite cokernel
                           d2 : H 0 (P1 , R1 f∗ ZY ) ,→ H 2 (P1 ; Z) = Z.                  (D5)
Indeed H 1 (Y ; Z) = 0 and H 2 (Y ; Z) is finite. Thus the image in (D5) is dZ for an integer d > 0;
for the stronger integral hypothesis H 2 (Y ; Z) = 0 one has d = 1. Choose γ mapped to d. By
Lemma 3.5, each γc ∈ H 1 (f −1 (c); Z) is nonzero. The coefficient morphism ZY → OY sends γ to
a global section of R1 f∗ OY . Coherent Leray and H 1 (P1 , O) = H 2 (P1 , O) = 0 identify this space
with H 1 (Y, OY ); let β be its inverse image.
    For every full fibre Yc , naturality of the edge maps and of restriction gives

                                   β|Yc = ιc (γc ) ∈ H 1 (Yc , OYc ),

where ιc is the coefficient map. This uses the natural coherent base-change homomorphism, but
does not require it to be an isomorphism. If Lr |Yc had finite order, the exponential sequence on
the full fibre would give an integer n > 0 and λ ∈ H 1 (Yc ; Z) with

                                          nr ιc (γc ) = ιc (λ).

Lemma 3.4 implies nrγc = λ in real cohomology. The group H 1 (Yc ; Z) is a finitely generated
free abelian group, and γc is a nonzero element of it. A nonzero integral coordinate of γc now

                                                   8
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


implies that r is rational, a contradiction. This works for every c and proves the simultaneous
assertion in Pic0 (Y ).
    For a component represented by a line bundle A, choose N > 0 with AN ∈ Pic0 (Y ) and write
AN = exp(2πib). Then
                                  Ar = A ⊗ exp 2πi(rβ − b)/N
                                                               

belongs to that component and satisfies AN    r = Lr . A group element has finite order exactly
when any fixed positive power of it has finite order. Therefore each Ar |Yc is non-torsion for every
irrational real r, proving the componentwise statement.

Proposition 3.7. Let f : Y → P1 be a holomorphic algebraic reduction of a compact complex
threefold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0 and a(Y ) = 1. At a general smooth fibre, the image of the
restriction H 1 (Y, OY ) → H 1 (F, OF ) contains the complex span of the coefficient homomorphism

                                                                                                  (D4)
                                                   ◦
                                ιF : H 1 (F ; Z)π1 (C ) −→ H 1 (F, OF ),

which is induced by ZF ,→ OF . The final spanning step of CDP’s rank argument reaches the
whole target exactly when this span is H 1 (F, OF ). Surjectivity of the full restriction map need
not have its image generated only by this lattice, so that last equivalence describes the stated
argument.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.1; proposition A.9;
proposition 3.4.

Proof. Let D1 , . . . , Dr be the prime components above ∆, and choose N > 0 annihilating the
finite group H 2 (Y ; Z). The logarithms, in the exponential identification Pic0 (Y ) = H 1 (Y, OY ),
of OY (N D1 ), . . . , OY (N Dr ) generate a free abelian subgroup of rank r − s + 1 = t0 . PHere is the
rank computation withP      its maps specified. The map is Zr → Pic0 (Y ), (ni ) 7→ OY (N ni Di ). A
relation means that N ni Di is the divisor of a meromorphic function. Since f is the algebraic
reduction, that function is f ∗ h for h ∈ M(P1 ). Its divisor is a sum of full fibres with total base
degree zero. Such relations have rank s − 1, and those given by divisors of rational functions
supported on ∆ already have this rank. Statement 3.1 gives the last equality.
    Over U = f −1 (C ◦ ) each of these divisor line bundles has its canonical trivialization. Exactness
of the exponential sequence therefore places its logarithm in the coefficient image of H 1 (U ; Z).
Coherent Leray identifies restriction H 1 (Y, OY ) → H 1 (U, OU ) with restriction of global sections
of E; this is injective because A.9 makes E locally free. Thus the rank-t0 group of logarithms
remains injective on U .
    Topological Leray on the punctured curve gives
                                                                           ◦
                       0 → H 1 (C ◦ ; Z) → H 1 (U ; Z) → H 1 (F ; Z)π1 (C ) → 0.

The first group’s coefficient image vanishes because H 1 (C ◦ , O) = 0. Conversely a class whose
coefficient image in H 1 (U, O) vanishes restricts to zero in H 1 (F, OF ); Lemma 3.4 makes its
integral restriction to F zero. Thus the coefficient image of H 1 (U ; Z) identifies exactly with the
invariant lattice in (D4). The logarithm group maps to a subgroup of the same rank t0 , hence
of finite index, in that lattice. Its complex span equals the span of the entire lattice, and the
restriction image is a complex vector subspace. This proves the assertion and the statement
about the last spanning step.

their quotient glues the construction to B ◦ . These are the maps asserted by Proposition 2, with
that equivariant choice made explicit. The later assertion in Kawai’s corollary about multiple
fibres is not used here.

logarithmic coordinates it fixes the two central generators and adds central vectors to the two base
generators. Its pullback fixes a, b and replaces each of c, e by itself plus a real linear combination
of a, b. Each of the four displayed classes therefore changes only by a multiple of the exact form
a ∧ b. Since the universal cover of P is contractible, a map of P and this group-model map
with the same induced fundamental-group map are homotopic. This computes the action of the
original biholomorphism and proves it is the identity on H 2 . In particular every monodromy
of our isotrivial family, whose action on the base H 1 was just proved to be the identity, acts
identically on H 2 (P ; C).

Proposition 4.8 (Proved exclusion of Inoue general fibres). Under the hypotheses of 4.9, the
very general smooth fibre is not an Inoue surface. More precisely, a proper holomorphic map
from a compact connected complex manifold to a compact Riemann surface, whose fibres over the
complement of a finite set are Inoue surfaces, has a class in H 1 (Y ; R) restricting nontrivially to
each such fibre. Thus these families cannot have b1 (Y ) = 0. This assertion permits arbitrary
multiplicities and arbitrary singularities of the omitted fibres.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 4.9; (Inoue, 1974, pp. 274,
278, 280); (Khaled and Teleman, 2026, Sections 2.1–2.3); equation (C.IN.2); equation (C.IN.3);
(Biswas et al., 2012, Theorem 3.2); (Biswas et al., 2012, Section 3.3); equation (C.IN.6).


                                                  23
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Proof. We first establish the precise family construction needed for the assertion about H 1 . Write
B ◦ for the complement of the finite set and Y ◦ = f −1 (B ◦ ). Put H = {w ∈ C : Im w > 0}. Each
Inoue surface is a quotient of H × C. In the three standard presentations the first coordinates of
all deck transformations have the form

                                w 7−→ aw + b,         a > 0,   b ∈ R.                       (C.IN.1)

They include a nonzero real translation and a transformation w 7→ αw, with α > 1. Inoue’s
original Propositions 2 and 5 establish infinitesimal rigidity for types SM and S − ; his Proposition
4 gives a locally complete one-parameter family for type S + (Inoue, 1974, pp. 274, 278, 280). In
that family the parameter changes only the second coordinate: local coordinate transitions have
the form
                                  wi = αmij wj + aij ,
                                                                                             (C.IN.2)
                                   zi = zj + bij wj + cij + t mij ,
where mij ∈ Z and the other coefficients are independent of t. In particular the real affine
transformations in the first coordinate are constant throughout this complete family. The
standard deck presentations are also recorded in (Khaled and Teleman, 2026, Sections 2.1–2.3).
   After shrinking a simply connected base disc V ⊂ B ◦ , local completeness identifies f −1 (V )
with the pullback of one of these families. Its universal cover over V is therefore H × C × V ,
with holomorphic covering map to f −1 (V ). In the S + case the parameter t in (C.IN.2) is a
holomorphic function on V ; the other two cases are products. The smooth real one-form

                                          θV = d log Im w                                   (C.IN.3)

is invariant under every deck transformation, where d is the exterior derivative on the whole
covering space. It thus descends to a closed real one-form on f −1 (V ).
    We prove that these forms agree on overlaps, including base directions. Over a simply
connected smaller overlap, a transition between the two family descriptions lifts holomorphically
to the universal covers. On each fibre its first coordinate is independent of z: composing with a
Cayley transform gives a bounded entire function of z, which is constant. Applying the same
argument to the inverse proves that the resulting first coordinate is an automorphism h of H.
This automorphism conjugates the first-coordinate deck groups. Their common fixed-point set
on ∂H = R ∪ {∞} is exactly {∞}: the nonzero translation has this as its sole fixed point, and
all their elements fix it. Consequently h(∞) = ∞ and h(w) = aw + b with a > 0 and b ∈ R. In a
holomorphic family of these transitions, a and b are holomorphic functions of the base parameter;
this follows, for example, by taking the w derivative and then evaluating at a fixed w. Their real
values force them to be locally constant. Therefore

                          d log Im(aw + b) = d log(a Im w) = d log Im w                     (C.IN.4)

as forms on the total family. Thus the θV glue to an actual closed form θ on Y ◦ . The same
argument includes a finite étale quotient of an Inoue surface. Locally over a simply connected
base disc its finite cover extends to the family: lift a differentiable marking by Ehresmann’s
theorem and equip the resulting covering space with the pulled-back complex structure. Passing
to the Galois closure when necessary gives a family of finite covers of Inoue surfaces; these
are again Inoue surfaces, as is also seen from their finite-index lattice presentations. Every
deck transformation of the quotient normalizes a finite-index Inoue deck group on H × C. Its
first-coordinate group still contains a nonzero translation and has common boundary fixed
point precisely ∞. The preceding conjugation argument therefore makes each quotient deck
transformation real affine in w, and its coefficients are constant over the base disc. Consequently
(C.IN.3) descends through the finite quotient as well. Its pullback to the Inoue cover has the
nonzero period log α, so the descended fibre class is nonzero. For a fibre loop represented on its


                                                 24
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


universal cover by the deck transformation w 7→ αw, its integral is log α 6= 0. Hence [θ] restricts
nontrivially to the fibre.

    For clarity, the exact topological extension is as follows. The map H1 (Y ◦ ; R) → H1 (Y ; R)
is surjective: loops can be moved away from a complex divisor. Its kernel is generated by the
meridians of the irreducible components of D. Indeed, a bounding real two-chain can be put
in general position, transverse to the smooth divisor locus and disjoint from its singular locus,
which has real codimension at least four. Removing small discs about its intersection points
leaves a chain in Y ◦ whose additional boundary circles are meridians. This proves the kernel
assertion, including relations and arbitrary singularities of D. The period homomorphism of θ
therefore factors uniquely through H1 (Y ; R) and defines a class

                                  θe ∈ H 1 (Y ; R),    θ|

Its restriction to an Inoue fibre is nonzero by (C.IN.3). This proves the asserted extension and
the obstruction b1 (Y ) > 0.
    We finish by explaining why a very general Inoue fibre in 4.9 places the entire smooth locus
in this situation. Ehresmann’s theorem identifies the diffeomorphism type, and in particular
the fundamental group, of all smooth fibres. The first two Betti numbers are then (1, 0). These
surfaces are minimal by 4.9 and non-Kähler. The compact-surface classification gives class VII
surfaces or non-Kähler elliptic surfaces (Biswas et al., 2012, Theorem 3.2). The Inoue group is
solvable and is not virtually nilpotent. For the latter assertion, its normal lattice is Z3 in type
SM , and a three-dimensional integral Heisenberg group in types S + and S − . Conjugation by a
generator of the cyclic quotient has an eigenvalue α > 1 on the rational abelianization of this
lattice. Every finite-index subgroup contains a positive power of that generator and a finite-index
sublattice, so the eigenvalue becomes αk > 1. In a nilpotent group repeated commutators make
every such conjugation unipotent on this rational abelianization. This proves the claimed failure
of virtual nilpotence.
    A Hopf group is virtually cyclic, and a Kodaira group is virtually nilpotent; neither can equal
this group. For a properly elliptic surface of Euler number zero the canonical bundle formula
makes the base orbifold hyperbolic: its orbifold canonical degree is positive exactly in Kodaira
dimension one. The elliptic fibration induces a surjection of its fundamental group onto the
orbifold group. That group has a finite-index closed surface group of genus at least two, and

                                                  25
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


hence is not solvable. This also cannot be a quotient of an Inoue group. The orbifold exact
sequence is the one used in (Biswas et al., 2012, Section 3.3). Thus every smooth fibre is an
Inoue surface. Applying (C.IN.6) contradicts b1 (Y ) = 0 and completes the exclusion.

Proposition 4.9. Let f : Y → C be a holomorphic algebraic reduction of a connected compact
complex threefold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0 and a(Y ) = 1. The base is C ≃ P1 . Every smooth fibre

Proposition 4.12 (Proved actual occurrence of both Hopf types). There are compact complex
threefolds with b1 = b2 = 0 and a = 1 whose holomorphic algebraic reduction is a smooth bundle

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 5.2.

Proof. On the normalization branch xi = 0, an ambient form maps to zero in the cotangent
bundle of that branch precisely when all coefficients except that of dxi vanish. Thus a coefficient
of dxi must Q  vanish on every branch xj = 0 for j 6= i. In the convergent power-series ring it is
divisible by j6=i xj . Its remaining factor is defined modulo xi , which gives exactly (A.6). The
coefficients of different dxi show injectivity. Coefficients of the coordinates not among x1 , . . . , xr
vanish on every branch and hence vanish in R. This proves surjectivity in every dimension.
    For r = 1 the map is a 7→ a dx. For r = 2 it is (a, b) 7→ ay dx + bx dy, and quotienting
by dF = y dx + x dy leaves the generator y dx = −x dy, annihilated by (x, y). For r = 3 the
branch generators are yz dx, xz dy, xy dz. Their sum is dF and their respective annihilators are
(x), (y), (z), proving (A.7). Multiplication of F by a unit and changes of coordinates were checked
in 5.2. Formula (A.6) is the restriction of the canonical fractional-ideal map, so it glues without
a chosen branch ordering, equation, or coordinate system.

Proposition 5.5 (Pinch points and cuspidal edges). At the pinch point F = x2 − y 2 z, with
normalization x = uv, y = u, z = v 2 , write B = C{u, v}. Then

               K = B dF,         T ≃ B/R ≃ R/(x, y),       τ = 2yz dx − 2xz dy − xy dz             (A.8)

is a torsion generator. At the cuspidal edge F = x2 − y 3 , with normalization x = t3 , y = t2 and
unchanged coordinate z, write B = C{t, z}. Then

                K = t−1 B dF,        T ≃ t−1 B/R ≃ R/(x, y 2 ),            τ = 2y dx − 3x dy.      (A.9)

The conductor is (x, y) for the pinch point and (x, y) for the cusp; in the cusp normalization
it is t2 B. An ordinary surface, meaning a surface whose singularities are double normal
crossings, triple normal crossings, and pinch points, satisfies canonically K = η∗ η ∗ N ∗ and
T = N ∗ ⊗ (η∗ OSe/OS ). For the cuspidal edge the additional quotient J −1 /B is generated by t−1
over C{z}.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. For the pinch point,

                 R = C{u, v 2 , uv} = C{v 2 } + uB,     J = (uv, uv 2 , u2 ) = u(u, v)B.

The equality of the two descriptions of J follows by separating even and odd powers of v. An
element q ∈ J −1 satisfies (qu)(u, v) ⊂ B. Since B is a regular local ring, HomB ((u, v), B) = B:
a meromorphic function whose products with u and v are holomorphic has no pole along any
divisor, and its possible isolated singularity is removable by the holomorphic extension theorem.
Hence qu = h ∈ B. The requirements hv, hv 2 ∈ R, restricted to u = 0, say respectively that

                                                   32
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


h(0, v)v and h(0, v)v 2 are even power series. The first requires h(0, v) to be odd and the second to
be even. Therefore h(0, v) = 0, so h ∈ uB and q ∈ B. The reverse inclusion follows either directly
or from (A.3). Also B/R is generated by v and its annihilator is (u, uv) = (y, x). Multiplying
dF by v = x/y gives the displayed τ .
    For the cusp, R = C{t2 , t3 , z} and J = (t3 , t4 ). A meromorphic q with qt3 , qt4 ∈ R has
no poles away from t = 0; writing its Laurent expansion in t shows that the lowest allowed
exponent is −1. Indeed an exponent −3 produces a forbidden t term after multiplication by t4 ,
an exponent −2 produces one after multiplication by t3 , and smaller exponents produce a pole.
Conversely every t−1 B has both products in R. Thus J −1 = t−1 B. Modulo R, the quotient
has the C{z}-basis t−1 , t; multiplication by y sends the first basis vector to the second, while
x and y 2 kill both. This proves the cyclic presentation and (A.9). The conductor calculations
follow directly from the displayed descriptions of R ⊂ B. Formula (A.2) and the three local
computations prove the ordinary-surface assertion by gluing.

Proposition 5.6 (Vertical residue poles at a tacnode–cusp intersection). For F = x2 − y 4 z 3 ,
normalization is x = u2 v 3 , y = u, z = v 2 . Put A0 = C{u, v 2 } and B = C{u, v}. Then

                             R = A0 ⊕ u2 v 3 A0 ,          c = u2 v 2 B,

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The element v = x/(y 2 z) belongs to the fraction field and satisfies v 2 = z. Adjoining
it gives the regular ring B, which is therefore the finite normalization. Separating even and
odd powers of v gives the displayed description of R. An even monomial ua v b belongs to the
conductor exactly when a ≥ 2 and b ≥ 2; an odd monomial already in R has a ≥ 2, b ≥ 3 and is
then in the conductor. Thus c = u2 v 2 B.
    The normalized Jacobian generators, with irrelevant nonzero constants removed, are
u v 3 , u3 v 6 , u4 v 4 . If qJ ⊂ R, the first product shows that q has no other polar divisor, with
  2

possible orders at most two along u = 0 and three along v = 0. A term of order v −3 would
produce a forbidden v 1 term in qu4 v 4 ; a term of order v −2 would produce one in qu2 v 3 . Both
coefficients must vanish, so q has order at least −1 in v. A coefficient a(v)u−2 would require

                              v −1 dF = 2y 2 z dx − 4xyz dy − 3xy 2 dz.

    For ordinary surfaces the exact ambient-vanishing criterion is (A.1) with K⊗A = η∗ η ∗ (N ∗ ⊗A).

Proposition 5.7 (A transverse cusp whose critical-curve equation is only a symbolic square).
Put
                     I = (y 2 − xz, yz 2 − x4 , z 3 − x3 y) ⊂ C{x, y, z},

independent over C{t5 }. Consequently this actual ring homomorphism is injective and has image
C{t5 , t6 , t7 }; it proves the stated normalization and the primeness of I. The three generators
are minimal. Indeed their initial terms have degrees two, three, three; after the degree-two
coefficient vanishes, the cubic terms yz 2 and z 3 are independent modulo the span of xg1 , yg1 , zg1 .
A height-two ideal with three minimal generators is not a complete intersection.

Proposition 5.10 (The hypotheses satisfied by the compact example). The threefold Y of
Statement 5.9 has H 1 (Y, Z) = 0, H 2 (Y, Z) ≃ Z11 , algebraic dimension 3, and e(Y ) = 24. Its
map g is holomorphic, proper, surjective, and has connected fibres. Thus it tests the fibrewise
inference in Section 7 of Campana et al. (2020a); it does not satisfy the vanishing of H 2 (Y, Z)
or algebraic dimension one required by that paper’s Theorem 2.2.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 5.9; Campana et al.

Proof. The residue calculation above gives KE = h∗ O(−1). Relative duality gives R1 h∗ OE =

and H 0 (E, KE⊗m ) = 0 for every positive m. Castelnuovo’s rationality criterion, in the form
q = P2 = 0 for a smooth projective surface, makes E rational. A rational smooth projective
surface is obtained from a minimal rational surface by point blowups; its first integral homology
vanishes and its second integral cohomology is free. Euler additivity gives e(E) = 12, since the
twelve nodal fibres each have Euler characteristic one and the smooth elliptic fibre has Euler
characteristic zero. Poincare duality gives b2 (E) = 10. The integral Kunneth isomorphism
for Y = E × P1 gives the asserted groups and Euler number. Projectivity and dimension give
a(Y ) = 3. Connectedness and surjectivity follow directly from the integral cubic fibres of h and
the second product factor.

    The construction in Statement 5.9 supplies the compact local counterexample, including

Proposition 5.11 (All thickenings and their lifting maps). Let S be any effective Cartier divisor
in a complex manifold, let E be any locally free sheaf on that manifold, and let Ek = E|kS . For
each k ≥ 2 there is a canonical exact sequence
                         0 −→ (E|S ) ⊗ (N ∗ )k−1 −→ Ek −→ Ek−1 −→ 0.                          (A.10)
Write Gk−1 = (E|S ) ⊗ (N ∗ )k−1 and let k : H 0 ((k − 1)S, Ek−1 ) → H 1 (S, Gk−1 ) be the connecting
map. Then
                     0 −→ H 0 (S, Gk−1 ) −→ H 0 (kS, Ek ) −→ ker k −→ 0.                      (A.11)
In particular H 0 (kS, Ek ) = 0 exactly when H 0 (S, Gk−1 ) = 0 and k is injective. Starting with
H 0 (S, E|S ), equations (A.10)–(A.11) compute the group on mS through all its extension maps.
The vanishing of every H 0 (S, Gj ), 0 ≤ j < m, is a sufficient criterion. These statements apply
to E = Ω1Y ⊗ B for every line bundle B, and include smooth, normal-crossings, and all other
reduced supports.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. With I = OY (−S), the sequence is the tensor product of E with 0 → I k−1 /I k →
OY /I k → OY /I k−1 → 0. The Cartier property identifies I k−1 /I k with (N ∗ )k−1 on S; local
freeness makes the tensor product exact. Taking global sections proves (A.11) and its equivalence.
Induction on k proves the sufficient criterion. No splitting of the thickening, cyclic base change,
or assumption about the normal bundle has been used.

Proposition 5.12 (Counterexample: Vanishing on the support alone does not imply vanishing
on a multiple fibre). There is a compact smooth complex threefold g : Y → P1 with connected
general fibre an abelian surface and a smooth fibre support S of multiplicity m, for every m ≥ 3,
and a line bundle B on Y , such that
                     H 0 (S, (Ω1Y ⊗ B)|S ) = 0,    h0 (mS, (Ω1Y ⊗ B)|mS ) = 3.                (A.12)
Its conormal has exact order m. The replacement is (A.10)–(A.11), with the graded twists
retained.

                                                  39
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Take an abelian surface F and a translation a : F → F of exact order m. Let ζ be a
primitive mth root of unity. The action generated by (p, z) 7→ (a(p), ζz) on F × P1 is free, so the
quotient Y is a smooth compact threefold and the quotient map is finite etale. The invariant
map t = z m gives g : Y → P1 . Away from 0 and ∞ its fibre is isomorphic to F : the m lifts of
a base point are permuted transitively and freely. At 0 the fibre is mS, where S = F /hai. Set
B = OY (−S).
    The connected cyclic cover F → S identifies N ∗ = B|S with the character line of weight
one. Its order is exactly m: otherwise a nontrivial proper character power would have a nonzero
invariant trivialization on the connected compact cover, whose holomorphic functions are constant.
Pullback to F splits the ambient cotangent bundle into two invariant tangent forms and the
normal form dz of weight one. Consequently
                                  (Ω1Y ⊗ B)|S ≃ (N ∗ )⊕2 ⊕ (N ∗ )2 .
The nontrivial flat lines on the abelian surface S have no holomorphic sections. For completeness,
their pullbacks to F are trivial; a section would be a constant function transforming by a
nontrivial character, which is zero. Since m ≥ 3, both characters in the preceding splitting are
nontrivial, proving the first equality.
    The inverse image of mS is the ringed space with structure sheaf OF ⊗ C[z]/(z m ). Write e for
the local generator of the pulled-back line B; it has weight one. All global sections on this inverse
image are linear combinations of z k α1 e, z k α2 e, z k dz e for 0 ≤ k < m, where α1 , α2 are a basis
of invariant one-forms on F . The first two have weight k + 1 and the third weight k + 2. The
invariant monomials are exactly z m−1 α1 e, z m−1 α2 e, z m−2 dz e. Taking invariants is exact over C,
by averaging over the finite group. These three monomials therefore give the claimed basis and
prove the second equality. Translations act identically on H q (F, OF ), whose dimensions are 2q .
                                                                                                     

The same calculation gives all fibre groups: hq (S, E|S ) = (0, 0, 0) and hq (mS, E|mS ) = (3, 6, 3)
for q = 0, 1, 2. For completeness, on the compact threefold itself the two tangent summands
pull back to OF  OP1 (−1) and have no cohomology. The normal summand is OF  Ω1P1 (−{0}).
Its first cohomology on P1 has the Cech basis dz/z, dz, of weights zero and one, respectively.
Indeed sections near zero are multiples of z dz, and sections near infinity are multiples of z −2 dz,
leaving exactly those two Laurent classes. Its invariant part is one-dimensional. Kunneth and
finite-cover descent therefore give hq (Y, E) = (0, 1, 2, 1) for q = 0, 1, 2, 3.

   For this example the complete dimensions on kS, 1 ≤ k ≤ m, are 0 for k ≤ m − 2, 1 for

Proposition 5.15 (Every reducible full fibre has generic ambient  vanishing). Let Y be a smooth
compact complex threefold with H 2 (Y, Q) = 0, and let F = i mi Si be an effective Cartier divisor
                                                          P
with connected reducible support. Every connected component of Pic(Y ) contains a dense open
subset, with proper closed analytic complement, on which

                                         H 0 (F, (Ω1Y ⊗ L)|F ) = 0.                                   (A.15b)

The multiplicities may be unequal. For a proper connected fibration over a compact curve, the
vanishing is simultaneous on all reducible full fibres after intersecting finitely many such open
sets. Consequently a full fibre with ambient sections for every Picard twist has irreducible support.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Every component Si meets a different component Sj , because the support is connected
and reducible. The canonical section of OY (Sj ) restricts to a nonzero section on Si . It is a
nonzerodivisor in every local ring of Si : otherwise one local branch of Si would be contained in
Sj , and analytic continuation on the global irreducible component would give Si = Sj . Its zero
scheme is therefore a nonzero effective Cartier divisor D on Si .
     For any fixed locally free sheaf E on the reduced irreducible compact surface Si , the injections

                                     H 0 (Si , E(−nD)) ,→ H 0 (Si , E)

form a decreasing sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces. Their intersection is zero. At a
point of D, a section in the intersection has its germ in every power of the Cartier ideal; the
Krull intersection theorem for the Noetherian analytic local ring makes this germ zero. The
identity theorem on the reduced irreducible surface, applied in local trivializations of E, then
makes the global section zero. A descending sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces stabilizes,
so H 0 (Si , E(−nD)) = 0 for all sufficiently large n.
    Fix a Picard component and a representative L0 in it. The integral class c1 (OY (Sj )) is
torsion because H 2 (Y, Q) = 0; choose a positive integer q killing it. Then OY (−qnSj ) belongs
to Pic0 (Y ) for every n. Apply the preceding argument to E = (Ω1Y ⊗ L0 )|Si . It supplies, in
the chosen Picard component, a twist L0 ⊗ OY (−qnSj ) with zero ambient group on Si . Local
holomorphic Picard families and proper semicontinuity show that the nonvanishing locus on that
component is a proper closed analytic subset. Its complement is dense and open. The same
argument works in every Picard component.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


   Choose an ordered list A1 , . . . , AN of the prime divisors Si , with Si repeated mi times, and
put F0 = 0, Fk = A1 + · · · + Ak . The exact Cartier sequences, tensored with the locally free
ambient bundle, are

                       0 −→ (Ω1Y ⊗ L ⊗ OY (−Fk−1 ))|Ak −→ (Ω1Y ⊗ L)|Fk
                                                 −→ (Ω1Y ⊗ L)|Fk−1 −→ 0.

This follows locally from multiplication by an equation of Fk−1 , and remains exact when a

intersection is dense open. Every displayed first term has no sections there, so induction from

    A proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact manifold to a smooth curve has finitely
many critical values, since its proper analytic critical-value set does not contain a general point.
Its smooth connected fibres are irreducible. Thus there are finitely many reducible fibres, and
a further finite intersection gives the asserted simultaneous vanishing. This proves the final
consequence and resolves the unequal-multiplicity transfer in this case without any assertion
about torsion-free differentials on individual components.

Proposition 5.16 (Both fibre groups on the specified W ). For the reduced normal-crossings
fibre W with normalization η : dP6 → W in the specified threefold X, and every L ∈ Pic(X), put

                        H 0 (W, Q ⊗ A) = 0,       H 0 (W, Ω1X |W ⊗ A) ≃ C.                   (A.15)

    The nonvanishing on the compact example and the torsion-free-cotangent vanishing are
contained in Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Theorem 10.5 and Section 10.4). The present calculation
sharpens the ambient section dimension to exactly one; that sharper equality and its proof are
distinguished from the source nonvanishing.

used is its specified normalization as the blowup of P2 at three points. A blowup at a smooth
point has π∗ O = O and R1 π∗ O = 0. The latter follows from the theorem on formal functions:
successive exceptional-neighborhood quotients are OP1 (k), k ≥ 0, whose first cohomology is zero.
Thus H 1 (dP6 , O) = H 1 (P2 , O) = 0. The exponential sequence makes c1 : Pic(dP6 ) → H 2 (dP6 , Z)
injective. The pullback of every line bundle on X has zero first Chern class and is therefore
trivial.
    The differential of normalization gives Ω1W → η∗ Ω1dP6 . Its target is torsion-free as an OW -
module, so it factors through Q. The resulting map is injective because it is an isomorphism on
the dense regular locus and its source is torsion-free. A holomorphic one-form on the blowup
restricts away from the exceptional curves to a one-form on P2 minus three points. Its coefficients
extend over these points by Hartogs’ theorem, and H 0 (P2 , Ω1P2 ) = 0 by the Euler sequence. Hence
H 0 (dP6 , Ω1 ) = 0. The projection formula and the triviality of η ∗ A prove the first equality in
(A.15).
     Because W is the full reduced fibre, its conormal is trivial. 5.4 identifies K ⊗ A with
η∗ η A = η∗ OdP6 . The normalization is connected and compact, so its global holomorphic
    ∗

Proposition 5.17 (Counterexample: A specific implication in the printed proof of Proposition
7.3). The implication that a ruled minimal surface S0 with a one-parameter family of numerically
trivial line bundles Mt and nonzero sections of Ω1S0 ⊗ Mt must be ruled over a curve of genus at
least two is false when the family Mt is allowed to be constant, as the printed proof explicitly
allows.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Take S0 = E × P1 for an elliptic curve E and take Mt = OS0 for every parameter. The
product cotangent decomposition gives

                              hq (S0 , Ω1S0 ) = (1, 2, 1),   q = 0, 1, 2.

Indeed the E cotangent summand contributes (1, 1, 0), while the P1 cotangent summand
contributes (0, 1, 1) by the Kunneth formula and h1 (P1 , O(−2)) = 1. A nonzero invariant
form on E provides the asserted sections for every parameter, whereas the ruling has genus one.
This refutes the stated implication. It is a counterexample to that implication with its explicit
data; it supplies no threefold satisfying all of Proposition 7.3’s ambient hypotheses.

Proposition 5.19 (Canonical triviality on an irreducible reduced torus fibre). Let g : Y → C be
a proper holomorphic map from a connected smooth compact threefold onto a smooth compact
curve, with connected fibres and general fibre a complex two-torus. Every irreducible reduced full
fibre S = g −1 (c) has ωS ≃ OS . When H 2 (Y, Q) = 0, it therefore satisfies hq (S, OS ) = (1, 2, 1).

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.2.

Proof. The coherent sheaf g∗ ωY is torsion-free: a nonzero function on an open subset of the
base cannot annihilate a holomorphic section of a line bundle on the dominating smooth total
space. It has generic rank one because the smooth torus fibre has one holomorphic top form;
after restricting to a base open set where Grauert base change holds, this identifies its rank. On
the smooth curve it is consequently a line bundle M . The evaluation morphism g ∗ M → ωY is
generically nonzero, so its zero scheme is an effective Cartier divisor D and ωY ≃ g ∗ M ⊗ OY (D).
No component of D dominates the base: on a general smooth torus fibre its defining section is a
nonzero holomorphic top form and is nowhere zero. Thus D is vertical.
    All vertical components meeting the specified irreducible full fibre are that fibre itself.
Consequently OY (D)|S is a power of OY (S)|S , and the latter is trivial because a coordinate
on C defines the full reduced fibre. The pullback g ∗ M |S is also trivial. Adjunction gives
ωS = (ωY ⊗ OY (S))|S ≃ OS . The fibre is reduced and connected, so h0 (OS ) = 1; it is a
Cartier divisor, hence Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein, so Serre duality gives h2 (OS ) = 1. The
divisor Riemann–Roch calculation in 6.2 gives χ(OS ) = 0 under the stated rational cohomology
hypothesis, yielding h1 = 2.

number is 4 + 2 = 6. The conductor is a cycle of six rational curves, with six nodes, so

counting the three preimages of each triple point once gives e(N ) = 6 − 2(3 − 1) = 2. Hence
e(S) = 2.

    Away from finitely many critical values the proper holomorphic map is a differentiable fibre
bundle, and a two-torus has Euler number zero. Additivity  for a stratification by this open base
and the exceptional points therefore gives e(Y ) = c e((Yc )red ). Nilpotents do not change the

underlying topological space. The assumed fibre classes and (A.18) give (A.19). The equality
with c3 is the complex-oriented Gauss–Bonnet theorem. Poincare duality for the connected

Proposition 5.22 (Unitary-flat differentials on every compact reduced complex surface). Let
S be a compact reduced complex surface, let A be a rank-one unitary complex local system on
its underlying topological space, and let A = A ⊗C OS be its associated holomorphic line bundle.
There is a canonical complex-linear injection

                                   H 0 (S, Ω
                                           e 1 ⊗ A) −→ H 1 (S, A).
                                             S                                                  (A.20)

The construction uses continuous local primitives that are holomorphic on the normalization; it
does not assert that those primitives are holomorphic on a non-seminormal surface.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let η : Se → S be normalization and choose a resolution π : Z → Se such that the
exceptional curves have normal crossings; the components of Z are compact smooth surfaces.
Pullback of Kähler differentials along h = η ◦ π : Z → S kills the torsion of Ω1S , because the
resulting form vanishes on the dense inverse image of Sreg and the target is locally free. Thus a
section α on the left of (A.20) gives a holomorphic one-form αZ with values in the unitary-flat
line h∗ A. This map on sections is injective for the same dense-open reason.
    Write ∇ for the flat unitary connection. Holomorphicity gives ∇αZ type (2, 0). The Hermitian
pairing identifies the tensor product of the flat line with its conjugate with the trivial local
system. Stokes’ theorem gives, on each connected component of Z,
                              Z                 Z
                                                               
                                 ∇αZ ∧ ∇αZ =       d αZ ∧ ∇αZ = 0.
                               Z                   Z

After multiplication by the fixed dimensional sign, the integrand is the nonnegative squared
norm of a (2, 0)-form times a positive volume form. Hence ∇αZ = 0.
     We prove the required local primitive assertion at a point x ∈ S. Trivialize A on a sufficiently
small connected neighbourhood V of x; complex analytic spaces are locally contractible, so such
a flat trivialization exists. The section α has a local lift to Ω1S ⊗ A, since the latter surjects onto
the torsion-free quotient. Its pullback to each reduced fibre of h over x is zero: the morphism of
that fibre to S is constant, so the induced morphism on Kähler differentials is zero.
     For each point x e ∈ η −1 (x), a sufficiently small regular neighbourhood of the exceptional fibre
  −1
π (e  x) in the good resolution retracts onto that fibre. This neighbourhood can be constructed by
plumbing the normal disc bundles of the exceptional curves at their transverse intersection points;
it is a neighbourhood of the entire fibre. A sufficiently small inverse image of a neighbourhood
of xe lies inside it by properness. In the smooth case one instead uses a coordinate ball. Every
period of αZ on the regular neighbourhood is zero, because the form is closed and its restriction
to the retracting fibre is zero. Integration from a fixed point therefore produces a single-valued
holomorphic primitive: a smooth primitive has differential of type (1, 0), so its ∂¯ is zero. Normality
and π∗ OZ = OSe descend that primitive to a holomorphic function b on a neighbourhood of x            e.
Choose its constant so that b(e     x) = 0. Perform this independently at every point over x and
shrink V so that all its inverse image is covered by these neighbourhoods.


                                                  47
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


    These primitives have equal values on every fibre of η over V . To see this, form the finite
analytic fibre product W = Se ×S Se with projections p1 , p2 . On the normalization of every
positive-dimensional irreducible component of Wred , the differential of p∗1 b − p∗2 b is zero on a dense
open subset: both differentials are pullbacks of the same local lift of α from S. The isolated
singularities of Se can be omitted for this comparison; holomorphicity then extends the equality.
Thus the difference is constant on each such component. The same conclusion is automatic on a
zero-dimensional component. Shrink V once more so that every component of the finite space
W |V meets the fibre over x; components disjoint from that fibre can be removed by properness.
Our normalization b(e   x) = 0 makes all these constants zero. Hence p∗1 b = p∗2 b as continuous
functions, proving equality on the fibres of η.
    A finite proper surjection is a topological quotient map. The functions b therefore descend
to continuous functions on V , holomorphic after pullback to normalization, whose differential
on the regular locus is α. On overlaps, any two such primitives differ by a locally constant
function: their difference is constant on each local normalized branch, and continuity identifies
the constants whenever branches meet. With the flat transition functions of A, these differences
define a Cech class in H 1 (S, A). Changing the chosen primitives changes it by a locally constant
coboundary. This defines the canonical linear map (A.20).
    If the resulting class is zero, adjust the local primitives by locally constant sections so that
they glue. Their pullback is then a global holomorphic section of the unitary-flat line on each
compact component of Z. Its squared norm is plurisubharmonic, so the maximum principle
makes the section parallel; its covariant differential is zero. Consequently αZ = 0, and injectivity
of pullback gives α = 0. This proves (A.20).

equation (A.22); proposition 5.22.

Proof. We specify all comparison maps used from 3.6. On a sufficiently small disc ∆ about c, put

                           π1 (U ) −→ S 1 ,    a 7−→ exp 2πirhγU , ai .                      (A.22)

Denote this local system by AU . 3.5–3.6 prove that γU restricts nontrivially to every nearby
smooth fibre. Irrationality of r therefore makes (A.22) nontrivial on such a fibre F .
    A nontrivial rank-one local system on the real torus underlying F has zero cohomology in
every degree. Explicitly, use the standard cellular cochain complex of the product of four circles
with coefficients in the character. It is the Koszul complex for the four scalars χ(ej ) − 1. At

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


fibre bundle. Its local-system Leray spectral sequence has zero fibre-cohomology sheaves, hence

     Inclusion induces a surjection π1 (U ∗ ) → π1 (U ): a loop in the smooth real six-manifold U
can be perturbed off the divisor, whose real codimension is at least two, relative to a base point

If a crossed homomorphism a : G → M becomes a(q(h)) = (χ(q(h)) − 1)v after pullback by a

Proposition 5.24 (CDP20 Proposition 7.3 with a complete replacement proof). Let Y be a
connected smooth compact complex threefold with H 1 (Y, Z) = H 2 (Y, Z) = 0, algebraic dimension
one and holomorphic algebraic reduction g : Y → C. There is a dense open subset of Pic(Y ),
whose complement is a proper complex analytic subset, such that

                             H 0 (Yc )red , Ω
                                            e1                                            (A.23)
                                                                   
                                              (Yc )red ⊗ L|(Yc )red = 0

for every singular reduced fibre support and every L in that subset. In fact the transgression
twists Lr of 3.6 satisfy (A.23) on every reduced fibre support, including smooth and reducible
supports, for every real irrational r.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.6; proposition 4.9;
proposition 5.23; (Schröer and Siebert, 2002, §1 and the central-extension diagram in the proof
of Lemma 1.1); (Albanese, 2020, §2.1.1 and Theorem 2.2); (Albanese, 2020, §2.1.2 and
Proposition 2.3); proposition 3.5; proposition 5.22; proposition 5.17; equation (A.24).

Proof. The independently rederived smooth-fibre classification 4.9 leaves complex tori, bielliptic
surfaces, primary or secondary Kodaira surfaces, and primary or secondary Hopf surfaces or
Inoue surfaces. We prove that for each such smooth fibre F and each nonzero γF ∈ H 1 (F, Z) the
local system
                         Ar,F : a 7−→ exp(2πirhγF , ai) (r ∈ R \ Q)
satisfies H 0 (F, Ar,F ) = H 1 (F, Ar,F ) = 0. Its character has infinite image, so the assertion in
degree zero is immediate.
    For a torus the Koszul argument in 5.23 applies. A bielliptic surface has a finite étale torus
cover. Pullback of the integral class is nonzero: transfer composed with pullback is multiplication
by the degree. The character stays nontrivial after pullback, and transfer with local coefficients
makes pullback on cohomology injective over C. Thus degree-one vanishing descends from the
torus cover.
    A primary Kodaira surface is a principal elliptic bundle over an elliptic curve, as described in
(Schröer and Siebert, 2002, §1 and the central-extension diagram in the proof of Lemma 1.1). Its
fundamental group has a central extension

                                  1 −→ Z2 −→ Γ −→ Z2 −→ 1.                                   (A.24)

For any nontrivial one-dimensional character χ of Γ, if its restriction to the central subgroup
is nontrivial, the latter’s cohomology with these coefficients is zero by the two-variable Koszul

                                                49
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


contraction. The Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence then gives H 1 (Γ, Cχ ) = 0. If its central
restriction is trivial, χ descends to a nontrivial character of the quotient Z2 . Centrality makes its
action on the cohomology of the central subgroup equal to that scalar character, and the same
Koszul contraction kills every term on the second page. Again H 1 (Γ, Cχ ) = 0. First cohomology
of a connected space with local coefficients is first cohomology of its fundamental group, so this
proves the required assertion. A secondary Kodaira surface has a finite primary cover; the same
transfer argument as above applies. Hopf surfaces have finite primary covers, and a primary
Hopf surface is diffeomorphic to S 1 × S 3 ; the cover statement and topology are recorded in
(Albanese, 2020, §2.1.1 and Theorem 2.2). The nontrivial circle character has an invertible
cellular differential, giving the required vanishing and its finite-cover descent.
    For completeness we also give the Inoue calculation, rather than assuming a generic-vanishing
theorem for its cotangent bundle. The explicit constructions in (Albanese, 2020, §2.1.2 and
Proposition 2.3) identify every Inoue surface with a mapping torus Nϕ of a compact three-
manifold N . In the SM cases N is a three-torus and the eigenvalues of ϕ∗ on H 1 (N, C) are
α, β, β̄, with α > 1 and |β| = α−1/2 < 1, after reversing the circle orientation when necessary.
In the S + and S − cases N is the nontrivial circle bundle over a two-torus; the nonzero Euler
class makes H 1 (N, C) the pullback of H 1 (T 2 , C) by its Gysin sequence. The monodromy on it
has eigenvalues α, α−1 or α, −α−1 , respectively. These assertions follow as well directly from the
conjugation relations displayed in that construction: on the abelian rank-three kernel the matrix
is M , and on the quotient of the Heisenberg kernel by its centre the matrix is N ∈ GL2 (Z) with
precisely those eigenvalues.
    None of these degree-one eigenvalues has modulus one. In particular there are no invariant
degree-one classes on N . The ordinary mapping-torus sequence therefore identifies H 1 (F, Z) with
the copy of Z from the circle, since the invariant subgroup of the torsion-free group H 1 (N, Z) is
zero. Thus Ar,F is pulled back from the circle, with monodromy λ ∈ S 1 of infinite order. The
local-coefficient Leray sequence for N → Nϕ → S 1 gives

                   0 −→ coker(λ − 1 : H 0 (N, C) → H 0 (N, C)) −→ H 1 (F, Ar,F )
                               −→ ker(λϕ∗ − 1 : H 1 (N, C) → H 1 (N, C)) −→ 0.

The first term is zero because λ 6= 1, and the last term is zero by the eigenvalue moduli. Using the
reciprocal convention for the circle local system replaces λ by λ−1 and gives the same conclusion.
This completes the degree-one calculation for every surface type in 4.9.
    Now repeat the neighbourhood argument of 5.23 with these two fibre-cohomology vanishings.
3.5–3.6 supply the same nonzero integral class on every nearby smooth fibre and the unitary local
system on every fibre neighbourhood. The only terms that can contribute to first cohomology of
the punctured neighbourhood are its degree-zero and degree-one fibre cohomology, just proved zero.
The fundamental-group surjection and proper base change therefore give H 1 ((Yc )red , Ar,c ) = 0
for every c. Applying 5.22 proves (A.23) for the single global twist Lr , simultaneously on all
reduced supports.
    Finally, the exponential sequence and the integral vanishings identify Pic(Y ) with the complex
vector space H 1 (Y, OY ). Choose holomorphic Cech cocycles representing a basis; exponentiating
their linear combinations gives a holomorphic family of line bundles on Y × H 1 (Y, OY ) whose
fibre is the indicated line bundle. There are finitely many singular fibre supports. For each
of them, tensor its fixed coherent torsion-free cotangent sheaf by this family and apply proper
semicontinuity: the locus where its space of sections is nonzero is a closed complex analytic
subset of the parameter space. Each is proper because it excludes Lr . Their finite union is
proper and has empty interior, giving the asserted dense open set. This proves the statement of
Proposition 7.3. The invalid genus-two deduction in its printed proof remains refuted by 5.17;
the proof above replaces that argument through the explicit maps (A.20)–(A.24).

Proposition 6.2 (Normal Gorenstein surfaces with vanishing first Chern class and Euler
characteristic). A compact connected normal Gorenstein complex surface S with c1 (ωS ) = 0 in
H 2 (S, Q) and χ(S, OS ) = 0 is smooth. Consequently every singular irreducible reduced divisor in
a compact complex threefold Y with H 2 (Y, Q) = 0 is nonnormal. In particular the assertion of
CDP20 Proposition 4.11 holds without its monodromy-dependent restrictions on the smooth fibre.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Peters, 2021, Theorem 2.2).

Proof. Let π : Z → S be the minimal resolution and set ` = h0 (S, R1 π∗ OZ ). Normality gives
π∗ OZ = OS , and the fibres have dimension at most one, so Leray gives χ(Z, OZ ) = −`. We first
prove ` = 0. The classification table in (Peters, 2021, Theorem 2.2), together with Noether’s
formula and invariance of χ(O) under blowing up, shows that a smooth compact surface of
negative holomorphic Euler characteristic is a blown-up ruled surface over a smooth curve B of
genus g ≥ 2. Indeed the sums c21 + c2 in every other row of that table are nonnegative. Thus,
when ` > 0, there is a ruling p : Z → B and χ(Z, OZ ) = 1 − g, giving ` = g − 1.
    An exceptional irreducible curve E of π dominating B would have h1 (E, OE ) ≥ g: normalize
E, apply Riemann–Hurwitz to its finite map to B, and use the normalization exact sequence
on E. The exact sequence 0 → IE → OZ → OE → 0, pushed forward by π, gives a surjection
R1 π∗ OZ → R1 π∗ OE because R2 π∗ IE = 0. It follows that ` ≥ h1 (E, OE ) ≥ g, a contradiction.
Hence every exceptional curve is vertical for p. The ruling is constant on each connected fibre
of π and descends to a holomorphic map pS : S → B: local holomorphic coordinate functions
descend by π∗ OZ = OS , and properness supplies the required neighborhoods. The map p is the
composite of blowups and a P1 -bundle, so R1 p∗ OZ = 0. The Leray sequence for p = pS ◦ π then
gives
                      0 = R1 p∗ OZ −→ (pS )∗ R1 π∗ OZ −→ R2 (pS )∗ OS = 0.
A nonzero sheaf supported at finitely many points cannot have zero direct image, so again ` = 0,
a contradiction. This proves rationality of all singularities.

                                                51
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


    We give the crepancy argument to specify the comparison of canonical bundles. Proper
duality applied to Rπ∗ OZ = OS identifies π∗ ωZ with the invertible dualizing sheaf ωS . A local
generator of ωS therefore pulls back to a holomorphic two-form on Z, agreeing with the usual
pullback off the exceptional set. Its zero divisor is effective and exceptional. These divisors glue
to D ≥ 0 with KZ = π ∗ KS + D. Every exceptional irreducible curve has arithmetic genus zero
by the same surjection to its first cohomology, hence is a smooth rational curve. Minimality
of the resolution gives E 2 ≤ −2, and adjunction gives D · E = KZ · E = −2 − E 2 ≥ 0. The
exceptionalPintersection matrix is negative definite. Thus a nonzero D would satisfy both D2 < 0
and D2 = E dE (D · E) ≥ 0. Therefore D = 0.
     Consequently c1 (KZ ) = 0 in rational cohomology. It follows by adjunction that Z contains
no (−1)-curve, so Z is a minimal compact surface; Noether’s formula gives c2 (Z) = 0. We
exclude rational curves on each surviving row of the classification. A ruled surface is excluded by
KZ · F = −2 on a ruling fibre. General-type surfaces have KZ2 > 0 and K3 and Enriques surfaces
have positive c2 , so none occurs. A torus has no rational curve because a map from P1 lifts to its
vector-space universal cover and is constant; the same holds for a finite etale quotient of a torus.
A primary Kodaira surface is an elliptic bundle over an elliptic curve, so a rational curve would
map constantly to the base and then constantly to a fibre; finite etale quotients have the same
property. A class VII surface here has b2 = c2 = 0, and the Hopf–Inoue classification gives no
rational curves. Equivalently one can use their standard universal covers: C2 \ {0} for a primary
Hopf cover and H × C for an Inoue surface. A map from P1 lifts and has constant coordinate
functions.
     It remains to check the properly elliptic row. For a minimal elliptic surface, the Kodaira fibre
list expresses c2 as a sum of nonnegative fibre Euler numbers, with zero contributions exactly
at multiples of smooth elliptic curves. Since c2 (Z) = 0, all fibre reductions are smooth elliptic
curves. The canonical bundle formula on a Kähler elliptic surface with χ(OZ ) = 0 has rational
first Chern class                                                   !

Proposition 6.5 (Uniform negative-degree vanishing for a fixed vector bundle). Let Z be a

with H 2 (Y, Z) = 0, the entire holomorphic Picard pullback is the zero map.

Proposition 6.6 (The ruled obstruction with a reduced conductor image). Let S ⊂ Y be

Proof. Write B = η∗ OT and Q = B/OS . We first specify conductor duality, including its

Numerical triviality and intersection with E force a = m − 1. The same numerical triviality

C{t2 , t3 }, the cusp ring. Thus Dν ≃ C ≃ B. This deduction also rules out any additional vertical
branch over the same image curve.

Proposition 6.7 (The genus of a horizontal conductor image from a local torus group). Let
f : Y → C0 be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold to a smooth
curve, with connected fibres and complex two-torus general fibre. Let S be an irreducible reduced
fibre support, η : T → S its normalization, and π : Z → T a resolution which is irrational ruled,

has just one horizontal irreducible component C, which is a section of p. Let D = ηπ(C) and let
Σ = Dν be its normalization. Then g(Σ) ≤ 1. In particular, when C → D has degree one, B is
elliptic. This applies to the horizontal-cusp case of DZ = 2C + V ; it allows arbitrary multiplicity
of the full fibre and arbitrary singularities or nonreduced conductor image on the finitely many
vertical curves.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.12; equation (A.Pi.1);
equation (A.Pi.2); (Łojasiewicz, 1964, §3, Theorem 2, p. 464); equation (A.Pi.4).

Proof. There is nothing to prove when Σ is rational, so assume g(Σ) ≥ 1. Statement 6.12
gives a holomorphic ruling pe : T → B with p = peπ. Identifying C with B by its section map,

vertical conductor component of T lies over one of finitely many points of B, so ψ is constant on
it. Its image under η has rational normalization: a vertical component is the image of a rational
curve on Z, and a nonconstant map from that curve to its image normalization is finite. Such an
image cannot equal D, because g(Σ) ≥ 1. Consequently these vertical images meet D at finitely
many points. Away from those points and from the finitely many singular points of D, every
normalization preimage of a point of D lies on C, and its ψ value is the unique corresponding
point of Σ. At a point outside D with more than one normalization preimage, all those preimages
lie on vertical conductor components. There are no other horizontal conductor components by
hypothesis. Thus there is a finite set A ⊂ Σ such that, for every s ∈ S, either ψ(η −1 (s)) is a
singleton or it is contained in A. One can take A to contain the constant values on all vertical
conductor components and all points of Σ above the singularities of D and its intersections with
the vertical image curves.
    Choose an embedded finite tree J in the underlying oriented surface Σ containing A, and let
q : Σ → Σ/J collapse that tree to one point. Such a tree is obtained by joining the finite set by
arcs and retaining a spanning tree after subdividing their finitely many crossings. Triangulate
the surface with J a subcomplex. A contractible subcomplex is a cofibration; contracting it gives
a homotopy equivalence of this CW pair. Concretely the homotopy extension property extends a
contraction of J and supplies a homotopy inverse to the quotient map. In particular

                                                                                           (A.Pi.1)
                                                 ∼

continuous map
                               a : S −→ Σ/J,        aη = qψ.                         (A.Pi.2)
Let δ : Σ → D ⊂ S be the curve normalization map. On its dense smooth locus, lifting through
C gives aδ = q. Continuity gives this equality everywhere. Equation (A.Pi.1) therefore makes a∗

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


surjective on fundamental groups, without any assertion that a finite point-identification quotient

Proposition 6.8 (The arithmetic genus of conductor images from coherent duality). Let
f : Y → C0 be a proper connected-fibre map from a smooth compact complex threefold with
H 2 (Y, Z) = 0 to a smooth curve, and let its smooth general fibre have trivial canonical bundle.
This includes complex two-tori and primary Kodaira surfaces. Let mS be a full fibre with
irreducible reduced nonnormal support S. Write η : T → S for normalization and π : Z → T for
a resolution. If the pullback homomorphism Pic(Y ) → Pic(Z) is nonconstant, then every reduced
irreducible component D of the conductor image scheme has arithmetic genus at most one. In
particular every such component whose normalization has positive genus is a smooth elliptic curve.
The conductor image scheme itself is allowed to be nonreduced, and no local-complete-intersection
assumption is imposed on its reduced components.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (A.CD.2);
equation (A.CD.3); equation (A.CD.1).


                                                 59
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Proof. First we determine exactly the needed canonical line on the reduced support, without a
multiplicity formula for the direct image. The sheaf f∗ KY is torsion-free of generic rank one on
the smooth curve and hence is a line bundle. Choose a frame near c = f (S) and evaluate it in
KY . A coordinate t on the base disc supplies the conormal frame dt, and adjunction identifies
KY |F with KF after dividing by this frame. Under that line-bundle isomorphism, the evaluated
section restricts on a general smooth fibre to a nonzero canonical two-form, which is nowhere
zero. Its zero divisor is therefore vertical. Shrinking the base disc to remove the other vertical
zero divisors, irreducibility of the support gives an effective divisor kS, with k ≥ 0, and an actual

             KY |U ≃ OU (kS),        ωS ≃ OY ((k + 1)S)|S ,      ωS⊗m ≃ OS .               (A.CD.1)

The last isomorphism uses the local base equation whose zero divisor is exactly the full fibre mS.
In particular no assertion k = m − 1 is used.
    Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch in 0 → OY (−S) → OY → OS → 0 gives χ(OS ) = 0: the rational

e = h0 (S, ωS ), we have

                   e ∈ {0, 1},     e = 1 ⇐⇒ ωS ≃ OS ,         h1 (S, OS ) = 1 + e.         (A.CD.2)

Here h0 (OS ) = 1 and Serre duality identifies h2 (OS ) with e.

connected and compact, so their global holomorphic functions are the same constants. The
normalization sequence consequently gives an injection and the indicated kernel:

     H 0 (S, Q) ,→ H 1 (S, OS ),   im H 0 (S, Q) = ker H 1 (S, OS ) → H 1 (T, OT ) . (A.CD.3)
                                                                                  


Because H 2 (Y, Z) = 0, Pic(Y ) is the connected exponential image of H 1 (Y, OY ). A nonconstant

(A.RC.3) applies without a reducedness assumption on Γ: Q = ωΓ ⊗ ωS−1 |Γ . Serre duality on that

                                 h1 (Γ, ωS |Γ ) = h0 (S, Q) ≤ e.                       (A.CD.4)
For any reduced irreducible component D of Γ, restriction of the line gives an exact quotient

again proving pa (D) ≤ 1. Finally, for a reduced irreducible curve the normalization exact
sequence gives pa (D) = g(Dν ) + length(ν∗ ODν /OD ). Positive normalization genus therefore
