Proposition 6.9 (The conductor bound when the general fibre has q = 1 and pg = 0). Let
f : Y → P1 be a proper connected-fibre map from a smooth compact complex threefold with
H 1 (Y, Z) = H 2 (Y, Z) = 0. Suppose its smooth general fibre has h1 (O) = 1 and h2 (O) = 0. Then

                      R1 f∗ OY = OP1 ,       R2 f∗ OY = 0,          Pic(Y ) = Cβ,          (A.Q1.1)

where the last identification uses the exponential coordinates of 3.6 and its nonzero transgression
class β. Every full fibre has structure-sheaf cohomology dimensions (1, 1, 0). For an irreducible
reduced support S, every nonconstant ambient Picard pullback to a normalization resolution forces
every reduced conductor component to have arithmetic genus at most one. In particular each
positive-genus component is smooth elliptic, without any lci or conductor-reducedness hypothesis.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.6; proposition A.9;
proposition 6.8.

Proof. By A.9, E = R1 f∗ OY is a line bundle. The section induced by 3.6’s integral transgression
class is nowhere zero: its image under the natural base-change map at each point is the nonzero
coefficient class on that full fibre. A zero of the section in E would have zero image under that
map. Thus E ≃ O. Coherent Leray now gives H 1 (Y, OY ) = Cβ. The exponential sequence and
the two stated integral cohomology vanishings give the Picard identification in (A.Q1.1).
    The coherent sheaf G =R R2 f∗ OY has generic rank zero, hence is a torsion sheaf. Riemann–
Roch on Y gives χ(OY ) = Y c1 c2 /24 = 0, since c1 (Y ) is zero in rational cohomology. The Euler
characteristic of coherent Leray is therefore

                             0 = χ(OP1 ) − χ(E) + χ(G) = length G.

Thus G = 0. Top-degree base change gives H 2 (F, OF ) = 0 for every full Cartier fibre F . The
multiplication-by-parameter sequence then gives H 1 (F, OF ) = E ⊗ C(c), of dimension one; A.9
gives h0 (F, OF ) = 1.
    For a full fibre F = mS with irreducible reduced support, the quotient OF → OS induces
a surjection on H 2 , because its kernel has support of dimension two and has no H 3 . Hence
h2 (S, OS ) = 0. Riemann–Roch in the Cartier sequence on Y gives χ(OS ) = 0 as in 6.8, so
h1 (S, OS ) = 1.
    Put Q = η∗ OT /OS for the normalization T and write Γ for the conductor image scheme.
Nonconstant Picard pullback has nonzero differential factoring through H 1 (S, OS ) → H 1 (T, OT ).
The source has dimension one, so this map has zero kernel. The normalization sequence (A.CD.3)
gives H 0 (Q) = 0. Conductor duality and Serre duality give

                             H 1 (Γ, ωS |Γ ) = 0,        H 1 (D, ωS |D ) = 0               (A.Q1.2)

for each reduced irreducible component D, where the second map is the restriction surjection
in the proof of 6.8. Adjunction makes ωS ambient, so deg(ωS |D ) = 0 by H 2 (Y, Z) = 0. Curve
Riemann–Roch yields 0 ≤ h0 (D, ωS |D ) = 1−pa (D). The normalization genus and its nonnegative
delta length then give the asserted smooth elliptic conclusion whenever that genus is positive.

Proposition 6.11 (A pure double conductor forces a smooth cusp image). Let S be a reduced
Gorenstein complex surface and π : S → S its finite normalization. Suppose that, over a
neighbourhood of a point p ∈ S, S is smooth and its conductor ideal is exactly OS (−2C) for
a smooth reduced divisor C; its local branches over p are disjoint. Suppose that the generic
transversal of S along the reduced image D = π(C) is an ordinary cusp. Then D is smooth at
p, C → D is an isomorphism near the preimage of p, and the germ of S at p is analytically a
product of an ordinary cusp and a smooth disc. No complete-intersection hypothesis on D is
required.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (A.J.13); equation (A.J.14);
equation (A.J.12).

Proof. Write R = OS,p and let R be its finite semilocal normalization. It is a product of regular
two-dimensional local analytic rings. Write c for the conductor, and set

                         A = R/c,         A = R/c,      Q = R/R = A/A.

We first give the exact duality comparison needed below. The R-module R is maximal Cohen–
Macaulay. Since R is Gorenstein, ExtjR (R, R) = 0 for j > 0. Its dual HomR (R, R) is precisely the
conductor, viewed as a fractional ideal: a homomorphism is multiplication in the total quotient
ring, and multiplication takes R into R exactly for conductor elements. Applying HomR (−, R)
to 0 → R → R → Q → 0 therefore gives

                                          Ext1R (Q, R) = A.                              (A.J.11)

The depth lemma shows that Q is a Cohen–Macaulay module of dimension one. Gorenstein duality
on such modules is the involutive functor M 7→ Ext1R (M, R). Consequently A is Cohen–Macaulay
and
                           Q ≃ Ext1R (A, R) = ωA ,     EndA (Q) = A.                  (A.J.12)
The final equality is the canonical multiplication map: duality identifies its endomorphism ring
with EndA (A) = A.
   The ordinary-cusp hypothesis says that A is generically reduced. Its nilradical is therefore
supported at finitely many points; a one-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay ring has no nonzero
submodule with that support. Hence A is reduced. Choose local coordinates (si , zi ) on the
normalization branches with C = (zi = 0). Put

component by component. The projection A → B is injective on A, since its kernel is nilpotent
and A is reduced. It identifies B with the finite normalization of the curve ring A.

Proposition 6.12 (Rational singularities for a vertically resolved ruled normalization). Let
π : Z → T be a resolution of a compact connected normal complex surface, where Z is an
irrational ruled surface with ruling p : Z → B. Suppose that every exceptional curve of π is
vertical for p. Then there is a unique holomorphic map pe : T → B satisfying p = pe ◦ π, and

                                   Rπ∗ OZ = OT ,          R1 pe∗ OT = 0.                       (A.J.17)

In particular all singularities of T are rational. For g = g(B), its complete structure-sheaf
cohomology dimensions are

                           (h0 (T, OT ), h1 (T, OT ), h2 (T, OT )) = (1, g, 0).                (A.J.18)

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (A.J.19).

Proof. The exceptional fibre of the proper birational map π over a point is connected, because T
is normal and π∗ OZ = OT . Its curve components are vertical by assumption, so their intersection
connectivity makes p constant on that whole fibre. It is also constant on the one-point fibres.
We verify holomorphic descent, rather than only descending the underlying continuous map.


                                                     66
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


    Fix t ∈ T and let U ⊂ B be a coordinate disc containing p(π −1 (t)). Properness makes
π(Z \ p−1 (U )) closed and disjoint from t. There is therefore an open neighbourhood W of t with
π −1 (W ) ⊂ p−1 (U ). The coordinate function of p on π −1 (W ) is a section of π∗ OZ (W ) = OT (W ),
so descends to a holomorphic function on W . Its values lie in the coordinate image of U ; the
inverse coordinate gives a holomorphic map W → U . These local maps agree after pullback to
the surjective map π, hence agree on overlaps. They construct the required unique pe.
    Contracting vertical ruling (−1)-curves factors p as
                                              b         p0
                                            Z−
                                             → Z0 −→ B,

where Z0 → B is a P1 -bundle and b is a finite sequence of point blowups. Every such blowup
has direct image O and no higher direct image of O: the successive layers on its infinitesimal
exceptional curves are OP1 (k) for k ≥ 0, whose degree-one cohomology is zero, and formal
functions gives the assertion. The bundle p0 has the same direct-image property by the cohomology
of P1 and local triviality. Composition consequently gives

                             p∗ OZ = OB ,         Rj p∗ OZ = 0   (j > 0).                    (A.J.19)

   The sheaf T = R1 π∗ OZ has finite support at the singular points of T . The low-degree Leray
sequence for p = pe ◦ π contains the actual arrows

                        0 −→ R1 pe∗ OT −→ R1 p∗ OZ −→ pe∗ T −→ R2 pe∗ OT .                   (A.J.20)

The last term is zero: the nonconstant proper map pe has fibres of complex dimension one. The
middle term is zero by (A.J.19). Thus R1 pe∗ OT = 0 and pe∗ T = 0. Pushforward is faithful on a
sheaf with finite support, since its stalk sections at finitely many points cannot disappear under
a proper map. Hence T = 0. Higher Rj π∗ vanish for j > 1 by the dimension of its fibres. This
proves (A.J.17) and the defining rational-singularity property.
    Finally (A.J.17) identifies every H q (T, OT ) with H q (Z, OZ ). Equation (A.J.19) identifies the
latter with H q (B, OB ). A compact connected smooth curve has dimensions (1, g) in degrees zero
and one and no higher cohomology, proving (A.J.18).

Proposition 6.13 (Arithmetic genus two and the embedded delta-one comparison). Let f : Y →

                              pa (D) = 1 + h1 (D, L) − h0 (D, L) ≤ 2,

   Let ν : D

      b > 0, every local delta is consequently at most one and their sum is at most one. We give
the analytic local rings at a point with delta one. Let A = OD,x and let B = ri=1 C{ti } be its
                                                                               L
finite normalization. Here dimC (B/A) = 1. The residue map of the local ring A has the same

    For r = 2, the subring

                         A0 = {(b1 , b2 ) ∈ C{t1 } ⊕ C{t2 } : b1 (0) = b2 (0)}

contains A and has colength one in B. Hence A = A0 . The explicit homomorphism
C{u, v}/(uv) → A0 sends u to (t1 , 0), v to (0, t2 ), and a constant to the corresponding equal pair.

embedding dimension at most two. In local coordinates of the smooth threefold, the tangent
space of D therefore has codimension at least one. There is an element z of its ideal with

the inverse image of a height-one ideal in the regular analytic ring C{u, v} = OY,x /(z). This ideal
is principal: a pure reduced curve in a smooth surface is a Cartier divisor, or equivalently its
reduced height-one ideal is a product of the prime factors in this factorial ring. Thus ID,x = (z, h),
a regular sequence. This proves the asserted lci embedding, including at the node and cusp.
Statement 6.10 now applies to the three specified generic transverse types and proves the final
smooth elliptic and constant-type conclusion.

Proposition 6.15 (A noncontracted horizontal cusp has zero Euler number). Let f : Y → C0
be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0, with
connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre with
irreducible reduced support, η : T → S its normalization and π : Z → T an irrational ruled
resolution with ruling p : Z → B. Suppose every exceptional curve of π is vertical and the
resolution conductor is 2C + V , where C is a noncontracted section and V is vertical. If the
generic transversal at D = ηπ(C) is an ordinary cusp, then D and C are smooth elliptic curves
and C → D is an isomorphism. The cusp type is constant along D. The normalization T is
a smooth minimal ruled surface over this elliptic curve, its conductor is twice a section, and
e(S) = 0. This permits an initially singular normalization; smoothness is part of the conclusion.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.13; proposition 6.10;
proposition 9.8; proposition 6.18.

Proof. A transverse cusp has exactly one normalization branch. The map from the horizontal
section to the normalization of its image consequently has degree one. Both curves are smooth,
so this finite map identifies C ≃ B with Dν . Its genus is positive. Statement 6.13, including its
actual delta-one lci comparison, and 6.10 therefore make D itself smooth elliptic and its cusp
transversal constant at every point. Thus C → D is an isomorphism, without any assumption
about the ambient Picard pullback.
    For the exact local normalization x = u3 , y = u2 , let CT ⊂ T be the image of C. The
normalization is smooth near this curve. Its normal line P = NCT /T has P 2 = R and P 3 = Q in
the degree-zero radical and Hessian quotient lines of 9.8. Hence deg P = 0. The normalization is
smooth near C, and no other conductor curve meets it. Factor π through its minimal resolution,
descending the ruling across its vertical exceptional blowdowns as in 6.18. On that minimal
resolution the section is isomorphic to CT in its unchanged smooth neighbourhood. It therefore
has self-intersection zero and is disjoint from the effective vertical conductor. The canonical
comparison is the actual line-bundle identity K + 2C + V = (ηπ)∗ ωS , of zero rational Chern
class.
    Apply (A.T.22) to each ruling blowdown. Its exceptional coefficient is exactly the multiplicity
at its centre minus one. No ruling (−1)-curve can meet C, since the intersection with K + 2C + V
would then be positive. On the minimal ruled bundle the vertical conductor is zero because it
is disjoint from a section. A first reverse blowup away from that section would have coefficient
−1, so there were no ruling blowups. All resolution-exceptional curves are vertical, and the
square-zero fibres of the resulting bundle cannot be exceptional. This identifies the minimal
resolution with T itself and proves the asserted smoothness and minimality.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                             Paper II


    Finally the normalization is an isomorphism off C and D. The exact Euler comparison is
e(S) = e(T ) − e(C) + e(D); all three terms vanish, since T is ruled over an elliptic curve and C, D
are elliptic. Thus e(S) = 0, also for the underlying topological space of the full fibre mS.

Proposition 6.18 (Every horizontal tacnode image is elliptic). Let f : Y → C0 be a proper
holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0, with connected fibres
and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre with irreducible reduced
support, η : T → S its normalization, and π : Z → T a resolution with an irrational ruling
p : Z → B. Suppose every exceptional curve of π is vertical and the conductor divisor on Z
is 2C + V , where C is a section of p and V is vertical. Let D = ηπ(C). Suppose the generic
plane-curve transversal to D in S is an ordinary tacnode.
    Then D is a smooth elliptic curve, B = C is elliptic, and C → D is an unramified double
cover. The transversal type along D is everywhere the same ordinary tacnode. The normalization
T is a smooth minimal ruled surface over this elliptic curve. Its conductor is twice a section, and
e(S) = 0. In particular its minimal resolution is the identity. In particular a rational image of
the horizontal tacnodal conductor cannot occur. The proof allows vertical conductor and rational
singularities of T ; it does not assume that the normalization map is immersive at the special
points under examination.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.13; proposition 6.10;
proposition 6.12; equation (A.T.3); proposition 6.17; equation (A.T.4); equation (A.T.5);
equation (A.T.7); equation (A.T.8); proposition 6.16; equation (A.T.9); equation (A.T.12);
equation (A.T.13); equation (A.T.15); equation (A.T.18); equation (A.T.20); equation (A.T.19);
proposition 9.8; equation (A.T.22).

isomorphism there, so Cmin 2   = 0. No other conductor or exceptional curve meets it. Hence
Vmin · Cmin = 0. No ruling (−1)-curve can meet Cmin : one in Vmin is disjoint from it, while one
outside Vmin would have

                  (KZmin + 2Cmin + Vmin ) · E = −1 + 2Cmin · E + Vmin · E ≥ 1,

contrary to the vanishing Chern class.
   Contract ruling (−1)-curves to a minimal ruled bundle. Every contraction therefore avoids
the section. For one blowdown σ : W → W 0 let D0 = σ∗ DW , let a be the coefficient of its
exceptional curve, and let d be the multiplicity of D0 at the centre. The actual divisor comparison
is
                           KW + DW = σ ∗ (KW 0 + D0 ) + (1 + a − d)E.                      (A.T.22)
Its intersection with E gives a = d − 1, so the log-canonical line and its zero rational Chern
class descend. The section remains disjoint from the effective vertical part at every step. On
a minimal ruled bundle every nonzero effective vertical divisor is a positive sum of fibres and
meets the section. The final vertical part is consequently zero. If there had been a blowup in
the reverse sequence, its first centre would be away from this section, and (A.T.22) would give
coefficient −1 on its exceptional curve. Its strict transform retains that negative coefficient under
subsequent blowups, a contradiction to effectiveness. Thus no ruling blowdowns were needed:
Zmin is already a minimal ruled bundle and Dmin = 2Cmin .
    All exceptional curves of πmin would be vertical. A minimal ruled bundle has irreducible
fibres of square zero, which cannot form the negative-definite exceptional divisor of a surface
resolution. Hence πmin has no exceptional curve and is an isomorphism. This proves the assertion
about T . Finally η is an isomorphism away from its conductor section CT and the elliptic image
D. Additivity of the topological Euler number on these actual decompositions gives

                     e(S) = e(T ) − e(CT ) + e(D) = e(P1 )e(B) − 0 + 0 = 0.                (A.T.23)

The full multiple fibre has the same underlying topological space and therefore the same Euler
number.

Connected double covers in the two non-lci cases. The non-lci calculation also excludes
a connected degree-two conductor cover when its covering curve is rational, for either of the two
image rings in (A.T.14). In the cusp-plus-line case the cleared quartic has degree 2q0 ≤ 0, so it

has no branch divisor at all. In the space-cusp case a rational double cover has branch degree
two. The already proved inequalities give
                                 2 ≤ 4 + 2q0 ,        2 ≤ −2q0 + 1,
so the integer q0 is −1. The cleared quartic then has degree two and exactly two simple branch
points. Only one point lies above the singular image germ. The other is a smooth simple
branch point, excluded by the actual coordinate reduction (A.T.10)–(A.T.12). Thus these two
non-lci images cannot support a connected double cover of any nonnegative genus in a torus
degeneration.

Proposition 6.19 (Ordinary-triple images have arithmetic genus at most one). Let f : Y → C0
be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0, with
connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre with
irreducible reduced support, and let D ⊂ Sing S be an irreducible curve with generic ordinary-
triple plane transversal. Then D is a local complete intersection in Y and pa (D) ≤ 1. The
possibilities for its underlying curve are a smooth rational curve, a rational curve with one
ordinary node or cusp, and a smooth elliptic curve. In the elliptic case the transversal type is
constant.
    When D is singular rational, every component of the normalized conductor curve dominating
D is rational, and its map to Dν ≃ P1 has degree one. Consequently, in the irrational ruled
setup of 6.18 with the generic transversal replaced by an ordinary triple point, the image of the
noncontracted horizontal section is either smooth rational or smooth elliptic. In the elliptic case
the horizontal cover is unramified of degree three, the normalization is smooth minimal elliptic
ruled, and the fibre has Euler number zero. In the rational case the horizontal cover has degree
two or three; these cases are not excluded by this statement.

proposition 6.10; equation (A.U.2); equation (A.U.4); equation (A.U.5); equation (A.U.1);
proposition 9.8.

Proof. By 6.13, pa (D) ≤ 2. If its normalization has positive genus, that statement and 6.10
already give a smooth elliptic curve of constant transverse type. Suppose its normalization

   We exclude every non-lci germ of delta at most two by its symbolic cube. The one- and

                                         I (3) = I 3 + F I.                              (A.U.2)

the cusp-plus-line germ it is t−2 uv on the cusp and s−1 v 2 on the smooth branch, so the pole

transition under a normal-coordinate change is therefore the actual cubic tensor in Sym3 N ∗ ⊗ M ;

The list of underlying curves follows from the delta-one classification in 6.13.
    We give the finite-cover comparison at a singular rational image. Here δ = 1, so (A.U.1) has
degree zero and its nonzero section is nowhere zero on Σ = P1 . The cubic defines a subscheme

coordinate chart, its derivative with respect to the root coordinate is nonzero, so the implicit
function theorem makes R3 → Σ a finite etale map of degree three. There is no component in a
whole projective fibre, since its nonzero discriminant forbids an identically zero cubic there.
    Over the generic point of D, normalization of an ordinary triple transversal separates exactly
its three tangent lines. This supplies an isomorphism between the function-field algebra of R3
and that of the normalized conductor curves dominating D, after their maps are factored through
Σ. Both are normal finite curves over Σ. Taking the integral closure of OΣ in this same algebra
therefore identifies the two finite covers everywhere. Every connected finite etale cover of the
simply connected Riemann sphere has degree one. Thus each of these conductor components is
rational and maps isomorphically to Σ, proving the second assertion.
    In the irrational ruled setting the horizontal section has positive genus. Its finite map to a
rational image normalization must have degree at least two. The preceding comparison excludes a
singular rational image, and the generic triple transversal bounds its degree above by three. The
remaining rational image is therefore smooth, with degree two or three. If the image is elliptic,
no vertical rational curve can dominate it, so all three branches belong to the horizontal section.
Statement 9.8 gives an unramified degree-three cover, normal degree zero and constant type. The
exact minimal-resolution factorization and blowdown argument (A.T.22) applies without change
to this coefficient-two section: its proof uses only those properties. It makes the normalization
smooth minimal elliptic ruled with conductor twice the section. The actual normalization Euler
formula (A.T.23) then gives zero.

Proposition 6.20 (Rational normalization bounds with the exact constant-sheaf map). Let

connected. Proper base change for the constant sheaf gives R0 π∗ CZ = CT . The degree-one

    6.3 gives the effective integral divisor D and the exact line-bundle relation KZ ⊗ OZ (D) ≃

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


D. Conversely, a positive-coefficient exceptional curve over a point outside the conductor would

and the zero-coefficient assertion. It also proves connectedness of Γred .

A normal complex surface has isolated singularities. The reduced local equation therefore has an
isolated critical point whenever that point is singular. Since the full fibre has equation uhm , the
isolated clause of 6.17 excludes it. This proves the final assertion and eliminates the displayed
sum by an actual local comparison with the nearby torus.
     We prove the asserted Euler bound for the conductor image, including its possible positive-
genus component. Put C = Γred . The normalization exact sequence for the connected reduced

Any component with genus one is smooth, is unique, and meets the remaining rational curves

increase the arithmetic genus to at least two. Each component of C is the finite image of a
strict conductor component of Dred . Riemann–Hurwitz therefore shows that its normalization is
rational or elliptic, with at most one elliptic-normalized component.
     Write n0 for the number of rational-normalized components of C, n1 ∈ {0, 1} for the number

   δp ≤ 1. A negative value could therefore only be −1, from one ordinary node. Indeed its curve

two points over that node are distinct on the elliptic normalization.
    Here the hypersurface embedding excludes this last case. At least one point t ∈ T over
the node receives both local conductor branches. Otherwise partition the local irreducible
hypersurface branches according to which of the two conductor branches they receive. Both parts
are nonempty. Two surface branches from opposite parts meet in a curve, since their distinct
equations in the regular three-dimensional ambient local ring generate an ideal of height two.
That intersection curve belongs to the conductor image, so is one of its two branches. Both
surface branches receive it, contradicting the partition. For a locally irreducible hypersurface
there is only one normalization point and the assertion is immediate.
    The connected resolution fibre π −1 (t) lies in Dred by the support equality proved above. The
strict conductor curves over the two branches are elliptic, because a rational curve cannot map
nonconstantly to an elliptic curve. There is at most one such curve on Dred . If the two strict
curves were different, they would already give total genus two. If they coincide, they meet π −1 (t)
at distinct points: the map of that normal elliptic curve factors through the normalization of its
image, so one point cannot map to both points over the node. The connected resolution fibre
then supplies an additional path joining those points, outside the elliptic curve. Its components

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


are rational, since T has rational singularities. This produces a graph cycle in addition to the
elliptic genus, again forcing pa (Dred ) ≥ 2. Both alternatives are impossible. Thus e(C) ≥ 0.

    We record the exact minimal-model calculation that follows from 6.20. This is a reduction of
the outstanding Euler calculation; the configurations with negative complement Euler number are
retained in the calculation. Choose any sequence of contractions of smooth rational (−1)-curves
from Z to a minimal rational surface Z0 , and let D0 be the pushforward of D. At one contraction
σ : Zi → Zi−1 , let E be the exceptional curve, a its coefficient in Di , and r the multiplicity of
Di−1 at the centre. The actual divisor comparison is

                         KZi + Di = σ ∗ (KZi−1 + Di−1 ) + (1 + a − r)E.                   (A.RT.11)

Both canonical-plus-boundary line bundles are trivial, so intersection with E gives a = r − 1.
In particular the centre lies on Di−1 , and effectivity is retained at every stage. If r = 1, the
centre is a smooth point of a reduced boundary component, a = 0, and the strict boundary is
isomorphic to the old boundary. The blowup increases its complement Euler number by one. If
r ≥ 2, the new reduced boundary is exactly the full inverse image of the old reduced boundary.
Both the surface and the boundary replace the centre by P1 , so the complement Euler number is
unchanged. Thus
                       e(Z \ Dred ) = e(Z0 \ (D0 )red ) + N0 ,    N0 ≥ 0,              (A.RT.12)
where N0 is the number of multiplicity-one centres in this specified sequence of reverse blowups.
Formula (A.RT.12) concerns the resolution complement. For the actual torus smoothing, the
isolated clause of 6.17 has already removed the off-conductor exceptional correction in (A.RT.4).
This local argument is needed: on an abstract minimal F2 , its exceptional (−2)-section can be
disjoint from an anticanonical divisor without having arisen from one of the N0 blowups.
    On P2 , the divisor D0 is an effective cubic. Its possible reduced supports and their complement
Euler numbers are
                           reduced support                e(P2 \ (D0 )red )
             smooth cubic, nodal cubic, cuspidal cubic       3, 2, 1

                    two distinct lines, or one line            0, 1.
For example the union of three concurrent lines has Euler number 6 − 3 + 1 = 4, whereas
e(P2 ) = 3. The last row retains respectively a double line plus a line, and a triple line. These
are all cubic possibilities: an irreducible singular cubic has arithmetic genus one and therefore
exactly a node or a cusp; the other degrees partition three as 2 + 1 or 1 + 1 + 1.
    On Fn , with n = 0 or n ≥ 2, write C02 = −n for a minimal section and F for a ruling fibre.
Then
                                       D0 ∼ 2C0 + (n + 2)F.                             (A.RT.14)
Its horizontal part has degree two over the ruling base. If that part consists of two distinct
sections C1 + C2 , write V for the vertical part, d for its total degree and k = C1 · C2 . Adjunction
on either section gives k + d = 2. Let q be the number of distinct intersection points of C1 and
C2 , and let r count those points whose ruling fibre occurs in Vred . A vertical fibre meets the two
sections in two points unless they coincide at that fibre. Additivity therefore gives the exact
formula
                     e((D0 )red ) = 4 − q + r,     e(Fn \ (D0 )red ) = q − r ≥ 0.           (A.RT.15)
This includes two sections and a fibre through their common point: that union has Euler number
four and complement Euler number zero.
    If the horizontal part is an irreducible bisection C, the same adjunction calculation gives
pa (C) = 1 − d, so d = 0 or 1. For d = 0, its Euler number is at most two, and the complement

                                                 90
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                            Paper II


Euler number is at least two. For d = 1, the bisection is a smooth rational curve, the vertical part
is one reduced fibre, and their set-theoretic intersection has one or two points. The complement
Euler number is respectively one or two.
    The remaining horizontal part is 2C, where C is a section. Write C ∼ C0 + kF . The vertical
divisor has total degree d = n + 2 − 2k, and, with v its number of distinct fibres,

                         e((D0 )red ) = 2 + v,           e(Fn \ (D0 )red ) = 2 − v.              (A.RT.16)

If C 6= C0 , positivity of intersection with C0 gives k ≥ n; hence d ≤ 2 − n and v ≤ 2. For n = 0
one also has d ≤ 2. Consequently the only negative values on a minimal ruled surface occur in

    There is a further fundamental-group restriction on precisely these negative minimal-model
configurations. Their reduced supports are unions of rational curves with simply connected
underlying spaces: three concurrent lines on P2 , or the section with its attached ruling fibres in
(A.RT.17). Every reverse blowup in (A.RT.11) preserves this property. A multiplicity-one blowup
leaves the support isomorphic to the preceding one. A positive-coefficient blowup at a smooth
point adds a rational leaf, at an ordinary double point subdivides the incidence edge, and at the
initial concurrent point replaces that vertex by an exceptional P1 with three attached branches.
Subsequent supports have only the resulting ordinary double points. None of these explicit
operations introduces a topological loop. Consequently Dred is simply connected throughout
these cases.

                                                              h|D
                                Dred ,→ Z,                      red

Indeed h is an isomorphism off these closed sets and the whole preimage of Γred is Dred . The
continuous map from this pushout to S is a bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space,
and hence is a homeomorphism. A triangulation of the pair (Z, Dred ) makes its inclusion a
cofibration. The double mapping-cylinder model for (A.RT.18) therefore has the same homotopy
type as the pushout, and van Kampen gives

                           π1 (S) ≃ π1 (Z) ∗π1 (Dred ) π1 (Γred ) ≃ π1 (Γred ).                  (A.RT.19)

All normalizations of the image components are P1 , by Riemann–Hurwitz. Gluing their finitely
many points over singularities identifies the topological curve with a graph of simply connected
spheres. Its fundamental group is a free group, of rank b1 (Γred ).
    That free group is a quotient of a metabelian group. To see the exact comparison, triangulate
(Y, S) and retract a small regular neighbourhood N onto S, as in 6.7. Properness puts a
sufficiently small full fibre tube U = f −1 (∆) inside N . Its retraction is surjective on fundamental
groups because it restricts to the identity on S. General position makes π1 (U \ S) → π1 (U )
surjective, and the torus bundle over ∆∗ has π1 (U \ S) = Z4 o Z. This last group has abelian
commutator subgroup, so its quotient (A.RT.19) is metabelian. A free group of rank at least
two is not metabelian: it maps onto S4 , whose commutator group A4 is not abelian. We obtain

                           π1 (S) ≃ π1 (Γred ) ∈ {1, Z},            b1 (Γred ) ≤ 1.              (A.RT.20)

                                                        91
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                                  Paper II


Under the full CDP Betti hypotheses, the nonzero class on every support from 3.6 excludes
the trivial group in (A.RT.20). This last use of the global transgression is separate from the
preceding b2 (Y ) = 0 calculations.
    For these two boundary classes one can further exclude a one-component image with first
Betti number one. Such an image has one two-branch singular point q; write α, β for its two
normalization points there. Any two normalization points of S above q receive a common local
conductor branch, because the corresponding two hypersurface branches meet in a curve. Thus
there cannot be both a point receiving only α and a point receiving only β. After interchanging
the labels, every normalization point above q receives α.
    Form the incidence graph with one vertex for each strict conductor component and one
vertex for each connected resolution fibre over a normalization point above q. Edges record
their intersection points, labelled by the branch α or β received there. Smooth resolution fibres,
consisting of one point, are included. The graph is a forest: it is obtained from the tree of
components and intersection points of Dred by contracting disjoint exceptional subtrees and
deleting the other incidence edges. Every strict conductor component maps finitely onto the sole
image component, so it has a preimage of β and therefore a β-edge. Every resolution-fibre vertex
has an α-edge by the preceding paragraph. Starting at any strict-component vertex, follow a
β-edge and then an α-edge, and repeat. This walk never immediately reverses an edge, because
its consecutive labels differ. It is an infinite nonbacktracking walk in a finite forest, which is
impossible. The contradiction proves the exclusion.
    Since every image component is rational-normalized, write nΓ for their number and βΓ ≤ 1
for the first Betti number. Their exact topological normalization formula now yields, on these
negative boundary classes,
                                     e(Γred ) = nΓ + 1 − βΓ ≥ 2.                        (A.RT.21)
For one component the excluded case is the only value below two; for at least two components
the inequality follows directly from βΓ ≤ 1.

Proposition 7.1 (Every torus-degeneration fibre has even Euler number). Let f : Y → B be
a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a smooth complex curve, with
connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. For every b ∈ B,

                                           e((Yb )red ) ∈ 2Z.                               (C.UN.1)

This assertion allows arbitrary multiplicities and singularities and imposes no Kähler or Betti-
number hypothesis on Y .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.UN.3);
equation (C.UN.4).

Proof. Take a sufficiently small closed coordinate disc ∆ about b, containing no other critical value.
Put U = f −1 (∆) and M = ∂U . Then U is a compact oriented smooth real six-manifold with
boundary, and M is the mapping torus of the orientation-preserving monodromy of a real four-
torus. The analytic central support S is a deformation retract of U . One precise construction
uses a controlled gradient for the real analytic function |f |2 on a Whitney stratification: it
decreases |f |, is tangent to the strata over zero, and has trajectories with a limit on the zero set
by the local analytic gradient inequality. Compactness of the zero set gives a common small disc,
and the resulting continuous limit homotopy fixes the zero set. Equivalently the triangulated
proper local tube is a regular neighbourhood of the zero fibre. Nilpotents do not change this
retraction. Thus e(S) = χ(U ).
    We give the parity calculation entirely over Q. Write si = rank(Hi (U ) → Hi (U, M )).
Exactness of the pair sequence, with Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, gives
                                                   5
                                                                                            (C.UN.2)
                                                   X
                   b0 (M ) + b1 (M ) + b2 (M ) =         bi (U ) − s0 − s3 − 2s1 − 2s2 .
                                                   i=0


                                                   95
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


Indeed, the summand bi (M ) is the sum of the ranks of Hi (M ) → Hi (U ) and Hi+1 (U, M ) →
Hi (M ); substitution of bi+1 (U, M ) = b5−i (U ) gives the formula. Here s0 = 0 and b6 (U ) = 0.
The map defining s3 is represented, after duality, by the middle-dimensional intersection pairing
of U . That pairing is skew-symmetric because the middle dimension is three, so s3 is even.
Consequently
                           χ(U ) ≡ b0 (M ) + b1 (M ) + b2 (M ) (mod 2).                 (C.UN.3)
  Let T act on H 1 (F, Q) for the four-torus fibre F , and set ai = dim ker(Λi T − I). Cutting the
mapping torus along one fibre gives the Wang exact sequence; hence

                       b0 (M ) = 1,   b1 (M ) = 1 + a1 ,   b2 (M ) = a1 + a2 .            (C.UN.4)

Orientation preservation says det T = 1. The transformation G = Λ2 T preserves the
nondegenerate symmetric wedge pairing on Λ2 Q4 and has determinant (det T )3 = 1. We verify
that rank(G − I) is even without a semisimplicity assumption. Complexify and split off the
generalized (−1)-eigenspace. Its dimension is even: all eigenvalues outside {1, −1} occur in
reciprocal pairs with equal algebraic multiplicity, and det G = 1. This generalized eigenspace is
nondegenerate and orthogonal to its invariant complement. On it G − I is invertible, of even
rank. On the complement G + I is invertible, and

                                          (G − I)(G + I)−1

is skew-adjoint for the symmetric wedge pairing. Multiplication by that nondegenerate pairing
represents it as a skew-symmetric matrix, whose rank is even. Its rank equals that of G − I
on the complement. This proves the assertion. Since dim Λ2 Q4 = 6, a2 is even. Equations
(C.UN.3)–(C.UN.4) prove (C.UN.1).

Proposition 7.2 (All even Euler numbers and an unbounded zero-Euler family). The set of
Euler numbers of reduced fibres among compact smooth threefolds fibred in two-tori is exactly
2Z. For each k ≥ 1 there is a smooth projective such threefold with one singular reduced
normal-crossing fibre of Euler number zero consisting of a blown-up abelian surface, k ruled
surfaces over a genus-two curve, and k projective planes. Their incidence graph is a chain of
the ruled components attached to the abelian component, together with k projective-plane leaves
attached to that component.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 9.6; proposition 7.1.

Proof. Use the explicit embedded genus-two curve C2 ⊂ A of 9.6. In A × P1 retain the smooth
horizontal surface R = C2 × P1 . First blow up C2 × {0}, as in 9.6. The strict transform of R is
still R, because its centre is a Cartier divisor in R. It meets the exceptional ruled surface in the
section corresponding to the base-normal direction; this section is disjoint from the intersection
with the strict abelian component. The map to the base is a submersion near this section.
     Blow up that section and repeat, always using the intersection of the strict transform of R
with the newest exceptional component. The next centre is a smooth genus-two curve in the
smooth locus of the reduced central fibre, disjoint from its double curves. Its normal sequence
splits: the normal line to the curve inside R maps isomorphically under df to the tangent line
of the base, and supplies a splitting of the normal sequence of the central surface. The two
line summands give two disjoint sections on the new exceptional projective bundle. One meets
the previous component; the other is the next centre. This proves by induction that all k
curve blowups are defined and that the reduced central support has the stated chain. In local
coordinates the comparison is always t = uτ as in 9.6, so every new component has multiplicity
one and no triple point is introduced.
     Finally blow up m ≥ 0 distinct points of the strict abelian component away from the genus-two
double curve. They introduce m projective-plane leaves, each meeting the blown-up abelian

                                                 96
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


component in one projective line. All maps are proper holomorphic blowdowns followed by the
original projection. Every nonzero fibre is biholomorphic to A.
    Each curve blowup increases the Euler number of the central support by e(C2 ) = −2:
the exceptional projective bundle has Euler number 2e(C2 ) and its intersection with the old
component has Euler number e(C2 ). Each point blowup increases it by two, because the old
surface gains one, the exceptional plane adds three, and their intersection subtracts two. Thus

                                           e(S) = 2(m − k).                                (C.UN.5)

Given any integer n, take k ≥ max(1, −n) and m = k + n. This realizes 2n; 7.1 supplies the
opposite inclusion. Taking m = k gives the asserted zero-Euler family.
   The integral cohomology of the total space is torsion-free. The excision and projective-bundle
comparison of 9.6 gives

                      (b0 , . . . , b6 ) = (1, 4, 7 + k + m, 8 + 4k, 7 + k + m, 4, 1).     (C.UN.6)

Its Euler characteristic is independently 2(m−k). The structure sheaf direct images of each blowup
are O in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, so (h0 (O), h1 (O), h2 (O), h3 (O)) = (1, 2, 1, 0).
The exact arithmetic and exterior-square checks are in code/root_unrestricted_euler.py
and its output. This family supplies further members of the requested unrestricted zero-Euler
classification; it does not claim that every zero-Euler fibre has this construction.

Proposition 7.3 (The same punctured torus family has non-bimeromorphic zero-Euler fillings).
Let A = E ×E, E = C/(Z+iZ). There are two proper smooth-total-space fillings of A×∆∗ over a
disc whose reduced central supports both have Euler number zero, but for which no bimeromorphic
map over the disc exists. One is A × ∆. The other is the local filling (D.23), whose central
support consists of a primary Kodaira surface and a primary Hopf surface meeting along one
elliptic curve. The nonexistence persists after every finite base change and resolution of the
normalized base change, with the given punctured family retained.
    These fillings occur in compact smooth threefolds: the principal A-bundle Y0 and the threefold
Y constructed in 14.6 are isomorphic away from the three specified fibres. That isomorphism does
not extend bimeromorphically, even after a finite base change of their base curve. In particular
smooth torus fillings, together with modifications by blowups and blowdowns over the central fibre,
do not generate all zero-Euler fillings of this punctured family.
    More strongly, the same punctured product has infinitely many pairwise non-bimeromorphic
zero-Euler fillings. They are obtained by replacing OV (R) in (C.UC.2) by OV (nR), n ≥ 1. This
distinction also persists after arbitrary finite base change and resolution.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 14.6; equation (C.UC.2);
(Abramovich et al., 2002, Section 1.2.4 and Lemma 1.3.1); equation (C.UC.1);
equation (C.UC.4); equation (C.UC.3); equation (C.UC.6); equation (C.UC.8);
equation (C.UC.9); equation (C.UC.10); equation (C.UC.7).

Proof. We first record the precise birational comparison used in the proof. Let φ : M 99K N
be a bimeromorphic map between smooth complex threefolds, and let P ⊂ M be a compact
irreducible divisor whose smooth resolution is not covered by rational curves. Then φ cannot
contract P to a subset of dimension at most one. Resolve the inverse meromorphic map by
smooth-centre blowups:

                                                                                           (C.UC.1)
                               a
                            b −−
                            N  → N,             b −→ M,
                                              b:N                  b = φ−1 a.

The elimination-of-indeterminacy construction has this form in the analytic category as well as
the algebraic one; see (Abramovich et al., 2002, Section 1.2.4 and Lemma 1.3.1). For maps of

                                                    97
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


proper disc models, the same construction is made on a smaller disc; its centres above the compact
central fibre are compact. For the compact threefolds in the statement the cited construction
applies directly.
    Since b is a proper modification of the smooth target M , the strict transform Pb maps
birationally onto P . Here is the analytic justification, without using a global function field. The
locus in M over which b has positive-dimensional fibres is analytic by properness. It cannot
contain a divisor: its preimage would then have dimension at least three while being a proper
analytic subset of the irreducible threefold N   b . Thus b is finite over a dense open subset of
P . A finite modification of the normal manifold M is an isomorphism, so its degree there is
one. If φ contracted P , then a would contract Pb. It would be an exceptional divisor of the
composition of smooth-centre blowups a. Every such divisor is birational to the exceptional
divisor created at one of those steps. In dimension three that divisor is P2 for a point centre, or
a P1 -bundle over a smooth curve for a curve centre. A divisor centre gives an isomorphism and
creates no exceptional divisor. Hence Pb, and therefore P , would be covered by rational curves,
a contradiction. Applying the same argument to the inverse shows that the surviving divisors
correspond birationally, rather than only by a generically finite map.
    We now give the actual local models. Put q = e−2π and

        V = Bl(0,0) (E × ∆),      R = Exc(V → E × ∆),          U = OV (R)× /q Z .         (C.UC.2)

The quotient map U → V is a principal elliptic bundle with fibre C∗ /q Z = E. It is smooth and
proper, since each bundle chart is the product with this compact elliptic curve. Composition
with V → ∆ is therefore a proper map from a smooth threefold. The canonical section of OV (R)
trivializes it on the punctured disc, giving the specified isomorphism

                                          U | ∆∗ = A × ∆ ∗ .                              (C.UC.3)

This is exactly the construction in 14.6, including its holomorphic gluing to the compact threefold.
   The strict transform E0 of E × {0} and the exceptional R meet transversely at one point.
The restrictions of OV (R) to them have degree +1 and −1, respectively. Their inverse images in
U are
                    P = OE (0)× /q Z ,      Q = OP1 (−1)× /q Z = (C2 \ {0})/hqi.          (C.UC.4)
They meet in a single elliptic fibre J, and the local equation of the map is xy = t along J.
The first surface is a primary Kodaira surface with b1 (P ) = 3: in its principal elliptic bundle
the primitive Chern class kills one of the two elliptic fibre cycles. The second is the indicated
primary Hopf surface, with b1 (Q) = 1. These identifications and the integral transgression are
also calculated in (D.23)–(D.25).
    Neither surface contains a rational curve. A holomorphic map P1 → P projects constantly
to its elliptic base and then constantly to its elliptic fibre. A map P1 → Q lifts to C2 \ {0},
since P1 is simply connected; its two holomorphic coordinate functions are constant. Thus their
resolutions are not covered by rational curves. A bimeromorphic comparison from U to A × ∆
over ∆ would, by (C.UC.1), have to carry each of P, Q birationally onto a central divisor. The
product has only the one central divisor A, and neither P nor Q is birational to it. Indeed
the first Betti number of a smooth compact surface is unchanged by point blowups: a ball is
replaced by the simply connected exceptional neighbourhood, and van Kampen gives the same
fundamental group. Resolution of a surface bimeromorphism therefore preserves b1 , whereas
b1 (A) = 4 differs from both values in (C.UC.4). This proves that there is no such bimeromorphic
comparison.
    All these supports have Euler number zero. For P and Q, their principal elliptic bundle
projections are locally trivial proper bundles, so their Euler numbers are the product of the Euler
numbers of base and fibre, hence zero. The intersection J also has Euler number zero. Additivity


                                                 98
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                               Paper II


gives
                               e(P ∪ Q) = e(P ) + e(Q) − e(J) = 0 = e(A).                            (C.UC.5)
    Here is the comparison after a finite base change, with its ramification retained. Locally
such a change has equation t = u(s)sm , u(0) 6= 0. Taking a local mth root of the unit replaces
its parameter by one with t = sm . At a general point of either P or Q the original map is a
submersion with coordinate x = t. Its base change is the smooth chart

                                                     x = sm ,                                        (C.UC.6)

with the two surface coordinates unchanged. The component over s = 0 thus maps with degree
one to the original component. At their intersection the normalized base change has equation
xy = sm , with one additional smooth elliptic coordinate. This is normal, with transverse rational
double point Am−1 when m > 1. A resolution adds ruled exceptional surfaces above J; the
strict transforms of P and Q remain birational to the surfaces in (C.UC.4). No choice of further
resolution changes those birational classes. The target base change remains the smooth product
A × ∆s . The argument using (C.UC.1) and their first Betti numbers again excludes every
bimeromorphic comparison over ∆s .
    Finally use the compact gluing of 14.6. The original principal A-bundle Y0 has a smooth
abelian central fibre at each of the three chosen base points. The replacement Y has the local
model (C.UC.2) at each point and is identified with Y0 elsewhere by (C.UC.3). An extension of
this isomorphism would respect the base, since the two base maps agree on its dense open graph.
Its restriction near any of the three fibres would be the already excluded comparison. The same
argument applies above every preimage of these points under a finite cover of the compact base,
using (C.UC.6). This proves the compact and base-change assertions.
    For the infinite family put

          Un = OV (nR)× /q Z ,          Pn = OE (n[0])× /q Z ,        Qn = OP1 (−n)× /q Z .          (C.UC.7)

The canonical section again trivializes the bundle off the central fibre. Thus the punctured
isomorphism is the same exact product (C.UC.3). The central support is Pn ∪J Qn ; all three
terms have Euler number zero by their principal elliptic bundle projections. Each Pn contains no
rational curve by its projection to E and then to its elliptic fibre. For Qn , the usual quotient
OP1 (−n)× = (C2 \ {0})/µn is explicit: a nonzero vector v represents v ⊗n in the nth tensor power
of the tautological line. Multiplication by q on that tensor power lifts to multiplication by the
positive real number q 1/n on C2 \ {0}. Hence

                         Qn = (C2 \ {0})/hµn , q 1/n i,          π1 (Qn ) = Z ⊕ Z/nZ.                (C.UC.8)

The two commuting generators are independent, because a nonzero power of q 1/n has absolute
value different from one. The action is free and properly discontinuous, and its covering space
retracts to the simply connected S 3 . This proves the fundamental-group calculation and also
proves that every map P1 → Qn is constant by lifting it to the cover.
    For completeness the corresponding calculation for Pn retains the extension class. A Hermitian
metric on OE (n[0]) identifies its nonzero total space smoothly with its unit-circle bundle times
R>0 . As q is positive real, its quotient is the unit-circle bundle times R>0 /q Z ≃ S 1 . The circle
bundle has Chern number n. Lifting the two generators of π1 (E), the attaching map of the base
two-cell has winding number n in the circle fibre. With a consistent orientation this gives the
exact presentation

        π1 (Pn ) = ha, b, c, d | [a, b] = cn , [a, c] = [b, c] = 1, [a, d] = [b, d] = [c, d] = 1i.   (C.UC.9)

There are no further relations: the homotopy sequence of the circle bundle has injective fibre
group because π2 (E) = 0, and the last factor is the displayed direct S 1 factor. Abelianizing

(C.UC.8)–(C.UC.9) yields

                      H1 (Pn , Z) = Z3 ⊕ Z/nZ,            H1 (Qn , Z) = Z ⊕ Z/nZ.        (C.UC.10)

Integral first homology, including its torsion, is invariant under a bimeromorphism of smooth
compact surfaces, by the same point-blowup comparison already used above. By (C.UC.1), a
bimeromorphism Un 99K Un0 over the disc must carry the two non-uniruled central divisors
birationally to the two such divisors on the target. The ranks in (C.UC.10) force Pn to correspond

(C.UC.6) still leaves these components birationally unchanged, and the resolution of xy = sm
adds only ruled surfaces over J. Further resolutions add only uniruled exceptional divisors. They
cannot replace a non-uniruled component under (C.UC.1), so the same torsion argument proves
persistence. Finally all Un have compact realizations: replace V by Bl(0,0) (E × P1 ) and use the
same line bundle O(nR). Its elliptic quotient is a compact smooth threefold, and the projection
to P1 restricts to (C.UC.7) near zero.

    The comparison obstruction specifies the limit of a particular proposed classification route. In
(Kajiwara et al., 2008, Sections 5.1–5.3), a nondegenerate logarithmic torus pairing is given first,
and a suitable complete fan produces a proper model of that logarithmic complex torus. The
theorem there supplies those models; an extension of an arbitrary punctured-family isomorphism
to a bimeromorphic map of its chosen fillings is an additional requirement. Statement 7.3 refutes
that additional requirement for the displayed fillings, even though the punctured family is a
product.

Proposition 7.4 (Every even Euler number occurs above each fixed torus filling). Let f : Y → B
be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a smooth complex curve, with
connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Fix b ∈ B and put S = (Yb )red .
For every integer k there is a finite composition of blowups with smooth compact centres in
successive fibres over b,

                          π : Ye −→ Y,        fe = f π,       e((Yeb )red ) = 2k.         (C.VR.1)

The map π is an isomorphism over B \ {b}. In particular every such filling is dominated by a
smooth filling whose central reduced support has Euler number zero. More precisely, every further
smooth model obtained by vertical blowups admits a zero-Euler refinement by additional vertical
blowups. Thus zero-Euler models are cofinal for this domination relation, in the explicit sense
that every object is dominated by one of them. Above every given filling there are such zero-Euler
refinements with arbitrarily many irreducible components of their central support.
    An elementary operation lowering the Euler number by two consists of one point blowup and
one smooth genus-three curve blowup. On integral cohomology its additional summands are Z2 in
degrees two and four and Z6 in degree three. In particular, whenever the Betti numbers are finite,

                    (∆b2 , ∆b3 , ∆b4 ) = (2, 6, 2),       ∆bj = 0     (j ∈
                                                                         / {2, 3, 4}).    (C.VR.2)

All the original positive full-fibre multiplicities are retained on their strict transforms. The
construction requires no normal crossings condition on the original support.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.VR.4);
equation (C.VR.6); equation (C.VR.8); equation (C.VR.9); proposition 7.1.

                          S 0 \ πZ−1 (Z) ≃ S \ Z,         πZ−1 (Z) = P(NZ/Y ).            (C.VR.3)

Compact complex analytic spaces admit finite triangulations, compatible with these closed
analytic subsets. Euler additivity, applied with compact supports on the complements, and the
projective-bundle formula therefore give

                                e(S 0 ) − e(S) = e(P(NZ/Y )) − e(Z)

   Choose a smooth point p of one component of S, away from every other component. Such
points form a nonempty open subset of each irreducible component. If the full fibre has multiplicity
m > 0 on that component, local holomorphic coordinates may be chosen with

                                             t ◦ f = xm .                                 (C.VR.5)

Consequently both E = (r = 0) and the strict component (u = 0) have multiplicity m. Formula

   Inside E take the Fermat quartic

                                 C = {X 4 + Y 4 + Z 4 = 0} ⊂ P2 .                         (C.VR.7)

Its three partial derivatives cannot vanish simultaneously at a projective point, so it is smooth.
It is connected: if the quartic were a disjoint union of distinct plane components, two such
components would meet by their positive intersection number; their intersection would be a
singular point. Adjunction gives KC = OC (1) and 2g(C) − 2 = 4, hence g(C) = 3 and e(C) = −4.

of the quartic and X are independent there. Thus C meets L transversely in exactly four points.

      The point blowup adds Z in each of degrees two and four. The genus-three curve blowup
adds H q−2 (C, Z), whose ranks in these three successive degrees are 1, 6, 1. This proves (C.VR.2)
and shows that pre-existing integral torsion is unchanged.
      Both steps are proper holomorphic maps from smooth threefolds. A blowup has connected
fibres and pushes its structure sheaf to the structure sheaf of the original smooth space. Stein
factorization therefore proves that their composition with f again has connected fibres. The
centres lie over b, so the resulting map is the same proper torus family over B \ {b}.
      Finally 7.1 writes e(S) = 2n for an integer n. To obtain 2k with k ≥ n, use k − n point
blowups. To obtain 2k with k < n, use n − k of the two-step operations just proved. At each stage
a fresh smooth point of a single component exists, and the construction can be performed there;
only finitely many centres are needed. Applying this same procedure to any given vertical blowup
model proves the asserted cofinality with its specified domination maps. After reaching Euler
number zero, compose one further point blowup with one of the two-step decreasing operations,
at fresh smooth points. Their net Euler change is zero, while they add three irreducible central
components. Repetition gives arbitrarily many components above the original filling. Each
repetition adds (3, 6, 3) to (b2 , b3 , b4 ) when those numbers are finite; the actual maps remain
the successive blowdowns already described. The exact chart, quartic, Euler, and cohomology
calculations are retained in code/E_vertical_refinements.py and its output.

Proposition 7.5 (The same non-uniruled components occur with every even Euler number).
Fix a proper holomorphic family p× : T × → ∆× of connected complex two-tori. A marked smooth
filling is a proper holomorphic map f : Y → ∆ from a smooth complex threefold with connected
fibres, together with a biholomorphism f −1 (∆× ) ≃ T × over ∆× . For each irreducible component
Si of (Y0 )red , let Zi → Siν → Si be a smooth compact resolution of its normalization. Write E(f )
for the finite multiset of bimeromorphism classes [Zi ] for which Zi is not uniruled. Here a smooth


                                                    102
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


compact surface is uniruled when it admits a dominant meromorphic map C × P1 99K Z for a
smooth compact curve C. Repetitions in the multiset record distinct components.
   For every integer k, the following equality holds between sets of finite multisets:

  {E(f ) : f is a marked smooth filling of p× } = {E(f ) : f is such a filling,
                                                                                                (C.EC.1)
                                                                                   e((Y0 )red ) = 2k}.

For each filling in the left-hand set, the representative on the right is obtained by the explicit
proper holomorphic vertical blowup map of 7.4. That map induces a bijection between the original
non-uniruled components and the resulting non-uniruled components, and a bimeromorphism of
their normalization resolutions. Every original full-fibre multiplicity is preserved by this bijection.
    The same assertion holds for compact smooth total spaces over a fixed compact base curve,
with the marked family fixed away from a finite set Q. One can prescribe an arbitrary even Euler
number at each point of Q simultaneously, preserving the multiset and multiplicity at each point.
In particular, the collection of non-uniruled surface classes which occur in arbitrary compact
torus-fibred fillings is exactly the collection which occur in compact fillings all of whose reduced
fibres have Euler number zero.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 7.4; equation (C.EC.2).

Proof. We specify the component comparison for one of the smooth blowups π : Y 0 → Y used in
7.4. Its centre C is a point or a smooth compact curve in the central support. The inverse image
of that support consists of the strict transforms Si0 of its original components together with the
exceptional divisor
                                       E = P(NC/Y ) −→ C.                                (C.EC.2)
Each restriction Si0 → Si is a proper holomorphic map and is an isomorphism over the complement
of C. Since C has smaller dimension than Si , this complement is dense. Thus this actual map
is bimeromorphic. Normalizing both surfaces and resolving them gives a bimeromorphism
Zi0 99K Zi : explicitly, take the closure of the graph of the isomorphism on the dense normal open
sets, normalize it, and resolve the resulting compact analytic surface. Its two proper holomorphic
projections resolve the stated meromorphic map. The pullback of the defining equation of the
full fibre has its original vanishing order at the generic point of Si0 , because π is an isomorphism
there. Hence its multiplicity is unchanged.
      Uniruledness is preserved by these bimeromorphisms. Indeed, composing a dominant
meromorphic map C0 × P1 99K Zi with either bimeromorphic inverse gives such a map for
Zi0 ; its dominance follows on the dense open set where that inverse is an isomorphism. Resolving
the graph makes the composition a well-defined meromorphic map. The same argument in the
reverse direction proves the equivalence.
      The newly introduced divisor in (C.EC.2) is uniruled. For a point centre it is P2 , which
is rational: the map P1 × P1 99K P2 given on the affine chart by (u, v) 7→ [1 : u : v] is
bimeromorphic. For a curve centre it is a projective line bundle over C. Its rank-two bundle is
meromorphically trivial on C: tensoring by a sufficiently positive line bundle supplies two global
sections independent at the generic point, and their ratio gives the meromorphic trivialization.
Projectivizing it gives a bimeromorphism C × P1 99K P(NC/Y ). Its subsequent strict transforms
remain uniruled by the same composition argument. Therefore a finite sequence of these blowups
introduces no new non-uniruled class and loses none of the original classes. It preserves their
repetitions and multiplicities as well.
      Starting from any marked filling, 7.4 constructs a finite sequence of exactly these maps
whose final reduced Euler number is 2k. Every centre lies over zero, so the blowdown is a
biholomorphism over ∆× and transports the given marking by composition. We have just proved
that its multiset is the original E(f ). This gives inclusion of the left side of (C.EC.1) in the right.

                                                 103
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


Inclusion in the other direction follows because each filling with Euler number 2k is among the
same marked fillings defining the left side. This also proves the assertion when there are no
fillings: both sets are empty.
     For the compact version, apply the same construction successively at the finitely many points
of Q. Every centre is a compact analytic submanifold of the current compact threefold. Its
global blowup is compact and smooth, and the composite with the fixed base map is proper
holomorphic with connected fibres, by the structure-sheaf and Stein-factor comparison in 7.4. Its
restriction off that point is an isomorphism. Thus a construction at one point preserves every
fibre and every marking already treated at another point. There are only finitely many critical
values of a compact proper map to a curve which is smooth generically: the image of its compact
analytic critical locus is a proper analytic subset of the curve. Taking Q to contain them all
and taking k = 0 at each of them proves the final assertion; the remaining smooth torus fibres
already have Euler number zero.

    For completeness, a surface dominated meromorphically by C × P1 has no nonzero
pluricanonical section. The pullback of such a section is nonzero, because a dominant
meromorphic map between smooth surfaces is generically of full rank. It is holomorphic away
from the finitely many indeterminacy points and extends over them by Hartogs’ theorem. Its
restriction to any {c} × P1 has degree −2m in pluricanonical degree m > 0 and must vanish.
This contradicts its being nonzero. Thus the equality applies in particular to a specified
general-type normalization class. It makes the occurrence problem for such a component part of
the unrestricted zero-Euler problem through the explicit maps just proved. It does not supply a
comparison between two independently specified marked fillings. The construction uses 7.4 only
and invokes no assertion that such a comparison extends across the central fibre.

Proposition 7.6 (No component of a torus degeneration has general-type normalization). Let
f : U → ∆ be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a disc, with connected
fibres and smooth fibres complex two-tori over ∆∗ . For every irreducible component Si of the
reduced central support, its smooth normalization resolution Zi satisfies

                                           κ(Zi ) ≤ 1.                                   (C.SC.1)

No Kähler, projectivity, Betti-number or Euler-number assumption is imposed on U or its central
fibre.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.SC.3); (Guillot, 2024,
Theorem 3.3, with its proof); Guillot (2019); equation (C.SC.6).

Proof. We first make the chosen component reduced by an actual finite base change. If its
full-fibre multiplicity is mi , put t = smi and normalize the fibre product. At a generic smooth
point of Si , away from the other components, the original equation is t = uz mi with u a unit.
The normalized base change has the explicit local maps

                                     wmi = u,         z = s/w.                           (C.SC.2)

It is therefore smooth at those points, and every central component above Si has multiplicity one
and maps generically finitely onto Si . Choose one such component and resolve the normalized
total space and central support, isomorphically over ∆∗ and generically along that component.
Write f 0 : U 0 → ∆s for the resulting proper map and E for the smooth strict component. The
space U 0 is smooth, E still has multiplicity one, and the smooth nearby fibres are the original
connected tori. Connectedness of all full fibres follows also from Stein factorization over the
normal disc, since its generic degree is one.


                                                104
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


    If Zi were of general type, so would be E. Here is the precise comparison. The map E → Si
factors through normalization and gives a generically finite meromorphic map E 99K Zi . Resolve
its graph to obtain a birational map a : E   b → E and a generically finite holomorphic map
b : E → Zi between smooth compact surfaces. The actual Jacobian map gives
    b

                                  KEb = b∗ KZi + R,       R ≥ 0.                           (C.SC.3)

Pullback of pluricanonical sections is injective. The generically finite pullback of a big canonical
line is big; equivalently a generically finite pluricanonical map of Zi remains generically finite
after composition with b. Equation (C.SC.3) therefore makes KEb big. Birational invariance gives
κ(E) = 2. In particular E is projective, as is every smooth compact complex surface of general
type.
    We construct a nonzero meromorphic vector field on E with single-valued solutions. Define
the coherent relative tangent sheaf by the actual kernel

                               TU 0 /∆s = ker df 0 : TU 0 −→ f 0∗ T∆s .                     (C.SC.4)
                                                                    

Its proper direct image is torsion-free on the disc: a section annihilated by a power of s vanishes
on the dense open punctured tube and hence vanishes identically. Its rank is two, because the
global holomorphic vector fields of a two-torus are its two translation fields. It is thus a locally
free rank-two sheaf after shrinking the disc. Choose a nonzero section v, viewed by adjunction as
an actual holomorphic vertical vector field on U 0 . At the generic point of E its order of vanishing
is a finite integer k ≥ 0. Set
                                             w = s−k v.                                      (C.SC.5)
This is a global meromorphic vector field on U 0 , with poles confined to the central divisor. At a
generic point of E, the multiplicity-one assertion makes s a local transverse coordinate. Since
v(s) = 0, write v = a(x, y, s)∂x + b(x, y, s)∂y . The integer k is the minimum of the two coefficient
orders along s = 0. Thus w is holomorphic and nonzero generically on E and has a well-defined
nonzero tangent meromorphic restriction wE to E.
    We use the precise closed-univalence theorem (Guillot, 2024, Theorem 3.3, with its proof): for
a holomorphic vector field on a complex manifold of any dimension, the locus where its maximal
solutions are single-valued is closed. Such a field is called semicomplete when that locus is the
whole manifold. The closure assertion is a path-continuation statement. A failure at a point is
witnessed by a nonclosed path in a solution leaf whose time-form integral is zero. Lifting the
time parametrization of this compact path through finitely many flow charts produces the same
nonclosed zero-time path through all sufficiently nearby initial points. This proves openness of
the failure locus and records exactly the comparison used here.
    Let P be the polar divisor of w and put W = U 0 \ P . On the dense open subset U 0∗ ⊂ W , w
restricts to a holomorphic vector field on each compact torus, multiplied by the constant s−k
on that fibre. Each such field is complete: its complex-time solution stays in the compact fibre,
so local existence extends it for all times. Consequently w is semicomplete on all of W by the
stated closedness theorem.
    The hypersurface E ∩ W is invariant. Indeed w(s) = 0, and at any point where w is
holomorphic, factoring the local equation of s into its irreducible components shows that w
preserves the ideal of each component. A solution starting in E ∩ W therefore stays there, and
its single-valuedness is the one inherited from w. The curve removed from E by the ambient
polar divisor may contain removable poles of wE . Apply the same closedness theorem once more
on E minus the actual polar divisor of wE . Its dense open subset E ∩ W is already semicomplete.
Hence wE is a nonzero semicomplete meromorphic vector field on the entire compact surface E,
in the precise sense of single-valuedness on its holomorphic locus.
    We finish by proving that a projective surface of general type admits no such field. Suppose
first that one maximal solution of wE has Zariski-dense image. The Main Theorem of Guillot

                                                105
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


(2019), including the clarification immediately following it, gives a birational model which is
an abelian surface or admits a rational or elliptic fibration. The holomorphic alternative is
covered there by Proposition 22; the dense leaf excludes a first integral in that alternative. All
these models have Kodaira dimension at most one, contradicting κ(E) = 2. Only single-valued
maximality, already proved, is needed in this application; the solution need not be entire.
    Here is the other case, with its actual fibration map. If every solution leaf is contained in a
proper analytic curve, the closures of the regular leaves are irreducible algebraic invariant curves
on the projective surface E. They cover its open regular foliation locus. Use the countably
many Hilbert polynomials and flattening strata of their universal families to parametrize reduced
irreducible curves. The locus of such integral curves is constructible. After clearing the polar
divisor, invariance is the vanishing of the induced normal-component map of the vector field
on the universal curve; on these strata it is a constructible condition. Thus we have countably
many irreducible locally closed parameter strata of integral invariant curves. Their incidence
images in E are constructible. If none were dense, their Zariski closures would be countably many
proper closed analytic subsets covering the regular foliation locus, contrary to the Baire theorem.
Choose a stratum whose incidence dominates E. Its generic curves are reduced and irreducible.
At a regular point of the foliation exactly one such irreducible curve can pass: two would contain
the same local solution germ and would coincide. Thus the parameter has dimension one and the
incidence map to E is generically one-to-one. Compactify and normalize this parameter curve
and close the incidence graph. Inverting its birational projection to E and projecting to the
parameter gives an actual meromorphic first integral. Resolve its indeterminacies and take its
Stein factor to obtain a morphism
                                            q : E 0 −→ C                                   (C.SC.6)
with connected generic fibre a smooth compact curve. The lifted meromorphic field remains
semicomplete: it agrees with the old field on the birational open set, and the same closedness
theorem extends single-valuedness over its full holomorphic locus. It is a nonzero tangent
meromorphic field on a generic fibre G of (C.SC.6).
    Such a field on a compact curve has no pole. A pole of order r ≥ 1 would have the local
form z −r a(z)∂z with a(0) 6= 0. Its time form is z r a(z)−1 dz, whose primitive has a zero of order
r + 1. The inverse solution therefore has r + 1 branches around that time value, all lying in the
punctured coordinate disc. This contradicts semicompleteness. The field on G is consequently
holomorphic and nonzero, so deg TG = 2 − 2g(G) ≥ 0 and g(G) ≤ 1.
    This also contradicts general type directly through pluricanonical maps. Adjunction on the
smooth generic fibre gives KE 0 |G = KG , of degree at most zero. Every linear system |nKE 0 |
therefore restricts to a constant map on G: a negative-degree line has no sections, and a degree-
zero line on a connected compact curve has at most one independent section. A generically finite
pluricanonical map of the general-type surface E 0 cannot contract its generic fibres in this way.
This excludes the all-algebraic- leaves case as well.
    Both cases contradict the general-type consequence of (C.SC.3). The chosen Zi cannot have
Kodaira dimension two. Since Si was arbitrary, (C.SC.1) follows for every component.

and with smooth complex two-tori over ∆∗ . Fix an irreducible central component Si of multiplicity

                                   aE ⊂ H 0 (E, TE ⊗OE ME )                             (C.CF.1)
of commuting meromorphic vector fields. Every member of aE is semicomplete on its holomorphic
locus. The map E → Si factors through normalization and is proper and generically finite.

    There are two exhaustive geometric alternatives for this particular space of fields. Its generic

    When a(Siν ) = 0, the unique minimal model of E is a two-torus or a Hopf surface. This last

Proof. Write f 0 : U 0 → ∆s for the resolved base change. The local equations wmi = u, z = s/w in
(C.SC.2), starting from t = uz mi , prove both multiplicity one and generic finiteness. Properness
and the universal property of normalization give the asserted factorization E → Siν → Si . These
