    Put O = C{s} and K = Frac(O). Let

                    M = (f∗0 TU 0 /∆s )0 ,    L = {v ∈ M ⊗O K : ordE (v) ≥ 0}.             (C.CF.3)

The order in this formula is the minimum of the coefficient orders in a local tangent frame at the
generic point of E. It is independent of that frame. The direct image is coherent by properness,
is torsion-free because its sections are actual vector fields on U 0 , and has rank two by base
change on the smooth torus locus. Consequently M is a free rank-two O-module. Its sections
are identified with actual holomorphic vertical fields by the definition of direct image. Any two
of them commute: their restrictions to a smooth torus are translation fields, so their bracket
vanishes on the dense punctured tube and hence everywhere.
    Here is a finite bound for the saturation in (C.CF.3). Choose an O-basis v1 , v2 of M . At a
generic point of E, multiplicity one makes s a coordinate, so the two vertical tangent coordinates
x, y give
                          (v1 v2 ) = (∂x ∂y )A,   d = ordE (det A) < ∞.                   (C.CF.4)
All entries of A are holomorphic there. The determinant is nonzero because the evaluation
of the two translation fields is an isomorphism on each nearby torus. In particular d ≥ 0.
For v = a1 (s)v1 + a2 (s)v2 ∈ L, the column Aa has nonnegative order along E. The identity
a = (det A)−1 adj(A)(Aa) shows that each aj has order at least −d. The order of a function of s
along E equals its s-adic order, again by multiplicity one. We obtain actual inclusions

                                             M ⊂ L ⊂ s−d M.                                (C.CF.5)

The set L is an O-submodule. Since O is noetherian, (C.CF.5) makes it finite; since it is
torsion-free of rank two over the discrete valuation ring O, it is free of rank two.
    Every member of L is a global meromorphic vertical field on a sufficiently small representative
of U 0 , regular at the generic point of E. Its restriction is therefore a global meromorphic section
of TE . Tangency follows from v(s) = 0 at the generic smooth point and then as an identity of
meromorphic sections. Restriction defines the exact map

                       resE : L −→ H 0 (E, TE ⊗ ME ),         ker(resE ) = sL.             (C.CF.6)

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


Indeed, zero restriction means order at least one along E; division by s then belongs to L.
Conversely, every member of sL restricts to zero. Thus

                                 L/sL ≃ C2 ,→ H 0 (E, TE ⊗ ME ).                            (C.CF.7)

Define aE to be its image. Since vertical fields annihilate functions of s, brackets of members of
M ⊗ K vanish. Hence the fields in (C.CF.7) commute.
    For completeness, semicompleteness applies to the entire space, not only to a selected nonzero
element. Given V ∈ aE , choose its representative v ∈ L. Its poles are confined to the central
fibre. On every punctured fibre it is a holomorphic translation field multiplied by constants,
and is complete. Remove the ambient polar divisor. The closedness of the uniformizability
locus for a holomorphic vector field (Guillot, 2024, Theorem 3.3) makes v semicomplete there,
since the punctured tube is dense. The component E is invariant: locally v(s) = 0 and
factorization of the local equation of s show that each irreducible component ideal is invariant
wherever v is holomorphic. Solutions in E inherit single-valuedness. Some removed curves may
be removable poles for V ; the same closedness theorem on E minus its actual polar divisor
extends semicompleteness across those curves. This proves the assertion for every constant linear
combination in aE .
    Take a complex basis V1 , V2 of aE . When V1 ∧ V2 is nonzero, it is the announced meromorphic
frame. Otherwise there is a globally defined meromorphic function h with

                                     V2 = hV1 ,         V1 (h) = 0.                         (C.CF.8)

The local coefficient ratios agree on their overlaps, which proves that h is global. It is nonconstant
by the complex-linear independence in (C.CF.7). The second identity follows from the vanishing
bracket. Resolve the graph of h : E 99K P1 and take the Stein factor of its projection to P1 . This
gives exactly (C.CF.2), with a finite map B → P1 . The lifted field is tangent to q and nonzero
on a general fibre. Its semicompleteness passes through the birational open isomorphism and
then over its full holomorphic locus by the same closedness theorem.
    A nonzero semicomplete meromorphic field on a smooth compact curve has no pole. At
a pole of order r ≥ 1 its expression is z −r a(z)∂z , a(0) 6= 0. The time form z r a(z)−1 dz has a
primitive vanishing to order r + 1; its inverse solution has distinct analytic continuations around
that time value. They all lie in the punctured coordinate disc, contradicting single-valuedness.
The restricted field is therefore holomorphic, so deg TG = 2 − 2g(G) ≥ 0 for a general fibre G.
This proves the rational-or-elliptic assertion.
    Finally suppose a(Siν ) = 0. The map E → Siν has a finite Stein factor E → T 0 → Siν , whose
first map is bimeromorphic. For a meromorphic function on T 0 , the elementary symmetric
functions of its values over the finite map are meromorphic on Siν . They give a monic algebraic
equation over M(Siν ). Thus the meromorphic function field extension is algebraic and

                                          a(E) = a(Siν ) = 0.                               (C.CF.9)

In particular (C.CF.8) cannot occur.
   Apply the compact-surface classification of semicomplete meromorphic fields (Guillot, 2024,
Theorem 9.2) separately to V1 and V2 . Its fibration alternative would give a nonconstant
meromorphic function on E; therefore each field is holomorphic on some smooth bimeromorphic
model. An algebraic-dimension-zero surface is not ruled. Its smooth minimal model E0 is
unique, and every smooth bimeromorphic model maps to it by successive point blowdowns.
Holomorphic fields descend under these actual maps: for a blowdown π the equality π∗ O = O
sends the derivation g 7→ V (π ∗ g) to a holomorphic derivation on the base. On the common open
isomorphism it is the original field. The two resulting holomorphic fields on the same E0 remain
complex-linearly independent and commute.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


   The complete list of minimal compact surfaces admitting a nonzero holomorphic field is
(Dloussky et al., 2001, Theorem 0.3). In algebraic dimension zero, its possibilities are two-tori,
Hopf surfaces, Inoue surfaces, and minimal class-VII surfaces with positive second Betti number.
The last class has at most one independent holomorphic field (Dloussky et al., 2000, pp. 256
and 260); Inoue surfaces also have at most one (Inoue, 1974, Propositions 2(ii), 3(ii) and 5). The
two independent fields on E0 exclude both of those alternatives. Hence E0 is a two-torus or a
Hopf surface, as claimed.

Proposition 7.9 (Every class VII normalization component has Hopf minimal model). For every
proper holomorphic degeneration of smooth complex two-tori with smooth three-dimensional total
space, each central component whose normalization resolution is of class VII has a Hopf surface
as its minimal model. This holds for arbitrary multiplicities, arbitrary central singularities, and
arbitrary Euler number. In particular no Inoue surface and no minimal class VII surface with
positive second Betti number is a normalization minimal model of such a component.
    The comparison proving this assertion is the cyclic cover obtained from t = smi for that
component. Its stabilizer acts on the minimal model of the covering component, and the quotient
is bimeromorphic to the original normalization.

                                                 111
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Bierstone and Milman, 1997, §1,
universal and canonical desingularization); equation (C.HQ.2); proposition 7.8; (Dloussky et al.,

(Khaled, 2024, Theorem 2.1); equation (C.HQ.6); equation (C.HQ.7); equation (C.HQ.8);
equation (C.HQ.10); (Dloussky and Teleman, 2012, Remark 2.7).

Proof. We first identify the quotient in the actual base change. Normalize U ×∆t ∆s , where
t = smi . Its cyclic group µmi acts over U . Choose a resolution of the total space and central
divisor equivariant for this finite group. Canonical analytic resolution has this property: the
invariants defining its centres are preserved by every local isomorphism, so the action lifts through
every blowup (Bierstone and Milman, 1997, §1, universal and canonical desingularization). The
algorithm is an isomorphism over the punctured tube and at the generic smooth points used in
(C.SC.2).
    Let E be a chosen smooth strict component above Si , and let G ⊂ µmi be its stabilizer. At a
generic point of Si the equations are exactly

                                      wmi = u,         z = s/w.                            (C.HQ.1)

Consequently the reduced inverse image over a dense smooth open subset of Si is a µmi -torsor.
The cyclic group permutes its connected components transitively. The stabilizer of a selected
component acts freely and transitively on each fibre of that component. Equivalently, the degree
of E → Si at the generic point is |G|, and quotienting by G gives degree one. The proper map
to normalization therefore descends to a proper bimeromorphic map

                                           E/G −→ Siν .                                    (C.HQ.2)

This argument remains valid when the root cover is disconnected over Si ; the stabilizer, rather
than the whole base-change group, is the group in (C.HQ.2).
    Write Zi for a smooth normalization resolution and Mi for its minimal model. The case
b2 (Mi ) = 0 already has Hopf minimal model by 7.8. Every minimal class VII surface with

treat a(Mi ) = 0, by an argument which also covers the zero-Betti case. The field comparison in
(C.CF.9) gives a(E) = 0, and 7.7 says that the unique smooth minimal model E0 is a torus or a
Hopf surface.
    Every element of G induces a birational automorphism of E0 . On a nonruled minimal
compact surface this is holomorphic, by uniqueness of the minimal model. Thus the contraction
ρ : E → E0 is equivariant: the identity ρg = g0 ρ holds on the common open isomorphism and
hence everywhere. It descends to a proper bimeromorphic map

                                          E/G −→ E0 /G.                                    (C.HQ.3)

The actions on E0 are faithful after removing their kernel, which does not change the quotient.
Resolving the graph of (C.HQ.2)–(C.HQ.3) gives actual proper bimeromorphic comparisons
between Zi and a resolution of E0 /G.
    We exclude the torus alternative by its first cohomology. For a finite holomorphic quotient
q : A → A/G, proper base change gives Rj q∗ Q = 0 for j > 0, and averaging gives (q∗ Q)G = Q.
Taking invariants is exact over Q, so the actual pullback map identifies

                                    H 1 (A/G, Q) ≃ H 1 (A, Q)G .                           (C.HQ.4)

For a complex torus the holomorphic action preserves H 1,0 ⊕ H 0,1 and conjugation interchanges
the two invariant summands. Hence the dimension in (C.HQ.4) is even. Each singularity
of a cyclic surface quotient has a resolution with a connected chain of rational curves: after

                                                 112
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


linearization, the quotient cone is the first quadrant in Z2 + n1 (a, b)Z, and a regular fan subdivision
gives that resolution. Removing pseudoreflections first only replaces the local coordinates by their
invariant powers. Thus every exceptional fibre has H 1 = 0 and is connected. Proper base change
and the degree-one part of Leray show that resolving A/G leaves H 1 unchanged. Birational maps
between smooth compact surfaces preserve H 1 , as follows from their factorization into point
blowups. The comparisons (C.HQ.2)–(C.HQ.3) would therefore make b1 (Zi ) even, contradicting
b1 (Zi ) = 1.
    It remains to prove that the cyclic quotient of the Hopf surface H = E0 is again Hopf. We
give the fixed-point and quotient argument explicitly. Let
                                          H = (C2 \ {0})/Γ.                                   (C.HQ.5)
The deck group contains an infinite cyclic subgroup of finite index generated by a holomorphic
contraction. Equivalently H has a finite unramified primary Hopf cover; the normal forms and the
finite-cover description are recalled in (Nakamura, 2008, §1.1) and (Khaled, 2024, Theorem 2.1).
Every deck transformation extends across the origin by Hartogs, as does its inverse. These
extensions fix the origin and are biholomorphic. The same is true for any lift ge of a holomorphic
automorphism g of H.
    Define the real character
                               δ : Γ −→ R,       δ(γ) = log | det(dγ)0 |.                     (C.HQ.6)
It is nonzero, since its value on a contraction is negative. For any automorphism lift, conjugacy
of derivatives gives
                                         δ(e  g −1 ) = δ(γ).
                                           g γe                                          (C.HQ.7)
A primary Hopf cover has rational Betti numbers (1, 1, 0, 1, 1): this follows directly from the
covering spectral sequence for C2 \ {0} ≃ S 3 and the infinite cyclic deck group, whose action
on H 3 (S 3 , Q) preserves orientation. Transfer from the finite primary cover gives b1 (H) ≤ 1 and
b2 (H) = 0, while (C.HQ.6) gives b1 (H) ≥ 1. Hence b1 (H) = 1. Equation (C.HQ.7) says that
every holomorphic automorphism acts identically on H 1 (H, R). Poincaré duality and its complex
orientation then give the identity action on H 3 as well. Its Lefschetz number is therefore
                                   L(g) = 1 − 1 + 0 − 1 + 1 = 0.                              (C.HQ.8)

    For a nonidentity finite-order automorphism, the fixed locus is a disjoint union of smooth
compact curves and isolated points, by finite holomorphic linearization. Each fixed curve C is
smooth. Since H 2 (H, Q) = 0, one has C 2 = KH · C = 0. The actual adjunction isomorphism
KC = (KH ⊗ OH (C))|C therefore gives 2g(C) − 2 = 0. Thus all the curve components of the fixed
locus have Euler number zero. For a finite-order map the topological Lefschetz number equals
the Euler number of its fixed locus. Indeed, use an equivariant triangulation and barycentric
subdivision; each invariant simplex is then fixed pointwise, so the alternating trace on simplicial
cochains counts exactly the fixed simplices. Equation (C.HQ.8) consequently shows that there
are no isolated fixed points.
    At any point of H, the stabilizer in the effective cyclic group G is cyclic. Its generator has a
fixed curve through that point and, in linearizing coordinates, acts by
                          (x, y) 7−→ (x, ζy),     C{x, y}hζi = C{x, y |Gx | }.                (C.HQ.9)
Here Gx denotes the stabilizer, and ζ has its full order; a finite-order germ with identity derivative
is the identity. This proves that the quotient Q = H/G is smooth, with the displayed local
quotient map even at its branch curves.
    The invariant-cohomology comparison in (C.HQ.4), now in every degree and combined with
(C.HQ.7), gives
                                    b1 (Q) = 1,       b2 (Q) = 0.                          (C.HQ.10)

                                                  113
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


The finite map H → Q injects every space of pluricanonical sections by the actual Jacobian
pullback. Since a Hopf surface has κ = −∞, this proves κ(Q) = −∞. Also Q is minimal:
an exceptional curve of self-intersection −1 would have a nonzero real H 2 class, contrary to
(C.HQ.10).
    There is a curve on Q. Explicitly, the primary Hopf normal form (z1 , z2 ) 7→ (αz1 + az2r , βz2 )
contains the elliptic curve given by z2 = 0; its finite image in H, and then in Q, is a nonempty
curve. A positive multiple of that curve is homologically trivial by (C.HQ.10). The divisor
classification (Dloussky and Teleman, 2012, Remark 2.7) applied to the minimal class VII surface
Q now gives a Hopf surface: its Enoki alternative has positive second Betti number and is
excluded by (C.HQ.10). We have proved the cyclic-quotient assertion by actual quotient maps,
including their branch points.
    Finally (C.HQ.2)–(C.HQ.3) make Zi bimeromorphic to this smooth Hopf surface Q.
Uniqueness of the class VII minimal model proves that Mi ≃ Q. This proves the assertion for
every component in the original, unaltered degeneration.

Proposition 7.11 (A component cover with a rank-two translation frame has coherent Euler

    The projected field has no pole. To verify this without an unproved descent assertion about

punctured disc about b avoiding all other bad values. The inverse image of the compact union of
these paths is compact. Both q and Y are holomorphic there, and Y has no pole there, since all
its polar curves are vertical and the disc was chosen accordingly. The usual continuation theorem
for holomorphic ordinary differential equations therefore lifts the whole time loop to a solution

is a nonzero holomorphic field on the compact curve B, and g(B) ≤ 1.

Proposition 7.12 (A cyclic torus quotient with nonnegative Kodaira dimension is a torus,
bielliptic, or K3). Let A be a compact complex two-torus, let G be a finite cyclic group of
holomorphic automorphisms acting effectively on A, and let Z → A/G be a smooth resolution.
Every positive plurigenus of Z is at most one. There are the following exhaustive alternatives for

                 linear part and action         minimal resolution type

In particular an Enriques surface is not bimeromorphic to a cyclic quotient of a complex two-torus.
    For the actual component cover in 7.7, suppose its minimal model is a two-torus. The quotient

Proof. The derivative of a holomorphic torus automorphism is constant in the translation
trivialization: its entries are holomorphic functions on a compact torus. Lifting to the universal
cover consequently writes the automorphism as z 7→ Lz + b, with LΛ = Λ for the lattice Λ. For
a finite-order automorphism, L is diagonalizable with roots of unity as eigenvalues.

                                                v

                                          A −→ A/G.
Here u is a sequence of point blowups and v is generically finite. Pullback of a pluricanonical form

                   H 0 (Z, mKZ ) −→ H 0 (A, mKA ) = C σ ⊗m ,         σ = dz1 ∧ dz2 .          (C.CQ.3)

Injectivity follows on the dense locus of the dominant map. The image is G-invariant, so a
nonzero image also requires (det L)m = 1.
    If the quotient map A → A/G is ramified along a curve, its generic local form is (x, y) 7→ (xe , y)
with e > 1. The Jacobian pullback of a holomorphic m-canonical form vanishes to order at least

              a branch curve in A −→ A/G         =⇒     Pm (Z) = 0     (m > 0).               (C.CQ.4)

This conclusion uses the actual ramification map, including when the quotient is smooth along
the branch image.
   When L = I, the group consists of translations. The action is free and its quotient is the
torus obtained by enlarging Λ by the finitely many translation vectors. This is the first row of
(C.CQ.1).
    Suppose that L has exactly one eigenvalue equal to one. Every power of L has that eigenvalue.
A nonidentity element of G with a fixed point therefore has a fixed curve, unless its derivative is
the identity; in the latter case it is a translation and has no fixed point. Thus a nonfree action
gives (C.CQ.4). A free action gives a smooth finite étale quotient. Its canonical line has finite

                        h1 (Z, OZ ) = 1,      h0 (Z, KZ ) = 0,      b1 (Z) = 2.               (C.CQ.5)

bielliptic presentation, without inferring it only from the numerical invariants. In particular this

derivative is invertible. Solve (I − L)p = b and translate the origin to p. The generator becomes
the linear map L and has a fixed point. Its order equals the order of L.

can have exactly one eigenvalue one; such a power would fix a divisor. If the order is n, each
eigenvalue of L is therefore a primitive nth root. After changing the cyclic generator, its local
representation is
                        (z1 , z2 ) 7−→ (ζz1 , ζ r z2 ), 1 ≤ r < n, gcd(r, n) = 1.         (C.CQ.7)
We give the precise local pluricanonical test. The quotient is the affine toric surface for the first
quadrant in

         N = Z2 + Z(1/n, r/n),         M = {(a, b) ∈ Z2 : a + rb ≡ 0      (mod n)}.        (C.CQ.8)

These are the cocharacter and character lattices: the invariant monomials are exactly z1a z2b with
(a, b) ∈ M . If (det L)m = 1, the form in (C.CQ.3) descends on the smooth locus as

                                                     dz2 ⊗m
                                                        
                                             m dz1
                                     (z1 z2 )      ∧         .
                                                z1    z2

Its order on the divisor of a primitive toric ray v = (v1 , v2 ) ∈ N is

                                           m(v1 + v2 − 1).                                 (C.CQ.9)

Indeed a unimodular toric chart expresses the monomial’s order as its character pairing with v,
while the logarithmic volume form has one simple pole along that divisor. The same formula
holds on a refinement, by its explicit monomial map.
   The vector (1/n, r/n) is primitive in N and can be included in a smooth fan subdivision of
the quadrant. To obtain such a subdivision, first insert this ray and then insert primitive lattice
rays until every adjacent cone has determinant one in a lattice basis; the Euclidean algorithm
terminates this two-dimensional procedure. When r < n − 1, (C.CQ.9) is negative on this ray.
The descended form cannot extend to that smooth resolution. Smooth resolutions have the
same pluricanonical sections under their actual common point-blowup resolution, by the Hartogs
comparison already used in (C.CQ.3). Therefore

              ker(L − I) = 0,    det L 6= 1    =⇒      Pm (Z) = 0    (m > 0),             (C.CQ.10)

also including the branch-curve case by (C.CQ.4).
    Finally let det L = 1. Every stabilizer acts with weights (1, −1) after choosing its generator,
so there are no branch curves. For a stabilizer of order n, the rays

                       (1, 0), ((n − 1)/n, 1/n), . . . , (1/n, (n − 1)/n), (0, 1)         (C.CQ.11)

give a smooth subdivision. Consecutive determinants are 1/n, the covolume of N , and all these
rays have height v1 + v2 = 1. Formula (C.CQ.9) shows that the invariant two-form extends
without a zero or pole across every exceptional divisor. Thus the simultaneous resolution Z0 has
KZ0 ≃ OZ0 . Its exceptional curves are the chains of rational curves given by (C.CQ.11).
    For clarity, its simple connectedness follows through the quotient map as well. Remove the
discrete set of points in C2 fixed by nontrivial elements of Γ = Λ o hLi. The complement is simply
connected: a compact loop bounds a disc in R4 , and a perturbation relative to its boundary
avoids the finitely many removed points met in a compact region. It is the universal cover of the
smooth quotient locus. Filling in a quotient point kills the normal closure of its finite stabilizer

                                                 121
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


in Γ, by van Kampen. For every λ ∈ Λ, the element (λ, L) has a fixed point, since I − L is
invertible. Thus all (λ, L) are killed, including (0, L); their products kill every translation (λ, I)
as well. The resulting fundamental group is trivial. Replacing a quotient point by the rational
chain in (C.CQ.11) imposes the same relation: its plumbing neighbourhood is simply connected
and has the same punctured boundary as the quotient ball. Hence π1 (Z0 ) = 1. Together with
KZ0 = O, this identifies Z0 as a K3 surface. It is minimal, since adjunction excludes a rational
(−1)-curve on a surface with trivial canonical line. This proves the third row.
    An Enriques surface has a nonzero even pluricanonical form, but has no nonzero canonical
form and has b1 = 0. None of the three nonnegative cases in (C.CQ.1) has those properties: the
torus and K3 have a canonical form, and the bielliptic case has b1 = 2. All the other cases have
no positive pluricanonical form. This proves the exclusion.
    We finish with the component comparison. The stabilizer of a component in the cyclic base
change of 7.7 is cyclic, and its quotient is properly bimeromorphic to the original normalization, as
in (C.HQ.1)–(C.HQ.3). If the minimal model of the covering component E is a torus A, its actual
minimal contraction E → A is equivariant. One way to verify the descent is to factor all the
exceptional rational curves: their maps to the torus are constant, and the equality ρ∗ OE = OA
descends the coordinate functions and hence every conjugate action. Thus the induced action on
A is holomorphic, and
                                   E     −→      A
                                    ↓            ↓        E/G 99K Siν                      (C.CQ.12)
                                  E/G −→ A/G
has a proper birational horizontal quotient map and the specified proper birational comparison
on the right. Resolving their graph identifies the pluricanonical spaces and minimal birational
type. Applying (C.CQ.1) gives exactly the last assertion. This statement concerns this actual
torus-cover branch; the separate rank-one fibration branch is handled by the different comparison
of 7.10.

    For comparison with the primary literature, the projective quotient classification is already
given by (Yoshihara, 1995, Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 3.4). Its Enriques cases have noncyclic
holonomy: the Klein four group or a dihedral group of order eight (Yoshihara, 1995, Example 2.3
and Lemma 3.6). The proof above includes nonprojective tori and supplies the actual cyclic
component-cover comparison needed here.

Proposition 7.13 (Every compact elliptic surface satisfies the intrinsic rank-one field condition).
Let q : X → B be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact connected complex surface to
a smooth compact curve, with connected elliptic general fibre. There are commuting meromorphic
vector fields V1 , V2 which are linearly independent over C, have generic rank one, and whose
every constant linear combination is semicomplete on its full holomorphic locus. Their ratio has
an actual graph resolution and Stein factor birationally equal to q.
    If a finite cyclic group G acts holomorphically on X and preserves q, the two-dimensional
space can be chosen G-stable. Thus the rank-one field-space condition of 7.7, even with this
equivariance, is satisfied by every specified compact elliptic surface and cyclic fibration action.
Any additional restriction on its occurrence as a degeneration component must use further data
of that degeneration.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 7.7; equation (C.FL.3);
(Guillot, 2024, Theorem 3.3).

Proof. The relative canonical line is the actual invertible sheaf
                                              −1
                             ωX/B = KX ⊗ q ∗ KB  ,        E = q∗ ωX/B .                     (C.FL.1)


                                                 122
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Proper coherence makes E coherent. It is torsion-free: a section of a line bundle annihilated by a
nonzero base function vanishes over the dense complement of its zero fibre and hence vanishes
identically. On a smooth elliptic fibre the canonical space has dimension one, so E has rank one.
It is therefore a line bundle on B.
    Choose a nonzero meromorphic section σ of E. This is an actual global choice: Riemann–Roch
on B gives a nonzero holomorphic section of E(D) for an effective divisor D of sufficiently large
degree, which is the required meromorphic section of E. Evaluation gives a nonzero meromorphic
section
                             a : OX 99K ωX/B from q ∗ E −→ ωX/B .                         (C.FL.2)
Here the dashed notation records poles of the section, not a replacement of the displayed sheaf
evaluation. On the smooth part of q, the canonical differential identification ωX/B = Ω1X/B
makes a an actual relative one-form.
    Its dual defines a global meromorphic vertical field V . The coordinate comparison at critical
fibres can be specified as follows. On a coordinate disc of B with coordinate z, set Ωz = a⊗q ∗ (dz),
a meromorphic section of KX . Define V by

                                          ιV Ωz = −q ∗ (dz).                               (C.FL.3)

Contraction by a nonzero meromorphic two-form is an isomorphism between the meromorphic
tangent and cotangent bundles, so this has a unique meromorphic solution. Under z 0 = φ(z) both
sides are multiplied by q ∗ φ0 (z); the solution is unchanged and therefore glues. The alternating
identity in (C.FL.3) gives dq(V ) = 0. On a regular fibre its relative time form is a, so a(V ) = 1
with the usual convention Ωz = q ∗ (dz) ∧ a.
     Remove finitely many base values so that q is smooth and the evaluated section is holomorphic
and nonzero on every remaining fibre. Such a removal is possible by generic base change for
q∗ ωX/B and the finite zero and pole divisors of σ. A nonzero canonical form on a compact
elliptic curve is nowhere zero. Thus V restricts on each of these fibres to a nonzero holomorphic
translation field and is complete there.
     Choose any nonconstant meromorphic function h on B, and put

                                     V1 = V,      V2 = (q ∗ h)V.                           (C.FL.4)

Their bracket vanishes because V (q ∗ h) = 0. They are independent over C since h is nonconstant,
and have generic rank one by the formula. For c, d ∈ C, the field W = (c + dq ∗ h)V is complete on
the dense union of the preceding compact smooth fibres away from the poles of h. Its coefficient
is constant on each such fibre; zero coefficients give constant complete solutions. Apply (Guillot,
2024, Theorem 3.3) to the complex manifold obtained by deleting the actual polar divisor of
W . The univalence locus is closed there and contains this dense union. It is therefore the whole
holomorphic locus, proving the asserted semicompleteness for every W .
     The ratio is q ∗ h, so the resulting map is the actual composite X −
                                                                           q
                                                                                 → P1 . The second
                                                                                 h
                                                                           →B−
arrow is finite. Its Stein factor is q itself: q∗ OX = OB , and B is the normalization in the field
of functions constant on the connected general fibres. This proves the precise first-integral
comparison.
     For the equivariant assertion, the finite orbit of V spans a nonzero finite-dimensional
representation of G by meromorphic vertical fields. A cyclic complex representation has an
eigenvector V 0 6= 0. On a general smooth fibre each orbit field is holomorphic and vertical, and
therefore a translation field. The same is true of V 0 ; after removing finitely many further values

                                          CV 0 + C(q ∗ h)V 0                               (C.FL.5)

is G-stable, with the same eigencharacter on its two displayed generators. Its members are

         PE = {[Re α] : α ∈ H 0 (E, KE )} ⊂ H 2 (E, R),      dimR PE = 2pg (E).            (C.PG.7)

subspace, and on their direct sum, follows from preservation of its positive intersection form.

This follows directly from the exterior-algebra identification of its integral cohomology: the three
complementary degree-two pairs give three hyperbolic blocks. Its positive index is therefore three.

Proposition 7.15 (Rank-one elliptic component covers have only smooth multiple fibres).
Let E be an actual multiplicity-one covering component constructed in 7.7, with its saturated
two-dimensional space of limiting translation fields. In the generic-rank-one branch, take the
actual graph resolution and Stein factor of their ratio. When its connected general fibre is elliptic,
the resulting relatively minimal elliptic surface

                                             q : E0 −→ B                                   (C.RG.1)

has identity integral H1 monodromy. Every fibre is a positive multiple of a smooth elliptic curve,
and all smooth fibres are torsors under one fixed elliptic curve. Moreover

                     R1 q∗ OE0 ≃ OB ,       pg (E) = g(B) ≤ 1,      χ(OE ) = 0.            (C.RG.2)

The maps to E0 are the specified point blowups resolving the first integral followed by vertical
exceptional-curve contractions. No extension of that first integral to an ambient neighbourhood is
assumed.
    Together with 7.11, this proves that every such root-cover component of nonnegative Kodaira
dimension has coherent Euler characteristic zero. In particular its minimal model is neither
K3 nor Enriques. Every original component of Kodaira dimension one has an isotrivial elliptic
Iitaka fibration over a curve of genus at most one; its possible singular fibres are retained by the
actual cyclic quotient comparison, and are not asserted to be smooth.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 7.7; proposition 7.11;

component. There is a nonconstant meromorphic function H on B such that

                                          V2 |E = (q ∗ H)V1 |E .                           (C.RG.3)

This is precisely the function and Stein map given by the original ratio, rather than a chosen

The direct image and the genus bound. Over a small smooth base disc, a local holomorphic

overlap map is the identity. The overlap maps are translations, which act trivially on H 1 (O).
At a multiple value use the actual normalized root family just described. It is smooth with
constant elliptic modulus. The cyclic action on its central elliptic fibre is free, since the map to
E0 is étale, and is therefore a translation. Its linear part on the neighbouring marked elliptic

Taking invariants in the local root disc consequently gives R1 q∗ O = O at the multiple value as

punctured discs. This proves the first assertion of (C.RG.2) with its actual descent map.

    Connected fibres give q∗ OE0 = OB . The coherent Leray sequence on the curve now gives
               H 2 (E0 , OE0 ) ≃ H 1 (B, OB ),   h1 (E0 , OE0 ) = g(B) + 1.              (C.RG.13)
Serre duality and birational invariance give pg (E) = g(B) and χ(OE ) = 0. The independent
compact-core inequality 7.14 gives pg (E) ≤ 1, and therefore g(B) ≤ 1.
    Every root-cover component of nonnegative Kodaira dimension has either generic rank two,
covered by 7.11, or rank one. In the latter case a rational general first-integral fibre would make
the surface uniruled and give Kodaira dimension −∞ by the actual adjunction argument in
7.10. Its general fibre is therefore elliptic and the present proof applies. This proves the stated
coherent-Euler and K3/Enriques exclusions on the covering components.
    Finally let an original component have Kodaira dimension one. Its actual generically finite
component cover has Kodaira dimension at least one by pluricanonical pullback, and at most
one by 7.6. Its elliptic fibration is therefore its connected-fibre Iitaka fibration. The cyclic
stabilizer acts on this fibration, since it acts on the pluricanonical field, and the proper quotient
and graph comparisons in 7.9–20 give the descended fibration on a smooth birational model of
the original component. Its base is the quotient of B, so has genus at most one. On a general
fibre, the subgroup fixing a general base point must act by translations: an origin-preserving
nontrivial linear part would give a rational general quotient fibre. Its normal line is trivial, so
adjunction restricts every positive pluricanonical line to OP1 (−2m); all pluricanonical sections
would then vanish on the dense family of these fibres, contrary to Kodaira dimension one. The
finite translation subgroup of the fixed elliptic curve is locally constant, because it consists of
points of bounded finite order. Thus the general quotient fibre is one fixed elliptic curve as well.
This proves isotriviality through the actual finite quotient, while leaving its exceptional and
singular fibres in place.
Proposition 7.16 (Nonnegative-Kodaira-dimension components have tightly specified cyclic
covers). Let f : U → ∆ be an unrestricted proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori
from a smooth threefold. Let Z be the smooth minimal model of the normalization of one central
component, with κ(Z) ≥ 0. There is an actual generically finite component cover E → S ν ,
obtained by the normalized root base change and resolution, with cyclic stabilizer G, such that
E/G is properly birational to S ν . Its smooth minimal model E0 satisfies one of these descriptions:

   • E0 is a complex two-torus;
   • E0 has an isotrivial elliptic fibration over a curve B with g(B) ≤ 1, identity integral H1
     monodromy, and only positive multiples of smooth elliptic fibres. In this case R1 q∗ OE0 = OB ,
     pg (E0 ) = g(B), and χ(OE0 ) = 0.

In both cases χ(OE0 ) = 0, and the action of G descends holomorphically to E0 .
    For the original minimal component the consequences are
                                 pg (Z) ≤ 1,     χ(OZ ) ∈ {0, 1, 2}.                       (C.CS.1)
Every component with κ(Z) = 1 has an actual isotrivial elliptic Iitaka fibration on Z, over a
curve of genus at most one. An Enriques component has an isotrivial elliptic fibration over P1 . A
K3 component is either the cyclic torus quotient of 9.10, with the exact orders and configurations
listed there, or has an isotrivial elliptic fibration over P1 through the non-torus-cover branch.
The singular and multiple fibres on these original quotient surfaces are retained by the quotient
maps; the smooth-multiple assertion concerns the specified cover E0 .

nontrivial linear part has a fixed point, and its quotient is rational by Riemann–Hurwitz. A
rational general fibre in (C.CS.4) would annihilate every positive pluricanonical section, contrary
to κ(Z) = 1. The translation points belong to the finite subgroup A[|K|], so they are locally
constant under the marked product identifications. Therefore the quotient general fibre is the
one fixed elliptic curve A/K. The quotient base has genus at most one by Riemann–Hurwitz
and g(B) ≤ 1.

On a minimal surface of Kodaira dimension one the canonical class is nef; this is the elliptic

    Now let Z be Enriques. Algebraic dimension is preserved by the actual generically finite
component map, by the symmetric-function field argument in (C.K3.2)–(C.K3.3). Thus E0 is
projective. If it has Kodaira dimension one, the preceding intrinsic Iitaka quotient argument
again gives an isotrivial elliptic fibration on a birational model of Z. If it has Kodaira dimension
zero, the surface classification and χ(OE0 ) = 0 make it Abelian or bielliptic. The Abelian case
is excluded by the exact cyclic quotient theorem 7.12. For the bielliptic case, use the actual
orbit fibration of its connected automorphism group. In its finite free product presentation
(A1 × A2 )/H, H acts by translations on A1 and has nontrivial linear action on A2 . The invariant
tangent fields are exactly the one-dimensional translation space of A1 . Thus the image of the
compact elliptic translation group A1 is the whole connected automorphism group, and its orbit
map is the explicit elliptic fibration to A2 /H ≃ P1 . Its fibres are smooth elliptic multiples; its
integral monodromy is the identity, since all actions on the fibre direction are translations. Every
automorphism normalizes the connected automorphism group, so preserves this orbit map and
acts on its connected-fibre base. It is therefore G-equivariant. The quotient (C.CS.4) is available
again. Its general fibre must be elliptic, since a rational general fibre would force the nonzero
even pluricanonical form of an Enriques surface to vanish.
    In either case, (C.CS.5) descends the elliptic map to the minimal Enriques surface: now KZ is
torsion, so its intersection term is zero. The Leray injection of H 1 of the base into H 1 (Z, OZ ) = 0
makes the base P1 . This proves the Enriques assertion through the actual quotient fibration.
    For a K3 target, the nonzero canonical form gives pg (E0 ) ≥ 1. If E0 is a torus, 7.12–24
give exactly the cyclic symplectic torus quotient already stated. Otherwise it has an elliptic
fibration of the specified fixed-modulus type. If κ(E0 ) = 1, use the equivariant Iitaka fibration.
If a(E0 ) = 1, use the intrinsic field identity M(E0 ) = q ∗ M(B) and the equivariant Stein factor
in (C.K3.4). The remaining projective Kodaira-dimension-zero case would be bielliptic, but has
pg = 0 and is excluded. Algebraic dimension zero has only the torus alternative by 7.7. Thus
these are all cases. Taking the quotient gives an isotrivial elliptic fibration, since its general fibre
cannot be rational on a K3 birational model. Formula (C.CS.5) with KZ = 0 descends it to Z,
and H 1 (Z, OZ ) = 0 again makes its base P1 .
    Finally 7.14 gives pg (Z) ≤ 1. The compact surface classification gives χ(OZ ) ≥ 0 when
κ(Z) ≥ 0: in Kodaira dimension zero its values are the explicit torus, bielliptic, Kodaira, K3 and
Enriques values; in Kodaira dimension one the relatively minimal elliptic surface has KZ2 = 0 and
nonnegative Euler number by Kodaira’s fibre list, so surface Riemann–Roch gives the inequality.
On the other hand
                                 χ(OZ ) = 1 − h1 (Z, OZ ) + pg (Z) ≤ 2.                       (C.CS.6)
It is an integer, giving (C.CS.1). The later exact quotient theorem 9.11 further identifies every
K3 component, in all algebraic dimensions, with the cyclic torus quotient family. The preceding
non-torus-cover comparison is retained as its explicit intermediate fibration map.
    All these comparisons retain the finite quotient’s singular fibres; they do not identify them
with the smooth fibres of its root cover.

    Let H be the kernel of G → Aut(B). On a general elliptic fibre it acts by translations.

a fixed subgroup of the constant elliptic curve, since points of bounded order are discrete. We

preserves the corresponding deck generator. Restriction to the central elliptic curve gives βτ = τ .
The finite-order endomorphism β 6= 1 satisfies 1 + β + · · · + β s−1 = 0. Applying it to τ yields
sτ = 0, so m | s.

surjective elliptic isogeny. Choose a lift of that point, and compose the lifted generator with a
deck transformation to make it fix the chosen lift. Its s-th power is a deck transformation fixing
a point of the central elliptic curve; the deck action there is free, so that power is the identity.
Therefore ρs = 1. Together with ρm having order s, this gives gcd(m, s) = 1. Since m | s, we
have
                                           m=1       (β 6= 1).                               (C.EQ.5)
This is the same explicit local comparison used in 9.11, and the argument did not use a canonical

    We finish by identifying the coherent invariants without adding any unproved occurrence
assertion. The singular values just listed are all the possible ones: a free base orbit is locally
unchanged, and the source had only smooth multiple fibres. A free cyclic action on an elliptic

whenever a + 1 6≡ 0 (mod n). Every Euler-twelve row of (C.EQ.11) has precisely that nontrivial
character. This argument uses pullback through the actual graph and Hartogs extension, and
does not infer extension of a form from numerical invariance alone.

or a properly elliptic component of coherent Euler characteristic one, the corresponding lower
bound is 6 + n.
     The existing monodromy theorem gives (U1 − I)2 = 0. In an oriented real basis of H1 (F, R),
all its possible Jordan forms give the following exact invariant forms:

       rank(U1 − I) nonzero values of U1 − I         dim ker(Λ2 U1 − I) (pU , qU , zU )

The two last rows record the two oriented real forms of that Jordan type. In particular rank-one

apply to arbitrary actual central fibres, with no normal-crossing, reducedness or Kähler hypothesis

Proof. The open set Zi◦ = Zi \ Di maps isomorphically to Si \ Sing S. It is therefore precisely
the part of this component where the reduced support is one smooth embedded surface. The
compact analytic set Di consists of curves and possibly isolated points. Its degree-two integral
cohomology is free, with one generator for each curve component. Indeed normalization of a
compact reduced curve changes only the identifications at finitely many points, which do not
change its degree-two cohomology; isolated points have none.

     Transfer an integral compact cycle by taking the sum of all its lifts under (C.CL.9), subdividing

     Transport the selected transferred basis cycles and extend by integer linearity. This defines

The axis Cα is C∗ /αZ , and its actual normal line is the quotient of C∗ × C by (z, v) 7→ (αz, βv).
If a positive tensor power n of this line is trivial, a nowhere-zero holomorphic function a on

αj = β n . Since |α| < 1, there is at most one such exponent, and there must be one. Its exponent
is positive because |β| < 1 and n > 0. Conversely that equality gives the explicit trivialization
a(z) = z j . It also gives the nonconstant invariant meromorphic function wn /z j on the Hopf
surface. Algebraic dimension zero therefore makes the normal of each axis non-torsion. Formula
(C.HB.1) excludes an entire such axis from the regular part of the reduced support.

    Finally let ν : H → S be the given smooth minimal Hopf normalization. Its conductor and
the inverse images of the other central components have curve support. Outside this support ν is
the actual isomorphism onto the regular locus of the reduced fibre. For clarity, there is no extra
isolated normalization defect: a hypersurface is Cohen–Macaulay, so its nonnormal locus is the
conductor curve locus; where it is normal, the normalization is an isomorphism, and smoothness
of H then gives smoothness there. An intersection with another central component is a Cartier
curve divisor and its finite pullback also has curve support.
    We also verify the curve assertion used in applying the obstruction. The inverse image of
a compact curve in the covering punctured plane extends analytically across the origin by the
removable-set theorem for analytic sets, since its dimension is one and the added set has dimension
zero. Its germ has a reduced equation a satisfying a ◦ F = va for a holomorphic unit v. After
shrinkingQto a contracting ball, the product solving the unit cocycle converges: if u = v/v(0),
then b = j≥0 u ◦ F j is a holomorphic unit and b ◦ F = b/u. Thus h = ba satisfies h ◦ F = v(0)h.
For the diagonal contraction, two distinct nonzero monomials in h would give αi β j = 1 for a
nonzero integer pair; because both moduli are less than one, this is a positive-power relation
between α and β and gives a nonconstant meromorphic invariant. In algebraic dimension zero
there is therefore just one monomial, so the curve consists of axes. For (C.HB.5), decompose
the convergent power series into weighted degrees with weights r, 1 on z, w. The contraction
preserves each finite-dimensional weighted piece and acts there with sole eigenvalue β d in degree
d. Their distinct moduli force an eigenfunction into one degree. Write it as wd P (z/wr ); after
taking out β d , invariance requires the polynomial P to be periodic under translation by β −r . It
is constant. Thus only the axis w = 0 occurs. Analytic continuation along the contraction orbits
gives this assertion on the entire punctured plane. Hence the only curves are the two disjoint axes
in (C.HB.4), or the single axis in (C.HB.5). Therefore an axis not contained in that boundary
is disjoint from it. The preceding neighborhood contradictions apply and force every axis into
the boundary. For a secondary Hopf surface, pull back the neighborhood and its canonical
trivialization along its finite unramified primary covering. The covering has the same algebraic
dimension: meromorphic functions descend through their elementary symmetric polynomials. A
curve outside the boundary would lift to an axis outside the pulled-back boundary, contradicting
the already proved primary calculation. This proves the stated descent and the theorem.

8    Irreducible and reducible torus-fibre Euler criteria
Proposition 8.1 (Every normal irreducible support is a smooth torus quotient). Let f : Y → B
be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a smooth curve, with connected
fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre whose reduced support
is irreducible and normal. Then S is smooth and e(S) = 0. More precisely, the normalized base
change t = sm gives a connected two-torus A and a finite unramified cyclic map
                                             A −→ S
of degree m. Thus S is a two-torus or a bielliptic surface. In the bielliptic case the order n of
KS is 2, 3, 4, or 6, and n | m; in particular a reduced normal fibre is a torus.

                                                150
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


   Every two-torus occurs with every positive multiplicity. Every bielliptic surface of canonical
order n occurs with every multiplicity divisible by n. These realizations can be made in smooth
compact threefolds over P1 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.17; (Buchdahl, 1999,
Theorem 11); (Catanese, 2002, Theorem 4.6); (Catanese, 2002, Definition 3.1 and
Theorems 3.2–3.3); equation (C.UNN.2).

Proof. A normal surface hypersurface has only isolated singularities. At a singular point of S,
write the actual map as t = uhm , with u a holomorphic unit and h a reduced local equation of S.
A local mth root of u gives t = (u1/m h)m . The isolated-hypersurface assertion of 6.17 supplies
an embedded vanishing two-sphere of self-intersection −2 in a small nonzero Milnor fibre of
u1/m h. This fibre is an open part of the actual nearby torus fibre of f . A sphere in a torus is
nullhomotopic, and hence has zero homology class and zero self-intersection. The contradiction
proves that S is smooth. This argument uses no Betti-number or Kähler hypothesis on the
ambient threefold.
    Shrink the base to a disc with coordinate t. Near any point of S write t = uz m with z a
smooth equation of S. The normalization U 0 of the base change t = sm is given locally by the
explicit maps
                             wm = u,      s = wz,      p : U 0 −→ U.                  (C.UNN.1)
Since u never vanishes, p is finite and unramified of degree m; these local normalizations glue
to the normalization of the actual fibre product. The map h : U 0 → ∆s has ds = w dz along its
central support, so that support is smooth and reduced. For each s 6= 0, the map p identifies
h−1 (s) with f −1 (sm ), a connected torus. The Stein factor of h has generic degree one over the
normal disc and is therefore the disc. In particular U 0 and its central fibre A are connected.
After shrinking the disc, h is a proper submersion. The deck action is w 7→ ζm w, so it is free also
on A, and its quotient there is exactly S.
     We verify that A is a torus through its actual Albanese map. Ehresmann’s theorem identifies
its integral cohomology ring with that of a real four-torus. Thus b1 (A) = 4, and (Buchdahl, 1999,
Theorem 11) makes A Kähler. The period-integral map a : A → Alb(A) is consequently defined
by its two independent closed holomorphic one-forms and induces an isomorphism on integral H 1 .
Both surfaces have the exterior algebra on this lattice as their integral cohomology ring. The
pullback of a top-degree generator is therefore a generator, so a has degree one; holomorphicity
fixes the positive sign. Its pullback on H 2 is also an isomorphism. A curve contracted by a would
pair to zero with every pullback class and hence with a Kähler class on A, contradicting positive
area. Thus a is finite of degree one and is an isomorphism. This proves the torus identification,
without imposing a metric on U 0 . It also agrees with the deformation theorem (Catanese, 2002,
Theorem 4.6).
     Write a generator of the deck group on A = C2 /Λ as g(z) = Lz + b. Every holomorphic torus
automorphism has this affine form: the derivative of a lift is periodic and hence constant on the
compact quotient. The matrix L preserves Λ and has finite order. If 1 were not an eigenvalue of
L, the equation (I − L)z = b in C2 would give a fixed point of g, contrary to the free deck action.
If L = I, the deck group acts by translations and S is the torus quotient by the resulting finite
subgroup.
     Otherwise the eigenvalues on C2 are 1 and a nontrivial root of unity ζ. The corresponding
integral real representation has characteristic polynomial (x − 1)2 (x − ζ)(x − ζ̄), so the order
n of ζ is 2, 3, 4, or 6. The images of I − L and of I + L + · · · + Ln−1 are elliptic subtori with
complementary tangent lines. Their addition map is an isogeny from a product of elliptic curves
to A. The kernel of the deck group’s linear representation consists of translations. Quotienting
by it first gives a torus A1 with a free cyclic action of order n and quotient S. On the canonical
form this action has character ζ, so KS has exact order n, while the invariant holomorphic

                                               151
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


one-form space has dimension one. Equivalently, lifting to the product isogeny and removing the
pure translation kernels gives the bielliptic presentation (E × F )/G, with G acting faithfully by
translations on E and with F /G ≃ P1 . These are precisely the bielliptic surfaces of (Catanese,
2002, Definition 3.1 and Theorems 3.2–3.3). The linear order divides the deck order m. In both
cases the unramified cover gives m e(S) = e(A) = 0.
   We finish with realizations and their multiplicities. Given any free cyclic torus quotient
A → S = A/hgi of degree m, set

               Y = (A × P1 )/h(a, z) 7→ (g(a), ζm z)i,          f ([a, z]) = z m .      (C.UNN.2)

The action is free, hence Y is smooth and compact. For t 6= 0, ∞ its m slices are permuted
transitively, and the quotient fibre is exactly A. The full fibres at 0 and ∞ are mS. Thus these
are actual compact realizations of the displayed support and multiplicity. For a prescribed torus
S, an index-m sublattice with cyclic quotient gives the required cyclic isogeny A → S for every
m ≥ 1.
    For a prescribed bielliptic surface, use its product presentation (E × F )/G. The linear
character G → µn is surjective, and its kernel acts by translations on both factors. Consequently
its canonical cyclic cover is a torus. Moreover the character factors through π1 (E/G) ≃ Z2 ,
because G acts on E by translations. A surjective character Z2 → Z/n lifts to a primitive integral
homomorphism Z2 → Z: choose integer lifts of its two coefficients, and change one by a multiple
of n to make their gcd one. The possible prime divisors of the other coefficient are avoided by
the Chinese remainder theorem; primes dividing n already cannot divide both coefficients. Pull
this homomorphism back along the connected elliptic fibration S → E/G and reduce it modulo
m = kn. Its kernel defines a connected cyclic unramified cover of degree m that factors through
the canonical torus cover. A connected finite unramified cover of a torus is the quotient of C2 by
a finite-index sublattice, so this new cover is again a torus. Applying (C.UNN.2) proves every
claimed bielliptic multiplicity.

    The statements 8.2–8.7 below retain the proved local and global reductions. The later 8.26
proves that the contracted irrational configuration has e(S) ≥ 2 and π1 (S) = 1. Together with
the CDP transgression, or the zero Euler conclusion 8.33, this excludes the configuration entirely
under the CDP hypotheses. The unrestricted genus assertion is separately proved in 8.9.

Proposition 8.3 (The ruling genus is at most two). In the situation of 8.2, the ruling genus is

zero-dimensional quotient of this ring. Purity hence forces the full conductor ideal to be exactly

Proposition 8.4 (The genus-two node alternative is excluded). In the genus-two situation of
8.3, the component of Γ through q = h(C) cannot have generic transversal an ordinary node.
Consequently the remaining genus-two alternative has an ordinary cusp at its generic point, and
exactly one strict conductor curve of coefficient two and degree one lies above that component.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.3.

Proof. We first record an additional consequence of the specified boundary blowups in C.2.CR.1:
every coefficient-one component of Dred is a leaf. This holds on the initial section-and-fibres
star. A smooth boundary blowup creates coefficient one only when the old coefficient is two, and
creates it as a leaf. A node blowup could create coefficient one only from an edge (1, 1), which
(C.CR.2) excludes. Subsequent blowups preserve the valence one of an existing coefficient-one
vertex: at its unique boundary node they merely subdivide that edge, and at a smooth point its
new exceptional coefficient is zero.
    Let E0 be the connected exceptional fibre containing C. In the boundary tree, the first
nonexceptional vertex on every path from C meets E0 , so its image passes through p. Its further
image is therefore a component of Γ through q. By 8.3 there is only one such component, denoted
G.
    Suppose its generic transversal were a node. Every strict conductor curve above G then has
coefficient one. Thus each first nonexceptional vertex just found is a leaf. Every strict conductor
curve is consequently such a leaf, attached at a single point to E0 . No additional exceptional
tail can meet it, since that would raise its boundary valence. The reduced conductor on T is
therefore a union of rational curves whose only possible multibranch point is p; every component
passes through p, is smooth away from p, and has only one branch at p.
    All their images pass through q, where Γ is smooth, so the conductor image has just the
one global component G. It also has no multibranch point elsewhere. Indeed, at x 6= q each
point of the normalization over x receives just one local branch of G. If G had two distinct
local branches there, their receiving normalization points would be distinct. The corresponding
irreducible hypersurface branches of S must intersect in a curve, because their distinct local
equations generate a height-two ideal in the regular local ring of the threefold. That intersection
curve is a conductor-image branch received by both normalization points, contradicting their
different singleton branch sets.
    The normalization of G is rational and all its germs are unibranch. The normalization map is
a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space and hence a homeomorphism.
Thus π1 (G) = 1, contradicting (C.CR.1). The generic cusp alternative is the only one left. Its
transverse normalization is unibranch with conductor exponent two, so it contributes exactly
one strict coefficient-two curve, of degree one over G.

Proof. Choose coordinates (x, y, z) with critical curve {x = y = 0}. The rank-one quadratic

                                            a(z)x2 .

homogeneous of degree three, so scaling all three coordinates by a holomorphic cube root of the

nonzero levels have uniformly transverse boundary. The full-critical- locus hypothesis ensures
that no other boundary singular curve has been omitted from this argument.

spherical cycle from (C.CR.18) can therefore be transported through regular target values to a

whose pullback has no exceptional pole. On the first plane blowup, with exceptional curve E, the

The coefficient of this pulled-back form along E is ord0 (a) + 1 − m. Hence
           m−1
     cD ⊂ mD       in the sense that every ambient representative has order at least m − 1.
                                                                                        (C.CR.22)
Adding a multiple of fD does not change this order bound, since fD has order m.
    At a general smooth point of any conductor component through q, the ambient coordinate
x remains in its conductor ideal and has a nonzero transverse linear part: its zero set is a
smooth ambient plane containing the conductor curve. Applying (C.CR.22) to a transverse plane
slice gives m ≤ 2. The slice is singular, so m = 2. Weierstrass preparation, completion of the
square, and absorption of a unit then put a reduced multiplicity-two plane curve in the form
u2 − v k+1 = 0.
    For k = 2s − 1, the two branches are u = ±v s ; their intersection multiplicity is s, and the
conductor on each normalized branch is (v s ). For k = 2s, the normalization is v = t2 , u = t2s+1 ,
whose semigroup has conductor 2s, giving (t2s ). These calculations specify both the coefficients
and the numbers of transverse branches; finite normalization over the global image component
expresses those numbers as the asserted sums of covering degrees.

Proposition 8.8 (A smooth full critical curve with generic node is a product node). Let a
reduced hypersurface germ {f = 0} in a smooth complex threefold occur in a fibre of a proper
torus-surface degeneration. Suppose that the full reduced critical locus of f is a smooth curve and
its generic transverse singularity is an ordinary node. There are local holomorphic coordinates in
which
                                              f = XY.                               (C.UNNODE.1)
The conclusion about the reduced hypersurface also holds when the actual map has a holomorphic
unit and a common positive multiplicity.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.UNNODE.2);
proposition 6.16; equation (C.UNNODE.3).

Proof. Choose coordinates (x, y, z) with critical curve Γ = {x = y = 0}. Since f vanishes on Γ
and its first derivatives vanish there, its transverse quadratic term is

                                          (x, y)Q(z)(x, y)t ,

where Q is a holomorphic symmetric 2 × 2 matrix. Its determinant is not identically zero. Shrink
the curve disc so that det Q(z) 6= 0 for z 6= 0. If Q(0) is invertible, the holomorphic Morse lemma
with parameter z gives f = X 2 + Y 2 , and a linear change gives (C.UNNODE.1).
    Suppose instead that Q(0) is singular. We construct arbitrarily small constant symmetric
matrices E for which Q(z) + E has a rank-one value at a simple zero of its determinant near the
origin. Choose z0 → 0 with Q0 (z0 ) 6= 0; such points exist because the nonconstant determinant
makes Q nonconstant. Choose a rank-one symmetric matrix R close to Q(0) with

                                      tr(adj(R)Q0 (z0 )) 6= 0.

This choice is possible also when Q(0) = 0: for a rank-one symmetric matrix with kernel spanned
by v, its adjugate is a nonzero scalar multiple of vv t , and the polynomial v t Q0 (z0 )v is not
identically zero. Thus the forbidden kernels form a proper finite set in the projective line, and
the rank-one matrix can be chosen as close to Q(0) as desired. Set E = R − Q(z0 ). Then E → 0,
and
                                        d
               det(Q(z0 ) + E) = 0,        det(Q(z) + E)        6= 0.           (C.UNNODE.2)
                                        dz                 z=z0

   Consider the actual perturbation fE = f + (x, y)E(x, y)t at (0, 0, z0 ). The rank-one Morse
lemma, retaining (y, z) as parameters after a linear normal-coordinate change, writes

                                      fE = X 2 + y 2 h(y, z).

The factor y 2 follows from fE (0, 0, z) = 0 and the vanishing of its normal first derivative along
the same curve. Equation (C.UNNODE.2) says exactly that h(0, z0 ) = 0 and ∂h/∂z(0, z0 ) 6= 0,
up to a nowhere-zero coefficient from the nondegenerate quadratic direction. Hence the actual
coordinate substitution Z = h(y, z) gives

                                          fE = X 2 + y 2 Z.                       (C.UNNODE.3)

The explicit construction in 6.16 gives a compact spherical class in a small nonzero level of
(C.UNNODE.3). Its square is −2(2/ gcd(2, 1))(1/ gcd(2, 1)) = −4. The construction supplies a
continuous map from S 2 representing this class; embeddedness is not required.
    Here is the precise transport into an original fibre. Choose a small closed ball whose boundary
is transverse to Γ and to the smooth stratum of f = 0. Along the compact boundary link of Γ,
the matrix Q is invertible. For all sufficiently small E, the parameter Morse lemma therefore

                                                 160
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


gives product-node charts there, retaining the curve coordinate. In these charts ∂/∂z is tangent
to every level of fE . A real radial curve-direction vector is transverse to the fixed boundary at
the critical link and remains transverse on its neighbourhood, uniformly for small E. On the
remaining compact boundary, ordinary transversality gives the same uniform conclusion for small
target values. The full-critical-locus hypothesis ensures that these charts cover every boundary
singular point requiring this argument.
     For a fixed small E, transport the spherical class from (C.UNNODE.3) through regular target
values to a fixed small value t1 , avoiding the finitely many nonzero critical values in the ball.
Choose E small enough that every critical value along the segment from E to 0 has modulus less
than |t1 |/2. This follows by compactness: a limit of critical points is a critical point of f with
value zero; the just-proved boundary charts rule out loss of transversality at the boundary. The
t1 -levels along that segment form a proper submersion with boundary. Ehresmann transport
therefore maps the actual spherical class to a class of square −4 in the original f = t1 level. Its
inclusion into the nearby torus preserves the square, since both the compact representative and
its intersection push-off lie in that open level. But this inclusion also maps its representing S 2 to
an aspherical torus, where it is nullhomotopic and has zero homology class. This contradiction
proves det Q(0) 6= 0.
     If the original map is uf m , replace the reduced equation by u1/m f using a local holomorphic
root of the unit. Its critical-set germ is still Γ: every critical component through the point has
constant value zero, and the singular locus of the reduced zero hypersurface is unchanged. The
argument then places the same class in the actual nearby level with base parameter tm        1 . This
proves the last assertion.

Proposition 8.9 (A contracted irrational horizontal section is elliptic without ambient Betti
assumptions). Let f : Y → B be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to
a smooth curve, with connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS
be an irreducible nonnormal full fibre. Write h = ηπ : Z → T → S for the normalization and
its minimal resolution. Suppose that Z is ruled over a curve of positive genus, that its effective
adjunction divisor is D = 2C + V , with C a section and V vertical, and that π contracts C.
Then the ruling base has genus one.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.2; proposition 8.3;
proposition 8.8; proposition 8.5.

Proof. We first supply the comparisons that previously came from the global Betti assumptions.
On a small full fibre tube U , the rank-one torsion-free sheaf f∗ KU is a line bundle. A generator
has no horizontal zeros, since its restriction to a smooth torus is a nonzero canonical form. Its
zero divisor is consequently kS for some k ≥ 0, after shrinking away other special fibres. Thus
the evaluation map gives the actual isomorphism

                            KU ≃ OU (kS),        ωS ≃ OU ((k + 1)S)|S .                 (C.UNCR.1)

The divisor mS is principal, so both these line bundles are torsion. The map to the smooth curve
is flat, and the holomorphic Euler characteristic of its full fibres is constant. The filtration of
OmS has quotients OS (−jS) for 0 ≤ j < m; each is a torsion line-bundle twist of OS . Analytic
Riemann–Roch gives the same Euler characteristic for these twists, since their rational Chern
characters are one. It follows that

                                     0 = χ(OmS ) = m χ(OS ).                            (C.UNCR.2)

The exact normalization and resolution duality maps therefore give KZ + D = h∗ ωS , with the
same effective divisor and torsion right-hand side as in 8.2–8.3.


                                                161
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


   Here are the parts of that argument needed here, with no transgression-class assumption.
Finite duality embeds ωT into the torsion line η ∗ ωS , with its sections vanishing on the nonempty
conductor. A nonzero section of a torsion line on a connected compact normal space is nowhere
zero: taking a trivializing power makes it a nonzero constant. Consequently H 2 (T, OT ) = 0.
The coherent Leray sequence then bounds length R1 π∗ OZ by h1 (Z, OZ ) = g, whereas formal
functions and restriction to the contracted section C give length at least h1 (C, OC ) = g at its
image point p. Thus equality holds at p and there are no further contributions.
   At q = η(p), fix a local generator of ωS . Finite duality identifies the branch conductor ideal
Ip with ωT,p , embedded as an actual ideal summand in OS,q . Proper duality and the residue
sequence of C give exactly
                   Ip = (π∗ ωZ (C))p ,    Ip /(π∗ ωZ )p ≃ H 0 (C, ωC ).                 (C.UNCR.3)
The equality of lengths follows from the preceding formal-functions computation. In the fixed
local dualizing trivialization these sheaves are OZ (−C − V ) and OZ (−2C − V ). The maximal
ideal of OS,q vanishes on C; its square supplies an additional order along C without losing
any prescribed order along V . Hence Ip ∩ m2q ⊂ (π∗ ωZ )p . The embedding dimension three and
Nakayama argument of 8.3 now give g ≤ 2. When g = 2 they give the actual conductor ideal
(x, y), a unique normalization point p above q, and generic transverse delta invariant one. Thus
the full conductor-image curve is smooth and reduced at q, and the generic transversal is a node
or a cusp.
     Every positive-dimensional critical component of the reduced surface is part of that conductor
curve; after shrinking, its full reduced critical locus is exactly the smooth curve just obtained.
The node case is a product node by 8.8. Its normalization has two smooth points above q,
contradicting the unique point p. The cusp case is a product cusp by 8.5. Its explicit normalization
(u, z) 7→ (X, Y, z) = (u3 , −u2 , z), after adjusting the harmless sign in X 2 + Y 3 , is smooth. This
contradicts a minimal normalization resolution contracting a positive-genus curve to p. Both
genus-two possibilities are excluded, and g = 1 follows.

Proposition 8.10 (The reduced horizontal case is a minimal elliptic ruled double-curve fibre).
Let f : Y → C0 be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold with
H 2 (Y, Q) = 0, with connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a
full fibre with irreducible nonnormal reduced support. Let h = ηπ : Z → T → S be the minimal
resolution of its normalization, and suppose that p : Z → B is an irrational ruling. Write the
effective divisor of 6.3 as DZ = H + V , where V is vertical and the horizontal part H is reduced,
of total degree two over B.
     Then B is elliptic, T = Z is a smooth minimal ruled surface over B, and DZ = H is a
disjoint union of smooth elliptic curves. The reduced conductor image is a disjoint union of
smooth elliptic curves. Its inverse image H maps onto it by a finite etale covering of total degree
two over each component. The support S has only ordinary double-curve normal crossings and
                                              e(S) = 0.                                     (C.IR.1)
No assumption on the initial normalization singularities or on the ambient Picard pullback is
made.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.3; equation (C.IR.3);
equation (C.IR.2); equation (C.IR.4); equation (C.IR.5); proposition 6.17; proposition 13.6;
proposition 6.13; equation (C.IR.6); proposition 6.16; proposition 6.10; proposition A.4.

Proof. All divisor intersections in this proof use rational Chern classes. The actual canonical
comparison in 6.3 gives
                             KZ + DZ = h∗ ωS ,         c1 (KZ + DZ ) = 0.                   (C.IR.2)

                                                 162
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


For an irreducible component Hi of the reduced horizontal part, adjunction therefore gives

                                2pa (Hi ) − 2 + (DZ − Hi ) · Hi = 0.                       (C.IR.3)

The second term is nonnegative. The normalization of Hi maps finitely onto the positive-genus
curve B; Riemann–Hurwitz makes its genus at least one. Equality in (C.IR.3) thus makes Hi a
smooth elliptic curve, makes B elliptic, and makes all horizontal components disjoint from each
other and from V .
   We give the required comparison under the ruling blowdowns. For one σ : W → W 0 with
exceptional curve E, put D0 = σ∗ DW , let a be the coefficient of E in DW , and let d be the
multiplicity of D0 at the centre. The exact divisor identity is

                           KW + DW = σ ∗ (KW 0 + D0 ) + (1 + a − d)E.                      (C.IR.4)

Intersection with E gives a = d − 1, so (C.IR.2) descends. An exceptional curve in the vertical
conductor is disjoint from H. An exceptional curve outside the conductor has DW · E = 1, and
therefore meets the horizontal part in at most one simple point; it cannot identify two horizontal
points or join a horizontal component to the vertical conductor. Thus the horizontal curves stay
smooth, disjoint, and disjoint from the remaining vertical conductor after each blowdown. On
the resulting minimal ruled bundle every nonzero effective vertical divisor meets the horizontal
part. Its vertical conductor is consequently zero.
    In the reverse blowup sequence a centre away from the current horizontal divisor would
have d = 0 in (C.IR.4) and create coefficient −1 on the new exceptional curve. That coefficient
persists on its strict transform under later blowups, contrary to effectiveness of the original DZ .
Every centre therefore lies on the smooth coefficient-one horizontal divisor and creates coefficient
zero. Induction gives
                                             DZ = H.                                       (C.IR.5)
This argument did not require the map h to factor through any ruling blowdown.
    We next prove that π has no exceptional curves, including horizontal ones. An exceptional
curve E of coefficient zero in (C.IR.5) satisfies KZ · E ≥ 0 on the minimal resolution: adjunction
and negative self-intersection give this inequality, the sole contrary possibility being a smooth
rational (−1)-curve, which minimality excludes. Equation (C.IR.2) then forces KZ ·E = H ·E = 0.
Such a curve is disjoint from H. A positive-coefficient exceptional curve is one of the mutually
disjoint elliptic curves Hi . Every connected exceptional fibre is therefore disjoint from the strict
conductor curves.
    The normal conductor ideal on T is the rank-one reflexive sheaf ωT ⊗ η ∗ ωS−1 , embedded in
OT by finite duality. On an open set without its conductor divisors it equals OT : equality off
a codimension-two set extends by reflexivity on a normal surface. Thus η is an isomorphism
near the image of every exceptional fibre just described. Such an image is an isolated normal
hypersurface singularity of S. The isolated-singularity clause of 6.17 excludes it from this actual
torus smoothing, including its full multiplicity m and its local unit. Hence π is an isomorphism.
In particular T = Z is smooth and its conductor is exactly the reduced divisor H.
    Let G be the conductor image. Its ideal is the contraction of the radical ideal of H under
the finite normalization, so it is radical. Thus G itself is reduced. Every local point of H
has a single smooth branch, whose image is one local branch of G. We claim that G has only
unibranch germs and that its distinct global components are disjoint. Otherwise choose two
local branches of G at a common point and points of T receiving the respective branches. These
points are different because H is smooth at each point. They correspond to different irreducible
hypersurface branches of S in the smooth threefold. Two such branches meet in a curve: their
distinct equations generate an ideal of height two in the regular three-dimensional local ring.
That intersection is a conductor-image branch received by both points of T . Each of those points
receives only one branch, contradicting the chosen distinct images. This proves the claim.

    The generic transverse curve has conductor exponent one on every normalized branch. The
branchwise conductor formula in the proof of 13.6 shows that it has exactly two smooth transverse

finite map H → G has total degree two over every irreducible component.
    Fix such a component Gj , with normalization ν : Ej → Gj . Each component of its inverse
image is elliptic. Riemann–Hurwitz gives g(Ej ) ≤ 1. We exclude Ej = P1 by an actual local

therefore at most two normalization points above its singular locus. At least one of the four
branch points lies over a smooth point of Gj .

        {a ∈ C{u, v} : a(0, v) ∈ C{v 2 }} = C{u, uv, v 2 } ≃ C{x, y, z}/(x2 − y 2 z).      (C.IR.6)
Here (x, y, z) = (uv, u, v 2 ), so every map in the comparison is specified. The pinch germ in

is a local complete intersection. On Ej let N be the dual of its pulled-back conormal bundle,

                          det N = KEj (Ξ) ⊗ ν ∗ KY−1 ,      deg N = 2δj .                  (C.IR.7)
The reduced equation of S belongs to the ordinary square of the ideal of Gj : the ideal is a regular

jet is therefore a holomorphic section of Sym2 N ∗ ⊗ M , where M = ν ∗ OY (S) has degree zero.

                                 deg (det N )−2 ⊗ M 2 = −4δj .                             (C.IR.8)

Thus δj = 0. The curve Gj is smooth elliptic and the determinant, now a degree-zero holomorphic
section, is nowhere zero. The holomorphic Morse lemma with the curve parameter gives the local

    There are no triple points, because H is smooth and its components are disjoint. Apply the

                                0 = e(Yt ) = m e(T \ H) = m e(T ),                         (C.IR.9)
because e(H) = 0. If N0 is the number of ruling blowups above a minimal bundle over the elliptic
