normalization is an isomorphism off H and G, so e(S) = e(T ) − e(H) + e(G) = 0. This proves
every assertion, with arbitrary full-fibre multiplicity retained.

    The elliptic ruled geometry in 8.10 has a direct literature comparison. Kamenova’s Theorem
3.1 in Kamenova (nd) treats semistable Kahler degenerations with trivial total-space canonical
bundle; its elliptic ruled cases have elliptic double curves arranged along a path or a cycle. Our
finite normalization T → S specifies the self-identification of the double curves in the irreducible
case. The proof above establishes this geometry from the actual conductor and the full-fibre
smoothing, retaining the multiplicity and proving the necessary local pinch exclusion. We have
not supplied a Kahler form or a trivialization of the total-space canonical bundle needed to apply
that theorem directly to our tube.

Proposition 8.11 (Proved anticanonical support comparison). Let Z be a smooth compact
surface of class VII, not necessarily minimal, and let D > 0 be an effective integral divisor
such that KZ + D is torsion in Pic(Z). Write R = Dred , and let r(R) be its number of rational
irreducible components. Then

                                 e(R) = r(R),         r(Z) ≤ b2 (Z),                      (C.VII.1)

where r(Z) counts all rational curves of Z. Every connected component of R has arithmetic
genus one. In particular a connected component containing an elliptic curve consists of that
single elliptic curve with trees of rational curves attached; it cannot contain a second elliptic
curve or a path joining two distinct points of the first one.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Dloussky, 2006, Theorem 0.2,
Proposition 2.29 and Theorem 2.38); (Dloussky et al., 2003, §1, pp. 284–285, and §3, p. 296);
(Dloussky, 2006, Corollary 2.25 and Proposition 2.27); (Dloussky et al., 2003, Introduction,
p. 283); (Dloussky, 2006, Lemma 2.22 and the following paragraph; Proposition 2.27);
proposition 4.5.

Proof. We specify the established surface results used in this comparison. For a minimal class
VII surface with positive second Betti number, existence of a numerically anticanonical divisor
implies existence of a global spherical shell by (Dloussky, 2006, Theorem 0.2, Proposition 2.29
and Theorem 2.38). The reduced support is one rational cycle with attached trees, one or two
rational cycles, or, in the parabolic Inoue case, a disjoint rational cycle and a smooth elliptic
curve. The intermediate graph and its actual curve configuration are described in (Dloussky et al.,
2003, §1, pp. 284–285, and §3, p. 296). The fact that no connected piece of the anticanonical
support is an isolated tree is (Dloussky, 2006, Corollary 2.25 and Proposition 2.27); Lemma 2.22
there shows that a curve meeting that support belongs to it. These statements apply to our
divisor with index one, since its twisting line is torsion and therefore flat. They give, on the
minimal model, arithmetic genus one for each connected component and Euler number equal
to the number of its rational components. The rational curve count is at most b2 , as stated
and used in (Dloussky et al., 2003, Introduction, p. 283). These are consequences of the proved
theorem about anticanonical divisors; no classification assertion about class VII surfaces without
such a divisor is used.
    There is a coefficient issue in the parabolic Inoue case which the torsion hypothesis resolves
explicitly. Write E for its elliptic curve and C for its reduced rational cycle. The exact canonical
relation is KZ0 + E + C = 0; the curves E and C are disjoint, E 2 = −b2 (Z0 ), and the intersection
matrix of the components of C has kernel generated by their sum (Dloussky, 2006, Lemma 2.22
and the following paragraph; Proposition 2.27). Consequently an effective integral divisor with
c1 (KZ0 + D0 )R = 0 has the form D0 = E + kC, k ≥ 0: intersection with E fixes its coefficient at
one, and the cycle intersection matrix makes all cycle coefficients equal. Our stronger torsion
relation thenR gives KZ0 + D0 = (k − 1)C torsion. For any Gauduchon metric ω, the degree
of O(C) is C ω > 0, whereas a torsion line has degree zero. Hence k = 1. In particular both
connected pieces of the stated reduced support really occur. This deduction uses the torsion
relation, not merely the vanishing of its real first Chern class.
    For a minimal model with b2 = 0, the nonzero effective divisor excludes the curve-free Inoue
surfaces. The Hopf alternative has only smooth elliptic curves, which are pairwise disjoint. This
follows as well from the explicit contraction description used in 4.5 and its finite unramified
quotient: the preimages of two distinct curves are disjoint elliptic curves, and the quotient is
locally biholomorphic. All assertions are then immediate on that model.
    We verify the transfer through the actual blowdowns. Let σ : Z → Z0 be a sequence of point
blowups from a minimal model. A torsion line is represented by a finite unitary character of
the fundamental group, and a point blowup induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups.

                                                165
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                          Paper II


Thus the torsion line KZ + D descends to Z0 . Pushing forward a meromorphic canonical section
with pole divisor D, or its torsion-trivializing power, gives an effective divisor D0 with KZ0 + D0
torsion. It is nonzero, since a torsion canonical bundle would give Kodaira dimension zero. At
each individual blowup the canonical divisor formula and the pushforward section give the exact
divisor equality
                                        Dnew = σ ∗ Dold − E.                               (C.VII.2)
The coefficient of E is multp Dold − 1. Effectivity forces the centre to lie on Dold . If this coefficient
is positive, the reduced support is its entire reduced inverse image: a smooth point acquires a
rational leaf, or an ordinary intersection is subdivided by the exceptional curve. These operations
preserve arithmetic genus and increase both the Euler number and the rational-component count
by one. If the coefficient is zero, the centre is a smooth point of a multiplicity-one component
and the new support is its strict transform, isomorphic to the old support. Thus all the stated
support properties transfer in the required direction. Finally each blowup increases b2 by one and
adds precisely its exceptional rational curve; every other rational curve is the strict transform of
one on the preceding surface. The curve-count inequality in (C.VII.1) follows.

Proposition 8.12 (Proved global conductor Euler bound). Let S be a compact irreducible
reduced hypersurface in a smooth complex threefold, with ωS torsion and χ(S, OS ) = 0. Let
η : T → S be normalization, let Γ be its conductor image scheme, and put C = Γred . Then
                                            χ(C, OC ) ≥ −1.                                    (C.VII.3)
Suppose in addition that the minimal resolution π : Z → T is a class VII surface. Then
                                               e(C) ≥ 0.                                       (C.VII.4)
The conductor scheme may be nonreduced and its generic transverse exponent is unrestricted.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.8; proposition 6.3;
proposition 8.11; equation (C.VII.5); equation (C.VII.6).

Proof. If the conductor is empty, both conclusions are immediate. We therefore assume that
it is nonempty. Put L = ωS and ε = h0 (S, L) ∈ {0, 1}. A nonzero section of a torsion line on
a compact connected reduced space trivializes it, by taking a torsion-trivializing power. Serre

constant holomorphic functions. The actual conductor duality of 6.8 is
                                           Q = ωΓ ⊗ L−1 |Γ .

h1 (C, L|C ) ≥ −1. If ε = 1, then L = OS and h0 (C, OC ) ≥ 1, while h1 (C, OC ) ≤ 2. This proves
(C.VII.3), including all nilpotents of the original conductor scheme in the comparison.
    Now assume that Z is class VII. 6.3 gives a nonzero effective integral divisor D with

                   X               X                  X               X

of C. Otherwise partition the irreducible local branches of the hypersurface germ S according
to the one conductor branch their normalization receives. Both parts are nonempty. Two
hypersurface branches from opposite parts intersect in a curve: in the regular three-dimensional
local ambient ring, the ideal of their two distinct equations has height two. That intersection
curve is contained in the conductor image and therefore is one of its two branches. Both surface
branches must receive it, contrary to the partition. With only one local surface branch the
assertion is immediate.
    Every π-exceptional curve not contained in Dred is disjoint from it. To see this, write E for
such a curve. Minimality of the resolution and adjunction give KZ · E ≥ 0, while D · E ≥ 0, and
(KZ + D) · E = 0 forces equality. In particular D · E = 0. A resolution fibre over a point of
the conductor must meet its strict transform, by properness. Since its fibre is connected, this
disjointness proves π −1 (t) ⊂ Dred for the normalization point just found.
    The strict curves over the two elliptic-normalized branches are elliptic: a rational curve cannot
map nonconstantly onto an elliptic curve. They meet the connected fibre π −1 (t). If the curves
are distinct, one connected component of Dred therefore contains two elliptic curves. If they are
the same elliptic curve, their meeting points with the fibre are distinct. This follows from the
exact factorization of a map from a normal curve through the normalization of its image: one
point cannot map to both points over the node in (C.VII.6). The connected resolution fibre
consequently gives a path in Dred joining these distinct points. Both possibilities contradict
C.2.VII.1: the first has two positive-genus components, and the second adds a graph cycle to
an elliptic component, giving arithmetic genus at least two. This excludes the only negative
possibility and proves (C.VII.4).

Proposition 8.13 (Proved sign for class VII normalization). Let f : Y → B be a proper
connected-fibre holomorphic map from a smooth compact complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0 to a
smooth curve, whose general fibre is a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre with irreducible
reduced nonnormal support, and suppose that the minimal resolution Z of its normalization is
class VII. Then
                                           e(S) ≥ 0.                                    (C.VII.7)
No restriction on the singularity type or conductor multiplicity of S is made.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.8; proposition 6.3;
proposition 8.11; proposition 8.12.

Proof. The canonical evaluation and adjunction comparison (A.CD.1) give ωS⊗m = OS . The
divisor sequence and Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch give χ(OS ) = 0, because c1 (OY (S)) = 0
rationally. These arguments require only b2 (Y ) = 0; the integral condition and Picard-variation


                                                167
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


assumption in the later part of 6.8 are not needed here. Let η : T → S, π : Z → T , and D > 0
be the maps and divisor of 6.3. Put C = Γred and A = (η −1 C)red ⊂ T . Thus KZ + D is torsion,
and 8.11–8.12 apply.
    We compute e(T \ A) through the actual resolution. As in 8.12, an exceptional curve E with
coefficient zero in D has KZ · E = D · E = 0. Adjunction and negative self-intersection then
give pa (E) = 0 and E 2 = −2. These curves are smooth rational and disjoint from Dred . Their
negative-definite intersection matrix makes each connected configuration a tree: a repeated edge
or a cycle would give a nonnegative square for a nonzero vector in the matrix. The intersections
are transverse, since their local intersection multiplicities are one; three curves cannot meet at
a point, since that would give a triangle. Connectedness of resolution fibres shows that a fibre
either consists entirely of these curves or lies entirely in Dred . The zero-coefficient fibres lie
outside A, since a fibre over A must meet the strict conductor.
    Let a be the total number of zero-coefficient exceptional curves, and let b be the number of
exceptional fibres lying in Dred whose images in T lie outside A. On Z \ Dred the former fibres
are still present and the latter are absent. A tree with aj rational curves has Euler number
aj + 1, so replacing it by its image point subtracts aj . Adding back the image point of an
absent positive-coefficient fibre adds one. Away from these finitely many fibres, π is the required
isomorphism of complements. Additivity of compactly supported Euler characteristic therefore
gives the exact equality

                             e(T \ A) = e(Z) − e(Dred ) − a + b
                                                                                           (C.VII.8)
                                      = b2 (Z) − r(Dred ) − a + b ≥ 0.

The inequality follows because the rational curves counted by r(Dred ) and by a are distinct, and
their total is at most b2 (Z) by 8.11. Finally η is a biholomorphism T \ A → S \ C. Hence

                                   e(S) = e(T \ A) + e(C) ≥ 0

by 8.12. This proves the assertion for the original reduced support and all full multiplicities.

    Now suppose that the Picard pullback is nonconstant. The argument of 6.8 applies to Pic0 (Y )

              H 1 (Y, OY ) −→ H 1 (S, OS ) −→ H 1 (T, OT ) −→ H 1 (Z, OZ ).             (C.VII.11)

    Assume e(S) = 0. Every rational curve in Dred must be resolution-exceptional, because its
image lies in C and cannot dominate an elliptic curve. A minimal class VII model with positive
second Betti number and a torsion anticanonical divisor is one of the proved configurations used
in 8.11. An intermediate or Inoue–Hirzebruch model has no elliptic curves, and therefore could
not dominate the nonempty elliptic conductor. A parabolic Inoue model has a rational cycle of
square zero and exactly b2 rational curves. Its point blowups therefore still have exactly b2 (Z)
rational curves. The equality b2 (Z) = r + a makes every one of them resolution-exceptional,
including any zero-coefficient blowup curves. Thus the full total transform of the minimal rational
cycle, whose square remains zero, would be exceptional. This contradicts negative definiteness
of a resolution’s exceptional intersection matrix. Consequently the minimal model is Hopf. All
rational curves on Z are now the exceptional curves of its point blowups, and their number
is b2 (Z). The equality b2 (Z) = r + a makes all of them resolution-exceptional. As in the last
paragraph of 8.30, a nonempty blowup sequence would have a last (−1) curve, contradicting
minimality of the resolution. Thus the normalization is already a smooth minimal Hopf surface.
Its reduced conductor curves are elliptic; their finite maps to the smooth elliptic curves of C
are unramified by Riemann–Hurwitz. Conversely those normalization and conductor data have
Euler number zero by the exact normalization formula. This proves the sharper equivalence.

component; a centre at a smooth coefficient-one point creates only a coefficient-zero leaf; and
a centre at a smooth point of coefficient at least two creates a positive leaf. These are all the
possibilities in the exact divisor formula Dnew = σ ∗ Dold − E. The r points of C so obtained are
distinct.
    If every component of Bj is π-exceptional, there has been at least one multiplicity-one
blowup centre above Fj . Indeed, in the absence of such a centre, every component of the entire
total transform of Fj has positive conductor coefficient. That complete ruling fibre, with its
positive multiplicities, has self-intersection zero. It cannot be supported on the negative-definite
exceptional matrix of a normal surface resolution. Distinct original fibres require distinct blowup
events. Hence at most N0 of the Bj can be entirely π-exceptional.
    Discard those fibres and the rdom fibres counted above. There remain at least
                                          k ≥ r − N0 − rdom                              (C.RA.23)
fibres with a surviving strict conductor component and none dominating H. Follow the connected
positive boundary from its point on C to the first component which is not π-exceptional. Its
image is a curve different from H meeting H at that point’s image. Every intervening connected
chain is contracted by π, so this is an actual intersection in S, not an identification imposed on
an auxiliary graph.
     Use the normalization-incidence graph of G = Γred : its vertices are the rational normalization
components and the singular points with more than one normalization branch, and its edges are
the individual branch preimages. The preceding k intersections give k distinct edges adjacent
to the vertex belonging to H. They remain distinct even when two of their images are the
same singular point: C → H ν is an isomorphism, and the points on C were distinct. Remove
that vertex and all its adjacent edges. Each of the c remaining connected components which
receives one of these edges contains a normalization vertex of a curve other than H. In particular
c ≤ nG − 1, where nG is the number of irreducible components of G.
     Contract a spanning tree in each of those c graph components. The k retained edges then
give a connected multistar with c + 1 vertices and k edges. Its first Betti number is k − c, so the
first Betti number β of the full incidence graph satisfies
                             k − c ≤ β ≤ 1,       nG ≥ k + 1 − β ≥ k.                    (C.RA.24)
The upper bound on β is the actual local torus-group quotient (A.RT.18)–(A.RT.20). Adding
genus-zero normalization components changes no graph first Betti number, and the normalization
quotient gives e(G) = nG + 1 − β ≥ nG . Combining (C.RA.23)–(C.RA.24) with the exact surface
Euler formula yields
              e(S) = 2 − r + N0 + e(G)
                                                                                         (C.RA.25)
                   ≥ 2 − r + N0 + nG ≥ 2 − r + N0 + (r − N0 − rdom ) = 2 − rdom .
This proves the assertion.

    The degree-one result accounts for every generic transverse type allowed by conductor
exponent two on that branch. It does not replace the other branches by a presumed ordinary
triple: those branches may have larger conductor exponents. The cases in which the horizontal
section is contracted, or maps with higher degree to a singular conductor image, require the
further arguments identified separately below.
Proposition 8.18 (Every rational degree-two tacnode cover has positive Euler number). Retain
the torus-fibre, rational-normalization and specified ruled-boundary morphism of 8.15. Suppose
C is not contracted, H = h(C)red has generic transverse type A3 , and the actual map C → H ν
has degree two. Then e(S) ≥ 1. No smoothness or local complete intersection assumption on the
image curve is required.

                                                175
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.15; proposition 6.18;
equation (C.RA.26); proposition 6.17; equation (C.RA.28); equation (C.RA.30);
equation (C.RA.31); proposition 8.17.

Proof. Write Σ = H ν ≃ P1 , G = Γred , δ = pa (H) ≤ 2, and s = #ν −1 (Sing H) ≤ 3 as in
(C.RA.5)–(C.RA.6). There are exactly two generic normalization branches above H, both
supplied by the degree-two map from C. Thus no vertical strict conductor component dominates
H.
    We first justify using the lci jet construction without assuming that property. The low-delta
classification in the proof of 8.15 applies to this same reduced image curve. Its three-independent-
axis germ is excluded by b1 (H) ≤ b1 (G) ≤ 1. The remaining non-lci possibilities are the space
cusp with semigroup h3, 4, 5i and a cusp with a transverse smooth branch. The genus-zero
double-cover calculation at the end of 6.18 excludes both: the space-cusp inequalities force
q0 = −1 and two simple zeros of the cleared quartic, one over Hreg , contradicting (A.T.12); for
the cusp-plus-line ring its cleared quartic has nonpositive degree and cannot have two branch
points. Therefore H is lci at all its points.
    Let Ξ be the normalization conductor divisor of H, and use the actual jet lines and sections
in (A.T.5)–(A.T.7). Put

     A = deg div(a) = −2 deg Q,        σ ∈ H 0 (Σ, L2 (4Ξ)),     deg div(σ) = 8 − A.     (C.RA.26)

Here A is a nonnegative even integer and σ is the conductor-cleared version of ∆ = ae − b2 /4.
The degree-two cover C → Σ has two branch points, exactly the odd-order zeros of σ. Let Bs
be the number of these branch points lying over singular points of H; there are 2 − Bs over
its smooth locus. Every smooth branch point has zero order at least three in σ, by the actual
coordinate exclusion (A.T.10)–(A.T.12).
    The section a must vanish at every point of Σ over a singular point of H. To see this, the
Hessian matrix has entries in OH . If its normalized scalar a is nonzero on one branch above p,
its primitive rank-one factor has a unit component there. A diagonal entry consequently has a
nonzero value at p. That same entry has the same nonzero value on every branch, so a is nonzero
at all normalization points above p. In that event (A.T.13) removes the conductor denominator:
∆ is holomorphic in L2 there. The orders of σ above p are at least those of 4Ξ, which are even.
Its total zero divisor must additionally contain the two parity contributions of the two branch
points, whether or not they lie over p. Thus

                         deg div(σ) ≥ 4 deg(Ξ|ν −1 (p) ) + 2 = 8δp + 2 ≥ 10,             (C.RA.27)

contrary to (C.RA.26). This proves the claimed vanishing.
   It follows in particular that
                                         A ≥ 2s − 2.                                     (C.RA.28)
For s ≤ 1 this is automatic; for s = 2 the two zeros give A ≥ 2. If s = 3, the bounds δ ≤ 2 and
b1 (H) ≤ 1 force exactly two singular points, each of delta invariant one: one node and one cusp.
The two node preimages contribute at least one each. At the cusp the ring is C{t2 , t3 }, so any
vanishing Hessian entry has order at least two. Dividing such a diagonal entry by the square of
a unit component of the primitive normalized factor shows that a has order at least two there.
Thus A ≥ 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 = 2s − 2.
    We now check exactly which smooth image points can receive two vertical boundary
attachments on their two conductor preimages. At a smooth point with a 6= 0, 6.17 gives
the constant A3 product and no vertical attachment. Suppose instead that a = 0 and ∆ is a
unit. In the actual coordinates (A.T.10), the coefficient b is then a unit. Substitute x = y 2 λ in
that equation and divide by y 4 . The result is holomorphic in (λ, y, z) and has, at the point in


                                                176
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


question, the simple root λ = −e(0)/b(0). The implicit-function theorem gives a holomorphic
λ(y, z) and an actual factorization

       f0 = F1 F2 ,     F1 = x − y 2 λ(y, z),     F2 |F1 =0 = y 2 u(y, z),   u(0) 6= 0.    (C.RA.29)

The last equality is the restriction of ∂f0 /∂x to F1 = 0; its quotient by y 2 has constant value b(0).
The branch F1 = 0 is smooth, and its conductor in the whole reduced hypersurface is exactly
the divisor 2{y = 0}, by the intersection factor in (C.RA.22). There is therefore no vertical
conductor near this normalization point. Its minimal resolution is an isomorphism there as well.
Since ∆ is a unit, this is one of the two distinct conductor preimages over the given point of Σ.
Consequently a smooth nonbranch value with two vertical attachments has a positive even zero
order of σ, at least two.
   Let dreg count distinct smooth values with two such attachments. The two branch points and
these distinct nonbranch zeros give

                                  3(2 − Bs ) + Bs + 2dreg ≤ 8 − A.                         (C.RA.30)

Among the s points above the singular locus, the Bs branch points each have only one preimage
on C. Thus at most s − Bs of these values can have two attachments. If d counts all values on Σ
with two attachments, (C.RA.28)–(C.RA.30) give

                                                                A
                                d ≤ s − Bs + dreg ≤ s + 1 −       ≤ 2.                     (C.RA.31)
                                                                2

    In fact d ≤ 1. If d = 2, (C.RA.31) requires A ≤ 2s − 2. For s = 0 this is impossible, and for
s = 1 it contradicts the vanishing of a over the singular point. For s = 2, it forces A = 2 and
the two singular preimages exhaust the zero divisor of a. For s = 3, it forces A = 4, exhausted
by the node and cusp orders 1 + 1 + 2 established above. In both remaining cases a is nowhere
zero over Hreg . The constant A3 product there has neither a cover branch point nor a vertical
attachment. Thus both cover branch points lie over Sing H, and only the other s − 2 ≤ 1 singular
preimages can have two attachments. This again contradicts d = 2. Consequently

                                                d ≤ 1.                                    (C.RA.31a)

    It remains to connect this local count to the exact surface Euler number. As in 8.17, at least

None maps onto H, so they give K distinct points of C anchored to image curves other than H.
After projection to Σ their number of distinct normalization-incidence edges is k = K − d0 where
d0 ≤ d ≤ 1: a degree-two fibre has at most two points, and the loss of one occurs precisely at
a value with two selected attachments. Apply the graph construction of (C.RA.24) to these k
distinct edges. It gives nG ≥ k and e(G) ≥ nG . The actual Euler decomposition therefore yields

                            e(S) = 2 − r + N0 + e(G) ≥ 2 − K + e(G)
                                                                                           (C.RA.32)
                                  ≥ 2 − K + k = 2 − d0 ≥ 1.

Every contraction, covering fibre and graph edge in this count comes from the specified maps
Z → T → S and C → Σ → H.

Proposition 8.19 (A locally unibranch tangent-root component gives positive Euler number).
Retain the torus-fibre, rational-normalization and specified ruled-boundary morphism of 8.15.
Suppose C is not contracted and maps with degree d = 2 or 3 onto a smooth rational curve H with
generic ordinary-triple transversal. Let q3 ∈ H 0 (H, Sym3 N ∗ ⊗ M ) be its cubic normal tensor,
where N = NH/Y and M = OY (S)|H . Suppose q3 is nonzero as a tensor at every point of H. Its


                                                 177
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


tangent-root divisor R3 ⊂ P(N ) is then finite of degree three over H. Let Rd be the component
corresponding to C over the generic point. If Rd is locally unibranch at every point, then

                                           e(S) ≥ d − 1 > 0.                                (C.RD.1)

In particular this applies when d = 2 and the only singularities of R2 are an A4 cusp or two A2
cusps.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.15; equation (C.RD.2);
equation (C.RD.4); proposition 8.17.

Proof. The nonzero cubic has three distinct roots over the generic point and is never identically
zero on a projective fibre. It therefore defines a reduced finite divisor R3 . The function-field
algebra of its roots agrees with that of the normalized conductor curves dominating H: a branch
of an ordinary triple is distinguished by its tangent line. Taking the integral closure of OH in
that algebra gives the exact finite-cover identification

                                           C ≃ Rdν   over H.                                (C.RD.2)

Thus two distinct points of C over one point p ∈ H give distinct root points of Rd , because
normalization of a locally unibranch reduced curve is bijective on its underlying points.
    We check what a simple root implies for the actual hypersurface, including its conductor.
In coordinates H = (x, y) = 0, with parameter z on H, the local equation f0 of S belongs to
(x, y)3 . The lower normal jets vanish on the reduced smooth curve, and the graded pieces of
its regular-sequence ideal are locally free, which justifies this membership. Choose the normal
coordinates so a specified simple tangent root is finite in x/y. Then

                            f0 (yλ, y, z)/y 3 = q3 (λ, 1, z) + y A(λ, y, z).                (C.RD.3)

The simple root gives a holomorphic solution λ = λ(y, z) by the implicit-function theorem.
Division by the monic linear factor yields an actual factorization

         f0 = (x − yλ(y, z)) G(x, y, z),      G|x=yλ(y,z) = y 2 u(y, z),       u(0) 6= 0.   (C.RD.4)

The unit is the derivative of the cubic with respect to its root coordinate, at the chosen simple
root. Hence this normalization branch is smooth and its conductor in S is exactly twice the
curve lying over H. There is no vertical conductor component there, and the minimal resolution
π is an isomorphism nearby.
    Two distinct C-points over p cannot both receive a vertical boundary attachment. Their root
points are distinct by (C.RD.2). If both could receive attachments, (C.RD.4) would make both
roots multiple, requiring total cubic degree at least four. Thus each point of H receives at most
one attachment from C.
    There are at most 3 − d generic normalization branches left to be supplied by vertical strict
conductor components. In the notation of 8.17 this gives rdom ≤ 3−d. At least K ≥ r −N0 −rdom
original positive vertical boundaries therefore survive with an image different from H. Their K
points of C give K distinct normalization-incidence edges at H, by the preceding paragraph.
Equation (C.RA.24) gives nG ≥ K, and the exact Euler decomposition gives

                           e(S) ≥ 2 − r + N0 + K ≥ 2 − rdom ≥ d − 1.

This proves the assertion. The final examples are locally unibranch by their displayed cusp
equations.

Proposition 8.23 (Global exclusion of connected positive-genus triple covers over a rational
image). Let Y be a smooth compact complex threefold with b2 (Y ; Q) = 0, and let f : Y → B be
a holomorphic map to a smooth curve whose smooth nearby fibres are complex two-tori. Fix
a fibre mS, with S reduced and irreducible, and restrict the base to a small coordinate disc
about it. Let H ⊂ S be a smooth rational curve along which the generic transversal of S is an
ordinary triple point. Suppose that the three generic normalization branches form one connected
degree-three cover C → H, where C denotes its smooth complete model. Then C is rational, and
the cubic normal jet of S vanishes identically on at least one normal fibre over H. In particular,
a positive-genus connected degree-three cover is impossible, and a primitive cubic normal jet is
impossible for any connected degree-three cover.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.D4.2); (Merle and
Teissier, 1977, Theorem 2.1.1 and Corollary 2.1.3); (Steenbrink, 1989, pp. 165–167); (Némethi,
1991, §1 and Example 2.4(a)); equation (C.D4.7); equation (C.D4.6); equation (C.D4.5);
equation (C.D4.9); equation (C.D4.12); equation (C.D4.4).

Proof. We construct all comparison maps, including the map into the actual nearby fibre. Put
N = NH/Y and M = OY (S)|H . The ambient Chern-class hypothesis gives M ≃ OH and
deg N = −2. The order-three normal jet is therefore an actual homogeneous function

                      P ∈ H 0 (H, Sym3 N ∗ ),        U = {v ∈ N : P (v) = 1}.              (C.D4.1)

The generic cubic has three distinct roots. The fibrewise Euler identity dP (v)(v) = 3P (v) proves
that U is smooth everywhere, including above a base point where the cubic degenerates. Above
a point where the entire cubic is zero there is no point of U .

Comparison with the actual fibre. Let t be the base coordinate, so f is a holomorphic
function on a neighbourhood of H. Locally f = usm , where s = 0 defines S and u is a unit. The
degree-3m normal jet of f is P m , after rescaling the chosen trivialization of M by a constant.
Indeed the ratio of the two jets is an invertible holomorphic function on H ≃ P1 , hence constant.
Take a smooth tubular map τ from a neighbourhood of the zero section in N to Y , whose
derivative on normal fibres is the specified complex-linear identification. For positive real s → 0,
Taylor’s formula gives

                  s−3m f τ (sv) −→ P (v)m in C ∞ on compact subsets of N.                  (C.D4.2)
                                

The order of vanishing is at least 3m along every point of H: its ideal is a regular codimension-two
ideal, and its ordinary powers are primary along the smooth curve, so the order verified at its
generic point extends over H.

                                                  185
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


    Choose any compact codimension-zero smooth submanifold K ⊂ U . On a neighbourhood
of K, the differential of P m has a smooth right inverse as a real map to C. The implicit-
function theorem, uniformly on K, or the corresponding right-inverse vector field, transports this
neighbourhood to the level s−3m f (τ (sv)) = 1. Composing with v 7→ τ (sv) gives an orientation-
preserving embedding into the actual fibre f −1 (s3m ). In particular, intersections of compact
two-cycles, computed with parallel perturbations inside K, are preserved. This construction uses
the actual function f and its leading normal jet; it makes no assertion that arbitrary changes of
local equations preserve a Milnor fibre.
    The algebraic surface U admits a compact smooth core whose inclusion is a homotopy
equivalence. For example, resolve the boundary in a projective compactification, triangulate the
resulting pair, take the complement of a sufficiently small regular neighbourhood of the boundary
and round its corners. The radial collars of this regular neighbourhood give the retraction. We
choose this core for K. Thus the preceding embedding induces one map carrying all of H1 (U )
and H2 (U ), together with their compact intersection pairing.
    Here is the precise torus obstruction we will use. For a map K → T 4 , let W be the rational
image of H1 (K) in H1 (T 4 ). The map lifts to the covering corresponding to its fundamental-group
image, a space homotopy equivalent to T r , where r = dim W . Its image on H2 consequently
lies in Λ2 W ⊂ Λ2 Q4 . For r ≤ 3 the wedge pairing on this image is zero, because Λ4 W = 0.
Consequently a compact core with b1 (U ) ≤ 3 and nonzero intersection pairing cannot embed by
(C.D4.2) into a nearby torus. This is a comparison of the actual homology maps.

The normal bundle and the root divisor. Write

                             N = OH (a) ⊕ OH (−2 − a),           a ≥ −1.                     (C.D4.3)

If a > 0, the coefficient of the cube of the first fibre coordinate vanishes, since it has degree −3a.
The other coordinate is then a global linear factor of the cubic. This contradicts connectedness
of the degree-three root cover. Thus a = −1 or a = 0.
    For a = 0, irreducibility of the generic cubic forces the coefficient of the first coordinate cubed
to be a nonzero constant. Along the trivial summand of N , the equation P = 1 therefore has
three constant sections. Each is a compact P1 in U with normal bundle OP1 (−2): the derivative
in the trivial summand is nonzero, so the implicit-function theorem identifies its normal direction
with the other summand. Its homology square is −2. Transporting its tubular neighbourhood by
(C.D4.2) gives a sphere of square −2 in a torus, whereas the torus has π2 = 0. This is impossible.
    We are left with N = O(−1)⊕2 and E = P(N ) ≃ P1 × P1 . Let A be the common zero divisor
of the cubic coefficients on the base, of degree v. Removing that scalar factor gives an integral
horizontal root divisor R of bidegree (3, 3 − v), where the first entry is its degree over H. Its
normalization is the given cover C: at a general point the maps identify a normalization branch
with its distinct tangent line, and both complete normal covers are the integral closure in this
same function field. Thus, writing g = g(C),

                                      0 ≤ g ≤ pa (R) = 4 − 2v.                               (C.D4.4)

For a primitive cubic v = 0. For a positive-genus cover with v > 0, the bound forces v = 1. We
treat these two cases. Their total root divisors are respectively

                                B = R(3,3) ,     B = R(3,2) + F(0,1) .                       (C.D4.5)

Both are reduced divisors of class (3, 3); the second has one simple verticalP

rp (B) is the number of analytic branches at a singular point. Their total delta invariants are
4 − g and 5 − g, respectively, so in the cases under consideration they are at most four.

Homology and the compact intersection pairing. The finite algebra in (C.D4.6) and

The irreducible components of D have independent homology classes. The exceptional classes
have a negative-definite intersection matrix. In the first case of (C.D4.5) the remaining class
pushes forward to the nonzero class of R; in the second, the two remaining classes push forward

the ample class B = (3, 3), whose square is positive. The Hodge index theorem implies that the
intersection form on this span is nondegenerate: its part orthogonal to the positive pullback class
is negative definite.
    Write nD for the number of boundary components. The exact homology sequence of the
pair (X, U ) identifies the map H2 (X; Q) → H2 (X, U ; Q) = QnD with intersection against these
components. Its surjectivity gives H1 (U ; Q) ≃ H1 (X; Q). Its kernel is the orthogonal complement

b2 (X) − nD . As D is connected, e(D) = nD + 1 − b1 (D), and consequently

                                               b1 (U ) = b1 (X) ≤ 2,

                                                              = e(U ) − 1 + 2b1 (X) − b1 (D).

Here the equality of ranks follows also for a degenerate pairing on H2 (U ): its kernel includes the
kernel of the map to H2 (X), and the induced form on its image is the nondegenerate form just
identified.

are ε independent relations, while their span still contains a positive-square class, the same pair

              rank intersection pairing on H2 (U ) = e(U ) − 1 + 2b1 (X) − b1 (D) + ε.

These identities concern the actual classes in the indicated cyclic cover. They will also be used

    To compute b1 (D), start with the normalizations of the c components of B, of total genus g,

    This excludes v = 0 for every connected triple cover and v = 1 for every positive-genus one.
By (C.D4.4) these are all possibilities for a positive-genus cover, proving the statement. The
genus-zero cases with v = 1 or 2 are not asserted to be excluded by this argument.

Proposition 8.24 (A rational ordinary-triple image has no positive-genus double branch
cover). Let f : Y → C0 have the torus-fibre and ambient hypotheses of 8.23. Let H ⊂ S be a
smooth rational curve with generic ordinary-triple transversal. Suppose two of the three generic
normalization branches form a connected degree-two cover C → H, and the remaining branch
forms a degree-one cover. Then the smooth complete curve C is rational. The assertion includes
all zeros, with their multiplicities, of the entire cubic normal tensor.

conductor with generic ordinary-triple transversal has smooth elliptic image. Its normalization is
smooth minimal elliptic ruled, the horizontal cover is unramified of degree three, and e(S) = 0.

(C.D4.1)–(C.D4.2), and write

N = NH/Y = O(a) ⊕ O(−2 − a),         a ≥ −1,       P ∈ H 0 (H, Sym3 N ∗ ),  U = {P = 1} ⊂ N.

The comparison embeds a compact core of U , including its compact intersection pairing, into an

    Put E = P(N ), using lines in N , and let L = OE (1), ξ = c1 (L) and F be the fibre class.

Proposition 8.25 (Rational connected triple covers have positive fibre Euler number). Retain
the torus-fibre, rational-normalization and specified Hirzebruch-boundary morphism of 8.15.
Suppose the horizontal section C is not contracted, its image H is smooth rational, the generic
transversal along H is an ordinary triple point, and C → H has degree three. Then e(S) ≥ 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.15; proposition 8.23;
proposition 8.17; proposition 8.19; proposition A.6; equation (C.D4.13); equation (C.D4.19).

Proof. Use the normal-cone construction of 8.23. That result forces N = O(−1)⊕2 and a common
cubic-coefficient divisor of degree v = 1 or 2. The horizontal root curve is integral of bidegree
(3, 3 − v), with rational normalization C. No vertical strict conductor component dominates H,
since all three generic branches are supplied by C.
     We first recall exactly how a finite attachment bound gives the Euler inequality. In the notation
of 8.15 let r be the number of original positive ruling fibres and let N0 count coefficient-zero
blowup events. At least K ≥ r − N0 of their positive boundary trees contain a strict conductor
curve. The negative-definite argument of 8.17 proves this bound without an assumption about
normalization singularities. They yield K distinct attachment points on C. Their images on
H give k distinct normalization-incidence edges. Put ` = K − k. The incidence graph has first
Betti number at most one, so the exact graph count (C.RA.24) gives e(Γred ) ≥ k. Consequently

                               e(S) = 2 − r + N0 + e(Γred ) ≥ 2 − `.                       (C.D4.13)

    At a point where the cubic is primitive, a simple tangent root gives a smooth normalization
branch with conductor exactly twice the horizontal curve. Indeed the ambient blowup chart
divides the reduced equation by the third power of its normal coordinate; the nonzero root
derivative solves the remaining coordinate holomorphically. The remaining quadratic factor has
nonzero value at the chosen simple root. Its restriction therefore gives the conductor factor
y 2 times a unit, even when its own two roots coincide. This is the explicit factorization and
conductor comparison of 8.19. Such a point cannot carry a vertical boundary attachment. If the
horizontal root curve is locally unibranch, a multiple root has just one point on its normalization.
A cubic has at most one multiple root unless all its roots are simple. Thus off the common divisor
each image value receives at most one attachment when that root curve is locally unibranch.

Proposition 8.26 (The irreducible local comparison and its rational and ruled consequences).
Let f : Y → B be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a smooth curve,
with connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Let mS be a full fibre with
irreducible reduced support, and let F be a nearby smooth fibre. Write T1 for the local monodromy
on H 1 (F, Q). Then
                                   m e(Sreg ) = det(1 − T1m ) ≥ 0.                        (C.UI.1)
For its normalization and minimal normalization resolution h = ηπ : Z → T → S, the following
statements hold.

   1. If Z is rational, then e(S) ≥ 2. More precisely, whenever H 1 (S, Q) 6= 0, one has e(S) = 2.

   2. Suppose Z is irrational ruled. A reduced horizontal conductor gives a smooth minimal
      elliptic ruled normalization, with disjoint smooth elliptic conductor curves and their finite
      etale double-cover maps to the conductor image. The support has ordinary double-curve
      normal crossings and Euler number zero.

   3. Suppose the horizontal conductor is twice a noncontracted section. The normalization is
      again smooth minimal elliptic ruled. Its conductor is twice that section; its image is smooth
      elliptic, and the map from the section is etale of degree 1, 2, or 3. The respective constant
      transverse types are the ordinary cusp, tacnode, and ordinary triple point. Every such
      support has Euler number zero.

   4. Suppose the horizontal conductor is twice a section contracted by π. Then e(S) ≥ 2 and
      π1 (S) = 1. In particular this case cannot occur under the full CDP hypotheses, since 3.6
      supplies a nonzero integral degree-one class on every fibre support there.

The alternatives in the last three items exhaust the irrational ruled case. No vanishing of b1 (Y )
or b2 (Y ) is used in the first four conclusions.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.6; equation (C.UI.2);
equation (C.UI.3); proposition 6.3; equation (C.UI.4); equation (C.UI.5); (A’Campo, 1975, §2
and §3); proposition A.4; equation (C.UI.6); equation (C.UI.7); proposition 8.32; proposition 6.7;
proposition 8.31; proposition 8.1; proposition 6.20; proposition 6.17; equation (C.UI.12);
equation (C.UI.11); proposition 7.1; proposition 8.10; proposition 6.13; proposition 6.18;

Proof.
The actual canonical and Chern-class comparisons. Choose a coordinate t on a small
disc ∆ about the chosen value and put U = f −1 (∆). The torsion-free rank-one sheaf f∗ ωU /∆ is a

two-form. Its divisor is therefore kS for some integer k ≥ 0. The coordinate dt identifies the

                         KU ≃ OU (kS),       OU (mS) ≃ OU ,             ωS⊗m ≃ OS .           (C.UI.2)

This restricts a section of the relative canonical line; it does not pull a three-form back as a
differential form to a surface.
    Here is the Euler calculation on this actual tube. The map is flat: its local rings are torsion-
free over the regular one-dimensional base ring. Proper flatness makes the holomorphic Euler
characteristic of its full fibres constant, so χ(OmS ) = χ(OF ) = 0. The Cartier filtration of
OmS has successive quotients OS (−jS), 0 ≤ j < m; by (C.UI.2) these are torsion line-bundle
twists. Each such twist has the same Euler characteristic as OS . One can check this without a
compact ambient manifold: use the normalization sequence and the resolution Leray sequence to
compute the Euler characteristic on the compact smooth surface Z, the conductor curve, and the
finite-support sheaf R1 π∗ OZ . Smooth-surface Riemann–Roch leaves the first term unchanged
under a torsion twist; curve Riemann–Roch, applied to the generic-rank filtration of the conductor
quotient, leaves the second unchanged; the finite lengths in the third are unchanged. These exact
sequences prove the assertion on S. Consequently, writing ci = ci (T U ), one has

                           0 = χ(OmS ) = mχ(OS ),

Indeed a first centre outside the existing exceptional locus lies in the singular locus of the reduced

For clarity, the local and global maps producing this identity are as follows. The real oriented

                             {(u1 , . . . , ur ) ∈ (S 1 )r : ua11 · · · uar r = eiθ }.       (C.UI.7)

An integral change of angular basis identifies this with gcd(a1 , . . . , ar ) copies of (S 1 )r−1 .
Monodromy permutes these copies and acts by translations on them. For r ≥ 2 the alternating
trace is zero, whether the permutation fixes a copy or not. For r = 1 it is a1 when a1 | j and zero
otherwise. The constructible higher-direct-image sheaves of this boundary projection carry those
stalk actions. Their cohomology spectral sequence computes H ∗ (F ) with its actual monodromy.
Triangulate the compact central divisor compatibly with the strata and these local systems.
On every open cell the alternating trace of compactly supported cochains is its signed cell
contribution times the stalk trace. Additivity and the spectral sequence prove (C.UI.6). The
proper modification is an isomorphism over ∆∗ , so these are the nearby fibre and monodromy of
the original map.
    This description also proves quasi-unipotence without an extra hypothesis. If N is a common
multiple of the finitely many ai , then T N is the identity on every stalk cohomology group in
(C.UI.7), since the finite permutation disappears and translations act trivially on cohomology. It
is the identity on the corresponding constructible cohomology sheaves, hence on the second page
of their cohomology spectral sequence. The finite filtration on H q (F ) has identity action on its
associated graded. Thus T N is unipotent on H q (F ).
    Put j = m in (C.UI.6). By (C.UI.5) only E0 contributes. The cohomology ring of the real
four-torus is the exterior algebra of its first cohomology, and a monodromy diffeomorphism acts
by the exterior powers of T1 . Therefore

The local degree-one class and the finite-character comparison. We record the exact

gives the specified class γU on the tube, whose restriction to S is γS .
    For injectivity upon restriction to F , the inclusion U ∗ = U \ S ,→ U surjects on fundamental
groups: loops can be perturbed off the real codimension-two divisor, avoiding its higher
codimension singular strata. If a rational degree-one class on U restricts to zero on F , the exact
homotopy sequence of the punctured-disc bundle makes its restriction to U ∗ a scalar multiple
a of the base-circle class. A small meridian at a smooth point of S is null-homologous in U

fundamental groups now makes the original class zero. In particular γU |F 6= 0.

The second equality is the bundle Leray comparison.

Proposition 8.27 (The unrestricted irreducible zero-Euler criterion). Let f : Y → B be a proper
holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold to a smooth complex curve, with connected

satisfies e(S) ≥ 0. Its Euler number is zero precisely in the following geometric cases, stated for
these actual maps.
    A normal support is a smooth torus or a smooth bielliptic surface, with multiplicities as in
8.1.
    A nonnormal support with irrational ruled normalization has smooth minimal normalization
ruled over an elliptic curve. Its conductor image and reduced inverse image are disjoint unions
of smooth elliptic curves. The transversal types and their finite conductor maps are exactly those

components. There are no contracted horizontal sections in the zero-Euler case.

Proposition 8.28 (Proved elliptic-image restriction). Let Y be a smooth compact complex
threefold with H 2 (Y, Q) = 0, let Si be an irreducible component of a connected reducible divisor S,
and let h : Z → Si ,→ Y be the minimal resolution of its normalization. Suppose that the minimal
model σ : Z → Z0 is a Hopf surface or a non-Kähler elliptic surface. Every strict transform
E ⊂ Z of an elliptic curve on Z0 has a one-dimensional image under h, and the normalization of
that image is elliptic. The actual restriction homomorphism Pic0 (Y ) → Pic0 (E) is nonconstant
for each such E. In particular such a component cannot meet a component whose minimal model
is an Enoki surface.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.INT.3); proposition 3.4;
equation (C.INT.1); equation (C.INT.2); (Brînzănescu and Moraru, 2005, Lemma 2.2 and §2);
(Dloussky and Teleman, 2012, Remark 2.7).

Proof. Choose an adjacent component Sj . The actual pullback of its canonical divisor section
gives a nonzero effective Cartier divisor

                              A = h∗ Sj > 0,      OZ (A) = h∗ OY (Sj ).                     (C.INT.1)

Its first Chern class is torsion. For some q > 0, OY (qSj ) ∈ Pic0 (Y ), so the restriction
homomorphism ρ : Pic0 (Y ) → Pic0 (Z) has in its image the line OZ (qA). That line has strictly
positive degree for every Gauduchon metric on Z.

                                                 203
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


    We spell out the blowdown comparison. Put A0 = σ∗ A. The difference A−σ ∗ A0 is exceptional
and has zero real Chern class: both A and its pushforward have zero real class. The negative
definite exceptional intersection matrix makes every coefficient of this difference zero. Thus

                                        A = σ ∗ A0 ,      A0 > 0.                             (C.INT.2)

Nonzeroness follows by the same negative definiteness if A0 were zero. Pullback is an isomorphism
Pic0 (Z0 ) ≃ Pic0 (Z); the integral blowup formula and Rσ∗ OZ = OZ0 identify both the lattice
and the coefficient space defining it. We therefore regard ρ as a map into Pic0 (Z0 ). Its image
contains OZ0 (qA0 ).
   We first prove the stronger assertion that the composite restriction to E cannot be zero.
Suppose that it is zero. This situation would in particular arise if h(E) were a point or had rational
normalization. In the latter case the map from the normal curve E factors as E → P1 → Y .
In both cases every line from Pic0 (Y ) restricts trivially to E. Here the pullback to P1 is in
Pic0 (P1 ) = 0; this is the specified map giving the vanishing. The restriction of σ to E is an
isomorphism onto its smooth elliptic image E0 .
   For a Hopf Z0 the homomorphism

                                       H 1 (Z0 , R) −→ H 1 (E0 , R)                           (C.INT.3)

is nonzero. On a primary Hopf surface this follows from its universal cover C2 \ {0}: a finite
image of π1 (E0 ) in π1 (Z0 ) = Z would lift a finite unramified cover of E0 to that cover. Its two
coordinate functions would be constant, contradicting the nonconstant inclusion of the curve. For
a secondary Hopf surface, pull back along a finite unramified primary cover. A component above
E0 is an elliptic curve. Transfer makes H 1 (Z0 , R) → H 1 (Z00 , R) an isomorphism between one-
dimensional spaces, and the preceding primary argument proves (C.INT.3) after this pullback,
hence before it. The real-to-holomorphic coefficient injection of 3.4, applied on E0 , shows
that H 1 (Z0 , O) → H 1 (E0 , O) is nonzero. Since Pic0 (Z0 ) = C∗ , the identity component of the
kernel of Pic0 (Z0 ) → Pic0 (E0 ) is zero. Connectedness of Pic0 (Y ) would therefore make ρ zero,
contradicting (C.INT.1)–(C.INT.2).
    For a non-Kähler elliptic p : Z0 → B, every curve on its minimal model is a reduced elliptic
fibre. The actual covering construction of (Brînzănescu and Moraru, 2005, Lemma 2.2 and §2)
provides a finite cyclic map ψ : Z00 → Z0 and a principal elliptic bundle p0 : Z00 → B 0 such that
a reduced fibre E 0 above E0 maps to E0 by a finite isogeny. To include multiple fibres, take a
base cover whose branching orders are divisible by their multiplicities and normalize the fibre
product. In the local cyclic presentation of a smooth multiple fibre, this removes the transverse
multiplicity and leaves a translation quotient on the reduced fibre, giving exactly the stated
isogeny. Extra branch points over ordinary fibres make the total map branched there, but its
map on the reduced elliptic fibre is an isomorphism.
    On this principal bundle the source’s explicit presentation is

        Z00 = Θ∗ /hτ i,   |τ | > 1,   deg Θ > 0,       Pic0 (Z00 ) = p0∗ Pic0 (B 0 ) × C∗ .   (C.INT.4)

In the last factor a scalar α is the automorphy factor of a line bundle. Its restriction to
E 0 = C∗ /hτ i is that same automorphy line; its kernel is the discrete subgroup hτ i. Consequently
the identity component of the restriction kernel is precisely the compact group p0∗ Pic0 (B 0 ). Our
assumed trivial restriction on E makes ψ ∗ ρ(Pic0 (Y )) lie in that identity component. Gauduchon
degree is a continuous additive homomorphism to R, and is zero on any compact subgroup. On
the other hand this image contains OZ00 (qψ ∗ A0 ), the line of a nonzero effective divisor, which has
strictly positive Gauduchon degree. This contradiction proves the first assertion in both cases,
and proves the stated nonconstant restriction. Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus at most one for the
normalization of the nonconstant image of E, so it is elliptic.


                                                   204
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


    For the last assertion, an effective divisor of zero real Chern class on a minimal class VII
surface is, by (Dloussky and Teleman, 2012, Remark 2.7), an elliptic divisor on a Hopf surface or a
positive multiple of the rational cycle on an Enoki surface. If the source states integral homological
triviality, first multiply the divisor by an integer killing its torsion integral class and use Poincaré
duality; the resulting support and coefficient conclusion descends to the original divisor. Formula
(C.INT.2) also applies to an Enoki minimal model. Thus the adjacent divisor on its resolution
is the full pullback of a rational cycle; all its curve images have rational normalization. On a
Hopf or non-Kähler elliptic neighbouring resolution, the adjacent divisor is the full pullback of a
nonzero divisor consisting of elliptic curves. At least one of their strict transforms must map
into the same intersection. It cannot map to a point or a rational-normalized curve by the result
just proved. This is the required contradiction.

class would therefore be zero and its self-intersection zero, contradicting −2. This contradiction
excludes the Enoki alternative.

the normalization formula gives e(S) = 0. The underlying spaces, and all comparisons just used,
are independent of the positive full-fibre multiplicities. This completes the proof including the
equality criterion.

Proposition 8.31 (The analytic support comparison used here). Let U be a smooth complex
threefold, let S ⊂ U be a compact divisor, and suppose that an embedded resolution r : U 0 → U is
a sequence of blowups with smooth compact centres in S, with D = (r−1 S)red a simple normal

crossings divisor whose components are projective. Let V be a finite-monodromy rational local

obtained from a projective hyperresolution is pure of weight k.
    In this assertion the support-to-restriction morphism is the actual morphism
                      RΓD (U 0 , r∗ V ) −→ colim RΓ(W, r∗ V ) = RΓ(D, r∗ V ).            (C.MH.1)
                                          D⊂W

Neither a Kähler metric on U nor a projective compactification of U is needed for this comparison.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.MH.2); (Steenbrink,
1999, Section 3, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2); (Steenbrink, 1999, Section 4, equation (3));
equation (C.MH.3); equation (C.MH.5).

Proof. First take constant rational coefficients. Write DI for the intersection of the components
indexed by a nonempty set I, and D[p] = |I|=p+1 DI . All these spaces are smooth and projective.
                                           `

The ordinary Čech de Rham complex on D[•] , with its Čech weight filtration and its differential-
form filtration, is therefore a cohomological mixed Hodge complex K(D) for QD . Its cohomology
in degree k has weights at most k.
    Here is the precise analytic construction of the other complex and of the arrow. For each
stratum C = DI , put
                                  K(C log D)C = Ω•U 0 (log D) ⊗ OC .                     (C.MH.2)
The tensor product in (C.MH.2) is a complex: in local normal crossings coordinates, the ideal
of C is preserved by the logarithmic differential. Endow it with the quotient residue filtration
and the filtration by form degree. The quotient map from the restriction of Ω•U 0 (log D) is a
filtered quasi-isomorphism to (C.MH.2). Its rational realization is i∗C Rj∗ QU 0 \D , where j is the

coordinate proof of (Steenbrink, 1999, Section 3, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2); it uses holomorphic
coordinates and the projectivity, or compact Kähler property, of the displayed strata. It does
not use a compactification of their ambient neighbourhood.
     Totalizing (C.MH.2) over D[•] gives the cohomological mixed Hodge complex K(D log D),
with rational realization i∗D Rj∗ QU 0 \D . The natural inclusion K(D) → K(D log D) is a morphism
of mixed Hodge complexes. Its mixed cone, shifted by [−1], computes cohomology with support
in D; the cone projection is exactly (C.MH.1). This is the excision comparison of (Steenbrink,
1999, Section 4, equation (3)), applied on the compact divisor. All complexes just used are
defined on that divisor, and all purity checks are on its projective strata.

Thom isomorphisms, gives

                                                210
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


residues commute with its inclusion maps, with the alternating signs fixed by the ordering of

comparisons agree on overlaps, since they are the residue maps for the holomorphic divisor line
bundles. Thus (C.MH.3) compares the actual support complex, including its arrow to K(D),
rather than only its unfiltered vector spaces. Its displayed term has pure weight q. In total

    Finite coefficients are handled by taking a finite étale cover on which V is constant and then a
rational direct summand of a finite direct sum of its regular representation. The inverse images of
the DI are still projective: a finite holomorphic étale cover of a projective manifold is projective,
since the pullback of an ample bundle is positive. The deck action acts on the displayed mixed
Hodge complexes. Rational idempotents consequently give exactly the same comparison and
weight bounds with coefficients in V .
    By the assumed punctured-tube acyclicity, the support long exact sequence makes (C.MH.1)
an isomorphism on cohomology. Properness of r identifies the punctured tubes upstairs and
downstairs, since its centres lie in S. The map is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures, whose
source has weights at least k and whose target has weights at most k. Strictness therefore proves
that H k (D, r∗ V ) is pure of weight k.
    We finally make the comparison with the original support explicit. The proper degree-one
map between the smooth ambient manifolds has the trace map, defined by oriented Poincaré
duality and proper pushforward, and the projection formula gives

                                r∗ r∗ = id : H k (U, V ) −→ H k (U, V ).                   (C.MH.4)

The same identity holds on every smaller ambient neighbourhood. Passing to the direct limit of
these identities gives an injection

                                   r∗ : H k (S, V ) ,→ H k (D, r∗ V ).                     (C.MH.5)

The identifications in this limit are the usual continuity identifications for a compact triangulable
subset. They can equally be made using cofinal triangulated regular neighbourhoods retracting
onto S and D. Properness ensures that inverse images of neighbourhoods are cofinal; thus the
map in (C.MH.5) is the pullback by D → S.
    This last map is a mixed Hodge morphism as well. One may construct the projective
hyperresolution of S from its projective normalization resolution and resolutions of the conductor
and exceptional curves. To compare it with D[•] , resolve their fibre products over S. Each such
fibre product is a closed analytic subspace of a product of projective spaces already occurring
in the two resolutions; Chow’s theorem makes it algebraic and projective, and its resolution
is projective. The resulting common hyperresolution realizes (C.MH.5) by pullbacks between
projective strata. Cohomological descent then identifies this with the stated mixed Hodge
structures. Injectivity into the pure target proves the assertion.

The second assertion is the Leray sequence of the punctured-disc torus bundle. This argument
uses the smooth fibres of the original map, so it also applies when the full central fibre is mS.
    Choose an embedded resolution of (U, S). Its strict transform is a blowup of Z, hence
projective. Every other exceptional surface is obtained by blowups from a projective bundle over
a compact smooth curve, or from P2 . It is therefore projective. All centres are compact and lie

                           0 −→ CV −→ H 3 (S, V ) −→ H 3 (T, V ) −→ 0,

This also covers the normal case, with the conductor terms zero. The left term is pure of weight

                                           H 3 (S, V ) ≃ H 3 (T, V ).                     (C.MH.11)

    For the resolution π : Z → T , the restriction H 2 (Z, V ) → H 2 (E, V ) to its exceptional curve
is surjective. Indeed V is constant on each exceptional fibre, since it is pulled back from T ; the
Gysin classes of its irreducible exceptional curves restrict by their negative-definite intersection
matrix. That matrix is invertible over Q, separately for each exceptional fibre and each coefficient
vector. The resolution descent sequence therefore gives

            H 3 (T, V ) ≃ H 3 (Z, V ),        H 4 (S, V ) ≃ H 4 (T, V ) ≃ H 4 (Z, V ).    (C.MH.12)

The last two identifications also follow directly because all the omitted loci have real dimension

Proposition 9.2 (Uniform multiple normal-crossings fibres). Let g : Y → C be a proper
holomorphic map from a connected smooth compact complex threefold with H 2 (Y, Q) = 0 to a
smooth compact curve, with connected fibres and smooth general fibre of Euler characteristic zero.

                                           e(S) = τ (S) ≥ 0.                               (C.NC.8)

The normalized base change t = sm is finite étale of degree m over a neighbourhood of S and has
reduced normal-crossings central fibre S 0 . Its possibly disconnected components do not affect the
comparisons e(S 0 ) = me(S) and τ (S 0 ) = mτ (S).

                                                     X

This proves (C.NC.8) directly, with no base-change assumption.
    To verify the additional comparison, locally write t = u(z1 · · · zr )m with u nowhere zero.
The normalization of sm = u(z1 · · · zr )m is given by wm = u and s = wz1 · · · zr . The derivative
of wm − u with respect to w is nonzero because w is a unit. Thus its map to the original

Proposition 9.3 (Reducible normal-crossings   P fibres with unequal multiplicities). Under the
hypotheses on g : Y → C in 9.2, let a fibre be i mi Si with connected reducible normal-crossings
support S. Its multiplicities may be unequal. Then

                                      τ (S) = 0,         e(S) = 0.                          (C.NC.9)

Every normalized conductor is a disjoint union of smooth elliptic curves, and every normalization
component has Euler number zero. More generally, any singular normal-crossings fibre support
under these hypotheses has either no triple point or exactly two triple points; in the latter case it
is irreducible and its normalization is rational.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 9.2; proposition 9.1;
(Peters, 2021, Theorem 2.2); (Biswas et al., 2012, Theorem 3.2).

Proof. First consider a normalization component Ti whose conductor Di is nonempty. If Ti is
Kähler and has nonnegative Kodaira dimension, choose a nonzero section of ωT⊗n           i
                                                                                           and denote
its effective zero divisor by E. The effective divisor E + nDi has rational Chern class zero by
(C.NC.6). Its integral against a Kähler form is positive because Di is nonempty, whereas its
cohomology class gives integral zero. This is impossible. A Kähler Ti is consequently rational or
a blown-up ruled surface. For a ruling Ti → B and a general ruling fibre F , one has KTi · F = −2,
hence Di · F = 2. Some conductor curve therefore dominates B. Its normalization has genus at
most one by 9.1, so Riemann–Hurwitz forces g(B) ≤ 1. The Kähler possibilities have χ(OTi ) = 1
in the rational case and 0 in the elliptic ruled case; their Euler numbers are nonnegative.
    For a non-Kähler Ti , the Enriques–Kodaira table (Peters, 2021, Theorem 2.2) leaves class
VII, Kodaira and properly elliptic minimal models. Class VII has c21 = −b2 and c2 = b2 , so
Noether’s formula gives χ(O) = 0. Kodaira surfaces have both Chern numbers zero. A minimal
non-Kähler elliptic surface has topological Euler number zero by Kodaira’s theorem in the precise
form (Biswas et al., 2012, Theorem 3.2); its canonical square is zero by the same classification
table, so Noether’s formula again gives χ(O) = 0. Blowing up preserves the holomorphic Euler
characteristic and adds one to the topological Euler characteristic. Thus every non-Kähler Ti
has χ(OTi ) = 0 and e(Ti ) ≥ 0. This derives all numerical classification facts used here from the
cited statements.
    A rational normalization component cannot meet a different global component of S. Indeed,
for j 6= i, pull back the canonical section of OY (Sj ) to Ti . It is a nonzero section whose zeros are
precisely the inverse image of Si ∩ Sj . Its line bundle has zero rational first Chern class. For a
smooth rational surface Ti , H 1 (Ti , O) = 0 and H 2 (Ti , Z) is torsion-free, by the corresponding
facts for P2 or a Hirzebruch surface and the blowup formula. The exponential sequence therefore
makes that pulled-back line bundle trivial. A nonzero section of a trivial line bundle on a
connected compact surface is a nonzero constant and has no zeros. Hence Si ∩ Sj is empty. This
proof places no restriction on intersections between two local branches belonging to the same Si .
    The intersection graph of the global components of a connected reducible fibre is connected.
Each component has nonempty conductor, and the preceding paragraph excludes rational
normalizations. Thus every χ(OTi ) is zero, and (C.NC.4) gives τ = 0. Each Cα is now elliptic and
has no marked point. The conductor covering is étale, so the normalized conductor components
are elliptic; there are no nodes of Di , since these would be preimages of triple points. Consequently
e(Di ) = 0. The weighted Euler formula now reads
                                                      X
                                        0 = e(Yt ) =     mi e(Ti ).
                                                     i

All summands are nonnegative and every mi is positive, so each e(Ti ) = 0. Formula (C.NC.5)
gives e(S) = 0.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


   For a singular irreducible support the conductor is nonempty and the same classification
argument gives χ(OT1 ) ∈ {0, 1}, with value one exactly in the rational case. Formula (C.NC.4)
then gives τ = 0 or 2, respectively. This proves the final assertion and also proves that any triple
point lies on an irreducible support with rational normalization.

Proposition 9.5 (Euler localization for torus fibrations). Let g : Y → C be a proper surjective
holomorphic map from a connected compact complex manifold to a compact Riemann surface,
with connected general fibre F . Let Σ ⊂ C contain every critical value. Then Σ can be chosen
finite, and
                                                                                          (C.1)
                                                     X
                             e(Y ) = e(C \ Σ)e(F ) +    e((Yc )red ).
                                                      c∈Σ

For
P a complex threefold with general fibre a complex two-torus this becomes
                                                                              R
                                                                               Y c3 (TY ) = e(Y ) =
  c∈Σ e((Yc )red ).


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The critical locus is a closed analytic subset of Y . Properness and the proper mapping
theorem make its image analytic in C; generic smoothness over characteristic zero makes
this image proper. Thus it is finite. Over C \ Σ, the underlying differentiable map is a
proper submersion. Ehresmann’s theorem makes it a smooth locally trivial fibre bundle. Euler
characteristic with compact supports is additive for the finite stratification by this open part
and the fibres; triangulating the base and trivializing over its cells shows that the open part
contributes ec (C \ Σ)e(F ). The real dimensions of a complex curve and its punctured strata are
even, so ec (C \ Σ) = e(C \ Σ). Nilpotents change no underlying topological space. This proves
(C.1). A two-torus has the cohomology of the real four-torus and Euler number (1 − 1)4 = 0.
Finally the top Chern class of the complex tangent bundle is the Euler class for the complex
orientation, giving the last identity.

Proposition 9.6 (Counterexample: Nonnegativity of every fibre in unrestricted torus fibrations).
There is a smooth projective threefold Y with a proper connected-fibre map Y → P1 , smooth
general fibre an abelian surface, and a reduced normal-crossing fibre of Euler number −2. There
is also such a threefold with a singular reduced fibre of Euler number zero whose three irreducible
components are a blown-up abelian surface, a ruled surface over a genus-two curve, and P2 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let C2 be the smooth projective completion of w2 = z 6 − 1. Its six simple branch points
and the unramified points at infinity give genus two by Riemann–Hurwitz. Let A = Jac(C2 )
and embed C2 in A by p 7→ O(p − p∗ ). This is injective because a principal divisor p − q for
distinct points would define a degree-one map C2 → P1 . It is an immersion because the canonical
system of a genus-two curve has no base point; the explicit differentials dz/w, z dz/w verify that
property, including at infinity. A proper injective immersion is an embedding. Adjunction on the
torus gives NC2 /A = KC2 .
    Blow up A × P1 along C2 × {0}, and denote the resulting smooth projective threefold by Y .
Compose its blowdown with projection to P1 . The exceptional divisor is E = P(KC2 ⊕ OC2 ).
The strict transform of A × {0} is A itself, since blowing up a Cartier divisor in a smooth surface
is an isomorphism. These two components meet along a section isomorphic to C2 . In local
coordinates (u, v, t) with centre (u, t) = (0, 0), a blowup chart has t = uτ , so the fibre is the
reduced normal-crossing divisor uτ = 0. The other chart and the complement give the claimed
global map and connectedness of its fibres. Euler additivity gives

                  e((Y0 )red ) = e(A) + e(E) − e(C2 ) = 0 + 2(−2) − (−2) = −2.

Every other fibre is A.


                                               218
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


    Now blow up one point of the strict-transform component A away from C2 . The new central
fibre has components Blp A, E, and P2 . Its pairwise intersections are C2 and P1 , with no triple
intersection. Its Euler number is

                                      1 − 4 + 3 − (−2) − 2 = 0.

Both modifications have smooth total space and reduced normal-crossing central fibre. For
completeness the integral cohomology is torsion-free. The Betti numbers of A × P1 are
(1, 4, 7, 8, 7, 4, 1); the blowup formula adds H k−2 (C2 , Z) in degree k, giving (1, 4, 8, 12, 8, 4, 1).
The point blowup adds one generator in degrees two and four, giving (1, 4, 9, 12, 9, 4, 1). These
formulas follow from excision for the exceptional projective bundle and its hyperplane class,
whose restriction identifies the new relative summands. Their Euler numbers are respectively
−2 and zero, independently checking the fibre computation. The exact arithmetic is in
code/C_euler.py.

Proposition 9.7 (Euler numbers in semistable toric rank-two models). Consider a rank-two
Mumford model with smooth three-dimensional total space obtained from a unimodular periodic
triangulation of R2 , divided by a rank-two translation lattice acting freely on the total model. Let
V, E, F be the numbers of vertices, edges and triangles in the quotient triangulation. Its reduced
central fibre has Euler number
                                      e(S) = F = 2V ∈ 2Z>0 .                                    (C.2)
Every positive even number occurs in this class. A rank-one model assembled from P1 -bundles
over elliptic curves with their boundary elliptic sections identified has Euler number zero.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Mumford, 1972, Section 6, especially
(6.3)–(6.7)).

Proof. The toric orbit strata of a rank-two central fibre have dimensions two, one and zero.
Its two-dimensional strata are copies of (C∗ )2 , its one-dimensional strata copies of C∗ , and its
zero-dimensional strata correspond to triangles of the quotient triangulation. The first two have
compactly supported Euler number zero. Hence the Euler number is F . The quotient complex is
a real two-torus, so V − E + F = 0, and every edge has two incident triangles, giving 3F = 2E,
with incidences counted even when a face has identified edges. Thus F = 2V .
    For existence, use the lattice N = Z2 ⊕ Z and the standard triangulation of R2 whose triangles
are
                 [u, u + e1 , u + e1 + e2 ],  [u, u + e2 , u + e1 + e2 ], u ∈ Z2 .
These are the Delaunay triangles for the positive integral quadratic form q(u1 , u2 ) = u21 −u1 u2 +u22 .
Take the cones over these triangles at height one and all their faces. They form a fan. Every
three-dimensional cone is generated by a basis of N , because its triangle is unimodular. Gluing
its affine toric charts therefore gives a smooth complex threefold X with a holomorphic map
to the affine line. On each maximal chart there are coordinates x1 , x2 , x3 in which the map is
exactly t = x1 x2 x3 . The central support is consequently reduced and has normal crossings. Over
t 6= 0 the fibre is the common algebraic torus (C∗ )2 .
    Let ΛN = Z(N e1 ) ⊕ Ze2 . For ` ∈ ΛN , the lattice shear

                                          (u, k) 7−→ (u + k`, k)

preserves the fan and induces an automorphism over the base. On the punctured torus chart it is

                                    (z1 , z2 , t) 7−→ (t`1 z1 , t`2 z2 , t).

Restrict to |t| <  < 1. This action is free: away from the central fibre, a fixed point would imply
t`i = 1 for both coordinates and hence ` = 0; on the central fibre, a fixed point would require its

bounded indexing face of the triangulation to be invariant under translation by `, which again
forces ` = 0.

chart of a triangle with vertices u1 , u2 , u3 , write
