On a compact subset of finitely many charts the |xj | are bounded. As t tends to zero, this gives
a uniform lower bound for every λj , and their sum then gives a uniform upper bound. Thus
v remains bounded there. Away from zero the same conclusion follows from compactness in
the torus charts. Translation by ` sends v to v + `. Consequently only finitely many elements
can carry a fixed compact set into itself, or make two fixed compact sets intersect. On the
central fibre this is also immediate from the finitely many indexing faces. The action is properly
discontinuous, so its quotient is a smooth complex threefold.
    The quotient map to the disc is proper. Indeed, translate any punctured-fibre point so that v
belongs to a fixed compact fundamental parallelogram for ΛN . Only finitely many triangles meet
that parallelogram. Choose one containing v; then all its barycentric coordinates are nonnegative,
so |xj | = |t|λj ≤ 1. These finitely many closed unit polydiscs provide compact representatives
for every sequence approaching the central fibre. The central fibre itself has finitely many toric
components modulo ΛN , and each is compact: the star of a vertex is a complete two-dimensional
fan. These facts prove compactness over every closed smaller disc. For t 6= 0 the quotient fibre is
explicitly
                                        C∗ /tN Z × C∗ /tZ ,
a product of elliptic curves. This supplies the actual convergent analytic degeneration, including
its smooth total space and properness, without inferring analytic convergence from a formal
model. The quadratic form supplies the usual polarization data: its difference under every lattice
translation is an integral affine function. Thus the construction is the analytic realization of the
polyhedral model described in (Mumford, 1972, Section 6, especially (6.3)–(6.7)). That source
formulates its construction over a complete discrete valuation ring; the preceding chart and
compactness argument is the complex-disc comparison used here.
    The quotient triangulation has V = N and F = 2N , as required. For rank one every
normalization component is a P1 -bundle over an elliptic curve, with Euler number zero, and the
identified boundary sections also have Euler number zero. Additivity gives the result.

Proposition 9.8 (The normal jets along cusp, tacnode and triple curves). Let Y be a smooth
complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0, let S be a reduced Cartier divisor, and let D ⊂ Sing S be a
smooth compact connected curve. Suppose the general plane section transverse to D has one of
the equations
                       x2 − y 3 = 0,      x2 − y 4 = 0,   xy(x − y) = 0.                (C.J.1)
Then g(D) ≤ 1. For g(D) = 1, the indicated transverse analytic type is constant along all of D.
The inverse image of D in the normalization is respectively an isomorphic copy, a finite etale
cover of degree two, or a finite etale cover of degree three. Each connected component C of that
cover has genus one and normal line of degree zero in the normalization, which is smooth near
C. At these three transverse types, the inverse Jacobian ideal pulls back into the line allowing at
most a simple pole on each normalization branch.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.J.2); equation (C.J.3);
proposition 5.5.



                                                  220
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


Proof. Put N = ND/Y and B = OY (S)|D . Since every ambient line bundle has zero rational
first Chern class, deg B = deg KY |D = 0. Adjunction for the smooth curve gives

                          det N = KD ⊗ KY−1 |D ,        deg N = 2g(D) − 2.                     (C.J.2)

A local defining section of S belongs to ID 2 . Its quadratic normal jet is a well-defined section of

Sym N ∗ ⊗ B. In the first two cases its generic rank is one. Its saturated radical R ⊂ N is a
     2

line subbundle on the smooth curve, and Q = N /R is a line bundle. The quadratic jet gives a
nonzero section of B ⊗ Q−2 , so deg Q ≤ 0.
    In the cusp case, the cubic jet on the radical is an intrinsic nonzero section of B ⊗ R−3 . To
check its independence, choose coordinates (x, y, z) with D = (x = y = 0) and R the y direction.
A change of lift of a radical vector changes the cubic by a Hessian term with one radical argument,
which is zero. Changing the local retraction to D differentiates the identity that the quadratic jet
vanishes on R, again giving zero. Thus the local cubics glue across all points, including possible
zeros of the quadratic coefficient. Consequently deg R ≤ 0. Equation (C.J.2) proves g(D) ≤ 1.
    In the tacnode case the radical cubic vanishes identically. Write the relevant normal terms as

                                          ax2 + bxy 2 + cy 4 .

Completing the square has invariant numerator

                            ∆ = ac − b2 /4 ∈ H 0 (D, B 2 ⊗ Q−2 ⊗ R−4 ).                        (C.J.3)

This numerator is holomorphic even at a zero of a. Under x 7→ x + uy 2 , the coefficients become
b + 2au and c + bu + au2 , and (C.J.3) is unchanged. Linear changes preserving the radical give
precisely the displayed line-bundle weights. Changes of the retraction to D add terms containing
the radical cubic or a radical Hessian argument, so also leave this quartic numerator unchanged.
These checks give its global definition. It is nonzero by the generic tacnode assumption. Hence

                 deg Q ≤ 0,       deg Q + 2 deg R ≤ 0,           deg N ≤ 12 deg Q ≤ 0.

This proves the same genus bound.
    For the ordinary triple case the quadratic jet is identically zero. The binary cubic normal
jet is a section of Sym3 N ∗ ⊗ B. Its discriminant is a nonzero section of B 4 ⊗ (det N ∗ )6 . The
discriminant has degree four in the cubic coefficients and weight six under a linear change of
the two normal coordinates; these weights also follow by writing it as the square of the product
of the three pairwise determinants of the linear factors. Its nonnegative divisor degree gives
deg N ≤ 0 and the genus bound again.
    When g(D) = 1, all the inequalities are equalities. In the cusp case both the quadratic and
radical cubic sections have no zeros. In the tacnode case a and ∆ have no zeros. In the triple
case the cubic discriminant has no zeros. The holomorphic splitting lemma with parameter z
completes the square in the first two cases. The remaining one-variable term is respectively a
unit times y 3 or y 4 ; taking a local root of the unit gives the corresponding equation in (C.J.1). In
the triple case its three distinct tangent lines split after an etale ordering cover; the holomorphic
implicit function theorem gives three smooth branches meeting transversely in each normal plane.
Straightening two branches to the axes and rescaling the third branch’s unit gives the third
equation. Thus these are constant transverse types throughout D. In particular no other singular
curve meets D.
    In the cusp normalization, x = u3 , y = u2 , up to the choice of which coordinate is the radical.
Its normal line P = NC/Se satisfies P 2 = R and P 3 = Q, so has degree zero. For the tacnode,
the two branches have x = ±y 2 and normal line the pullback of R, again of degree zero. Their
permutation cover is etale because ∆ is nowhere zero. For the ordinary triple, order the three
tangent lines by a finite etale cover. Three pairwise transverse line subbundles in a rank-two

                                                 221
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


bundle make it a sum P ⊕ P : the third is a graph of an isomorphism between the first two. Since
the determinant has degree zero, deg P = 0. Each normalization branch has this tangent-root
normal line. Etale descent gives the claimed degrees and covers before ordering.
    Finally the inverse-Jacobian assertion can be checked on these exact transverse equations.
For the cusp, R = C{u2 , u3 } and J −1 = u−1 C{u}, as in 5.5. For the tacnode, normalization
functions are pairs whose constant and linear terms agree. A putative pole of order two in a
fractional multiplier has leading coefficients (a1 , a2 ). Multiplication by 2x forces a1 = −a2 at
order zero, while multiplication by −4y 3 forces a1 = a2 at order one. Thus both vanish. For the
ordinary triple, use branches (0, u), (u, 0), (u, u). The partial derivatives have leading coefficient
vectors (−1, 0, 1) and (0, 1, −1) at order two. A pole of order two would make both products
constant on all three branches, forcing all its leading coefficients to vanish. A pole of larger order
is already excluded by regularity of these products on normalization. These computations prove
the simple-pole bound. The covariance and leading-coefficient equations are checked exactly in
code/C_jets.py.

permutation is killed its action is a translation on the torus and induces the identity on cohomology.

cohomology sheaf. It acts identically on the corresponding cohomology groups of those sheaves

difference from the identity is nilpotent on that cohomology. This proves quasi-unipotence using
the actual analytic normal-crossings comparison; no ambient Kähler assumption enters. In

    They preserve SNC supports as well. Choose the point on a single component away from the

transverse to that line. Near any of their four intersection points write the map as t = (ru)m , with
exceptional component r = 0, old component u = 0, and quartic centre (r, v) = (0, 0). Its blowup

component is still a coordinate hyperplane; away from these four points the same assertion uses
only two coordinates. These explicit charts verify the claimed SNC zero-Euler realization of
every row. After the Euler number is zero, one additional +2 operation and one −2 operation
over the same value leave it zero and introduce exceptional components. Performing this at both
0 and ∞ ensures precisely two reducible singular fibres, including the identity-monodromy row.
All other fibres remain the original smooth tori.

matrix-to-signature map itself forgets information: for example I4 and I4 + E12 have the same
characteristic polynomial and zero signature, while their minimal polynomials differ. The table
therefore records precisely the stated invariant and does not supply an analytic isomorphism
classification of fillings.

Proposition 9.10 (K3 components are elliptic in positive algebraic dimension; algebraic
dimension zero has an exact occurrence criterion). Let f : U → ∆ be a proper holomorphic map
from a smooth complex threefold, with connected two-torus fibres over ∆∗ . Let Si be an irreducible
component of its central support, and suppose that a resolution of Siν has a K3 minimal model
M . If a(M ) > 0, there is an actual elliptic fibration M → P1 .
    Among K3 surfaces of algebraic dimension zero, the minimal birational classes which occur in
this way are exactly the minimal resolutions of cyclic quotients of complex two-tori by nontrivial
symplectic automorphisms without eigenvalue one on the tangent space. After translating the
origin, the generator is linear of order n = 2, 3, 4, or 6. The quotient singularities and exceptional
configurations are exactly

           n quotient singularities number of exceptional curves e(A/hgi)
           2         16A1                       16                  8

Here the cyclic quotient in the criterion is required to have algebraic dimension zero; the table
applies to the cyclic K3 quotient models in every algebraic dimension.
    Every cyclic quotient K3 minimal class just described is realized by a compact smooth threefold
over P1 with connected torus general fibre and with both special reduced supports of Euler
characteristic zero. The central support has a component whose normalization resolution has
exactly that K3 minimal model. The total space and construction are projective when the given
torus is projective.

    The two-dimensional space of fields on E in 7.7 has generic rank one or two. In rank one, 7.10
gives an actual rational or elliptic fibration on a birational model of M . The rational alternative
would make all positive pluricanonical sections vanish, by restricting them to its smooth general

    In rank two, 7.11 gives χ(OE ) = 0 and its precise torus or elliptic-fibration alternatives. First
suppose a(M ) = a(E) = 1. In the elliptic alternative, the connected-fibre map q : E 0 → B has

                                          M(E 0 ) = q ∗ M(B).                                  (C.K3.4)

Indeed every meromorphic function is algebraic over any one nonconstant function on B and
hence constant on the connected general fibres; the proper graph descends it, as in (C.RF.9). The
equality makes this field intrinsic and therefore G-invariant. Resolve the graph of q equivariantly
and take its Stein factor. The group acts on that factor, and the actual finite quotient is a map
to B/G whose general fibre is F /K, with K = ker(G → Aut B). This is the same quotient and
Stein comparison proved in 7.10. Its general fibre is connected and rational or elliptic; the K3
form again excludes the rational case. In the torus alternative the minimal model of E is a torus
and the cyclic quotient argument below applies.
     Now suppose a(M ) = a(E) = 2. We work on the smooth projective minimal model E0 , to
which the finite action descends. In rank two, (C.K3.3) and χ(OE0 ) = 0, together with the
compact surface classification already used in 4.9 (Peters, 1990, Theorem 3.1), leave the following
possibilities. If κ(E0 ) = 0, it is an Abelian surface: K3 and Enriques surfaces have coherent Euler
characteristic 2 and 1, and bielliptic surfaces have pg = 0. If κ(E0 ) = 1, its elliptic Iitaka fibration
is intrinsic. More explicitly, G acts on each space of pluricanonical sections, so a sufficiently large
pluricanonical map, its equivariant graph resolution, and its Stein factor are all G-equivariant.
The connected general fibres are elliptic. Taking the quotient gives the actual fibration with
general fibre F /K just described. It is elliptic because its total quotient has the K3 minimal
model. Thus the only remaining positive-dimensional case is a cyclic quotient of a two-torus.

to M itself. Take an actual common resolution

    Finally we prove the occurrence assertion with its specified compact comparison. Start with
any torus A and one of the actual cyclic symplectic actions above, of order n. Form the finite

           W = (A × P1s )/h(a, s) 7→ (g(a), ζn s)i,       W −→ P1t ,   t = sn .         (C.K3.10)

and at a generic point of each of these two original components. The strict transform of the
latter maps properly birationally to the specified torus quotient. Its normalization resolution
therefore has the K3 minimal model already proved in 7.12. The resulting smooth compact
total space has connected fibres: its Stein factor over P1 has generic degree one and hence is the
identity finite map to the normal base.
    Each of its two reduced special supports has even Euler characteristic by 7.1. Apply the
actual vertical point and quartic-curve blowup operations of 7.4 separately over zero and infinity.
They change the reduced Euler number by +2 or −2 until it is zero, preserve the punctured torus
family, and leave the original strict component birational to the same torus quotient. Resolution
and these blowups are projective morphisms when A is projective. This supplies all asserted
compact realizations, including every class of algebraic dimension zero in the criterion.
    The algebraic-dimension-zero occurrence criterion is thus an equivalence. In positive algebraic
dimension the theorem gives the elliptic-fibration restriction and realizes its cyclic quotient
subfamily by the explicit compact construction.

Proposition 9.11 (K3 components in arbitrary torus fillings are exactly the cyclic generalized
Kummer surfaces). The K3 minimal birational classes occurring as normalization components
of proper two-torus degenerations are exactly the minimal resolutions of cyclic quotients of
complex two-tori by nontrivial symplectic automorphisms. The generator has no eigenvalue one
on the tangent space and, after an actual translation of the origin, is linear of order 2, 3, 4, or
6. The exceptional configurations are those of (C.K3.1). This criterion holds in every algebraic
dimension.
    Every such class occurs in a smooth compact filling with both special reduced supports of
Euler number zero, by the explicit quotient and balancing construction of 9.10. In particular the
algebraic-dimension-zero equivalence of that statement extends to all K3 components.

The corrected analytic contraction theorem and its application. We use the Main
Theorem of (Nakano, 1970, p. 484), in its corrected and strengthened form in (Fujiki and

projective-space bundle, the condition that its ambient normal line restricts to O(−1) on every
projective fibre produces a smooth analytic blowdown with that bundle as its exceptional divisor.
The supplement repairs the cohomology argument and proves that this normal condition suffices.
These are the versions read and used here; their local blowdown maps glue by the actual
isomorphisms off the exceptional divisor.

The Hopf boundary is the individually marked diagonal pair. Pull KH + D ≃ OH back

reduced nonempty pullback boundary cannot satisfy K + D = 0 there.
    For a diagonal contraction, the lifted anticanonical section is g(z, w)∂z ∧ ∂w , where Hartogs
extends g across zero and
                                     g(αz, βw) = αβg(z, w).                              (C.CZ.11)
In the nonresonant case its only possible monomial is zw. In the resonant case a further central
power has multipliers (γ p , γ q ), with coprime positive p, q. Its monomials have weight p + q.
For p, q > 1 this again gives only zw. For p > 1, q = 1 the equation is g = w(az + bwp ), and
reducedness requires a 6= 0. The triangular coordinate change z 7→ z + (b/a)wp commutes with
the contraction and gives the two axes. The symmetric case is identical. When p = q = 1,
the reduced quadratic is a product of two distinct linear forms, and an invertible linear change
commuting with the scalar contraction gives the axes. Thus the pulled boundary is exactly two
axes in every case.
    Their unique logarithmic two-form, up to a constant, is dz/z ∧ dw/w. A deck lift preserving
both axes individually is diagonal by the contraction-unit argument of 11.14 and fixes this form.
A lift interchanging the axes is a diagonal map followed by the interchange and negates the form.
The nonzero section of KH (D) pulls back to a deck-invariant section, so no interchange occurs.
Consequently the two images are distinct elliptic curves, the full deck group is diagonal, and the
original marked pair is precisely one of the diagonal primary or secondary Hopf pairs of 11.12.

order, since the homotopy sequence injects π1 (C∗ ) when π2 (E) = 0.

Realization with a nowhere-zero local volume. For every such marked cycle, 11.12 gives
the actual proper plumbing, the compact two-ended period family, and its exact punctured-family
gluing. It retains all marked components and elliptic maps. We check the required local canonical
condition on this construction.
    On its common period charts put

                                          Ω = dt ∧ dη1 ∧ dη2 .                           (C.CZ.13)

Here η is the common vector coordinate obtained from each component chart by its actual
moving frame Pi (t). Thus every overlap has identity linear part in this common frame. Every
period and affine edge translation depends holomorphically on t; its differential changes the vector
differentials only by multiples of dt. Thus this three-form descends through the actual lattice
and collar maps. It is nonzero on component cores. At a double curve the relative two-form is a
holomorphic unit times dx/x ∧ dz, where z is an elliptic coordinate and xy = t. Hence

                                 dt ∧ (dx/x ∧ dz) = dy ∧ dx ∧ dz.                        (C.CZ.14)

The right side is holomorphic and nowhere zero. The moving Hopf and ruled frames have nonzero
determinant at the central value, so the displayed unit never vanishes after shrinking the disc.
The form therefore extends across all of S as a nowhere-zero three-form. Its evaluation orders
are equal to zero. The compact realization in the statement now follows from 11.12, with the
same verification at its conjugate fibre. The smooth torus case is its literal product family.

Exact relation to the primary modification literature. Kulikov’s definition of a good
degeneration in (Kulikov, 1977, p. 958) is the smooth-total, reduced SNC condition used here. Its
Lemmas 2.1–2.2 give the same principal-divisor and coherent-stratum maps as (C.CZ.5)–(C.CZ.8).
The general canonical modification statement is (Kulikov, 1981, Theorem 10 ): a good degeneration
of surfaces with trivial canonical class admits a good modification with trivial total canonical
class precisely under its stated minimum-order condition on class VII components. The present
equal-order hypothesis gives the actual identity comparison to such a target through Ω/f k . The
zero-case classification above is proved on that given neighbourhood and supplies the explicit
marked-cycle maps and compact occurrence. The 1981 appendix also records the correction to
the 1977 Enriques modification assertion; the cited line and Euler comparisons are the displayed
1977 lemmas.
    Kamenova’s author-hosted primary text (Kamenova, nd, Theorem 3.1) assumes a Kähler
total space and trivial KX . Its necessary list contains a smooth torus, elliptic-ruled paths and
cycles, and a rational case with a triangulated torus as dual complex. The residue and finite-trace
maps in (C.CZ.10) exclude a terminal elliptic bisection, so the path alternative contributes
no additional zero-Euler support in the stated smooth-component setting. This sharpens that
necessary list. In the Kähler case Hopf components are also excluded by restriction of the Kähler
form: their vanishing real H 2 would make its positive square integrate to zero by Stokes. The
present proof keeps the actual component and collar maps without a Kähler hypothesis and
supplies compact occurrence of every marked zero-Euler cycle specified in the statement.

maximum case. Pull (C.MR.5) to its primary contraction cover. Its only curves are the two axes.
If both occur, the anticanonical eigenfunction equation gives αa1 −1 β a2 −1 = 1. Since |α|, |β| < 1
and ai ≥ 1, both exponents are zero. If only one occurs, the same equation gives a positive
integral resonance between α and β, contradicting algebraic dimension zero. Thus this case has
exactly the two equal-order boundaries.

its neighbours at that same maximum. An equal-order edge cannot lead to one of the strict-

displayed cycle or smooth torus. If the orders are not all equal, a maximum Hopf leaf exists. Its
boundary is elliptic and its normal line has finite exact order.
The actual field space aligns a vertical elliptic fibration. We record the comparison needed
to propagate from that leaf. On any component T of the current reduced smooth SNC family,
the actual multiplicity-one construction (C.CF.3)–(C.CF.7) gives two independent commuting
meromorphic fields, all of whose constant combinations are semicomplete. Their polar divisors
are confined to the boundary of T . Indeed the original module consists of holomorphic fields on
U ; multiplying its basis by meromorphic functions of t introduces poles only in the central fibre.
Cancelling the generic order on T makes the restriction holomorphic at every point of T away
from its intersections with the other components. This is a restriction on the original component,
with no different covering surface substituted.
    Let q : T → B be an actual connected-fibre elliptic map for which every boundary is vertical.
Over the complement of finitely many values the fields are holomorphic on the entire compact
fibres. Their coefficients in a base direction are holomorphic functions on each such fibre and
hence constant. Proper Stein descent gives commuting meromorphic fields on B.
    The projected fields have no poles, by the exact continuation argument in (C.RF.1). At a pole
of order r, the primitive of the one-dimensional time form vanishes to order r + 1. Continue one
inverse branch around its time value, using a small loop whose lifted base paths avoid all other
bad values. The preimage under q of the compact union of these paths is compact and contained
in the holomorphic locus. The upstairs solution therefore continues along that whole loop. Its
endpoint has a different base value, contradicting semicompleteness. This proves holomorphy of
the projected fields without an assumed descent theorem for semicompleteness.
    If a projection is nonzero, any other commuting projection is a constant multiple of it: the
derivative of their meromorphic ratio along the nonzero field is zero. Subtracting that constant
multiple upstairs gives a nonzero vertical commuting field. The actual period-preservation map
(C.RF.2) for this transverse/vertical pair shows that the integral elliptic periods are constant
and monodromy is the identity. If both projections are zero, the two fields are translation fields
on each regular elliptic fibre. Their nonconstant meromorphic ratio is constant there, so its
connected Stein fibres are exactly those of q. Applying 7.15 to this actual first integral gives the

A torsion-normal elliptic boundary on a ruled component. Consider a component T
meeting a known elliptic boundary C whose normal line is torsion. It has C 2 = 0. A minimal
rational surface contains no such elliptic curve. On P2 a smooth elliptic curve has degree three

a > 0. Its arithmetic genus equation is

It is distinct from C0 and has b ≥ na. The only possibilities have a = 2, b = n + 2, n ≤ 2, with
square eight, or a = 3, n = 1, b = 3, with square nine. These include F1 . None has square zero.

Proposition 9.15 (A torsion-normal elliptic boundary cannot lie on a rational component). Let
f : U → ∆ be a proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori, with smooth total threefold
and full reduced SNC central fibre. Let P be a rational component, with no minimality assumption.
It cannot have a smooth elliptic boundary curve J whose normal line NJ/P is torsion and which
is disjoint from every other boundary curve on P .
     In particular a rational component, including a rational elliptic surface and any point blowups
of a rational surface, cannot be adjacent to an elliptic Hopf component or a nonlinear Hopf
component. No Hopf leaf can have a rational parent. The assertion permits rational double curves
and triple points elsewhere in the central fibre. It imposes neither a zero-Euler hypothesis nor a
minimality hypothesis on the other components.
     The obstruction is obtained on the actual component. Its torsion normal produces the connected
elliptic pencil |mJ|, where m = ord NJ/P . The actual limiting translation fields force this pencil
to have identity integral monodromy. After its vertical exceptional curves are contracted, it has
only smooth multiple fibres and coherent Euler characteristic zero, contradicting χ(OP ) = 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (C.RH.1);
equation (C.RH.4); proposition 7.7; (Kodaira, 1963, Theorem 6.2; Section 8(iv)(11), p. 585);
Ulmer and Urzúa (2021, Section 2.3, pp. 5–6); equation (C.RH.8); equation (C.RH.7);
proposition 10.11; proposition 11.5; proposition 11.8.

Proof. The exact pencil made by the torsion normal. Suppose that such a component
and curve exist, and put N = NJ/P , with exact order m ≥ 1. The degree of N is zero, hence
J 2 = 0. For every k ≥ 1 use the actual divisor restriction sequence

                        0 −→ OP ((k − 1)J) −→ OP (kJ) −→ N ⊗k −→ 0.                        (C.RH.1)

For 1 ≤ k < m, the last line is a nontrivial degree-zero line on the elliptic curve. It has both H 0
and H 1 zero: a nonzero section would be nowhere zero, and Serre duality gives the H 1 assertion.
Since P is rational, H 1 (P, OP ) = 0 and H 0 (P, OP ) = C. Induction in the actual long exact
sequences gives

                   h0 (P, OP (kJ)) = 1,     H 1 (P, OP (kJ)) = 0    (0 ≤ k < m).           (C.RH.2)

At k = m, the restriction in (C.RH.1) is onto H 0 (J, OJ ) = C. Thus

           h0 (P, OP (mJ)) = 2,       H 0 (P, OP (mJ)) −→ H 0 (J, OJ ) is onto.            (C.RH.3)

One section has divisor mJ; a second restricts to a nonzero constant on J. Their common zero
locus is empty: on J the second does not vanish, and off J the first does not vanish. They define
the actual holomorphic map

                                q0 : P −→ P1 ,         q0−1 (∞) = mJ.                      (C.RH.4)

    We check its connectedness through the Stein map, rather than assuming that a pencil has
connected fibres. Write P −

The actual translation fields align this pencil. The component has full multiplicity one.
The saturated relative translation module of 7.7 supplies two commuting meromorphic fields
V1 , V2 on P , independent over C, all of whose constant combinations are semicomplete. Their
polar divisors are contained in the boundary of P . Indeed they are obtained from holomorphic
ambient relative fields by meromorphic base coefficients; cancelling the generic order on P leaves
a holomorphic restriction at every point of P away from the other central components. This is
the original surface and its actual fields, not a replacement cover.
     Remove the finitely many base values supporting a boundary, a singular fibre or a vertical
zero of the relevant field. On each remaining compact elliptic fibre the fields are holomorphic.
Their base coefficients are holomorphic functions on that fibre and hence are constant. The
connected-fibre map therefore descends them to commuting meromorphic fields on B = P1 .
     These projected fields have no poles. For clarity, at a pole of order a > 0, the primitive of
the one-dimensional time form has a zero of order a + 1. Continue one inverse branch around its
corresponding time value. Choose the small loop so that its lifted base paths avoid every other
bad value. Their compact union has a compact inverse image under the proper map q, contained
in the holomorphic locus of the upstairs field. The upstairs solution therefore continues along
the entire loop. Its final base value is a different inverse branch, contradicting the single-valued
maximal solution of a semicomplete field. This is the actual continuation map used in (C.RF.1)
and (C.MR.8); it does not require a minimal surface.
     If one projection is nonzero, the other is a constant multiple, because the derivative of their
meromorphic ratio along a nonzero commuting curve field is zero. Subtract that constant multiple.
The resulting nonzero vertical field is a translation field on each compact regular elliptic fibre.
Its commuting transverse field identifies neighbouring fibres and preserves its time form. Its
two marked integral periods are therefore locally constant and, by analytic continuation on the
connected smooth base, globally single-valued. Integration of a nonzero elliptic time form is
injective on H1 (F, Z); the integral monodromy is the identity.
     If both projections vanish, the fields are vertical translation fields on each regular fibre.
Their meromorphic ratio is a nonconstant function pulled back from B, since the two fields are
independent over C. Its connected Stein fibres are exactly those of the map q just constructed. The
actual ambient return germs (C.RG.4)–(C.RG.12) apply to this same first integral: λi = di − ki H
for its two continued integral periods. The right-hand side is single-valued, and injectivity of
elliptic period integration again gives identity integral monodromy. No elliptic pencil on an
ambient neighbourhood has been assumed.
Relative minimization and the exact singular-fibre comparison. Contract only the
vertical (−1)-curves of q. Each contraction is the actual smooth surface blowdown of a rational
exceptional curve, and q descends because that curve is one fibre of the blowdown and maps to a
point of B. There are finitely many such steps, since each lowers b2 . The resulting map
                                          qmin : Pmin −→ P1                               (C.RH.7)
is relatively minimal. It has the same marked smooth fibres and the same identity monodromy.
Moreover χ(OPmin ) = χ(OP ) = 1, by the direct-image equality for every ordinary point blowup.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


   We now use the relatively minimal singular-fibre classification, precisely in its stated scope:
(Kodaira, 1963, Theorem 6.2; Section 8(iv)(11), p. 585) and Ulmer and Urzúa (2021, Section 2.3,
pp. 5–6). Its nonmultiple non-smooth types have monodromies conjugate to nontrivial unipotent
matrices, their negatives, or the nonidentity finite-order matrices of orders 2, 3, 4, 6. Only the
smooth type I0 has identity monodromy.
    For a full multiple fibre write its local function as t = uha , with u a unit and the divisor of h
primitive. Normalize the actual base change t = sa by

                                          wa = u,         s = wh.                           (C.RH.8)

The resulting surface map is étale over the original surface, because w is a root of a unit. Its
monodromy is the a-th power of the original one and is therefore the identity. It is still relatively
minimal by the following canonical intersection comparison. For every irreducible component C
of a fibre F below, F · C = 0 gives C 2 ≤ 0. Adjunction gives KPmin · C = 2pa (C) − 2 − C 2 ≥ 0,
except possibly for a smooth rational curve of square zero or minus one. The latter is excluded
by relative minimality. In the square-zero case, all intersections with the other fibre components
vanish. Connectedness would give F = bC, contradicting KPmin · F = 0. Thus every component
has nonnegative canonical intersection. Their positive weighted sum is KPmin · F = 0, so each
intersection is zero. For the actual étale covering map π in (C.RH.8), Kup = π ∗ Kdown . Any
vertical (−1)-curve E upstairs would then satisfy Kup · E = deg(E → C)Kdown · C = 0, contrary
to adjunction, which gives minus one. This uses the cycle pushforward and does not assume that
the image curve is embedded or nonsingular. Its primitive Kodaira fibre must consequently be
I0 . Thus every fibre of qmin is a positive multiple of a smooth elliptic curve.
     The oriented period ratio is now a single-valued holomorphic map from a punctured P1 to
the upper half-plane. Its bounded Cayley transform extends across the missing points and is
constant on P1 . All regular fibres have one fixed Jacobian. Their transition maps are translations,
since the integral monodromy is the identity. At a multiple value use (C.RH.8). The free central
elliptic inertia is a translation, and its action on H 1 (O) is trivial. Taking the actual invariant
coefficient functions gives

                         (qmin )∗ OPmin = OP1 ,       R1 (qmin )∗ OPmin = OP1 .             (C.RH.9)

The coherent Leray sequence now yields χ(OPmin ) = 1 − 1 = 0, contradicting the preserved value
one in (C.RH.7). This proves the obstruction without applying a minimal-only assertion to the
original P .
The Hopf interface. On an elliptic Hopf component every curve is a fibre support and has
normal of finite exact order, by the actual normalized-root map in 10.11. A nonlinear Hopf has
its one axis, whose normal has exact resonance order, including the secondary comparison of
11.5. Distinct Hopf curves are disjoint. There can therefore be no triple point on an interface
with a Hopf component: such a point would make two different boundary curves meet inside
that Hopf surface. The actual xy = t normal-product map gives

                                          NJ/P ⊗ NJ/H = OJ .                              (C.RH.10)

It makes NJ/P torsion, and the same absence of triple points makes J disjoint from every other
boundary curve on P . The obstruction just proved applies.
    Every terminal Hopf pair has one of these torsion-normal axes, by the exact one-boundary
canonical and character comparison in 11.8. The two nontorsion axes of an algebraic-dimension-
zero diagonal Hopf cannot form such a leaf. This proves all the asserted parent and interface
exclusions.

curves and cannot contain a nodal rational cycle. The other nonrational possibility is the Hopf

in (C.ER.2) force m = m0 .

The inverse image of the original singular point is a chain of two projective lines. In the first chart
of (C.CP.7) the old and new curves have equations (a, h) = (0, 0) and (a, s) = (0, 0); they meet
once transversely. Charts (C.CP.6)–(C.CP.7) complete each to a projective line. No exceptional
divisor is introduced. Outside the origin the respective ideals are Cartier, so these maps are
isomorphisms there.
    The blowups globalize without an analytic gluing choice. The ideal (u, a) is the ideal of
the Weil diagonal R ,→ X. The ideal (u, b) is the Weil graph of the global automorphism
(x, y, t) 7→ (ρx, y, t) of R; after the first blowup take its strict transform. Each of these divisors is
Cartier off the six specified singular points. Their projective blowups therefore give a smooth
projective threefold Y and a proper small map π : Y → X, with precisely the local charts above.
Set f = gπ, using the common projection of the fibre product. It agrees with the original product
of elliptic curves away from the six values. Its fibres are connected, because the product fibres
and every fibre of the two blowdowns are connected.
    The original central support at each of the six values is the product S0 = C × C of a cuspidal
cubic with itself. It is reduced and irreducible. Since π has no exceptional divisors, the full
fibre upstairs is its single strict transform, still reduced. Its normalization resolution is rational:
the function field is unchanged from that of the finite birational parametrization P1 × P1 → S0 .
This assertion is birational; we do not discard the exceptional curves of the actual normalization
resolution.
    Topologically a cuspidal cubic is S 2 . Its finite normalization is bijective, so compactness
makes it a homeomorphism. Hence S0 is homeomorphic to S 2 × S 2 . The restriction S → S0 is
an isomorphism off the cusp-pair point and replaces that point by the chain E of two projective
lines. The quotient S/E → S0 is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff
space, hence a homeomorphism. Choose a finite triangulation of (S, E). Its cofibration sequence
identifies the reduced homology of S/E with the relative homology of (S, E). Since H2 (E, Z) = Z2
and E is simply connected, the long exact sequence gives
                            H4 (S, Z) = Z,       H3 (S, Z) = H1 (S, Z) = 0,
                                                                                               (C.CP.8)
                                0 −→ Z −→ H2 (S, Z) −→ Z2 −→ 0.

The last sequence splits as a sequence of abelian groups. Van Kampen for the same cofibration
shows π1 (S/E) = π1 (S)/hhπ1 (E)ii. Thus π1 (S) = 1. Universal coefficients now give the integral
cohomology in (C.CP.1), and its Euler number is 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.
   The fibre product is a local complete intersection in R × R, cut out by the inverse image of
the base diagonal. Adjunction and (C.CP.4) give

                                ωX = p∗1 KR ⊗ p∗2 KR ⊗ f ∗ TB ≃ OX .                          (C.CP.9)

Its generator pulls back to a nowhere-vanishing canonical form on Y away from the small
exceptional curves. Its coefficients and the coefficients of its inverse extend across that codimension-
two set by Hartogs’ theorem in a local canonical frame. Hence KY = OY . Adjunction makes
ωS = OS . Proper flatness over the smooth base preserves the holomorphic Euler characteristic,
so χ(OS ) = χ(OEt2 ) = 0. Connectedness and Serre duality then give (h0 , h1 , h2 )(OS ) = (1, 2, 1).
    We include the ambient groups, with their comparison maps. A type-II local elliptic
monodromy has characteristic polynomial x2 − x + 1, so T − I is an integral isomorphism.
This also follows directly from the cyclic sixth-root trivialization of y 2 = x3 + τ . The smooth
part of the fibration has fundamental group generated by its fibre lattice and base meridians.
Its inclusion into Y is surjective on fundamental groups, by perturbing loops off the central
divisor. The pair of zero sections extends over every special value and kills each base meridian
in Y . Conjugation by one such meridian therefore kills the image of T − I on each of the two
elliptic lattices. Since those two maps are unimodular, the whole fibre lattice is killed. Thus
π1 (Y ) = 1. Projectivity and KY = OY give (h0 , h1 , h2 , h3 )(OY ) = (1, 0, 0, 1) by Hodge theory
and Serre duality. The identical argument for R gives b1 (R) = 0. Its six cuspidal fibres give
e(R) = 12, hence b2 (R) = 10. Moreover KR = g ∗ O(−1) makes every positive plurigenus zero.
The surface classification therefore makes R rational, so its Picard group has rank ten.
    Let K = C(t) and let EK be the generic elliptic curve of R. Restriction of divisors gives
a surjection Pic(R) → Pic(EK ): close a generic divisor in the smooth surface. Its kernel is
generated, up to linear equivalence, by the full fibre, because every fibre is irreducible. The
zero section splits the degree map on Pic(EK ), whose degree-zero part is EK (K). Consequently
EK (K) has rank eight.
    Apply the same divisor restriction to Y and its generic fibre AK = EK × EK . It is surjective
and its vertical kernel has rank one, since all six singular fibres of Y are irreducible. The
degree-zero Picard group of AK is its dual abelian variety’s K-points, which have rank sixteen
under the product principal polarization. Its Néron–Severi group has rank four. To verify this
last number explicitly, use the two factors, the diagonal, and the graph of the automorphism ρ.

    Euler localization now gives e(Y ) = 6 · 6 = 36. Poincaré duality and b1 = 0 yield b3 = 8; the

    Finally a sufficiently small compact fibre tube retracts onto S. Its fundamental group is
therefore trivial. There is no nontrivial finite local system there, and no nonzero integral degree-
one class to restrict to the nearby torus. The example consequently disproves the proposed
unrestricted replacement for the character construction itself, with its actual comparison map.
The exact coordinate identities, intersection matrix, and all displayed integer ranks are checked
in code/root_cusp_product.py and its saved output.

used here.

under its strict scalar contraction forces every power-series coefficient to vanish. Hence pg = 0.

    Finally, a rational curve in Pm would lift through the finite étale map (C.PE.12), since P1
is simply connected. Its two projections to the positive-genus curves would be constant. The
Hopf components have no rational curve either: a map from P1 lifts to C2 \ 0, and its coordinate
functions are constant. The inverse-map resolution comparison in 7.3 prevents contraction of any
of these surfaces in a bimeromorphic map between smooth threefold fillings. A finite base change
t = sd is generically, along Pm , the graph x = sd for the local transverse coordinate x = t. Its
normalized strict component maps with degree one to Pm ; resolution preserves that birational
component. The distinct plurigenus slopes 2(1 − 1/m) distinguish the unique properly elliptic
components, and hence the fillings for different m.
    This is an explicit signed logarithmic-transform example. The prior Kodaira-dimension-one
occurrences discussed after 10.1, including (Fujimoto, 1988, Example 3.4(1)), are retained as the
literature comparison.

                        C × E −→ B,            (z, y, [u]) 7−→ [` = u2 , a = y/u].         (C.EN.11)

It is étale, including at the four root values, by the two Jacobians in (C.PE.13). Its deck involution
is
                                     η : (z, y, [u]) 7−→ (z, −y, [−u]).                     (C.EN.12)
The translation [u] 7→ [−u] is a nonzero two-torsion translation, so η is free. Thus B = (C ×E)/hηi
is bielliptic. The involution (C.EN.8) lifts to

          k : (z, y, [u]) 7−→ (−z, y −1 , [u−1 ]) or    (z, Y, [u]) 7−→ (−z, Y, [u−1 ]).   (C.EN.13)

These formulas commute with η.
    On C, the involution j : (z, Y ) 7→ (z, −Y ) and kC : (z, Y ) 7→ (−z, Y ) each act by −1 on
dz/Y . The latter has four fixed points, the two points over each of 0, ∞. Their product jkC has
no fixed point: over zero its equation would require Y = 0, and at infinity it exchanges the two
points. It is consequently a nonzero two-torsion translation of the elliptic curve C. It follows
that η and ηk are free on C × E, whereas k has exactly 4 · 4 = 16 fixed points. They occur in
eight free η-orbits. At each, the derivative of k is (−1, −1).
    The quotient B/hhi therefore has exactly eight A1 singularities and no branch curve. Its
minimal resolution M is Enriques. One exact verification uses the intermediate quotient (C ×
E)/hki. Its minimal resolution is K3 by 7.12. The involution η extends over its sixteen exceptional
curves, permuting them in pairs. It is free away from them because both η and ηk are free
upstairs, and free on them because they are paired. Its quotient is precisely M . Equivalently,

                                                     271
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


the canonical form has character −1 under η and +1 under k; its square descends through the
explicit crepant A1 resolutions, while pg (M ) = q(M ) = 0. Thus KM has exact order two and
e(M ) = 12. This is an actual noncyclic product quotient, consistent with the two Enriques
holonomy cases of (Yoshihara, 1995, Theorem 2.1 and Example 2.3).

Proposition 10.9 (Every fixed-modulus elliptic quasi-bundle over a rational or elliptic curve
occurs unchanged). Let q : S → B be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth compact connected
complex surface to a smooth compact curve with g(B) ≤ 1. Assume that every fibre is a positive
multiple of a smooth elliptic curve, that its smooth fibres have one fixed elliptic modulus, and that
its integral H1 monodromy is the identity. Then there are a smooth compact complex threefold Y ,
a proper holomorphic map f : Y → P1 , and a specified isomorphism from S to a component of
its reduced zero fibre, with the following properties:

   • the component S is unchanged and has multiplicity one in the full fibre;
   • over P1 \ {0} the map is an actual product with a fixed product of two elliptic curves, and
     hence has connected torus fibres and identity monodromy;
   • the reduced zero fibre has simple normal crossings, all its components are smooth elliptic
     quasi-bundles, all its double curves are smooth elliptic, and it has no triple points;
   • every reduced fibre, including the zero fibre, has Euler characteristic zero.

This realizes every elliptic covering model in 7.11 and 7.15. The prescribed surface is retained
through its full holomorphic torsor class, including its degree-zero parameters and its individual
multiple-fibre translations.

Proposition 10.10 (Every prescribed cyclic smooth-multiple elliptic quotient occurs in a zero-
Euler torus filling). Let q : E → B be a connected compact smooth elliptic surface with a fixed
elliptic Jacobian F , identity integral H1 monodromy, and only smooth multiple fibres. Suppose
g(B) ≤ 1. Let Q be a finite cyclic group acting holomorphically on E, preserving q, and acting
faithfully on B. The trivial group is allowed. The smooth minimal model of E/Q occurs as the
minimal normalization model of a component of a fibre in a smooth compact threefold over P1
whose general fibre is a complex two-torus. It also occurs in such a fibre with reduced-support
Euler number zero. The construction retains the given surface and its given action before taking
the quotient: the distinguished component of the constructed covering threefold is Q-equivariantly
isomorphic to E over B.
     Consequently the minimal normalization models of nonnegative Kodaira dimension occurring
in arbitrary two-torus degenerations are exactly the following two explicitly specified classes:

   • the minimal resolutions of finite cyclic quotients of complex two-tori that have nonnegative
     Kodaira dimension;
   • the minimal models of E/Q in the preceding construction that have nonnegative Kodaira
     dimension.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


The same two classes occur among zero-Euler fillings. The torus-quotient class is described
completely in 7.12 and 9.11. In the second class, all multiplicities, translation gluing, and the
cyclic action are part of the specified input; none is discarded by the occurrence construction.

    One has H 2 (C, K) = 0. Indeed finite-group invariants on complex vector spaces are exact by
averaging. On each finite root chart the higher invariant direct images therefore vanish, and the
invariant direct image of a coherent sheaf is coherent on the coarse curve. Coherent cohomology
in degree two on a compact complex curve is zero. The same averaging for Q proves the asserted
vanishing on C. The long exact sequence of (C.EO.5) consequently supplies an actual T -torsor

full cocycle identity; they are not merely isomorphisms of underlying line bundle classes.
An invariant meromorphic frame. The faithful action on B makes L = C(B) a cyclic
extension of k = C(B/Q). At the generic point the root inertia is absent. The monomial descent
of (C∗ )2L defines an algebraic k-torus Tk , and the generic fibre of P is an algebraic torsor under it.
To see algebraicity directly, pull back to B and choose meromorphic sections of its two associated
orbifold line bundles. Such sections exist: after separating the finitely many root weights, this is
the ordinary meromorphic-section theorem for line bundles on a compact curve. The equivariant
descent isomorphisms are then monomials multiplied by meromorphic functions on B, which
belong to L. Their existing cocycle identities give precisely this algebraic generic torsor.
    It has a k-rational point. This is the rank-two torus case of Steinberg’s theorem (Steinberg,
1965, Theorem 1.9); the independent curve-field and cyclic-lattice proof below establishes the
required vanishing for exactly the representations used here.
An independent calculation of the generic torus torsor. Here is a direct verification of
the required vanishing for the actual cyclic rank-two torus. Put K = C(B/Q). The splitting
action on its character lattice has order d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}; if the base group is larger, pass first to
the fixed field of the kernel of this lattice action. This gives the actual cyclic splitting extension
L/K of degree d. We prove
                                             H 1 (K, T ) = 0.                                (C.EO.H1)
The cohomology here is the Galois cohomology of the algebraic torus obtained by descent of the
two-dimensional split multiplicative group, and classifies its actual torsors over K.
    First every function field K 0 of a smooth compact complex curve has the following elementary
property: a homogeneous polynomial of degree a in b > a variables has a nonzero zero over K 0 .
To verify it, let g be the genus of the curve, choose a point P , and choose an effective divisor
D bounding the poles of all coefficients. Seek each variable in H 0 (O(rP )). For large r there
are b(r + 1 − g) scalar unknowns, whereas the polynomial value belongs to H 0 (O(arP + D)), of
dimension ar + deg D + 1 − g. Its vanishing imposes at most that many homogeneous equations
of positive degree. For large r the number of unknowns is strictly larger. The height bound for
an ideal generated by that many elements gives an affine homogeneous zero set of dimension at
least one. Over C it contains a point other than the origin. This yields the asserted nonzero zero
over K 0 .
    Consequently, for every finite field extension L0 /K 0 the norm map is surjective:

                                      NL0 /K 0 : (L0 )∗ −→ (K 0 )∗ .                         (C.EO.H2)

Indeed, for c ∈ (K 0 )∗ , choose a K 0 -basis of L0 of size a = [L0 : K 0 ] and apply the preceding
property to NL0 /K 0 (x1 e1 + · · · + xa ea ) − cz a . This has degree a in a + 1 variables. A nonzero
zero cannot have z = 0, because the norm of a field element vanishes only for the zero element.
Dividing by z gives an element of norm c. Every intermediate field used below is again the
function field of a smooth compact complex curve, so the same proof applies to it.

Exhaustion of the nonnegative classes. Let Z be a minimal normalization model of
nonnegative Kodaira dimension in an arbitrary two-torus degeneration. 7.16 provides its actual
cyclic component cover and equivariant minimal contraction. A torus cover gives exactly the
first class in the statement. In the remaining case 7.11 and 7.15 give a fixed-Jacobian, identity-
monodromy fibration with only smooth multiples over a rational or elliptic curve. We specify
why an appropriate such fibration is preserved by the cyclic action.
     For a cover of Kodaira dimension one it is the intrinsic connected Iitaka fibration. In algebraic
dimension one its base is the intrinsic meromorphic function field, and the equivariant Stein
factor of 7.10 applies. The non-torus projective case of Kodaira dimension zero is bielliptic. Use
its actual finite free product description (F1 × F2 )/Γ, with Γ acting by translations on F1 and
with a nontrivial linear action on F2 . The invariant holomorphic vector fields on the product are
exactly the constant fields in the F1 direction. These integrate to the connected automorphism
group of the quotient, an elliptic quotient of F1 . Its orbit map is

                                    (F1 × F2 )/Γ −→ F2 /Γ ≃ P1 .                            (C.EO.16)

Every automorphism normalizes the connected automorphism group and hence preserves this
orbit fibration. Its local stabilizers act by free translations on F1 ; its root charts are (C.EO.1).
Therefore it has the required identity monodromy and only smooth multiples. This is the
preserved fibration used in the bielliptic case.
     Let H be the kernel of the cyclic action on the chosen base. Its action on a general elliptic fibre
is by translations: a nontrivial linear elliptic automorphism has rational quotient, which would
make the quotient surface ruled and annihilate all positive pluricanonical sections, contrary to
κ(Z) ≥ 0. The exact translation and reflection charts (C.EQ.3)–(C.EQ.4) show that quotienting
the cover by H is again a smooth elliptic surface with fixed Jacobian, identity monodromy, and
only smooth multiples. The residual cyclic group acts faithfully on the base. Its quotient is the
same actual surface quotient as before, through the finite quotient maps. It is therefore one of
the inputs already constructed above.

first, take the compact diagonal quotient (A × P1t )/G using a faithful character on t, resolve it,
and use the same 7.4 balancing; the exact component comparison is 9.10. All occurrences may
therefore be chosen with zero-Euler support, proving both asserted equalities of classes.

Proposition 10.11 (Occurrence of every Hopf surface of algebraic dimension one). Let H be
any primary or secondary Hopf surface with a(H) = 1. There is a proper holomorphic map from
a smooth compact complex threefold to P1 , with connected fibres and smooth two-tori away from
one value, whose fibre over that value contains H itself as a smooth component of multiplicity
one. Its reduced special fibre has simple normal crossings and Euler number zero. Over the
complement of the special value the family is the actual product of two fixed elliptic curves with
the base.
    The map used to apply 10.9 is the actual connected elliptic reduction

                                           q : H −→ P1 .                                  (C.EH.1)

Every fibre of q is a multiple of a smooth elliptic curve, the modulus is constant, and the integral
H 1 monodromy is the identity. The assertion includes secondary Hopf surfaces without imposing
a cyclic condition on their finite primary cover.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 10.9; equation (C.EH.2);

character γ 7→ log | det(dγ)0 | gives b1 ≥ 1. This is the comparison proved in (C.HQ.5)–(C.HQ.7).
Thus it applies to secondary surfaces as well.
   Choose a nonconstant meromorphic function h on H. Its effective zero and pole divisors
have no common irreducible component and have intersection number zero by (C.EH.2).
Local intersection multiplicities of distinct effective curves on a smooth surface are positive.
Consequently those two divisors are disjoint. In a local coprime expression h = f /g, an
indeterminacy point would belong to both (f = 0) and (g = 0), so no such point exists. The

                               2pa (C) − 2 = (KH + C) · C = 0.                       (C.EH.4)

    This finite gluing is Hausdorff. Indeed at the boundary kxk = r of a core overlap the core
point is absent, and at its other boundary kxk = R the neck point is absent. Thus the graph
of each identification is closed relative to the two pieces. The same holds for y; distinct necks
have disjoint overlaps in a given core, and the preceding r2 inequality excludes an additional
identification through the opposite core. This also proves separation for the resulting finite
equivalence relation. The quotient is a smooth complex threefold Y with the holomorphic map
t. At the two double curves it has the exact coordinates xy = t; at zero its fibre is the two
unchanged Hopf surfaces with the asserted two inversion identifications.

    The map is proper after the indicated restriction to the disc. Choose r < r0 < R0 < R. Over
a closed subdisc, the two compact sets {να ≥ r0 , νβ ≥ r0 } in the Hopf copies, together with the
two closed neck sets kxk, kyk ≤ R0 , cover the entire inverse image. For a core point missing its
compact set, the small normal coordinate is less than r0 and the other neck coordinate has norm

belongs to its compact set. All these closed sets are compact: their bases are compact elliptic
curves and their vector-bundle coordinates are bounded. They cover the closed inverse image,
proving properness. This argument also explicitly verifies compactness of the fibres.

Every secondary Hopf surface H of algebraic dimension zero has an actual finite quotient
presentation of one of the forms
                     Hα,β /h(z, w) 7→ (ζna z, ζnb w)i, gcd(a, n) = gcd(b, n) = 1,
                                                                                             (C.SH.1)
                     Hr (β)/h(z, w) 7→ (ζnr z, ζn w)i, gcd(r, n) = 1.
The first primary contraction is (αz, βw) with no multiplicative resonance, and the second is
(β r z + wr , βw), where 0 < |α|, |β| < 1. This is an exhaustive presentation, without a uniqueness
assertion about the displayed parameters.
      Every prescribed such surface occurs itself as a smooth multiplicity-one component of a reduced
SNC fibre of a proper map from a smooth compact complex threefold to a smooth compact curve,
with connected fibres and general fibre a complex two-torus. All reduced fibre supports can have

component). For every smooth compact connected complex curve C, there is a smooth compact

of such a morphism are rational. If that neighbour also has an algebraic-dimension-zero Hopf
minimal model, this same curve is one of its minimal axes. Its diagonal rule would force equal
ratios, contradicting (C.HA.2); its non-diagonal rule would force the opposite strict inequality.
Neither is possible. The diagonal–diagonal case merely repeats the equality (C.HA.1). The
theorem gives these exact adjacency restrictions and does not infer a global nonexistence assertion
from a local decrease.

Proposition 11.2 (The diagonal Hopf cycle criterion and the complete two-component case).
Consider a reduced SNC fibre of an actual smooth-total degeneration of two-tori, all of whose
irreducible components are unblown diagonal Hopf surfaces of algebraic dimension zero. Primary
and secondary Hopf surfaces are both allowed. Its components form a cycle: each of the two axis

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


Every actual torus degeneration in the stated SNC branch has M = I. The definition of M , its

    For two components, the criterion is more explicit. The two Hopf surfaces are isomorphic.
After an actual diagonal automorphism of one of them, both gluing maps are inversion on the

Proposition 11.4 (Exact nonlinear Hopf star criterion and compact realization). Let S be
a specified compact SNC surface with components P, H1 , . . . , Hn , n ≥ 1, and no triple points.
Suppose q : P → B is a connected fixed-Jacobian elliptic quasi-bundle: its only nonsmooth scheme
fibres are multiples of smooth elliptic curves, and its integral H 1 monodromy is the identity.
Each Hi = Hri (βi ) is a nonlinear primary Hopf surface as in (C.NH.1). It meets P along its
unique axis, identified by a specified holomorphic isomorphism with a distinct reduced fibre Ji of
q. There are no other intersections.
    The following assertions are equivalent.

   1. S is the reduced full central fibre of a proper one-parameter degeneration of two-tori with
      smooth total space.

   2. S is the reduced full special fibre of a smooth compact threefold over P1 , all of whose other
      fibres are smooth two-tori.

   3. The normal lines on every double curve are dual; B is elliptic; all ri equal one integer r;

Proposition 11.7 (The weighted root criterion, exact inertia and compact occurrence). Let
S be a simple normal-crossing oriented cycle with at least two embedded components, which
are specified unblown diagonal primary or secondary Hopf surfaces Hi of algebraic dimension
zero, with their two axes joined by specified elliptic isomorphisms between distinct components.
Assign positive integers mi to its components. The compatible weighted normal data   P defined in
(C.WH.1)–(C.WH.2) give an explicit smooth proper local plumbing with full fibre i mi Hi .
    There is the following complete test for its general fibre to be a connected two-torus. Put
N = lcmi (mi ), form the finite cyclic component covers (C.WH.3), and join their axes by the
normalized root necks (C.WH.4). Their graph must be connected, and the product M of their
actual rank-three integral complement lattice maps must be the identity. Every actual smooth-total
torus degeneration with the given weighted support supplies these data and satisfies this test.
Conversely every weighted support passing this test occurs, with its specified reduced surface and
component multiplicities, over a compact rational base, with a smooth compact total threefold
and Euler number zero for every reduced fibre support. The compact construction chooses
normal-product constants; it does not identify different full analytic neighbourhoods without a
comparison.

connected strict covers of every Hi , with r | gcdi mi . Write

Proof. The curves and the actual restriction maps. A Hopf surface has H 2 (H, Q) = 0.
For an irreducible compact curve C ⊂ H, adjunction gives pa (C) = 1. A map from P1 to H lifts

of C hence cannot be rational. The equality pa (C) = g(C ν ) + δ(C) now gives g(C ν ) = 1 and
δ(C) = 0. Thus C is smooth elliptic. Two distinct such curves have intersection number zero,
since H 2 (H, Q) = 0; positivity of every local intersection forces them to be disjoint. These are
the same explicit curve comparisons used in 10.11. It follows at once that the present support
has only elliptic double curves and no triple point.
    We prove nonvanishing in (C.HR.1), including secondary surfaces. First let H 0 = (C2 \
{0})/hF i be a primary Hopf surface. The constant additive deck cocycle 1 represents a nonzero
class in H 1 (H 0 , OH 0 ). Indeed, a trivialization would be a holomorphic function b on C2 \ {0}
satisfying b(F z) − b(z) = 1. Hartogs extension to the origin and evaluation there give a
contradiction. Since h1 (H 0 , OH 0 ) = 1, this class spans the group.
    For every elliptic curve C 0 ⊂ H 0 , its lift can have finitely many branches permuted by F .

The scalar and nonlinear-axis cases are included. The actual map C∗ /hF d i → C 0 induced by

successively determine nonzero values at all other vertices. Thus the tree rows of d1 are
independent and have a one-dimensional kernel. In particular if the whole graph were a tree, d1
would be surjective and H 2 (S, OS ) = 0.
    The map f is flat: multiplication by its nonzero local parameter is injective in each regular
local ring of the smooth total space, and torsion-free modules over the base discrete valuation
ring are flat. Upper semicontinuity for this proper flat family gives h2 (S, OS ) ≥ h2 (F, OF ) = 1.
The central fibre is the reduced S by hypothesis, so no thickened-fibre cohomology has been
substituted here. The tree case is impossible.
     7.21 gives a surjection from π1 (S) to the incidence graph group, and π1 (S) is a quotient of
Z4 because the full fibre is reduced. The free graph group is therefore abelian and has rank at
most one. Together with the preceding paragraph this proves that the graph is unicyclic and
|E| = |V |.
    There is now just one row left after the spanning-tree equations. Writing its endpoints using
the successive nonzero values shows that it vanishes precisely when the product of the actual
ratios rv,e /rw,e around the cycle is one. If it did not vanish, d1 would have rank |V | and again
H 2 (S, OS ) = 0. The product is consequently one, the rank is |V | − 1, and (C.HR.6) gives exactly
(C.HR.3). A vertex-basis change cancels between the incoming and outgoing ratios; an edge-basis

change cancels inside its ratio. This proves the asserted independence without discarding the

The full algebraic-dimension-zero branch. The actual primary and secondary curve
computations in 7.19 and 10.14 give two possibilities in algebraic dimension zero: a nonlinear
Hopf surface has just one elliptic curve, and a diagonal Hopf surface has just its two distinct
axis elliptic curves. The diagonal finite action cannot exchange them: such an exchange would
force equal positive powers of the two contracting multipliers, giving a nonconstant meromorphic
invariant and algebraic dimension one. Thus every vertex of the present graph has degree at
most two.
    A connected unicyclic finite graph with all degrees at most two is a cycle and has every
degree equal to two. Indeed its equality |E| = |V | gives average degree two, so no smaller degree
is possible. Consequently there is no nonlinear component and no attached tree. There is no
loop at a single vertex, since the components of the specified SNC surface are smooth embedded
components: such a loop would be a self-identification, not a double curve between distinct
components. Hence there are at least two components.

Proposition 11.12 (The exact marked-cycle criterion without an algebraic-dimension restriction).
Specify a connected oriented cycle of marked surfaces, each either a diagonal primary or secondary
Hopf surface with its two distinct axes, or P(OE ⊕ L) with L ∈ Pic0 (E) and its zero and infinity
sections. Specify the elliptic gluing maps and duality of the actual axis or section normal lines.

supports which admit a smooth-total two-torus smoothing. Every such support occurs as a full
reduced fibre of a smooth compact complex threefold over P1 . The construction retains each
component and every specified elliptic gluing map. Its only other singular fibre is the complex
conjugate marked support, and every reduced fibre support has Euler number zero. No restriction
on the algebraic dimension of the diagonal Hopf components is imposed. The construction chooses
normal-product constants.

Proposition 11.14 (All multiplicities and all diagonal Hopf and ruled vertices). Specify a
simple-NC cycle of smooth embedded marked surfaces, with edges between distinct components.
Each vertex is a diagonal primary or secondary Hopf surface with its two axes, or P(OE ⊕ L)
with E elliptic and L ∈ Pic0 (E), marked by its two sections. Specify their elliptic gluing maps,
positive multiplicities mi , and the actual compatible weighted normal lines, sections and boundary
maps of (C.WH.1)–(C.WH.2).
    Put N = lcmi mi . Form the actual normalized N th-root component covers and the compressed
necks uv = shi . The root graph is connected and its rank-three integral complement-lattice product
is the identity precisely when the specified weighted normal plumbing has connected two-torus
fibres. Every actual smooth-total torus degeneration with the specified marked support yields these
data and passes this test.
    Every weighted support passing the test occurs over P1 in a smooth compact complex threefold.
The construction retains all marked components, elliptic gluing maps and multiplicities. Its only
other singular fibre is the complex conjugate weighted support. All reduced fibre supports have
Euler number zero. Normal-product constants are chosen in this compact realization. There is
no algebraic-dimension restriction on the Hopf vertices, and an all-ruled cycle is included.
    The complete component, axis and inertia comparisons in (C.WH.0), and the ruled-cover
identities (C.WM.2)–(C.WM.7), hold in this scope. In common root-complement coordinates the
finite deck linear part fixes the primitive total normal period. Its other eigenvalue is a root of
unity of order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6. The compact construction retains this linear part and every affine
deck constant.

proposition 11.7; proposition 11.11; proposition 11.6; proposition 11.10; equation (C.EW.3);

equation (C.EW.15); equation (C.EW.14); proposition 11.12; equation (C.EW.12);

lattice cover constructed there. Coordinate powers extend it across both axes, and the actual
contracting generator and free finite angular characters identify its finite normalization with a
smooth diagonal Hopf surface. This comparison does not require nonresonant multipliers.
    On a ruled vertex the proof (C.WM.4)–(C.WM.7) applies without any Hopf assumption. It
gives the actual finite normalization P(OE 0 ⊕ L0 ) → P(OE ⊕ L), with an étale base map π, fibre

weighted normal line is pulled back on each entire section chart by its transferred flat connection;

Proposition 11.15 (Exact pruning and compact reinsertion classify every reduced all-Hopf
support). Let S be a specified compact connected reduced SNC surface whose smooth components
are primary or secondary Hopf surfaces. Its elliptic gluing maps are part of the specified surface.
The following finite geometric test is necessary and sufficient for S to occur as the full central
fibre of a proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori with smooth total space.

   1. The actual normal lines on every double curve are dual, and the incidence graph has exactly
      one independent cycle.

   2. If a diagonal algebraic-dimension-zero component occurs, the whole support is its diagonal
      cycle and its integral lattice product M is the identity, as in 11.2.

   3. In the remaining case every algebraic-dimension-zero vertex is a nonlinear leaf. Every other
      vertex has its actual elliptic reduction to P1 , and every multiple fibre of that reduction is
      one of its marked double curves.

   4. Let me be the exact order of either normal line at an edge, and let hv be zero on the cycle
      and the sum of the me along the path from the cycle to v. There is an integer R > 0 such
      that every nonlinear leaf has hv = R and every other vertex has hv < R. If there is no
      nonlinear leaf, any R > max hv passes this test.

   5. Perform the exact leaf-pruning operations specified below, including the full integer secondary
      framing and all torsor maps. The resulting marked Hopf/ruled core cycle has integral
      complement-lattice product M = I.

    In the second case the tests referring to elliptic tree vertices are unneeded. In the remaining
case the pruning operations always exist under the preceding geometric requirements. Each
terminal step is one of two explicit operations: the inverse logarithmic chart of 11.5 for a primary
or secondary Hopf pair; or removal of the product pair (F × P1 , F × {∞}). The latter leaves the
parent surface unchanged. After its children have been removed, every vertex has exactly one of
these two forms. The pruned core and its test are independent, up to the stated actual marked
isomorphisms, of the order of pruning disjoint branches.
    Every support passing the test has a realization over P1 with smooth compact total threefold.
It retains all the original components, their analytic torsors and every specified elliptic gluing
map. Its other singular support can be taken to be the complex conjugate of its pruned core cycle.
All reduced fibre supports have Euler characteristic zero.

with the old model minus its marked central elliptic curve. In a compact Hopf fundamental

Proposition 11.16 (The exact rooted elliptic-tree criterion and compact occurrence). Let S be
a specified compact connected reduced SNC surface whose incidence graph is a nontrivial tree.
Distinguish one smooth component P , with no initial restriction on its geometric genus or surface
type. Every other component is either a primary or secondary Hopf surface, or is equipped with a

fibres and only smooth multiple fibre supports. In the latter case every boundary curve is a fibre
support of the specified map. Retain the actual elliptic gluing maps and the complete analytic
torsors. The following finite geometric test is necessary and sufficient for S to occur as a full
fibre of a smooth-total degeneration of connected complex two-tori.

      with identity integral monodromy and only smooth multiple supports. Its marked boundary

      either a nonlinear algebraic-dimension-zero Hopf leaf or an elliptic quasi-bundle over P1 of
      the stated type, whose multiple fibres are all marked double curves.

    We now identify every marked elliptic curve on P with a fibre of one such elliptic fibration.
On a torus an elliptic curve is a translate of an elliptic subtorus: lifting its map to universal
covers makes its derivative a periodic holomorphic function, hence constant. Two different elliptic
directions give an isogeny from their product to the two-torus, so their translates intersect. The
pairwise disjoint boundary curves therefore have the same direction and are fibres of the actual
quotient by that elliptic subtorus.

restriction to that curve has positive ramification, a contradiction. If there is no multiple fibre,
q is a principal F -torsor. A nonvertical elliptic curve would give a section after its finite base
pullback. Pullback on H 2 (B, ΛF ) multiplies its Chern vector by the positive covering degree.
The vector group is torsion-free, so the original vector would be zero. Formula (C.PT.8) then
makes P a torus, already handled above. Otherwise all marked curves are vertical. Since every
reduced fibre is one smooth elliptic curve, each is exactly a marked fibre support. This proves
the required actual fibration qP in all cases.

Proposition 11.17 (Unicyclic quasi-bundle supports with all torsors retained). Let S be a
specified compact connected SNC surface with smooth embedded components. Each component is
either a nonlinear primary or secondary Hopf surface of algebraic dimension zero, or is equipped
with an actual map
                                        qv : Tv −→ P1                                  (C.QT.1)
with connected fibres, every fibre a multiple of a smooth elliptic curve, fixed elliptic Jacobian, and
identity monodromy on the integral first cohomology of the regular fibre. Every boundary curve
on Tv is a fibre support of this specified map. The elliptic gluing maps, the surfaces and their
complete analytic torsors are part of the data.
    The following geometric test is necessary and sufficient for S to occur as a full reduced fibre
of a smooth-total degeneration of connected complex two-tori.

   1. The actual boundary normal lines are dual, and the incidence graph has exactly one
      independent cycle. Nonlinear Hopf vertices are leaves.

   2. Every multiple fibre of every map (C.QT.1) is marked by a boundary curve. Let me be the
      exact order of its normal line, also the normal order at the other endpoint. At a nonlinear
      endpoint this is its resonance.

   3. Set hv = 0 on the cycle and set hv equal to the sum of the me along its path from the cycle.
      There is an integer R > 0 for which every nonlinear leaf has height R and every elliptic
      quasi-bundle vertex has height strictly smaller than R. With no nonlinear leaves one may
      choose any R > maxv hv .

   4. Apply the exact inverse-logarithmic and product-cap pruning maps of 11.15, retaining their
      full integer framings and all torsor identifications. The resulting marked diagonal Hopf or
      degree-zero ruled core cycle has integral complement-lattice product M = I.

All pruning operations in this test exist under its preceding requirements. Their marked result
is independent of the order of disjoint branch operations. Every support passing the test has a
realization over P1 with smooth compact total space, retaining every original component, analytic
torsor and specified elliptic gluing map. The only other singular support is the complex conjugate
of its pruned core. Every reduced fibre support has Euler number zero.
    In particular the statement includes elliptic quasi-bundles of Kodaira dimension one and
coherent Euler characteristic zero, together with the genus-zero quasi-bundle components of
Kodaira dimension zero and the Hopf and ruled components in the same explicitly specified class.

12 Actual contractions, canonical reduction and finite generation
Proposition 12.1 (Maximum components without a minimality assumption). Let f : U → ∆ be
a proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori from a smooth threefold. Let its full central
fibre S = v Tv be reduced and simple normal crossing, without triple points. No minimality
           P
assumption is made on any Tv . Write kv for the actual canonical evaluation orders.
    At a local maximum Tv of these orders, precisely one of the following descriptions applies:

  1. Every adjacent component has order kv .

  2. The component is an unblown terminal ruled surface meeting its parent in a section, with
     order drop one, or an unblown terminal plane meeting its parent in a line, with order drop
     two. These are the actual contractions of 9.12.

  3. The component is an unblown terminal Hopf surface, with the exact axis normal order and
     positive canonical drop of 11.5 and 11.13.

In the second alternative the ruled base has positive genus. Thus, when the orders are not all
equal, a global maximum is one of the two kinds of strict-drop leaves.
    Moreover every rational double curve can be removed by a finite sequence of the actual
plane-line contractions of 9.12. At each step the other double curves and their neighbourhoods

are unchanged. If r0 is the number of connected rational double curves of the original support,
the resulting actual torus degeneration has no rational double curve and satisfies
