There are exactly r0 point contractions. Reversing their recorded ordinary blowups recovers the
original support, including its original smooth threefold neighbourhood. In particular the rational
double edges are removed as terminal edges of the actual incidence graph; none belongs to a cycle.

A positive-square rational curve on a component. We shall use the following implication
for any component, not only a maximum:

        a smooth rational curve of positive square on T            =⇒   T is rational.      (C.NM.4)

Here is the comparison with its actual minimal-model map. For a nonrational ruled minimal
model, every rational curve maps to a point of the positive-genus ruling base. A surviving
such curve is a ruling fibre, of square zero; its strict transform has nonpositive square. Every
exceptional curve also has negative square. On the Hopf minimal model supplied by 7.9 there are
no rational curves, since a map from P1 lifts to C2 \ {0} and has constant coordinate functions.
Hence a rational curve on a blowup of that model is exceptional and has negative square.
    The remaining actual minimal models have Kodaira dimension zero or one by 7.6. In this

Following rational edges gives actual point contractions. Take a rational double curve
and orient it toward its higher-height endpoint. Equation (C.NM.3) makes the height difference
nonzero; at that higher endpoint its square is positive, equal to one or two. By (C.NM.4) the
endpoint surface is rational. The pencil (C.NM.6) makes every other boundary on it rational.
Hodge index leaves at most one positive-square boundary, the incoming one. Every other
boundary therefore has negative square by (C.NM.3), and its neighbour has strictly higher height.
Follow one of those edges when it exists.

rational component having exactly its one incoming boundary. It has K = −aC, with (a, C 2 )
as in (C.NM.8). The same integer-intersection argument excludes every (−1)-curve, so it is an
actual 9.12 leaf. Its ruled section possibility has just been excluded by (C.NM.10). It is therefore
a plane-line leaf, and 9.12 contracts it to a smooth point of the smooth central locus of its parent.
    Every other boundary misses that line, so the actual blowdown is an isomorphism on its
neighbourhood. It removes exactly one rational double curve, creates no new double curve or
triple point, retains the punctured torus family, and decreases e(S) by two. Apply the argument
to the new actual degeneration until no rational double curve remains. Exactly r0 steps have
been made; (C.NM.1) and the recorded ordinary-blowup reconstruction follow.

with smooth torus Euler number zero, gives e(Y ) = 2d + 2d = 4d. This completes the compact
occurrence construction.

    For later comparison, let φ : X 99K X 0 be an actual bimeromorphic map over the disc
between smooth total spaces. Pullback of a holomorphic top form is holomorphic wherever

coefficient in smooth coordinate volume frames gives a holomorphic form on all of X. The inverse
map gives the inverse pullback, since their compositions agree on their common biholomorphic

In particular normalized generators agree under pullback up to a base unit. At the generic point
of a divisor which survives the comparison, the map is a biholomorphism of the corresponding
divisorial local rings, so its canonical order is unchanged.
Why every Hopf-birational component is retained. A holomorphic map from P1 to a Hopf
surface is constant: lift it to the universal cover C2 \ {0} and use the two constant coordinate
functions. Every rational curve on a point blowup of that surface is therefore exceptional over
the Hopf minimal model. A finite sequence of point blowups has only finitely many such curves.
These surfaces cannot be covered by rational curves. They are also not projective: their first


                                                  407
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


Betti number is one, unchanged by point blowups, whereas a projective surface has even first
Betti number.
    In the recorded local σ-maps, a divisorial exceptional component over a general point of
a curve centre is ruled by complete rational fibres. A component lying over an isolated point
is projective, as a component of a projectivized normal cone. Here the contradiction with the
original compact component uses the proper composite graphs, not a comparison of local analytic
patches. Suppose a strict transform were removed for the first time. For a curve centre, choose a
general complete rational exceptional fibre through a generic strict-transform point. The proper
preceding graph maps this curve meromorphically back to the original compact component.
The map is nonconstant, since at that generic point the strict-transform comparison is a local
biholomorphism. Varying the fibre gives rational curves through a dense open subset of the
original component, contradicting the finite exceptional-curve description above. For a point
centre, restrict the proper preceding graph to the compact projective exceptional component
containing the generic strict-transform piece. Its image back in the original compact component
is closed and contains that open piece, and therefore is the whole component. The comparison
has generic degree one. Resolving this surface graph gives a bimeromorphic comparison with
a projective surface; point blowups preserve b1 , again contradicting b1 = 1. Thus the strict
transforms through the finite chart record retain a prime divisor of that birational type. The
restored overlap maps identify these strict transforms by their actual generic-point maps. Hence
a component in H survives to the endpoint.
    At a canonical-flat smooth endpoint a nowhere-zero three-form generates f0∗ KX0 , so every
canonical order is zero. Equation (C.KG.6) then proves ki = 0 for every i ∈ H. This proves

    Here termination is an actual finite induction, rather than a decrease of an unspecified
complexity. Let R = max ki . Every removed old component has level k ∈ {1, . . . , R}. It
produces only finitely many new components, all at level k + 1, and produces none when k = R.

produced. Continuing through the fixed finite set of levels proves that all removals terminate.

The source’s actual overlap maps glue global graphs. The bare two-cover definition of

    For a finite σ-chain, its composite graph is obtained as the closure of the common
biholomorphic graph in the proper image of the fibre product of its arrow graphs. Both

     If one of these lists is nonempty, choose a component of largest canonical order among the
globally occurring last locally blown-up branches. Use an auxiliary resolution a : X      b → X 0 as

last-locally-blown-up case: its boundary is connected and no missing links are inserted. This does

    This cleanup terminates without inserting an ambient resolution into the record or estimating
orders of arbitrary resolution divisors. Label every current global component by its order in
{0, . . . , M }. A removal deletes a positive label q, adds finitely many labels q + 1 when q < M ,
and adds none when q = M . There are finitely many removals at level one, hence finitely many
objects ever created at level two, and inductively at every level through M . This is the finite
game of (Kulikov, 1981, §9), now applied also to the cleanup removals.
    When cleanup stops, no recorded locally exceptional branch remains. The defining contraction
lists of the sigma-atlas are empty; their terminal smooth NC charts are therefore the current
charts. The total space is smooth and its full fibre is reduced NC. Its normalization components
are smooth. Other global components may retain self-incidences. At a maximal Hopf the intrinsic
argument (C.HM.2)–(C.HM.5) excludes rational self-incidences. No elliptic self-incidence was
introduced: type-I and type-II changes use rational exceptional curves; in a local ruled contraction
the horizontal parent has order one lower, so a maximal-order Hopf can only meet that contraction
in vertical rational curves. Thus the maximal Hopfs are again smooth embedded components,
and their ordinary point maps to their Hopf minimal models are available for the next step.
Termination of the whole procedure. Perform a type-I or type-II step whenever the chosen
last point gives the first or second case. In the third case perform the finite ruled removal and
cleanup just specified. Across the entire procedure there are only finitely many divisorial removal
blocks: the same fixed-level game counts all their positive component labels together. Between
these blocks every step strictly decreases the finite integer (C.HM.8). More explicitly, if cj counts
the retained global components of order j, the block-level potential is

                            (c1 , c2 , . . . , cM , h) in lexicographic order.           (C.HM.10)

A whole-component removal decreases its first changed cj , whatever finite next-level additions or
Hopf point changes occur inside the block. A type-I or type-II step chosen on a last Hopf point
leaves all the cj unchanged and decreases h. Lexicographic order on this fixed finite product
of nonnegative integers has no infinite strictly descending sequence, by the same successive-
coordinate induction. This potential is attached to the specified finite blocks, not to every
auxiliary arrow in their graphs. An infinite procedure would therefore have either infinitely many
divisorial removals, contradicting that game, or an infinite tail of strict decreases of h. Both are
impossible.
    At the endpoint a nonminimal maximal Hopf would still have a last point blowup and one of
the three alternatives, so every such Hopf is minimal. Its curves are the disjoint smooth elliptic
curves proved above, and hence no triple point meets it. The original Hopf primes survive with
unchanged orders by 12.7, and each additional prime used in the record is ruled. The same
actual proper graphs and restored overlap isomorphisms give the asserted reversible comparison.
Their annular gluing and normal-cone Euler terms are exactly those of 12.7. This proves the
statement in its specified scope.

Proposition 12.10 (Every point-exceptional prime of an aligned parent is an actual boundary).
Let P , π : P → Z, and qZ : Z → B be the actual component and maps of 12.2. Write DP for
the reduced union of its intersections with the other central components. There is a nonzero
constant linear combination of the two restricted saturated ambient translation fields which is the
meromorphic lift of a nowhere-zero holomorphic vertical field

                                WZ ∈ H 0 (Z, TZ ),      dqZ (WZ ) = 0.                      (C.EP.1)

On every smooth elliptic fibre its complex-time period lattice is the same fixed lattice. The field
extends without a zero or a pole across every smooth multiple fibre of qZ .



                                                  417
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


     Every prime exceptional for the specified point map π is a polar divisor of its meromorphic
lift WP . Consequently
                                          Exc(π) ⊂ DP .                                  (C.EP.2)
In particular, a last point-exceptional curve for π is an actual boundary curve. This assertion
concerns the exceptional primes of this actual map: it makes no assertion that every rational
(−1)-curve on P is exceptional for π. The component and its ambient neighbourhood are not
changed.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 12.2; proposition 7.7;
equation (C.EP.6); equation (C.EP.7); equation (C.EP.3); equation (C.EP.10);
equation (C.EP.9); equation (C.EP.11).


Proof. The actual field space and its polar locus. Use the two-dimensional saturated field
space of 7.7 on the original multiplicity-one component P . In this full reduced situation no root
cover of P is needed. Denote a basis of its restrictions by X, Y . They are independent over C,
commute, and are meromorphic fields on P .
   Their actual ambient representatives are linear combinations of holomorphic relative fields
with coefficients meromorphic in the disc coordinate. They therefore have polar divisors only in
the central fibre. Saturation removes their pole along the generic point of P . On P \ DP the
central fibre has just this one smooth branch, so restriction gives

                                   X, Y holomorphic on P \ DP .                              (C.EP.3)

This is the exact restriction comparison used in (C.MR.8) and 12.2. It applies to every constant
linear combination. All boundary and exceptional curves of the specified map π are vertical for
q = qZ π.
     Remove finitely many values from B so that π is an isomorphism over their complement B ◦ ,
all fibres are smooth, and the fields and their projected coefficients are regular. On a compact
elliptic fibre the latter coefficients are holomorphic functions and hence constants. Thus X, Y
project to meromorphic vector fields on B, exactly as in the alignment proof.
Rank one: the period identity gives a constant combination. Suppose the meromorphic
rank of hX, Y i is one. Alignment identifies its connected elliptic first integral with the actual
map q. Thus
                                         Y = (q ∗ H)X                                     (C.EP.4)
for a nonconstant meromorphic function H on B. The actual return-germ calculation
(C.RG.4)–(C.RG.12), performed on the original ambient representatives, gives time periods
λ1 , λ2 of X and constants di , ki ∈ C such that

                                λi = di − ki H,         λ2 /λ1 = τ ∈ H.                      (C.EP.5)

The formula continues on B ◦ with these same constants. This uses the actual global ratio H,
the continued integral cycles, and the identity theorem; it does not extend q to a threefold
neighbourhood.
   Take
                                  W = d1 X − k1 Y = λ1 X.                           (C.EP.6)
A nonzero integral cycle on an elliptic curve has nonzero time period, so W is nonzero on every
fibre under consideration. Multiplying a field by λ1 divides its time periods by λ1 ; the two periods
of W are exactly 1, τ . Thus (C.EP.6) is a constant linear combination with a fixed nonzero
period lattice. In an integration coordinate on each fibre it is the fixed invariant translation field.


                                                  418
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


Rank two: commuting transverse transport preserves the periods. Suppose instead
that the meromorphic rank is two. The two projected fields on the curve B commute. Two
nonzero commuting meromorphic fields on a connected curve have constant ratio: writing them
locally as a(z)∂z and b(z)∂z , the bracket equation is ab0 − ba0 = 0. The ratio therefore continues
as a constant. They cannot both project to zero, since vertical fields on an elliptic fibre have
meromorphic rank at most one. After interchanging the basis if necessary there is consequently
a constant c for which

                         W = Y − cX 6= 0,         q∗ W = 0,          q∗ X 6= 0.            (C.EP.7)

On the compact fibres over B ◦ , W is a nonzero translation field. The local flow of the transverse
field X, constructed on an entire compact fibre for sufficiently small time, identifies neighbouring
elliptic fibres. Since [X, W ] = 0, this identification preserves the time form and its two integral
periods. Thus their lattice is locally constant and hence constant on connected B ◦ . This is the
actual compact-fibre flow comparison of (C.RF.1)–(C.RF.2). A constant rescaling of W makes
one nonzero period equal to 1. Once again W is a constant combination of the original two
restricted fields.
Extension on the specified minimal elliptic model. On qZ−1 (B ◦ ), push W through the
open isomorphism of π. Integration of its fixed lattice identifies each small smooth fibre tube
with a torsor under one fixed elliptic curve F . Every overlap has translation linear part, so its
derivative preserves the same invariant field of F .
   At a multiple value, use the actual normalized root chart of 12.2 and (C.RG.13):

                         (F × ∆z )/h(u, z) 7−→ (u + η, ζm z)i,         t = zm.             (C.EP.8)

The translation η gives the free cyclic action on the total space. The invariant vertical field on
F × ∆z is fixed by this action and is nowhere zero. On the punctured root disc our field agrees
with it: its coefficient relative to the invariant frame has the fixed nonzero time periods and
therefore is the same constant. It follows that the agreement extends across z = 0 and descends
through the actual etale quotient. These extensions agree on overlaps with the previously fixed
field. This proves (C.EP.1), including every zero or pole that might have been hidden at an
omitted base value.
    The meromorphic lift of WZ through π agrees with the constant combination (C.EP.6) or
(C.EP.7) on their common open isomorphism, and therefore agrees everywhere as a meromorphic
vector field. In particular its polar divisors are contained in DP , by (C.EP.3).
Every exceptional valuation is polar. Let E be any prime exceptional for π, with image
p ∈ Z. The nowhere-zero field WZ has a holomorphic flow box (z, w) centred at p in which

                                   WZ (z) = 1,         WZ (w) = 0.                         (C.EP.9)

Both pullbacks vanish to positive order along E. Work at a generic smooth point of E and let s
be its local equation. Write

                             π ∗ w = sb u,    π ∗ z = sa v,       a, b ≥ 1,              (C.EP.10)

where u, v are holomorphic units after shrinking this generic neighbourhood.
    Suppose the lifted derivation D = WP were holomorphic there. The identity D(π ∗ w) = 0,
divided by sb−1 and reduced modulo s, gives

                                      b u D(s) = 0     (mod s).                          (C.EP.11)

Characteristic zero and the fact that u is a unit imply D(s) ∈ (s). Thus D preserves the ideal of

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


the exact pulled-back identity D(π ∗ z) = 1. Hence E is a polar divisor. The argument applies
directly to every exceptional prime, including all infinitely-near point divisors; it does not assume
that a first pole survives an unexamined modification.
    Combining this with (C.EP.3) proves (C.EP.2). The exact period rescalings, the root-
chart invariance, and finite toric valuation certificates for (C.EP.9)–(C.EP.11) are executed in
code/A_translation_exceptions.py. The general exceptional-prime assertion is the local

Proposition 12.11 (Finite removal of all vertical point defects at the marked Hopf interfaces).

an embedded minimal fixed-Jacobian elliptic quasi-bundle. Its full elliptic fibres are multiples of
smooth elliptic curves, its integral linear monodromy is the identity, and every one of its boundary

    Every retained global component has canonical order between 0 and the original M . Whole-
component removals delete a component of positive order q; their preliminary additions, when
needed, have order q + 1 ≤ M , and there are no additions at q = M . The record retains its
actual centres, local maps, normalization branches and restored overlaps, so reversing it recovers
the original family. For a given compact family the same modifications are performed on that

interfaces. In particular an equal-order interface with a nontorsion normal line is not among

in (C.AP.2), and every boundary is a fibre support. All new self-incidences created by the
type-I/type-II and ruled sigma charts are rational exceptional curves. None can remain on these
parents, since their rational boundary would have to be exceptional for a point map of defect
zero. No elliptic self-incidence was introduced: a ruled removal has only one horizontal boundary
section, and all its other changes are at its rational fibre curves. The designated parents are
consequently embedded, with disjoint elliptic boundaries and no triple point.
    Every arrow used above is one of the actual two-ruling, curve, point, or restored sigma-atlas
maps already specified. The inverse record, including all normalization branches and overlap
restrictions, reconstructs the given family. The proper graph gluing and annular comparison of
12.7 give the same record on a compact base, and its normal-cone Euler formula applies at every
retained step. This proves the stated marked-interface reduction in its exact scope.

Here H 0 (KT ) = 0 and H 1 (KT ) = H 1 (OT )∗ = 0 by Serre duality. Consequently H 0 (ODT ) = C.
An effective divisor with disconnected support has independent constant functions on its disjoint
components, so its support is connected. Since C is isolated in that support and has coefficient

Keeping the marked curve through the surface point maps. Take an actual sequence of

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


contraction is an isomorphism near C. If its coefficient is zero, (C.ML.5) says that the old divisor

image meets it. Equivalently, a curve of multiplicity r at the centre has total intersection r with
the exceptional divisor; here r = 1. This proves the assertion by induction through the specified
point maps. Write C0 = π(C).

ruling. The elliptic curve C0 cannot be contained in a rational ruling fibre. Its map to B is finite,

                                     DT0 · F = −KT0 · F = 2.                                (C.ML.6)

vertical part. If C0 has degree two over B, (C.ML.6) gives DT0 = C0 . This connected anticanonical

functional equation is the constant-Jacobian equation from (C.HA.5) and (C.CZ.11).
    For a nonlinear contraction (z, w) 7→ (β r z + wr , βw), its only possible eigenfunction is a
nonzero multiple of wr+1 , with r ≥ 1. Its single curve has coefficient at least two, contradicting
the given simple factor.
    For a diagonal contraction without a resonance, the section is a multiple of zw. In the
resonant case pass through the actual finite unramified central-power cover, so its multipliers
are (γ p , γ q ), with coprime positive p, q. Its monomials have weight p + q. The exact equation
pi + qj = p + q gives i = 1 + q`, j = 1 − p` for an integer `, by coprimality. For p, q > 1,

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


nonnegative exponents force ` = 0, so the only monomial is zw. For p > 1, q = 1, the section has

Propagation through the actual central support. The preceding arguments apply to the

normalization branches and introduce no new component order.

the first assertion.

canonical direct-image line. For M > 0, the first assertion excludes coefficient one on any such
boundary.

Proposition 12.14 (The highest Hopf order can be made the global maximum). Let f : X → ∆
be a proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori with smooth total space and full reduced

                                          h = max ki > 0.                              (C.TK.2)

    At all retained global stages the canonical orders lie between zero and the original R. A
whole-component removal has positive order q; its possible added components have order q + 1,
bounded by the current maximum, and there are no additions when q is that maximum. The
removed q is not required to exceed h. The termination potential therefore counts every positive
order, including orders at most h.

overlaps. Reversing it recovers the given analytic family. On an original compact family it gives
the same actual modification over its compact base. Its Euler changes are the signed normal-cone

complete one-triple ruling curve. At a singular sigma chart, the last locally blown-up branch
of largest order supplies the same one-section configuration. These are the actual two-ruling,
complete-curve and sigma-atlas maps recorded in 12.7 and 12.8.

                                      ksection parent = q − 1.                         (C.TK.3)

of (Kulikov, 1977, Lemma2.19) makes the boundary connected and no insertion is made. In

Why selection remains available above h. The proper composite-graph argument in 12.7
proves that every Hopf-birational prime survives every recorded removal. A general complete
rational exceptional fibre cannot cover a point-blown-up Hopf surface; a compact projective
point exceptional cannot map bimeromorphically onto it. The actual canonical direct-image

over the specified centre, so it is not Hopf-birational. It follows that the set of Hopf orders, with
its original labels, is unchanged. In particular its highest value remains h.

Exact reversal and the converse construction. Every preceding ambient map is one of the
ordinary holomorphic blowdowns of 9.12. Reverse the finite record on the actual endpoint family.
A point step replaces a smooth point of one central component by its exceptional plane. A curve
step has the exact normal sequence (C.NT.1). These comparisons are the actual local blowup
charts and glue with the original isomorphism off each exceptional divisor. They recover the
given U over the disc, not just the birational classes of its components.
    For clarity, the same charts prove the converse directly. At a curve centre choose coordinates
(z, w, t) with the centre (z, t) = 0 and f = t. The blowup charts t = zs and z = tr have fibre
equations zs = 0 and t = 0. At a point centre blow up the ideal (x, y, t); the chart y = xu, t = xv
has fibre equation xv = 0, and the other two charts give the same ordinary normal-crossing
comparison. The centre avoids all pre-existing double curves, so no third component meets either
exceptional pair. The full exceptional multiplicity is one, since t has order one along the centre.
Thus each step retains a smooth total space and a full reduced SNC fibre without triple points.
Its punctured family is unchanged. Properness is retained by the proper blowup map.
    On a curve centre B in the smooth central locus the actual canonical divisor is supported
on boundaries away from B. Its restriction trivializes KP 0 |B . Adjunction therefore gives
NB/P 0 ≃ KB , and the normal sequence with the quotient df 0 is precisely (C.NT.1). No curve of
genus zero can be such a centre: the compact submersion transport (C.NM.10) would again put
its square-minus-two sphere into the nearby torus. Points and smooth curves of positive genus
are exactly the centre types used in the reconstruction.
    When the original total space is compact, the actual local blowdowns glue to the identity off
their exceptional divisors by 9.12. Their targets remain compact and the map to the compact
base descends. Conversely every listed compact centre has its ordinary global blowup. This
proves the compact version without assuming an isomorphism between unrelated realizations of
a marked core.
Euler balance and the intrinsic double-curve record. All four cores have Euler number
zero. A point blowup replaces one point by P2 and adds two to the Euler number of the support.
A curve blowup replaces B by its projective-line bundle of Euler number 2e(B), and so adds
e(B) = 2−2g(B). Additivity along the actual blowup maps gives (C.NT.2), and its zero condition
is exactly (C.NT.3).

Identification of the endpoint and the retained analytic scope. Every endpoint component
and double curve has topological Euler number zero, so e(S∗ ) = 0. The exact invariant relative
cohomology frame gives pg (Z) = g(B) for a quasi-bundle. The common regular Jacobian is
retained by the actual normal-root maps: along an edge joining two quasi-bundle vertices, the
dual normal lines have the same exact order, and inversion identifies their connected root covers of
the elliptic double curve. These are exactly the two regular elliptic fibres, by (C.QT.2)–(C.QT.3);
their translations are retained in the gluing record. At a nonlinear Hopf leaf the same root cover
is instead its exact period cover of 11.5. Such leaves do not interrupt propagation through the
connected quasi-bundle region, and their actual leaf periods and finite characters are retained by
that comparison. The compact-core bound 7.14 therefore permits at most one genus-one base. If
there is one, that normalization has pg = 1. 7.22 gives the actual surjection from its fundamental
group onto that of the full support. The graph-of-spaces comparison gives a surjection from the
support fundamental group to that of its incidence graph, and kills the image of this component’s
fundamental group. The graph fundamental group is therefore trivial, so the connected graph is
a tree. The exact coherent restriction and fundamental-group comparisons of 11.16 then give its
rooted-tree support, with the actual integral Chern and recursive period conditions. If there is
none, 11.17 gives the unicyclic support and its exact torsor, height and common-period conditions.
Its nonlinear leaves retain the secondary finite characters of 11.5. These applications keep the
original surfaces and gluing maps; they do not replace the actual endpoint smoothing.
    All prior operations are the actual finite diagrams already used in 12.7, 12.8, 12.11 and

analytic family. Equation (C.GP.1) is the telescoping normal-cone formula on that finite record,
including its restored-overlap subdivision. Annular gluing to an unchanged compact outside
gives the same actual modifications when the starting total space is compact.

   The data in the following construction include analytic neighbourhoods and their transition
maps. This is essential when an inverse operation uses a normal extension or higher transverse
terms. We first specify those data without referring to a family to be reconstructed.

Finite admissible data. The following are the inputs and the checks on them.

   1. An actual proper smooth-total core family f∗ : X∗ → ∆s , with its labelled analytic charts
      and overlaps and its punctured torus-family comparison, is given. Its full reduced central

      elliptic quasi-bundle/Hopf support of 11.16–11.17. The core chart functions, including their
      transverse terms, are retained.

   2. A finite inverse overlap-compatible sigma record on that actual core is given. Each arrow
      includes the local blowup or contraction map, its centre and ideal, the target charts, and
      the isomorphism on the restored overlap. The maps and their inverse comparisons are
      checked on these charts as in 12.7. The resulting space Z is smooth and proper over ∆s ,
      with full reduced SNC central divisor. The record is an isomorphism on the punctured
      family.

   3. A finite cyclic birational action on the core, over s 7→ ζs, is given, where ζ has order N .
      Conjugating it by the specified inverse record gives holomorphic maps on every chart of
      Z, including the central divisor. Their compositions satisfy the cyclic group law. Thus it
      is an actual regular action of G = µN on Z, not only a central action or an action on its
      meromorphic function field.

   4. A labelled equivariant toric coarsening q : Z → YN is given. Its local semigroup charts,
      units and maps are explicit normalized monomial-ideal blowups in the reverse direction.
      The finite quotient charts of YN have invariant ring OY , with smooth coordinates in which
      the descended function is

annulus. This is the compact version of the same definition.

Proposition 12.18 (Complete rooted generation and the zero-Euler criterion for arbitrary
fibres). Every proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori from a smooth threefold, with
arbitrary full central fibre, is the output of the finite admissible construction above. Conversely
every such input produces a proper degeneration of connected complex two-tori from a smooth
threefold. The inverse record recovers the supplied family exactly. For compact threefolds over
compact curves, the same assertions hold for the compact data.

13    Global CDP replacement and normalization resonance
Proposition 13.1 (The CDP Euler sign and its complete geometric equality criterion). Let Y
be a connected smooth compact complex threefold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0, and let f : Y → B be
a proper surjective holomorphic map with connected fibres and smooth general fibre a complex
two-torus. No condition on the singularities or multiplicities of its fibres is imposed. Then B ≃ P1
and
                         c3 (Y ) = e(Y ) ∈ {0, 2},    b3 (Y ) = 2 − c3 (Y ).                  (C.G.1)
Every reduced fibre support has nonnegative Euler number. An irreducible singular support with
rational normalization resolution has Euler number two; every other irreducible support has Euler
number zero.
    The equality c3 (Y ) = 0 holds precisely when every fibre support has one of the following
geometric descriptions. An irreducible smooth support has a finite unramified torus cover. An
irreducible singular support has smooth minimal elliptic ruled normalization, or has normalization
resolution of class VII. A reducible support has normalization a disjoint union of smooth minimal
Hopf or non-Kähler elliptic surfaces; its reduced conductor image and inverse image are disjoint
unions of smooth elliptic curves, and the maps between these curves are finite unramified covers.
These descriptions concern the actual normalization and resolution maps of the given fibres; all
conductor multiplicities and full-fibre multiplicities are retained.
    In the ruled case the geometric alternatives in (C.IZ.1) are exhaustive. A contracted horizontal
section is excluded by C.2.UN.7: its fundamental group would be trivial, whereas 3.6 supplies
a nonzero integral degree-one class on this support. The class VII data necessarily satisfy the
exact equalities (C.VII.9), sharpened to (C.IZ.2). This criterion does not assert that an arbitrary
abstract collection of such surface and curve data admits a torus smoothing.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.6; proposition 6.2;
proposition 6.3; proposition 8.32; proposition 8.10; proposition 6.18; proposition 6.15;
proposition 6.19; proposition 8.23; proposition 8.26; proposition 8.34; proposition 8.14;
proposition 8.30; proposition 9.5; equation (C.G.2).

Proof. The injection H 1 (B, Q) → H 1 (Y, Q) in the connected-fibre Leray sequence gives g(B) = 0.
We may therefore apply the local transgression and finite-character constructions over P1 .
    First let the support S be irreducible. A normal singular support is excluded by 6.2. A
smooth support has Euler number zero. More explicitly, for a full fibre mS the normalized base
change t = sm is the finite unramified map of A.3.4: in a local equation t = uz m it is given by
wm = u and s = wz. Its central reduction is smooth, and its nearby fibres are the original tori.
Proper smooth deformation identifies their integral cohomology and transports the first Chern
class of the relative tangent bundle, so the central cover has b1 = 4 and rational first Chern
class zero. A compact complex surface with even b1 is Kähler. In the surface classification a
Kähler surface with rational first Chern class zero has Kodaira dimension zero: a nonminimal
model has a (−1)-curve pairing nontrivially with its canonical class; a minimal rational or ruled
surface has a line or ruling fibre with negative canonical degree; and positive Kodaira dimension
would give a nonzero effective pluricanonical divisor pairing positively with a Kähler class. The
Kodaira-dimension-zero list and b1 = 4 therefore identify the cover as a torus. One may also



                                                453
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


compute e(S) = 0 directly: the Cartier-divisor Riemann–Roch calculation gives χ(OS ) = 0, and
adjunction gives c1 (KS ) = 0 rationally, so Noether’s formula gives e(S) = 0.
    For a nonnormal irreducible support let Z → T → S be its minimal normalization resolution.
The effective nonzero resolution conductor D satisfies KZ + D torsion by 6.3 and the canonical
evaluation near this full fibre. If any positive tensor power of KZ had a nonzero section, taking a
further power killing that torsion would give a nonzero section of OZ (−aD) for some a > 0. On
a compact connected surface such a section would be a holomorphic function vanishing along
a nonempty divisor, which is impossible. Thus κ(Z) = −∞. The surface classification gives a
rational surface, an irrational ruled surface, or a class VII surface, with the actual blowup and
normalization morphisms retained.
    For rational Z, 8.32 gives e(S) = 2. For irrational ruled Z, the reduced-horizontal case is
8.10. The coefficient-two horizontal cases are the cusp and tacnode comparisons 6.18 and 6.15
and the complete ordinary-triple comparisons 6.19 and 8.23–2. When the horizontal curve is
not contracted, these prove that the ruling base is elliptic and the normalization is smooth and
minimal. A contracted section cannot occur: 8.26 gives π1 (S) = 1 in that case, contradicting
the nonzero restriction of the integral class of 3.6. We make the exhaustion explicit. For a
noncontracted 2C, degree one over the normalized image makes that image have positive genus;
no vertical rational curve can dominate it, so conductor exponent two is the single-branch
ordinary cusp. In degree two the two horizontal branches each have conductor exponent two.
They are smooth, and their total intersection contributions allow precisely contact two between
them, or simple intersections with one additional smooth branch: the tacnode and ordinary triple
types. Degree three permits precisely three transverse smooth branches. Degree at least four
would already give conductor exponent at least three on each branch, since each meets the other
three branches, and is impossible. Together with the reduced-horizontal case and the exclusion
of a contracted section, these exhaust the horizontal degree two of the anticanonical divisor on a
ruling fibre. 8.32 now gives e(S) = 0 for all of them. Finally 8.34 gives e(S) = 0 for class VII Z,
retaining the exact equality data proved in 8.14.
    Every reducible support has nonnegative Euler number by 8.30. That theorem gives both
directions of precisely the normalization, elliptic-conductor and unramified-cover description
stated here. Its proof works on the whole reduced support and retains the unequal multiplicities
of the original fibre, so it applies to the remaining fibres without a base-change substitution.
    The critical values are finite and the map is a smooth locally trivial bundle away from them, as
proved in 9.5. The Euler number of its torus fibre is zero, so that theorem and complex-oriented
Gauss–Bonnet give
                                                                                             (C.G.2)
                                                    X
                                  c3 (Y ) = e(Y ) =    e((Yb )red ) ≥ 0.
                                                  b∈B

Poincaré duality on the smooth oriented six-manifold gives e(Y ) = 2 − b3 (Y ). Its nonsingular
middle pairing is skew-symmetric, so b3 (Y ) is an even nonnegative integer. Together these facts
give (C.G.1). All summands in (C.G.2) are nonnegative; their sum is zero exactly when every
summand is zero. The irreducible calculation and the reducible equivalence give the stated
complete criterion.

Proposition 13.2 (A geometric replacement on an explicit fibre class). Let f : Y → P1 be
a connected-fibre holomorphic map from a compact connected complex threefold with b1 (Y ) =
b2 (Y ) = 0, and smooth general fibre a complex two-torus. Suppose every full fibre has one of
the following forms: a reduced irreducible normal-crossing surface; or a smooth torus family
modulo a finite free cyclic action over a cyclic base cover, so that its reduction is smooth and its
multiplicity is the covering order. Let

                                      0 6= γ ∈ H 0 (P1 , R1 f∗ Z)



                                                 454
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


be a generator, and suppose that, for every singular reduced full fibre S, its pullback to H 1 (S,
                                                                                                e Q)
under normalization is nonzero. Then a dense open subset of every component of Pic(Y ) satisfies

            H q (Y, TY ⊗ L) = 0   (0 ≤ q ≤ 3),         χ(Y, TY ⊗ L) = 0,    c3 (Y ) = 0.     (C.15)

The generator exists under the stated rational Betti-number assumptions. Its normalization
condition is a condition on an explicit integral cohomology class, with no tangent-cohomology
vanishing assumed.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 5.20; proposition 5.4;
proposition 5.21; proposition 9.5.

Proof. The integral Leray sequence gives an injection

                                H 0 (P1 , R1 f∗ Z) −→ H 2 (P1 , Z) = Z

whose cokernel injects into the finite group H 2 (Y, Z). Thus its source is infinite cyclic. The
degree-one specialization argument of Part D identifies its stalk at every fibre with a nonzero
integral class: a class in the preimage of a small disc that vanishes on a nearby fibre comes from
the meridian of the punctured disc; a normal disc to any irreducible component makes a nonzero
multiple of that meridian nullhomotopic, forcing the class to vanish. The real-to-holomorphic
cohomology map on a compact connected complex space is injective on real classes, as proved
there by the pluriharmonic maximum principle. Coherent Leray therefore supplies β ∈ H 1 (Y, OY )
whose restriction to every full fibre is the image of γ.
     Fix a real irrational number r and put Mr = exp(rβ), with the exponential normalized by
2πi. On each fibre this line is represented by the unitary character exp(2πirγ). It is nontrivial,
and on a singular fibre its normalization pullback is nontrivial by the hypothesis on γ. To see this
directly, triviality of an nth tensor power would place nrγ in the integral lattice after applying
H 1 (R) → H 1 (O); real injectivity makes this an equality in H 1 (R), which is impossible for an
irrational multiple of a nonzero integral vector.
    The same construction works in every Picard component. Each component contains a finite-
order line bundle P : for a representative P0 , a positive power P0m lies in the complex vector
group Pic0 (Y ), where division by m is possible. Dividing P0 by the resulting line makes its mth
power trivial. Replacing Mr by Mr ⊗ P retains nontrivial unitary restriction on each fibre and
on each specified normalization. Indeed an mth power eliminates P and reduces a purported
trivialization to the preceding irrationality contradiction.
     Set L = KY ⊗ (Mr ⊗ P )−1 . On every full fibre F the Serre-dual bundle for degree two is

                            (TY ⊗ L)|∗F ⊗ ωF = Ω1Y |F ⊗ (Mr ⊗ P )|F ,

because F is a Cartier fibre and ωF = KY |F . At a smooth torus fibre both the conormal
line and the intrinsic cotangent bundle are trivial; nontrivial unitary degree-zero lines on the
torus have zero cohomology. The ambient space of sections is therefore zero. At a reduced
irreducible normal-crossing fibre, Statement 5.20 proves the torsion-free cotangent vanishing for
every nontrivial unitary line. The normal-crossing kernel in 5.4 is the normalization pushforward,
and its sections vanish because the pulled-back unitary line is nontrivial. A holomorphic section
of a unitary line on a compact connected complex manifold has constant norm by the maximum
principle and is either zero or a trivialization. Thus the ambient group vanishes there as well.
    On a cyclic-cover neighbourhood of a smooth multiple fibre, the covering map to Y is finite
etale. The pulled-back line restricts nontrivially to the covering central torus: finite etale
pullback is injective on rational degree-one cohomology by its trace, and r is irrational. The
scheme-theoretic inverse image of the full fibre is the corresponding thickening of this torus.


                                                 455
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


Each layer in its ideal filtration is the same ambient cotangent restriction tensored with this
nontrivial line, since the covering base coordinate trivializes the conormal. Every layer has zero
cohomology. The exact filtration sequences therefore give zero sections on the full thickening.
Taking finite-group invariants, an exact functor, proves the required ambient vanishing on the
original full fibre.
    Top-degree coherent base change now gives R2 f∗ (TY ⊗ L) = 0. For sufficiently large integer
n, Serre vanishing on the base gives

                                H 1 P1 , R1 f∗ (TY ⊗ L) ⊗ O(n) = 0.
                                                               


Projection formula and the two-column Leray sequence imply H 2 (Y, TY ⊗ L ⊗ f ∗ O(n)) = 0. This
is an actual twist in the same Picard component up to the fixed finite-order class of f ∗ O(n);
choosing n divisible by the finite order of its Chern class keeps the component unchanged.
Semicontinuity in the explicit Picard family of C.1 makes the degree-two zero locus dense open
in that component. Intersect it with the dense open endpoint-vanishing loci from C.1. On this
intersection χ(TY ⊗ L) = −h1 ≤ 0.
     Statement 5.21 gives Euler number zero or two for each reduced irreducible normal-crossing
fibre; the positive case has rational normalization. Our normalization hypothesis excludes that
case, since rational smooth surfaces have H 1 (−, Q) = 0. Smooth torus fibres and the smooth
finite etale quotients in the second fibre class have Euler number zero. Therefore 9.5 gives
c3 (Y ) = 0. The index formula in C.1 gives χ = 0, forcing h1 = 0 on the same dense open set.
This proves all of (C.15).

Proposition 13.4 (The finite singular-fibre test and a fixed unavoidable fibre). Let f : Y → P1

Proof. The universal Picard family constructed in C.1 restricts to a holomorphic family on the

    Let h : Z → S ⊂ Y . 6.3 supplies an effective conductor divisor DZ with

                            KZ + DZ = h∗ (KY + S),          DZ · F = 2                        (C.22)

for a general ruling fibre F . Its horizontal part is therefore either reduced of total ruling degree
two, or 2C for a section C. We record the comparison through each ruling blowdown σ : Z → Z 0
used below. Put D0 = σ∗ DZ , let a be the coefficient of its exceptional curve E in DZ , and put
d = multσ(E) D0 . Then

                            KZ + DZ = σ ∗ (KZ 0 + D0 ) + (1 + a − d)E.                       (C.22b)

Intersection with E, using c1 (KZ +DZ ) = 0 and E 2 = −1, gives a = d−1. Thus the log-canonical
divisor is the exact pullback of KZ 0 + D0 , and the latter again has zero rational Chern class. No
factorization of h through the blowdown is asserted or needed.
    We first treat the reduced horizontal part H. If a component is exceptional for the
normalization resolution, every ambient line restricts trivially to it. Its normalization maps
finitely onto B, and the norm composed with pullback on Pic0 (B) is multiplication by the
covering degree. Hence this restriction has finite kernel; the connected ambient Picard image
is trivial, giving (C.21). We may therefore assume that the horizontal components map to
conductor curves. Adjunction on each of them gives

                                2pa (Hi ) − 2 + (DZ − Hi ) · Hi = 0.

The second term is nonnegative. Since Hi dominates a positive-genus base, its arithmetic genus
is at least one. Thus the base has genus one, each Hi is smooth elliptic, and the horizontal
curves are disjoint from each other and from the vertical part. Contract ruling (−1)-curves to a
minimal bundle. A contracted curve outside DZ has DZ · E = 1, so cannot identify two horizontal
points or create a horizontal node. A contracted curve in the vertical part is disjoint from H.
Downstairs the horizontal curves remain smooth and disjoint, and any nonzero vertical divisor on
a minimal ruled bundle meets them. Consequently the downstairs vertical part is zero. Reversing
the contractions, a blowup away from the horizontal conductor would give coefficient −1 on
its exceptional curve in (C.22), which persists under further strict transform and contradicts
effectiveness. A blowup at a smooth point of a coefficient-one horizontal curve gives exceptional
coefficient zero. Hence DZ = H has no vertical component. Every codimension-one singularity of
S is then an ordinary node, and A.2 identifies the inverse-Jacobian kernel with the normalization
kernel globally, including its codimension-two points. A section of a topologically trivial line on
the Kahler resolution has an effective zero divisor of zero Kahler volume, so is nowhere zero.
Persistence for all twists therefore makes all ambient pullbacks trivial and proves (C.21).

Proposition 13.7 (An unrestricted geometric replacement for CDP20 Theorem 2.2). Let
f : Y → P1 satisfy the integral CDP hypotheses. For each critical full fibre with irreducible
nonnormal reduced support S, let ηS : TS → S be its normalization. Then a general line bundle
L ∈ Pic(Y ) satisfies
                                 H q (Y, TY ⊗ L) = 0 (q 6= 1)                        (C.VC.1)
exactly when, for every such S, the holomorphic pullback homomorphism

                                          Pic(Y ) −→ Pic(TS )                              (C.VC.2)

is nonzero. Equivalently, its differential H 1 (Y, OY ) → H 1 (TS , OTS ) is nonzero. In this case
χ(Y, TY ⊗ L) ≤ 0 and c3 (Y ) ≤ 0. If one map (C.VC.2) is zero, then H 2 (Y, TY ⊗ L) 6= 0 for every

criterion.

proposition 6.9; proposition 13.5; proposition 3.8; proposition 5.24.

Proof. The classification and exclusions cited in 13.6 leave exactly the two cohomological cases
used in that proof: torus general fibre, or h1 (O) = 1, h2 (O) = 0. The Picard group of Y is
the connected exponential image of H 1 (Y, OY ). A holomorphic group homomorphism out of
this group is zero precisely when its differential is zero. For each fixed critical full fibre, the
ambient-section nonvanishing locus is closed analytic in this group, as in 13.4. 5.14 makes it
proper when the support is smooth, and 5.15 makes it proper when the support is reducible.
A connected normal support is irreducible and is smooth by 6.2, so these cases leave just the
supports in the statement.
    Suppose the nonvanishing locus for F = mS is the whole Picard group. The proof of 13.6,
beginning with its fixed-fibre persistence assertion, proves that (C.VC.2) is zero. Its steps

transverse-type calculations. Each is independent of the Euler number once persistence has been
given.
    Conversely, suppose (C.VC.2) is zero. The last nonzero ideal layer of the full fibre is an actual
subsheaf
                        (Ω1Y ⊗ M ⊗ OY (−(m − 1)S))|S ,→ (Ω1Y ⊗ M )|mS .                     (C.VC.3)

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II

actual twists Lr = KY ⊗ Mr−1 for real irrational r. 5.24 and the smooth-fibre conormal sequence
make their R2 f∗ (TY ⊗ Lr ) torsion. The fixed full-fibre obstruction again makes that torsion

complex line Pic(Y ) = Cβ. A closed complex analytic subset of that line containing them is the
whole line. This proves all-twist nonvanishing in the second case and completes both implications
of the criterion.

    For every member in question, H 2 (Y, Z) is a finite group. For the original affine family this

automorphism of P1 and multiplication by a constant of modulus strictly less than one on C∗ .
Its quotient is a P1 -bundle over the elliptic curve given by that multiplicative period. The cusp
normalization is bijective; a proper continuous bijection between these compact Hausdorff spaces
is a homeomorphism. Hence e(Ccusp ) = 0. This proves (C.TEST.2).
    Finally the explicit good-reduction covers in 15.8–15.9 and the original root charts have
the stated orders. Their reduced central fibres are smooth finite unramified torus quotients,
and their Euler numbers are zero. 5.14 applies to their actual full fibres, proving the asserted
generic ambient vanishing. Euler localization therefore gives c3 (Y ) = 2 in all three rows, while
the nonreduced fibres satisfy the complete multiple-fibre test. This is the required test of the
proposed additional nonreduced-fibre necessity.

Proposition 14.1 (Proved obstruction). A compact complex threefold with b1 = b2 = 0 and a
holomorphic connected-fibre map to a curve, with general fibre a two-torus and trivial rational
monodromy, has reducible fibres. More precisely, for every nonempty set of s removed values
containing all critical values, their reduced fibres have r = s + 3 irreducible components in total.
Every component of each reducible fibre has no compact Kähler resolution. Consequently no such
fibration can have all its fibre components admitting compact Kähler resolutions.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.1; proposition 4.3.

Proof. The base is P1 by 3.1. Trivial monodromy on the four-dimensional H1 (F ; Q) gives t0 = 4,
so the corrected formula gives r = s + 3. If all removed fibres were irreducible one would have
r = s, which is impossible. The assertion about each component is Statement 4.3, applied to this
threefold. The last assertion follows by combining these two conclusions.

Proposition 14.3 (Proved sign in the full normal-crossings class). For the threefolds and maps
in D.2 whose reduced fibre supports all have normal crossings, the Euler number is

                                     c3 (Y ) = 0,         b3 (Y ) = 2.

All multiplicities, including unequal multiplicities on a reducible support, are allowed. In this
class there are no positive-Euler-number examples with trivial monodromy.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 9.4; proposition 9.2;
proposition 14.2; proposition 14.6.

Proof. Statement 9.4 gives c3 (Y ) = 2r, where r counts the irreducible fibre supports with rational
normalization. A fibre of that kind is necessarily mS for one positive integer m. Choose a small
disc around its value and perform the normalized base change t = um . Statement 9.2 identifies
the resulting map to the original neighbourhood as finite étale of degree m, and its central fibre
S 0 as reduced with normal crossings. The total space is therefore smooth. Its nearby fibres are
the original connected tori. Stein factorization over the normal disc shows that its central fibre
is connected as well: the finite Stein factor has generic degree one and is the disc itself.
     Normalization commutes with this étale base change. Each normalized component of S 0
is an unramified finite cover of the smooth rational normalization T of S. Since T is simply
connected, these normalized components are copies of T , and all have geometric genus zero. The
local monodromy after base change is the mth power of the original monodromy, so remains the
identity on H 1 . This contradicts 14.2. Therefore r = 0, proving c3 (Y ) = 0. Poincaré duality and
b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0 give c3 (Y ) = 2 − b3 (Y ), hence b3 (Y ) = 2. The example of 14.6 realizes this
normal-crossings class.

Proposition 14.4 (Proved unrestricted sign under trivial monodromy). Let f : Y → P1 be
a proper surjective holomorphic map with connected fibres from a compact connected complex
threefold with b1 (Y ) = b2 (Y ) = 0. Suppose its smooth general fibre is a complex two-torus and its
monodromy representation on H1 (F, Q) is trivial. Then

                                     c3 (Y ) ≤ 0,         b3 (Y ) ≥ 2.                        (D.S.1)

The fibres may have arbitrary singularities and arbitrary multiplicities. In particular this proves
the sign assertion of D.2 for a holomorphic algebraic reduction; no existence assertion is required
for the conclusion.

proposition 14.2.

Scope of 14.5. For a fibration over P1 with globally trivial marked H 1 monodromy, the local
constructions glue to a smooth proper torus group family over P1 . The period map may be
nonconstant, as the explicit family in 3.12 demonstrates. The local filling in 14.6 proves that the
marked Albanese map need not extend to the given model. Its inclusion of a nearby fibre kills
the nonzero cycle w in (D.25). An extension U → A × ∆ of the marked fibre isomorphisms would
induce a map on H1 whose composite with that inclusion is the identity on H1 (A; Z), which is
impossible because it would send w both to zero and to w. This exact topological obstruction
explains why the extending group family does not imply nonexistence in D.2.

Proposition 14.6 (Proved existence). There exists a smooth compact connected complex threefold

           [C1 ] = e3 ∧ e4 ,   [C2 ] = −e2 ∧ e3 + e3 ∧ e4 ,       [C3 ] = −e2 ∧ e4 + e3 ∧ e4 .

They form an integral basis of the rank-three quotient. Consequently (D.32) is zero, including its
torsion. The attached program constructs both full signed Mayer–Vietoris matrices: their sizes
are 15 × 15 and 29 × 30, the first has determinant +1, and all nonzero Smith entries of both are
1. It also checks the six-dimensional relation matrix in (D.32).
    Each central component is an elliptic bundle over a compact curve and therefore has Euler
number zero; their intersection is elliptic and also has Euler number zero. The three central
fibres have Euler number zero. The smooth torus fibre has Euler number zero, so additivity over
the base gives e(Y ) = 0. Gauss–Bonnet and Poincaré duality now give c3 (Y ) = 0 and b3 (Y ) = 2.
    Finally every effective divisor on Y is vertical. If an irreducible divisor dominated the base, its
restriction to a general Kähler torus fibre would be a nonzero effective divisor. Its rational Chern
class is zero because H 2 (Y ; Q) = 0; integration against a Kähler form gives the contradiction of
a strictly positive number equal to zero. A meromorphic function therefore has only vertical zero
and pole divisors, and its restriction to a general compact fibre is a holomorphic nowhere-zero
function, hence constant. It consequently descends to a meromorphic function of the base. To
verify extension at a special value with parameter t, choose N so that multiplication by f ∗ tN
removes the pole order on every component of the full fibre. The product has no polar divisor
and is holomorphic on the smooth total space, by the local normality criterion for a meromorphic
function. Properness, connected fibres and normality of the base give f∗ OY = OP1 by Stein
factorization. The product therefore descends to a holomorphic function, proving the required
meromorphic extension after division by tN . Thus M(Y ) = f ∗ C(t) and a(Y ) = 1. The universal
coefficient theorem also gives H 1 (Y ; Z) = H 2 (Y ; Z) = 0 from (D.31)–(D.32). This proves every
assertion in (D.21).

Literature comparison. The construction uses explicit principal elliptic bundles, one ordinary
point blowup in each local quotient surface, and the specified integral clutchings. Searches for

“complex threefold, Kodaira, Hopf, fibre, monodromy”, “algebraic dimension, S 3 × S 3 , torus”,

example in the sources inspected. The complete construction and integral calculation above
are independent of a literature classification of such fillings. They also show why extending the

Proof. Write E = R1 f∗ OY . Statement 3.9 gives its local freeness, full-fibre base change, and

                          H 1 (Si ; Z) = H 1 (Ui ; Z) = {λ ∈ Λ∗ : λ(wi ) = 0}.                  (D.36)

     Each annihilator in (D.36) has real dimension three, so its complex span in the two-dimensional

consequently extend as a frame of E across zero.

therefore glue to E ≃ O⊕2 on P1 . The cup-product isomorphism in 3.9 gives R2 f∗ OY ≃ det E ≃ O.
Connected fibres give f∗ OY = O. Leray on P1 proves all four dimensions in (D.33), and evaluation
of the trivial rank-two bundle, followed by the proved base-change isomorphism, proves coherent
surjectivity.

constant smooth-fibre lattice. Their defining equations are λ3 = 0, λ2 + λ4 = 0, λ1 + λ4 = 0. The

primitive solution is (1, 1, 0, −1), giving (D.34). In particular all three extra fibre components

Proposition 14.8 (Proved existence and exact Euler number). The class of compact complex
threefolds with b1 = b2 = 0, a proper connected-fibre map with smooth two-torus general fibre,
and trivial rational monodromy is nonempty. Every member satisfies

                                       c3 (Y ) = 0,         b3 (Y ) = 2.

Every individual reduced fibre support has Euler number zero and the geometric description of
13.1. Arbitrary singularities and full-fibre multiplicities are allowed. There is an example with
integral H1 (Y, Z) = H2 (Y, Z) = 0 and algebraic dimension one.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 13.1; proposition 14.4;
proposition 14.6; proposition 14.2.

Proof. The unrestricted lower bound of 13.1 and the independent trivial-monodromy upper
bound of 14.4 give c3 (Y ) = 0. Poincaré duality gives b3 (Y ) = 2 − c3 (Y ) = 2. 13.1 expresses c3
as the sum of the nonnegative Euler numbers of the reduced fibre supports, so each summand
vanishes and satisfies that theorem’s exact equality criterion. Statement 14.6 constructs the
asserted example with integral homology vanishing and algebraic dimension one. 14.2–4 also
give a separate local proof of the equality when all supports have normal crossings.

Proposition 15.1 (The infinitesimal map and the rank-two boundary). Let g : Y → C be a
proper connected-fibre map from a compact complex threefold whose smooth general fibre is a

                                  g∗
                 0 → H 1 (C, TC ) −→ H 1 (Y, g ∗ TC ) → H 0 (C, TC ⊗ R1 g∗ OY ) → 0.              (3)

                               δ : TC ⊗ R1 g∗ OY |U −→ R2 g∗ TY /C |U .

At a smooth torus fibre F , write its Kodaira–Spencer tensor as κ = u1 ⊗ η1 + u2 ⊗ η2 , where
η1 , η2 is a basis of H 1 (F, OF ) and ui ∈ Lie(F ). Then

                              δ(aη1 + bη2 ) = (bu1 − au2 ) ⊗ (η1 ∧ η2 ).

H 1 (Y, g ∗ TC ) lies in g ∗ H 1 (C, TC ). For C = P1 this image is zero.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition A.9.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


Proof. The projection formula gives Rq g∗ g ∗ TC = TC ⊗ Rq g∗ OY , and the coherent Leray spectral

Proposition 15.2 (Stability of a rank-two torus fibration). Let g : Y → P1 be as in 15.1
and suppose its Kodaira–Spencer tensor has rank two at one regular value. For every proper
deformation Y → (S, 0) of Y over a complex analytic germ, including a nonreduced germ, there
is, after shrinking S, a holomorphic map

                                          G : Y −→ P1 × S

over S whose central restriction is g. Every Gs is surjective with connected fibres and smooth
general fibre a complex two-torus. With b2 (Y ) = 0, every sufficiently small deformation has
algebraic dimension one.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 15.1; (Horikawa, 1974, §4,
equations (4.3)–(4.5), and §6); equation (4); equation (3); (Douady, 1966, Section 9,
Theorems 1–2, pp. 83–85); (Douady, 1966, Section 10.1, Proposition 1, p. 86); (Douady, 1966,
Section 10.2, Theorem 1, p. 87); (Buchdahl, 1999, Theorem 11); proposition 2.3.

Proof. We prove the lifting assertion at every Artin order; this is more than the tangent-space
assertion of 15.1. The obstruction calculations below use the Cech construction of holomorphic-
map deformations in (Horikawa, 1974, §4, equations (4.3)–(4.5), and §6); we spell out the portions
needed here. The injectivity hypothesis on degree-two tangent cohomology in its Theorem 6.1 is
replaced here by the explicitly proved unobstructedness of the torus source.
    First fix a rank-two regular fibre and its embedding i : F ,→ Y . The normal line is canonically
N = OF ⊗ Tc P1 . The tangent sequence and 15.1 imply that

                            H 1 (F, TF ) −→ H 1 (F, i∗ TY )   is surjective.                        (4)

Let A0 → A be a small extension of local Artin complex algebras, with kernel I annihilated by
the maximal ideal. Suppose an embedding iA : FA ,→ YA deforming i and a deformation YA0
lifting YA have been specified. The deformation functor of a complex torus is smooth: with a real
lattice marking its small complex structures are graphs of arbitrary small complex linear maps
between the two complementary Hodge subspaces; constant Beltrami tensors have zero bracket.
This gives a smooth four-dimensional miniversal germ for F . In particular FA has a lift FA0 .
     Choose local lifts of iA on sufficiently small coordinate charts. They exist because the target
deformation is smooth over A0 . Their differences on overlaps form a one-cocycle in i∗ TY ⊗ I.

                                                 482
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


Changing the lifted transition functions of FA0 by a cocycle vij ∈ TF ⊗ I changes this obstruction
by di(vij ). Such changes are precisely the action of H 1 (F, TF ) ⊗ I on the set of lifts of FA ; their
cocycle law has no quadratic term because ImA0 = 0. Surjectivity (4) therefore makes the map
obstruction zero. A zero-coboundary correction glues the local maps. The resulting proper map
is a closed immersion: the map on local rings is surjective modulo the nilpotent ideal, hence
surjective by Nakayama, and its underlying central map is the embedding i. Thus the given
embedded torus lifts in every ambient small extension.
    Now suppose gA : YA → P1A has been lifted and that YA0 is prescribed. Choose local lifts
ti of the target coordinate of gA ; on overlaps their discrepancies define the holomorphic-map
obstruction
                                       α ∈ H 1 (Y, g ∗ TP1 ) ⊗ I.
Coordinate changes on the target give exactly the transition factors of g ∗ TP1 , and the triple-
overlap relation gives its Cech cocycle law. A coboundary makes the local maps agree, so α = 0
is sufficient as well as necessary.

                                     (ti − tj )|F = ηi |F − ηj |F .
This is exactly the assertion that the restricted obstruction cocycle is a coboundary in N ⊗ I.
    By (3) and H 1 (P1 , TP1 ) = 0, α is a section of the locally free sheaf TP1 ⊗ R1 g∗ OY , tensored
with I. Its evaluation at every rank-two regular fibre is zero. That set is open dense; hence the
section and α are zero. The map therefore lifts across every small extension.
    We pass from the formal assertion to an analytic map and specify the relative parameter
space, including its nilpotents. Let H be the germ at the graph of g in the absolute Douady
space of Y × P1 , and let π : R → H be its universal compact flat family. Douady’s existence and
finiteness theorems (Douady, 1966, Section 9, Theorems 1–2, pp. 83–85) apply to this analytic
ambient space; its local rings and those of the parameter space may have nilpotents.
    After shrinking H, one has
                                             π∗ OR = OH ,
compatibly with base change. To check this without assuming a reduced parameter space,
represent Rπ∗ OR near the central point by a finite complex of finite free analytic modules. On
the central fibre the unit spans H 0 (Y, OY ) = C. Split off this unit in degree zero. The differential
is injective modulo the maximal ideal on the complementary degree-zero summand; an invertible
minor cancels that summand with its image in degree one. The resulting complex begins with OH
in degree zero and zero differential from it. This proves the displayed equality and its base-change
assertion on the full analytic germ.
     Embed a representative of (S, 0) in a polydisc. The coordinate functions of the map R → Y →
S are now pullbacks of unique holomorphic functions on H. They satisfy the defining equations
of S, because their pullbacks do and the unit map just proved is injective. They therefore define
a holomorphic morphism H → S, and the universal subspace lies scheme-theoretically in

                                           (Y ×S H) × P1 .

The projection of this subspace to Y ×S H is a proper morphism between two proper flat families
over H and is an isomorphism at the central point. By the isomorphism-locus criterion (Douady,
1966, Section 10.1, Proposition 1, p. 86), it is an isomorphism after restricting to an open
neighbourhood of that point. The proof of that criterion uses the finite direct image, flatness and

                                                  483
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


Nakayama’s lemma, and applies to nonreduced H. On this open locus the universal subspace is
the graph of an actual map to P1 .
    The universal property of the absolute Douady space consequently identifies this open
locus with the germ H → S of relative maps from Y/S to P1 × S/S. This is the relative
version of Douady’s graph construction (Douady, 1966, Section 10.2, Theorem 1, p. 87); the
argument above supplies the variation of the compact source explicitly. The just-proved lifting
property for every small Artin extension says that this morphism is formally smooth at [g]. The
local analytic smoothness criterion identifies a formally smooth morphism of finite-dimensional
analytic germs with a projection S × (Cr , 0) → S after shrinking. One can see the criterion on
presentations of their convergent local algebras: lifting across all square-zero quotients makes the
relative conormal obstruction zero, and the analytic implicit function theorem eliminates the
corresponding equations. The zero section of this product supplies the required holomorphic
family of graphs. This argument applies to nonreduced S.
    At one regular value, the family G remains a proper submersion near the central compact
fibre. Its nearby fibres are connected deformations of a torus. Each map Gs is nonconstant,
and hence surjective. Its Stein factorization has finite degree one because it has a connected
regular fibre in this neighbourhood. Thus every fibre is connected. Over the connected smooth
locus of Gs , Ehresmann’s theorem identifies the differentiable fibres with T 4 . Every compact
complex surface with this differentiable type is a torus: its even first Betti number makes it
Kähler by (Buchdahl, 1999, Theorem 11); its Albanese has dimension two; the exterior algebra
on its four integral degree-one classes shows the Albanese map has degree one; and a nontrivial
exceptional curve of this degree-one map would include a (−1)-curve, impossible for the even
intersection form of T 4 . Hence the general fibre is a complex two-torus. Finally b2 is constant in
the differentiable deformation family, and 2.3 proves a(Ys ) = 1.

Proposition 15.5 (Counterexample: A fixed positive-genus target in the unrestricted stability
assertion). The assertion that every small deformation of a fibration extends over its original
fixed positive-genus target curve C is false even for a torus fibration with Kodaira–Spencer rank
two at a regular value.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (3); proposition 15.1.

Proof. Let S → P1t be the rational elliptic surface obtained by blowing up the nine base points
of the Hesse pencil x3 + y 3 + z 3 − 3txyz = 0. Its critical values are {1, ω, ω 2 , ∞}, where ω 3 = 1,
ω 6= 1. Pull another copy back by φ(t) = 1/(t − 4); its critical values are {4, 5, 4 + ω, 4 + ω 2 },
disjoint from the first set. Their fibre product Z → P1 is a smooth projective threefold, since
at every point at least one elliptic-surface map is a submersion. Its general fibre is a product
of two elliptic curves. Both elliptic j-functions are nonconstant, so their two Kodaira–Spencer
derivatives are simultaneously nonzero off a finite set. The tensor of their product is then diagonal
of rank two.
    Let Cs be the smooth genus-two double cover

                     y 2 = (t − 10)(t − 11)(t − 12)(t − 13)(t − 14)(t − 15 − s)

of P1 , for s in a small disc. All its branch values avoid the critical values of Z. Thus Ys = Z ×P1 Cs
is a smooth projective deformation of a compact threefold, and gs : Ys → Cs has connected torus
general fibre and rank two at a regular value. The Kodaira–Spencer class θC ∈ H 1 (C0 , TC0 ) is
nonzero: any infinitesimal isomorphism of the hyperelliptic covers descends through their unique
hyperelliptic involutions to an infinitesimal projective transformation fixing five distinct branch
values; it is zero, whereas the sixth branch value moves with derivative one.
    All the cohomology used for the obstruction is explicit. Put L = πC             ∗ O (1) on C ; the

Proposition 15.6 (All coprime (3k, 4l) multiplicities). Fix admissible logarithmic-transformation
data with multiplicities r = 3k, s = 4l, where k, l > 0 and gcd(r, s) = 1, in the family constructed
from the original elliptic-surface data. For every member which is diffeomorphic to S 6 , as in
(Viaclovsky, 2026c, Theorem labelled t:main),

                                       h• (X, TX ) = (1, 1, 1, 0),

its Kuranishi germ is a smooth reduced line, and varying the nonzero linearization scale with those
data fixed is locally miniversal. For the original (3, 4) affine-twist family, the same statements
hold whenever p 6= 0, including |p| > 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Viaclovsky, 2026c, Theorem labelled
t:main); proposition 15.3.

Proof. Put Br,s = P(r, s). The root morphism σ : Br,s → B3,4 over the identical coarse P1 sends
the two root sections to their kth and lth powers. In line notation σ ∗ OB3,4 (1) = OBr,s (kl). The
vertical transition matrices and the action on fibre O-cohomology depend only on the linear
monodromy. The extra affine translations act trivially on both. The same cusp comparison used
in Paper I, Theorem 3.9 therefore gives the actual bundles

                          E = G = O ⊕ O(−kl),             R2 f¯∗ OX = O(−kl),

and

  0 → f¯∗ E → T := TX (− log W ) → f¯∗ L → 0,         L = O(r + s − rs),       KX = f¯∗ O(kl − r − s).

For example the normal-cover coordinate at the first finite point is u = v k , and differentiation
changes the ordinary root tangent line from the old one to TBr,s ; the vertical bundle and its
cohomology are pulled back through u = v k . This specifies the comparison rather than identifying
the two horizontal tangent lines. At the cusp W remains the same normal-crossing divisor, so its
logarithmic base correction is −p0 = −rs and its normal quotient is η∗ KdP6 .
    Locally σ∗ O = O and its positive direct images vanish: the additional cyclic group has
invariants C{v}µk = C{u}, and averaging is exact. Consequently the cohomology of the pulled-
back lines O(−kl) and O(−2kl) is the cohomology of the original O(−1) and O(−2), hence zero.
Projection and Leray give h• (X, f¯∗ E) = (1, 1, 0, 0). For the horizontal line, its coarse direct image

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


is OP1 (−1): a vector field on a root disc must have its coefficient divisible by the root parameter, so
ρ∗ TBr,s = TP1 (−p1 −p2 ), and the extra −p0 gives the asserted degree. Moreover L and L⊗O(−kl)
have negative orbifold degree, so have no global sections. Thus H 0 (X, f¯∗ L) = H 1 (X, f¯∗ L) = 0.
The two exact tangent sequences now give h0 (X, TX ) = h1 (X, TX ) = 1.
    We compute degree three independently. On the smooth torus locus, the boundary on a
relative holomorphic one-form is the transpose of the Kodaira–Spencer tensor. The latter is
generically invertible by 15.3. Hence every ambient holomorphic one-form on an inverse-image
base disc is horizontal. It is the pullback of a base one-form. At a finite root point the root map

                                            f¯∗ Ω1X = Ω1Br,s .

                            h3 (X, TX ) = h0 Br,s , O(kl − 2r − 2s) = 0.

For the last equality, a weighted monomial of that degree would give nonnegative integers a, b
with 3k(a + 2) + 4l(b + 2) = kl. Reduction modulo k makes b + 2 a positive multiple of k, since
gcd(k, 4l) = 1. The second term alone is then at least 4kl, a contradiction. On a six-sphere
χ(TX ) = 1, giving h2 = 1. For the original affine-twist family, r = 3, s = 4, and the horizontal

and the quotient η∗ KdP6 gives h• (TX ) = (1, 1, 1, 0) directly for every admissible affine twist. This
computation does not require the integral homology to be that of a sphere.
    The scale derivative changes the fourth torus period by a nonzero constant multiple of the
parameter derivative in Paper I, Theorem 3.9, so its restricted torus class is nonzero. A first-order
trivialization of the compact member would turn the given fibration into a first-order deformation
of the fixed map f with fixed source. Such deformations are H 0 (X, f ∗ TP1 ) = H 0 (P1 , TP1 ), by
connected fibres and the projection formula. Thus they are precisely infinitesimal projective
transformations of the base. The two multiple critical values and the hexagonal critical value
remain the same three constant sections in this scale family; the local equations t = v r , t − 1 = v s ,
q = xyz show this also over the dual numbers. The base vector field is therefore zero. The
nonzero torus class cannot be trivialized, proving the nonzero global scale derivative. The
one-dimensional tangent space and the analytic local-algebra argument at the end of Paper I,
Theorem 3.9 prove smoothness, reducedness and miniversality.

    We construct a family with this full tangent space. All nearby root-period sections have
normal bundle V ⊗ G, tangent space H 0 (A), and obstruction space H 1 (A) = 0. This section germ
can be realized using an ordinary coarse Grassmannian bundle and finite analytic conditions.
Split the equivariant bundle as F ⊕ G on a finite-cover chart and write a nearby plane as a
graph matrix. Dividing the invariant-generator factors shows that a holomorphic lift requires
one entry to vanish at p1 and two at p2 . At p1 the entry is from the nontrivial Hodge line to
the trivial quotient line. At p2 it is that entry and the entry between the two nontrivial lines.
These are linear conditions on the values of the local graph matrix. Their normal sheaf is A.
The Cech gluing obstruction across a small Artin extension lies in H 1 (A) = 0; each local graph
chart and its stated conditions is smooth. The finite-dimensional Douady section germ with
these conditions is therefore smooth of dimension 8m + 1. This description does not require a
global manifold cover of the root curve.
    These sections produce compact threefolds even though their limiting periods are allowed to
vary. At a finite point the equivariant lift is a small deformation on the compact good-reduction
cover. Admissibility is open there. The affine action has the same real formula x 7→ T x + v/n; it
is holomorphic for the new equivariant periods and stays free because its real action is unchanged.
At the hexagon the transverse graph chart is open, and its periods are
                                                 log q
