                                                  2πi
with H holomorphic and uniformly bounded on a smaller parameter polydisc. The translations
with unit factors exp(2πiHij ) preserve the same toric fan. On logarithmic radii their action is
r 7→ r + (I + O(1/ log |q|))λ; it is uniformly proper and free for small q. A fixed finite collection of
toric unit polydiscs gives compact representatives. Thus the filling is proper with local equation
q = x1 x2 x3 , and its total space is smooth over the parameter. Varying H(0) varies gluing units
and preserves these estimates and local equations. On the compact complement of the critical
discs admissibility is open. The annular gluings extend holomorphically with their fixed integral
classes: the lattice–Lie–torus exact sequence and Cartan vanishing on an annular product extend
the original translations. This constructs a proper holomorphic family with all 8m + 1 period
directions and the specified central member.
     Its Kodaira–Spencer map is injective. A first-order trivialization would make its map
variation a section of H 0 (Xm , f ∗ TB ) = H 0 (B, TB ). The three critical values remain constant by
the equations w3 , w4 , x1 x2 x3 , so that base vector field vanishes at three points and is zero. The
trivialization would then be fibre preserving. On a marked smooth torus the period derivative is
the corresponding constant Dolbeault tensor in Lie(F ) ⊗ H 1 (F, OF ). A nonzero constant tensor
cannot be a Dolbeault coboundary, since derivatives of periodic coefficients integrate to zero.
Thus a period section giving a trivial total-space deformation vanishes on every regular fibre,
and hence identically. Its Kodaira–Spencer map is an isomorphism onto the already computed
H 1 (TXm ). The inverse-function argument of 15.8 then makes the Kuranishi ideal zero, proving
smoothness, reducedness and miniversality. The topology theorem of the comb construction
identifies these manifolds with S 6 ; 2.3 and 15.2 give algebraic dimension one throughout their
small deformation germs.

Proposition 15.11 (Rank divisors from the root Kodaira–Spencer morphism). We use the
logarithmic Kodaira–Spencer morphism at the specified degenerate fibres and the ordinary morphism
on the finite smooth torus covers. For the original affine-twist family, including every |p| > 1, its
only rank defect is rank one at the order-three point. The logarithmic cusp has rank two. For the
(3k, 4l) logarithmic transforms, on their full root covers the ranks at the two multiple values are
respectively                       (                 (
                                     1 k = 1,          2 l = 1,
                                                                                            (E.16.1)
                                     0 k > 1,          0 l > 1.
Every other smooth point and the logarithmic cusp have rank two.
    For the two-parameter family the logarithmic rank is one at each of its two rank-one nodal
values, zero at the order-four root point, and two everywhere else, including the hexagonal fibre.
Its determinant has simple coarse zeros at the two nodal values and order four in the root
coordinate at the multiple value. For the Liu–Rollenske central family the logarithmic rank is
two at both the cuspidal and hexagonal fibres and throughout the remaining smooth locus; at the
order-four root point it is zero, and its determinant has order four there.
    For a specified positive comb section σ of degree parameter m, let x, y be root coordinates of
weights 3, 4, with y = 0 at the order-three point. There is a nonzero homogeneous polynomial
Pσ (X, Y ) of degree 4m, uniquely determined up to an overall nonzero scalar by the marked period
section, such that
                                       det κσ = y 2 Pσ (x4 , y 3 ).                       (E.16.2)
The rank-defect set is exactly its zero divisor. At any such point the rank is zero exactly when all
four entries of the actual Kodaira–Spencer matrix vanish; otherwise it is one. Formula (E.16.3)
below computes those entries from σ. No unspecified choice of a comb section is assigned a fixed
root set. The polynomial is nonzero at the hexagonal cusp, so that cusp always has rank two.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (E.16.3); proposition 15.4;
proposition 15.8; proposition 15.9; proposition 15.10; proposition 15.3.

Proof. Adding a linearization constant or changing only the admissible affine lifts does not change
the derivative of the marked period matrix. 15.4 therefore proves the first assertion. On a root
cover of a higher logarithmic transform the original local good-reduction coordinate is s = uk at
the first multiple value and s = ul at the second. The lifted period map is its actual holomorphic
pullback, not a change of frame with a pole. The chain rule gives kuk−1 κ(s) or lul−1 κ(s). 15.4
gives rank one at the original order-three centre and rank two at the original order-four centre.
The covering derivative is nonzero off its centre, proving (E.16.1) and the absence of further
defects. The cusp coordinate is unchanged.
    For the two-parameter family 15.8 proves, with its extension maps,

                  E = G = O ⊕ O(−1),          κ : O(−7) −→ E ⊗ G       on P(1, 4).

Thus the four entries have weights 7, 6, 6, 5. Write x for the weight-one coordinate vanishing
at the root point and y for the weight-four coordinate. Every monomial of these respective

                                                498
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


weights is divisible by x3 , x2 , x2 , x. Consequently the entire matrix vanishes at the root point,
and its determinant is divisible by x4 . The determinant is a section of O(12), whose coarse
degree is three. At each of the two rank-one Mumford values, the limiting logarithmic derivative
is the nonzero rank-one integral monodromy operator in the local torus frames. Its determinant
therefore vanishes at least once, whereas its matrix has rank one. These two coarse zeros, together
with the root zero of order at least four, account for all of the degree of O(12). The determinant
is nonzero because the logarithmic rank at the hexagonal cusp is two. All the stated orders
are therefore exact, with no remaining zeros. This proves the two-parameter assertion without
assuming a theta identity for its varying section.
    For the Liu–Rollenske central member 15.9 proves the analogous map from O(−3) on P(1, 4).
Its entries have weights 3, 2, 2, 1; these spaces consist respectively of multiples of x3 , x2 , x2 , x.
The determinant is a section of O(4) and is a constant multiple of x4 . The constant is nonzero
by the hexagonal local monodromy. Hence the only rank defect is the root point, where all four
entries vanish. In particular this calculation determines the value of the extended logarithmic
boundary at the cusp, even though its fibre is not normal crossing.

                    det V = det G = O(24m − 1),          κσ : O(−5) −→ V ⊗ G.

The determinant is a section of det V ⊗ det G ⊗ O(10) = O(48m + 8). On P(3, 4) every weighted
monomial xa y b of this degree satisfies b ≡ 2 (mod 3) and a ≡ 0 (mod 4). Factoring y 2 therefore
gives exactly the polynomial in (E.16.2), of coarse degree 4m.
    Here is the exact computation of that polynomial for any of the period sections in the
construction. On a marked local root disc let the two columns of a holomorphic 4 × 2 matrix
U frame the Hodge subbundle of the canonical flat extension. Let ∇ be its explicitly marked
Gauss–Manin connection, and let D be the local generator of TB (−p0 ): ∂s away from the cusp
and q∂q at the cusp. Then

    κσ = (∇D U ) mod im U,         det κσ is represented by det(U1 , U2 , ∇D U1 , ∇D U2 ).     (E.16.3)

The first expression uses the quotient frame of G and the dual frame of V = F ∗ ; it specifies every
matrix entry and therefore also the rank-zero test. Changing the Hodge frame multiplies the
determinant by the square of its determinant, exactly its transition in det V ⊗ det G ⊗ TB (−p0 )−2 .
Changing a root parameter gives the inverse square of the tangent-frame change. Thus the local
calculations glue to the stated global section and determine Pσ from the actual period data. In
the cusp comparison of 15.3 and 15.10, the logarithmic derivative has the fixed invertible integral
leading matrix; its determinant is nonzero. This proves both the nonzero-polynomial assertion
and the exact rank-divisor description.

Proposition 15.12 (Counterexample: The embedded-component omission in the divisor-twisting
lemma). CDP98, Proposition 1.1, in its printed generality of arbitrary nonreduced compact spaces,
is false. The exact replacement is as follows. For an effective Cartier divisor D on a compact
complex space Z and a locally free sheaf V, the spaces H 0 (Z, V(−kD)), viewed inside H 0 (Z, V),
stabilize for k  0 at
                             {s ∈ H 0 (Z, V) : supp(s) ∩ |D| = ∅}.
In particular they eventually vanish when Z has no embedded associated components and D meets
every irreducible component. This last case applies to every full Cartier fibre used in A.7.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition A.7.

Proof. Let C = P1 , let p, q be distinct points, and form the square-zero complex space

                  |Z| = C,       OZ = OC ⊕ C p ,       (a, u)(b, v) = (ab, av + bu).

                                                 499
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


Near p its analytic local ring is C{z, e}/(ze, e2 ), and away from p it is the ordinary smooth curve.
These charts glue through the quotient by e, so this specifies a compact connected complex space.
It has one irreducible component, of positive dimension, and an embedded associated point at p.
The divisor D = q is effective Cartier: its local equation is a coordinate at q and a unit near p.
For every integer k there is the exact, split description as an OC -module

                                   OZ (−kD) = OC (−kq) ⊕ Cp .

It gives every cohomology group:

              h0 = max(1 − k, 0) + 1,       h1 = max(k − 1, 0),         hj = 0   (j ≥ 2).

In particular the nonzero section of the square-zero summand survives for every k ≥ 1, refuting
the printed proposition.
    For the replacement, the descending spaces in theTstatement are finite dimensional, hence
stabilize. A section in their intersection belongs to k ID      k V = 0 at every z ∈ |D|, by Krull
                                                                   z
intersection in the analytic local ring. Its coherent support is therefore disjoint from D. Conversely
a section with support disjoint from D vanishes near D and is a section of V(−kD) for every k.
This proves the exact stable-space formula. When there are no embedded associated components,
every nonzero submodule of a locally free sheaf has support containing an irreducible component
of Z. Such a support cannot avoid D under the stated intersection hypothesis, proving the
vanishing.

Audit of the printed non-holomorphic proof. We now give its entire chain of reductions
and identify its dependencies. CDP20, Section 3, first uses constancy of the index under Picard
twists and Riemann–Roch to deduce its parts (b) and (c) from generic vanishing. Serre duality
reduces generic vanishing to degrees zero and two. Degree zero invokes CDP98, Corollary 1.3;
that corollary uses only Proposition 1.1 on the smooth manifold, a multiple of an effective divisor
lying in Pic0 , and semicontinuity. 15.12 proves the version of Proposition 1.1 needed there, and
A.7 spells out the exponential-family semicontinuity argument. Thus this dependency is valid
and involves none of the cotangent or monodromy steps.
    For degree two the printed proof resolves the meromorphic pencil by σ : Yb → Y , with a
connected map h : Yb → P1 , and writes

                                     h∗ O(1) = σ ∗ P ⊗ O(−E),

where E is the exceptional divisor of the pulled-back base ideal. The map on second cohomology
from Y to Yb is an isomorphism, since a composition of smooth blowups has Rσ∗ O = OY . The
divisor sequence reduces vanishing on Yb to vanishing after −tE and to H 2 (tE, σ ∗ W ) = 0. The
printed proof asserts the exceptional higher-image vanishing needed for this step. For this
particular pencil divisor it has the following direct justification. Pull back the evaluation sequence
on P1 and tensor by σ ∗ P −t to obtain, for t ≥ 1,
                                                    ⊕t
                         0 −→ O(E) ⊗ σ ∗ P −(t+1)         −→ (σ ∗ P −t )⊕(t+1)
                                −→ O(−tE) −→ 0.

The evaluation sequence remains exact under pullback because it is a sequence of vector bundles
with locally free quotient. The middle term has zero R2 σ∗ , by the projection formula and
Rσ∗ O = OY . Every coherent sheaf has zero R3 σ∗ because the fibres have dimension at most two.
Hence R2 σ∗ O(−tE) = 0; the divisor sequence now gives

                                     R1 σ∗ OtE = R2 σ∗ OtE = 0.


                                                 500
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


The support of σ∗ OtE has dimension at most one, so Leray and the projection formula give
the required H 2 (tE, σ ∗ W ) = 0. No identification of this pushforward with a structure sheaf is
needed.
    This special verification matters. The analogous assertion for an arbitrary exceptional divisor
is false. Blow up a point p ∈ P3 and then a smooth plane cubic in the exceptional P2 . For the
second exceptional divisor S, projection to that cubic is a P1 -bundle; thus h• (S, OS ) = (1, 1, 0)
and the composite contraction to P3 has R1 σ∗ OS = Cp . This example, also given in Lehn et al.
(2019), concerns arbitrary exceptional divisors and does not refute the just-proved assertion for
the divisor of a resolved pencil. The graph proof of A.7 avoids the distinction by computing its
own higher direct images from its hypersurface equation.
    The printed argument then replaces its twist M by M ⊗ P t+k and applies Leray to h. It
must prove
                                    R2 h∗ σ ∗ (W ⊗ M ⊗ P k ) = 0
and then the vanishing of H 1 of the corresponding R1 twisted by O(t); the latter is ordinary
Serre vanishing on P1 . For the former it uses top-degree base change and fibrewise Serre duality.
It invokes CDP98, Proposition 1.1, first on components meeting E, and then successively on
components at increasing graph distance from them. Coefficients in an auxiliary effective divisor
are chosen in reverse order of this distance, and the power of E is chosen last. A.7 gives
this argument with the actual pullback maps, full multiplicity filtrations, and a finite-support
argument establishing uniformity. These fibres are Cartier in a smooth threefold and have no
embedded components, so 15.12’s proved version of the twisting lemma applies.
     These are the only earlier CDP results invoked in Section 3: CDP98, Corollary 1.3 and
Proposition 1.1. Its opening reference to CDP98, Theorem 2.1 identifies the proof being rewritten,
rather than using that theorem as a premise. CDP98, Lemma 1.5 is not invoked; its erroneous
replacement of fibrewise vanishing by generic vanishing is precisely what the full component
argument removes. No result from CDP20, Sections 4–7 is used. In particular the cotangent-
filtration and monodromy failures treated in Parts A and D do not enter A.7. The supplied
LRS graph proof has the same dependency on the no-embedded-component twisting lemma, and
supplies its own higher-image calculation. Its displayed adjunction formula has a sign misprint:
for a Cartier fibre F ⊂ Y it is ωF = (KY + F )|F , not (KY − F )|F . A.7 uses the actual dualizing
line and includes nonreduced fibres, so that misprint has no role in the proof here.

theta quotient for the point P = 1/2 identifies this line bundle with O(P − O). The last lattice
generator acts by (z, a) 7→ (z + 3, exp(2πiβ)a). Its elliptic translation is −6P = 0 in the elliptic
curve; its scalar is a holomorphic contracting linearization. This constructs the family from an
elliptic family, a section and a linearization explicitly.
     There is a specified relation to the symmetric period matrix Ω = ( µτ µv ). Adjoining (µ, v)
enlarges Λτ to the lattice generated by (1, 0), (0, 1), (τ, µ), (µ, v); its index is six, because 6(µ, v) =
(3, β) and no smaller multiple belongs to the original real lattice. Identity on C2 induces a finite
holomorphic isogeny of degree six between these families. Its differential is the identity on the Lie
spaces and its pullback on complex first cohomology is an isomorphism. The Kodaira–Spencer
tensors therefore have the same rank under these explicitly given comparisons.
     The identity ϑ1 (1/2 + z, τ ) = ϑ2 (z, τ ) and evenness of ϑ2 give ∂µ log ϑ1 (1/2, τ ) = 0. Since
µ0 = 0, the proposed square is zero. The actual determinant, by the proved heat-equation
formula, is

16 Connected deformation chains and two independent periods
Corollary 16.1 (arbitrary connected deformation chains). The ordered coprime pair (3k, 4l) is
constant in every proper smooth holomorphic family over a connected complex analytic base which

                                                   502
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


contains a constructed sphere member. Two constructed members are deformation equivalent
through such families, allowing arbitrary intermediate members and finite chains, if and only
if their pairs agree. Moreover different pairs cannot occur in one continuous family in the C ∞
space of integrable complex structures on S 6 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.2; corollary 16.31;
proposition 16.27; proposition 16.29; theorem 16.30.

Proof. The detailed proof is 16.2–16.31 below. The intrinsic pencil persists for either canonical
slope, the limiting period stays in the admissible interior, and the two finite root charts and
the actual analytic cusp are recovered. 16.27 then identifies every full punctured-disc smooth
completion with the prescribed member. The additional step 16.29 propagates from any nonempty
known open subset of a disc: finitely many successive discrete analytic exceptional sets are filled
in reverse order. 16.30 uses a finite local projection and normalization of a curve through two
specified points to pass to arbitrary analytic bases and deformation chains. The classical C ∞
Kuranishi local theorem then gives the continuous-family conclusion in 16.31.
    Local miniversality alone would prove only openness. Nor does a boundary point of an
arbitrary open locus necessarily admit a holomorphic disc whose punctured image lies in that
locus. The generic-disc propagation and finite-projection steps are the substantive additions
which establish the required closedness.

in a local trivialization, and the common ideal is generated by s0 . The analogous assertion
holds on the other chart. These local generators define a nonzero section of L0 ⊗ h∗0 O(−1) and
an effective Cartier zero divisor E0 . This gives the stated factorization of L0 with no residual
codimension-two base locus.

Proposition 16.3 (positive canonical slope preserves the fibration). Under the hypotheses of
16.2, suppose D > 0. Then E0 = 0 and e = 1. After shrinking the disc and choosing a frame of
π∗ L, its evaluation defines a proper flat holomorphic map

                                          g : X −→ P1 × ∆

which is the intrinsic algebraic reduction on every fibre. Its smooth general central fibre is a
complex two-torus.
    In particular, two families of the type in 16.2 with positive canonical slope cannot have
the same smooth central manifold unless their multiplicity pairs agree. A positive-slope and a
negative-slope family cannot have a common smooth central manifold either. This proposition
concerns a common smooth specialization. The additional propagation and closure arguments for
arbitrary connected chains are 16.29–16.31.

Proof. Choose a very general smooth fibre F of g0 , avoiding the images of all vertical components

Remark 16.4 (Scope after 16.3). 16.2 proves that the central meromorphic reduction is
holomorphic, and 16.3 removes its fixed divisor and degree loss for D > 0. The positive-slope
proof alone does not exclude the effective antipluricanonical divisor allowed by the restriction
identity when D < 0. 16.7–16.9 remove that possibility by the horizontal-divisor vanishing
argument. 16.14 and 16.20–16.27 then recover the finite charts, cusp, and actual smooth
completion. The separate generic-disc propagation and closure arguments in 16.29–16.31 prove
16.1 for arbitrary analytic bases, deformation chains, and continuous complex structures. The
present proposition retains its stated one-sided, positive-slope scope.

proposition 16.7; proposition 16.9; proposition 16.14; proposition 16.20; proposition 16.27;
proposition 16.29; corollary 16.31; corollary 16.1.

Remark 16.6 (Scope and subsequent completion). For either canonical slope, 16.9 supplies
the fibration-persistence hypothesis of this proposition, so a one-sided smooth specialization has
an interior period value. Equality of that value with an existing model does not by itself prove
uniqueness of its smooth completion. 16.10–16.12 exclude critical values appearing only at the
central parameter; 16.14–16.25 recover the actual finite and cusp charts, and 16.27 proves the
full one-sided identification. The distinct problem of propagation through arbitrary deformation
branches is settled by 16.29–16.31.

A restriction on the negative-slope fixed divisor

Proposition 16.7 (horizontal divisors force non-Kähler fibre normalizations). Let X be a
compact complex threefold diffeomorphic to S 6 , and let f : X → P1 be a surjective holomorphic
map with connected fibres. Suppose that a smooth general fibre F has b1 (F, Q) = 1. Then every
reduced fibre of f is irreducible, and the monodromy on H 1 (F, Q) is trivial.
    If H ⊂ X is a horizontal prime divisor, the normalization of every reduced fibre lies outside
Fujiki’s class C. Equivalently, no such normalization admits a Kähler resolution. In particular
no fibre has Moishezon normalization.

                                                508
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


    Without the hypothesis b1 (F ) = 1, every irreducible component of a reducible fibre of any
such connected map from a complex S 6 also has normalization outside C.
    Consequently, in 16.2 with D < 0, a horizontal component of E0 is possible only if every
reduced fibre of the central algebraic reduction g0 is irreducible and has normalization outside
C. This necessary condition does not exclude non-Kähler normalizations and does not prove
persistence of the relative pencil in the negative-slope case.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.2; Campana et al.
(2020b, Lemma 4.2); Fujino (2021, Lemma 3.3 and Corollary 3.4); proposition 16.3.

Proof. Choose a nonempty finite set Σ ⊂ P1 containing all critical values; a regular value can be
added if necessary. Write s = |Σ|, put A = f −1 (Σ)red , and let r be the number of irreducible
components of A. The compact analytic set A is triangulable. Each of its irreducible two-
dimensional components has its complex fundamental class, and their intersections have real
dimension at most two. Hence
                                       H 4 (A, Q) ≃ Qr .
Alexander duality in the oriented six-sphere gives
                                          b1 (X \ A, Q) = r.
On the other hand, f : X \ A → U := P1 \ Σ is a proper smooth fibre bundle. The base U has
the homotopy type of a graph with s − 1 loops. The degree-one Leray–Serre sequence therefore
gives an exact sequence
                  0 −→ H 1 (U, Q) −→ H 1 (X \ A, Q) −→ H 1 (F, Q)π1 (U ) −→ 0.
In particular, the correct formula retains the invariant subspace:
                               r = s − 1 + dim H 1 (F, Q)π1 (U ) ≤ s.
Every nonempty fibre over Σ has at least one irreducible component, so r ≥ s. Equality follows
throughout. Thus every fibre over Σ has precisely one reduced irreducible component and the
invariant subspace is all of the one-dimensional H 1 (F, Q). Fibres outside Σ are smooth and
connected, hence irreducible. This proves both assertions without assuming monodromy triviality
at the outset. It is the rank-one repair of the component-count argument; the unrestricted
formula in Campana et al. (2020b, Lemma 4.2) is not being used.
    Let S = f −1 (t)red . A horizontal prime H maps surjectively to the base by properness, so
H ∩ S 6= ∅. Since S is irreducible, S ⊂ H would imply S = H, contrary to horizontality. The
canonical section of OX (H) consequently restricts to a nonzero section on the reduced irreducible
space S, with a nonempty zero set. Its zero divisor is a nonzero effective Cartier divisor on S.
Indeed the section cannot vanish identically on any local irreducible branch: its pullback would
then vanish on an open subset of the irreducible normalization, hence everywhere by analytic
continuation. In the reduced local ring it consequently avoids every minimal prime and is a
non-zero-divisor, including at self-intersections.
    Let ν : S ν → S be the normalization. If S ν were in C, it would have a compact Kähler
resolution µ : Sb → S ν ; this precise surface statement is Fujino (2021, Lemma 3.3 and
Corollary 3.4). The pulled-back line bundle
                                      L = (νµ)∗ (OX (H)|S )
has c1 (L) = 0 integrally, since H 2 (X, Z) = 0. Its pulled-back section is nonzero and has zeros:
normalization is finite surjective, and modification is proper surjective. Thus it defines a nonzero
effective divisor B on S.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


a contradiction. The argument applies to the reduced support even when the original fibre is
nonreduced. Moishezon spaces are in C, so the stated consequence follows.
     For the assertion about a reducible fibre, let Si be one of its reduced irreducible components.
The fibre is connected, so another component Sj meets Si ; otherwise Si would be an open-and-
closed component of its support. Distinctness ensures Si 6⊂ Sj . Apply exactly the preceding
canonical-section and positivity argument to OX (Sj )|Si . Its first Chern class is zero because
H 2 (X, Z) = 0, whereas its effective Cartier zero divisor is nonempty. This proves the additional
assertion without any hypothesis on the general fibre’s first Betti number.
     For the application, choose a very general smooth fibre F of g0 meeting a horizontal component
of E0 and avoiding its vertical components. As in 16.3, adjunction gives c1 (KF ) = 0 and F is
minimal. The identity of 16.2 now restricts to

                              KF−A = OF ((−D)E0 |F ),         −D > 0,

with a nonzero effective divisor on the right. If a positive power KFm had a nonzero section,
multiplying a suitable power of that section by the mth power of the displayed anticanonical
section would give a nonzero holomorphic function with zeros on F . Compactness forbids this.
Thus κ(F ) = −∞. Moreover F is not Kähler, since its nonzero effective divisor (−D)E0 |F has
zero real Chern class. The Enriques–Kodaira classification then places F in class VII and gives
b1 (F ) = 1; see Barth et al. (2004, Chapter VI, Theorem 1.1 and Table 10, pp. 243–244). The
preceding argument applies with f = g0 and any horizontal prime component H of E0 .

    The proof supplies a necessary restriction on an unknown smooth specialization. It neither
classifies the singular non-Kähler normalizations nor replaces the unresolved non-normal-fibre
step in the holomorphic-fibration argument of Campana et al. (2020b, §7). That step is not used
here: 16.8–16.9 prove the needed horizontal-divisor vanishing, and 16.27–16.31 complete the
actual specialization and deformation-chain arguments.

Removing the negative-slope horizontal fixed part

Proposition 16.8 (no horizontal divisor when all fibres are irreducible). Let X be a compact
complex threefold diffeomorphic to S 6 , and let f : X → P1 be a surjective holomorphic map with
connected fibres. If every reduced fibre is irreducible, then X has no horizontal prime divisor for
f.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.7; Ramis and Ruget
(1970, §3, Theorem 1, p. 81, and the complete-intersection calculation on p. 91); (Bănică and
Stănăşilă, 1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.12(ii)); (Bănică and Stănăşilă, 1976, Chapter III,
Theorem 4.1).

Proof. Suppose that H is such a divisor. It is Cartier because X is smooth. Since H is horizontal
and every reduced fibre S is irreducible, H meets S and does not contain it. As in 16.7, restriction
of its canonical section is a non-zero-divisor on every local branch of S.
    We first record the elementary vanishing used below. On a compact reduced irreducible
complex space S, let D be a nonzero effective Cartier divisor and V a vector bundle. Multiplication
by the powers of the canonical section identifies

                            H 0 (S, V (−nD)) ⊂ H 0 (S, V ),     n ≥ 0,

with a decreasing sequence of finite-dimensional vector spaces. A section in their intersection
vanishes to every order along D. Krull intersection in a local ring at a point of D makes its germ



                                                510
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


zero. After pullback to the irreducible normalization, analytic continuation makes the section
zero everywhere. The decreasing sequence therefore stabilizes at zero. In particular

                         H 0 (S, V (−nD)) = 0    for all sufficiently large n.

The same conclusion holds for a vector bundle on a thickened fibre mS. Indeed S is Cartier in
X, and the finite filtration by powers of its ideal has successive quotients

                                 V |S ⊗ OS (−jS),       0 ≤ j < m.

Apply the preceding reduced-space statement to these finitely many vector bundles, with the same
nonzero divisor H|S , and then use their exact sequences. This also proves that the multiplication
maps used here remain injective on mS: its only associated component is S and H contains none
of its local branches.
    Let B be any holomorphic vector bundle on X. The map f is flat, since its local rings are
torsion-free over the discrete valuation rings of the smooth base. Every analytic fibre Ft is a
Cartier, Cohen–Macaulay, Gorenstein surface, possibly nonreduced. Its dualizing line is

                                            ωFt = KX |Ft ,

where the constant one-dimensional factor from the target has been trivialized. Serre duality on
this compact Gorenstein surface gives

                     H 2 (Ft , B(nH)|Ft )∗ ≃ H 0 Ft , (B ∗ ⊗ KX )(−nH)|Ft .
                                                                         


The compact-space duality being used includes singular Cohen–Macaulay spaces; it is the absolute
duality theorem of Ramis and Ruget (1970, §3, Theorem 1, p. 81, and the complete-intersection
calculation on p. 91), already specified in Paper I, Proposition 23.7, not a smooth-fibre replacement.
The preceding filtration argument makes the right hand side zero for all sufficiently large n, for
each t.
    For fixed n, the nonvanishing locus

                              Zn = {t ∈ P1 : h2 (Ft , B(nH)|Ft ) > 0}

is closed by semicontinuity. Multiplication on the dual section spaces gives Zn+1 ⊂ Zn . Their
intersection is empty by fibrewise vanishing. Compactness of P1 therefore supplies a single N
with ZN = ∅. Constant-zero cohomology and analytic cohomology-and-base-change (Bănică and
Stănăşilă, 1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.12(ii)) give

                                          R2 f∗ (B(N H)) = 0.

Higher direct images vanish in degrees greater than two by the fibre dimension. The coherent
sheaf R1 f∗ (B(N H)) has vanishing first cohomology after a sufficiently positive twist on P1 . The
projection formula and Leray sequence consequently give, for some integer a  0,

            H 2 (X, B ⊗ M+ ) = H 3 (X, B ⊗ M+ ) = 0,         M+ = OX (N H) ⊗ f ∗ O(a).

All coherence, semicontinuity and constant-zero base-change uses are the proper analytic theorems
audited in Paper I, Proposition 23.7; the argument does not infer base change from coherence
alone.
    Independently, the reduced-space vanishing argument applied to the connected smooth
manifold X and its nonzero divisor H gives

                      H 0 (X, B ⊗ M− ) = 0,        M− = OX (−bH),        b  0.


                                                 511
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


We must arrange these different vanishings for one line bundle. The exponential sequence gives

                                       Pic(X) ≃ H 1 (X, OX )

because H 1 (X, Z) = H 2 (X, Z) = 0. Let `− , `+ be the corresponding additive classes. The affine
line
                               `(z) = (1 − z)`− + z`+ ,      z ∈ C,
is realized by a holomorphic family of line bundles on X × C: choose additive holomorphic Cech
cocycles representing the two classes and exponentiate their linear combination. Equivalently,
use the integrable Dolbeault operators obtained by a holomorphic linear combination of fixed
closed (0, 1)-form representatives. Thus no representability or universal-Picard-space assertion is
needed here.
    For the proper projection X × C → C, the cohomology jumping loci

                          Tj = {z : hj (X, B ⊗ Mz ) > 0},      j = 0, 2, 3,

are closed analytic subsets of C by the proper analytic finite-complex theorem (Bănică and
Stănăşilă, 1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.1): the condition is expressed by the rank minors in a
local finite free complex. In particular no closedness claim from the corrected Grauert Section 7,
Satz 2 is used. The set T0 omits z = 0, while T2 and T3 omit z = 1. Each is therefore proper,
and their finite union cannot fill the irreducible complex line. Choose z outside that union. Then

                              χ(X, B ⊗ Mz ) = −h1 (X, B ⊗ Mz ) ≤ 0.

Every line bundle on X is topologically trivial, so Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch makes this Euler
characteristic equal to χ(X, B).
   Finally take B = TX . Since H 2 (X, Z) = H 4 (X, Z) = 0, the only contributing term in its
Riemann–Roch formula is
                                      1               1
                           χ(X, TX ) = hc3 (X), [X]i = χtop (S 6 ) = 1.
                                      2               2
This contradicts the preceding inequality. Hence no horizontal prime H exists.

Proposition 16.9 (persistence for either canonical slope). Under the hypotheses of 16.2, for
every nonzero D = kl − 3k − 4l one has E0 = 0 and e = 1. After shrinking the disc, the evaluation
of π∗ L gives a proper flat holomorphic map

                                          g : X −→ P1 × ∆

whose restriction to every fibre is its intrinsic algebraic reduction. A smooth general central fibre
of g is a complex two-torus. Its normalized punctured period has an interior limit as in 16.5.
    Two families satisfying 16.2 cannot have the same smooth central manifold unless their
ordered multiplicity pairs agree, regardless of the signs of their canonical slopes. Uniqueness of a
smooth completion at an interior period and the arbitrary deformation-chain statement 16.1 are
not asserted.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.2; proposition 16.5;
corollary 16.1; proposition 16.3; proposition 16.7; proposition 16.8.

Proof. The case D > 0 is 16.3. If D < 0 and E0 had a horizontal prime component, the final
part of 16.7 would give b1 (F ) = 1 for a smooth general fibre of g0 and would make every reduced
fibre of g0 irreducible. 16.8 would then forbid precisely that horizontal component. Thus for
either sign E0 is vertical.

                                                512
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


    The connected-divisor-limit argument in the middle of the proof of 16.3 only uses verticality,
not the sign of D. Its generic choice of pencil section has central zero support equal to the
disjoint union of the vertical fixed part and e distinct regular fibres. The total divisor is reduced
and irreducible with connected central support after normalization and Stein factorization.
Consequently E0 = 0 and e = 1. Surjectivity of evaluation, flatness and the torus assertion follow
from the remainder of that same proof. The hypothesis of 16.5 is now satisfied for either sign,
and gives the interior period limit.
     Suppose two such one-sided families have the same central manifold X0 . Its algebraic reduction
is intrinsic, so both pencil lines are the same line L = g0∗ O(1) up to isomorphism. With indices
i = 1, 2, the two root identities give
                                  Ai
                                 KX0
                                     = LDi ,             LD1 A2 −D2 A1 = O.

The line L is not torsion, because a positive power has a nonzero section with zeros. Hence
D1 /A1 = D2 /A2 . Paper I, Proposition 23.6 recovers the ordered coprime multiplicity pair from
this rational number. This proves the common-limit assertion without identifying the limit with
a member of the given period construction.

   The vanishing argument is an application of standard proper cohomology, duality and
Riemann–Roch machinery; no novelty claim is intended. It proves the needed absence of a
horizontal fixed divisor under the rank-one hypothesis. It does not establish the different claim
that every holomorphic Hopf-surface fibration on a complex six-sphere is impossible.

An extension criterion at an isolated base point

Proposition 16.10 (purity with a smooth torus Jacobian). Let B ⊂ C2 be a sufficiently small
bidisc about 0, put U = B \ {0}, and let g : X → B be a proper flat holomorphic map from a
connected smooth complex (n + 2)-fold, with connected fibres of dimension n. Let G → B be a
smooth proper holomorphic family of complex n-tori with a holomorphic zero section and its
group law. Suppose that XU → U is a holomorphic GU -torsor. Then g is a submersion on all of
X, and the given action extends uniquely to make X → B a holomorphic G-torsor.
    No polarization, Kähler metric on X, or section of the given torsor on U is assumed. The
smooth extension G is an explicit hypothesis.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Shrink B so that the holomorphic Lie bundle of G has a frame e1 , . . . , en . Its period local
system has a basis of holomorphic sections
                                                                         2n
                                                                         X
                        λ1 (b), . . . , λ2n (b) ∈ Cn ,      G b = Cn /         Zλa (b).
                                                                         a=1

Indeed the lattice is locally constant over the simply connected bidisc, and the local inverses
of the relative exponential map make its sections holomorphic. The periods are a real basis at
every b.
    The infinitesimal torsor action gives holomorphic vector fields V1 , . . . , Vn on XU . Flatness
makes Z = g −1 (0) have complex codimension two in X. Hartogs extension in local coordinates
therefore extends each coefficient of each Vj uniquely across Z; uniqueness glues these local
extensions to holomorphic vector fields on X. This use of Hartogs applies to functions on the
complement of an analytic set of codimension at least two in a complex manifold, hence also


                                                     513
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


coefficientwise to any locally free sheaf. It does not assert extension across a divisor. The
identities
                                   dg(Vj ) = 0,   [Vi , Vj ] = 0
hold on the dense open subset XU and consequently on X.
    Every Vj , and every linear combination with coefficients pulled back from B, is complete. Its
integral curve stays in a compact fibre; a finite endpoint of a maximal solution would have an
accumulation point in that fibre, where the holomorphic ordinary differential equation extends
the solution. The flows thus define a holomorphic action of Cn on X over B.
    For a = (a1 , . . . , a2n ) ∈ R2n take the time-one flow of the vertical holomorphic vector field
whose Lie coordinate is
                                              X2n
                                                  aj λj (g(x)).
                                            j=1

These maps depend smoothly on a and add under composition: all their coefficients are constant
along every vertical flow. For a ∈ Z2n the map is the identity on XU , hence everywhere by
holomorphic uniqueness. We obtain an action of the fixed compact real torus T = R2n /Z2n by
holomorphic automorphisms of X, over B. On the fibre over b, it is the holomorphic action of
Gb obtained by factoring the Cn action by its period lattice. The action of T is free on XU . The
variable period identities also make the holomorphic Lie-bundle action descend to a holomorphic
action G ×B X → X. Its restriction therefore acts on each scheme-theoretic fibre, including its
nilpotent structure.
    We show that its stabilizers have dimension zero everywhere. Let x ∈ X, b = g(x), and let H
be the identity component of the stabilizer. Viewed in Gb , it is a compact complex subgroup: it
is the identity component of the inverse image of x under the holomorphic orbit map Gb → Xb .
Put
                                    Kx = ker(dgx ) = Tx (Xb ),
where the right-hand side is the Zariski tangent space of the scheme-theoretic fibre. Differentiating
the holomorphic Gb action on this fibre gives a holomorphic representation H → GL(Kx ). It
is trivial, because every holomorphic function on the compact connected complex group H is
constant. The induced representation on Tx X/Kx is also trivial: this quotient injects into Tb B
by dgx , and every group element acts over B. Averaging a Hermitian inner product over the
compact group H gives an invariant complement to Kx . The full derivative representation on
Tx X is therefore trivial.
    Here the required local linearization has a direct proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates z
centred at x and a sufficiently small H-invariant neighbourhood on which all z(hy) are defined.
Such a neighbourhood exists by compactness of H and continuity of the action. With normalized
Haar measure set                                Z
                                        Ψ(y) =     z(hy) dh.
                                                  H
This map is holomorphic, invariant under H, and has derivative the identity at x. It is a
holomorphic coordinate system after shrinking. Its invariance then forces every h ∈ H to be the
identity near x, and hence on connected X. This contradicts freeness on XU unless H is trivial.
Thus every stabilizer is finite, and the n vector fields Vj are linearly independent everywhere.
   Their commuting flows give local holomorphic coordinates (z, s) ∈ Cn × C2 in which they
span the z directions: choose a transverse complex surface and apply the holomorphic inverse
function theorem to the flow map. In these coordinates g has the form

                                            g(z, s) = h(s).

Equidimensionality implies that the germ h−1 (b) is zero-dimensional. Consequently the germ
h : (C2 , 0) → (B, b) is finite; this is the local finiteness criterion obtained by Weierstrass division

                                                  514
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


for an isolated fibre. If dgx failed to have rank two, the determinant of dh would vanish at s = 0.
It is not identically zero, since the map is a submersion away from Z. Its zero set would therefore
contain a complex curve through 0. Finiteness sends that curve to a curve of critical values. This
contradicts smoothness over B \ {0}. Hence g is a submersion everywhere.
     The Gb orbits now have the full dimension of every smooth connected fibre and are compact.
Each fibre is a single orbit. Its finite stabilizer acts trivially on its tangent space, because Gb
is abelian; it also acts trivially on the base tangent quotient. Averaging as above, now over
that finite group, again makes its full derivative trivial and then makes the action locally trivial.
Freeness on XU forces the stabilizer to be trivial. Thus the extended action is free and transitive
on every fibre. Local holomorphic sections of the submersion identify X with G over small base
opens, which proves the torsor assertion. The extension is unique because it agrees with the
original one on the dense open subset XU .

Remark 16.11 (Scope and literature check). This is a conditional extension criterion, not a
general purity theorem for proper flat maps. In particular it does not apply to B.4.15: that
construction has vertical threefolds over the bidisc origin and is not flat over the bidisc. Searches
on 15 November 2026 for purity and discriminants of complex-torus fibrations, Hartogs extension
of torus actions, and isolated critical values did not locate the exact statement under these
hypotheses without an added Kähler assumption. The complete argument is given above.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the argument and qualifications
immediately following.

Proposition 16.12 (no additional central critical values). In the smooth-specialization setting
of 16.9, let
                                    g : X −→ P1 × ∆
be the extended intrinsic fibration, and let c1 (s), c2 (s), c0 (s) be the three labelled critical-value
sections of 16.5. The critical values of g0 are exactly the distinct points among c1 (0), c2 (0), c0 (0).
In particular, no additional critical value occurs only on the central target curve.
    If the normalizing projective transformations As of 16.5 have a degenerate limit, the central
regular fibres are isomorphic complex two-tori and g0 has at most two critical values. If the
constant image of the limiting rank-one matrix is 0 or 1, this torus is the corresponding finite-root
abelian surface. If that image is an ordinary source point, it is the ordinary torus at that point
and need not be an abelian surface. The cusp cannot be the constant image.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.9; proposition 16.5;
proposition 16.10.

Proof. 16.5 gives 0 < |z(0)| < Rk,l . A local logarithm therefore extends the normalized parameter
c(s) holomorphically to the disc. The critical image is closed and contains the three punctured
sections, so it contains their three limiting points. Suppose that a different central critical value
b0 = (v0 , 0) exists. Take a small bidisc B about b0 which avoids all three section closures and all
other central critical values. Put U = B \ {b0 }. The restricted family over U is a proper smooth
family of complex two-tori. We verify that its Jacobian extends to a smooth holomorphic torus
group family over B, so that 16.10 applies.
    The normalized source coordinate is t = As (v). Represent As by a matrix with holomorphic
entries, after clearing poles and removing a common power of s, so its central matrix is nonzero.
If that matrix is invertible, t extends holomorphically near b0 and its value there is ordinary: a
marked value would put b0 on the corresponding section closure. The ordinary period model
with parameter c(s) then gives the desired smooth Jacobian over B.
    Otherwise the central matrix has rank one. Denote its constant image by t∗ and its exceptional
target point by v∗ . For each marked source value different from t∗ , its preimage tends to v∗ . At

                                                  515
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


least two of the three marked values are different from t∗ , so v∗ belongs to at least two labelled
section closures. Consequently v0 6= v∗ . After shrinking B, the function t(s, v) tends uniformly
to t∗ there. For an ordinary t∗ the ordinary period model again extends directly.
    Suppose instead that t∗ = 0 or 1, and use a local coordinate ξ at that marked point. The
divisor of ξ(t(s, v)) on B is supported on s = 0, since B avoids the corresponding critical-value
graph. Consequently
                                 ξ(t(s, v)) = sn u(s, v),   n > 0,
where u is a nowhere-zero holomorphic function. This also explains why no zero of the leading
coefficient may be overlooked: such a zero would put the point on the labelled graph closure.
Choose a nearby v1 for which (v1 , 0) is regular. The actual family over the full s-disc at v1 is
smooth, so its integral degree-one monodromy is the identity. The parameter c(s) has no winding.
By the marked comparison of 16.5, this monodromy is An1 or An2 , respectively. Their orders are
three and four, so e | n, where e = 3 or 4. A holomorphic eth root of u exists on the bidisc, and

                                       r(s, v) = sn/e u(s, v)1/e

is an actual holomorphic root coordinate on B. Pull back the smooth finite-root torus period
model by (c(s), r(s, v)). This produces the required smooth torus group family G → B. The larger
multiplicities 3k, 4l do not change this Jacobian argument: their additional deck transformations
are translations, and the linear Jacobian model is the original order-three or order-four root
model.
     For completeness t∗ = ∞ is impossible. In the cusp coordinate the same divisor argument
gives q = sn u with n > 0. The smooth family at v1 would have monodromy An0 . But A0 = I + N ,
N 2 = 0, and N u b=w  b 6= 0, so An0 6= I.
     It remains to identify G|U with the actual Jacobian, rather than merely comparing individual
tori. The punctured bidisc U is simply connected. Its integral first-homology local system
therefore has a global marking. Over s 6= 0 that marking agrees with the reference period
marking, after one constant integral change of basis; the transition comparisons of Paper I,
Corollary 23.3 have identity linear homology action at fixed marked parameter. Both holomorphic
period subbundles extend on U , and they agree on its dense open subset s 6= 0. They agree
everywhere on U . Equivalently, the two quotients of their holomorphic Lie bundles by the same
marked period lattice are isomorphic torus group families on U . This is a Jacobian identification
and makes no assertion that the actual affine torsor has a section on B.
    The total space is smooth and g is proper and flat. The only possible nonsmooth fibre over
B lies above b0 , and its codimension in the total space is two. All hypotheses of 16.10 now hold.
That lemma makes g smooth also above b0 , a contradiction. The central critical-value set is
therefore precisely the set of labelled limits.
     For the final assertions, in the rank-one case every ordinary central target point different
from v∗ has the same limiting marked torus: it is obtained from (c(0), t∗ ), or from the finite-root
value (c(0), r = 0). Equality of the extended period subbundles proves this assertion without
assuming separatedness for threefold completions. All marked values except possibly t∗ have
their preimages tending to v∗ . Hence there are at most two central critical values; if t∗ is ordinary,
there is exactly one. At t∗ = 0 or 1, the finite linear automorphism of the root torus has complex
eigenvalues 1 and a primitive third or fourth root of unity. The rational idempotents for these
two distinct cyclotomic factors split that torus, up to isogeny, as a product of two elliptic curves.
It is therefore an abelian surface. This argument makes no projectivity assertion for an ordinary
limiting torus, and supplies no polarization on the whole central threefold.

Remark 16.13 (Scope of 16.10–16.12). Purity here is obtained from the explicit good Jacobian

a general purity theorem. These results do not give uniqueness of an interior smooth completion,

Proposition 16.14 (persistence of an isolated finite multiple fibre). In the setting of 16.9,
suppose the central value of one finite labelled critical section is distinct from the limits of the other
two labelled sections. Write its multiplicity as m, with m = 3k or 4l, and its linear monodromy
order as e = 3 or 4, respectively. Near that section, normalize the base change taking an mth
root of its defining equation.
    The resulting total space is smooth, and its map to the root bidisc is a proper smooth family
of two-tori. The deck group acts freely on the total space. Consequently the actual central reduced
finite fibre is smooth, has exactly multiplicity m, and belongs to the same smooth family of finite
free affine quotients as the punctured reduced finite fibres.
    This applies to both finite fibres when the three labelled critical values have distinct limits. In
the two-critical-value collapsed-target case, it applies to the isolated finite labelled fibre.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.9; proposition 16.12;
proposition 16.10.

Proof. Choose target coordinates (v, s) in a bidisc about the section, and let Γ be its graph.
Take a local defining function ξ for Γ. On the smooth fourfold the divisor identity is

                                              g ∗ Γ = mD,

where D is the prime closure of the punctured reduced multiple-fibre family. Indeed this equality
holds away from s = 0. The only possible extra divisorial component would be X0 , but g0 is
nonconstant, so X0 is not mapped into the point Γ(0). The closure D is Cartier because the
total space is smooth. Thus locally, even if its central restriction is initially singular or reducible,

                                               g ∗ ξ = am u

for a local equation a of D and a holomorphic unit u.

including over a = 0. This is an assertion about the normalized cover; the unnormalized fibre
product generally has intersecting branches.
    The induced map g 0 : Y → B 0 is proper and equidimensional of relative dimension two.
Since both source and base are smooth, the two pulled-back base parameters form a regular
sequence in each local ring, giving flatness. Over s 6= 0 this is the actual smooth root torus
family. Its connectedness makes Y connected and its generic fibre connected. The Stein factor
of g 0 is finite birational over the normal bidisc and hence is the bidisc itself, so all fibres are
connected. Equivalently this follows from normality of Y and the finite birational form of its

Remark 16.15 (Scope of the finite-chart argument). This argument identifies the smooth
root charts at the isolated finite critical values. The excluded target-collision cases are treated
in 16.16–16.18. The actual cusp is recovered separately in 16.20–16.25, and 16.27 glues these
comparisons into the full one-sided completion theorem.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.16; proposition 16.18;
proposition 16.20; proposition 16.25; proposition 16.27.

Proposition 16.16 (extension of the circle field and exclusion of finite-root collapse). In the
setting of 16.9, the normalized vector field δ of the punctured family extends to a holomorphic
relative vector field on X after shrinking the parameter disc. Its time-one flow is the identity,
and its real circle action on the central fibre is equivariantly diffeomorphic to the prescribed circle
action on the punctured fibres. In particular its central fixed locus is a smooth rational curve with
normal bundle O(−1) ⊕ O(−1) and the same two opposite circle weights.
    The rank-one limit of the normalizing projective transformations As cannot have constant
image 0 or 1. More generally, a collapsed constant image is impossible whenever the limiting
torus’s complex δ line has two real-linearly independent periods. Thus the finite-root isotrivial
possibilities in 16.12 are excluded.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.9; proposition 16.12;
proposition 16.10.

Proof. Let π : X → ∆ be the original proper holomorphic submersion. The coherent sheaf

                                             H = π∗ TX /∆

                                                  518
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


is torsion-free: multiplication by a nonzero base function is injective on the vector bundle upstairs
and hence on its sections. Its generic rank is one by Paper I, Theorem 23.4. On the smooth disc
it is therefore locally free of rank one. Choose a generator V after shrinking the disc. On ∆∗ it
has the form
                                           V |Xs = b(s)δs ,
with b holomorphic and nowhere zero there. The normalized fields δs agree on overlaps of local
classifying maps: at fixed discrete data the comparison maps of Paper I, Corollary 23.3 have
fibre-linear part the identity and fix the marked period δ.   b Their translations also preserve the
invariant vector field. Moreover V is vertical for g, because this holds on the dense punctured
family.
    Choose a regular central target value and a small bidisc around it on which g is smooth. The
ordinary or finite-root comparison used in 16.12 supplies its smooth marked Jacobian, with the
marked period δb extending as a nonzero holomorphic Lie section. The resulting invariant field
δB on the actual torsor is nonvanishing there. Comparing one nonzero coefficient of δB with V
shows that b(s) extends holomorphically to s = 0. Its independence of the target coordinate
follows from that equality on s 6= 0 and holomorphic uniqueness.
    If b(0) = 0, the restriction V |X0 vanishes on a nonempty open subset of connected X0 , and
therefore vanishes everywhere. In local coordinates for the submersion π, every coefficient of V
is then divisible by s. The quotients glue uniquely to a global holomorphic relative vector field
V /s. This contradicts the fact that V generates the free module H. Hence b(0) 6= 0, and V /b(s)
gives the required global extension of δ.
    The extended field is complete on each compact fibre of π. Its time-one flow is the identity
on the punctured family and hence on the whole family by holomorphic uniqueness. Its real
flow consequently defines an action of R/Z on X over the parameter disc. Average a smooth
metric and an Ehresmann horizontal distribution over this compact group. Parallel transport
then gives equivariant diffeomorphisms of the fibres. The central action is therefore the same
effective semifree action, with a single fixed two-sphere, as on the prescribed fibres.
    The fixed set of a holomorphic compact-group action is a complex submanifold, as follows
from the averaging coordinates used in 16.10. Here it is a proper smooth family of curves of
genus zero, and hence each fibre is P1 . Its two holomorphic normal weight lines have the same
degrees as in the punctured family. Those degrees are −1, −1 by C.3.11, or directly by the two
fixed toric edge normals. The characters distinguish the lines, so their central restrictions are
exactly O(−1) ⊕ O(−1).
    Suppose now that As has rank-one limit with constant image a finite marked value. 16.12
identifies every central regular torus, with its marked δ direction, with the corresponding finite-root
torus at parameter c(0). The invariant lattice of Aj has rank two and spans its one-dimensional
complex fixed subspace. It contains δ;   b its second primitive period is independent over R. The
complex fixed subspace is precisely the δ line, since the other complex eigenvalue is a primitive
third or fourth root of unity. Consequently, in the normalization in which the δ period is 1, there
is a constant second period
                                               κ ∈ C \ R.
This is a period of the invariant field on every central regular fibre. The time-κ flow is therefore
the identity on their dense union, and hence on all of X0 .
   The flow of the nonzero field δ0 thus factors through a nontrivial holomorphic action of the
compact elliptic curve E = C/(Z + κZ). Such an action has no fixed point on a connected
complex manifold unless it is trivial. Indeed its derivative at a fixed point is a holomorphic
representation of the compact complex group into a general linear group, so is constant. Averaging
local coordinates over the compact group then makes the action trivial near that point, and
holomorphic uniqueness makes it trivial everywhere.


                                                 519
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


    The elliptic action here is nontrivial because δ0 6= 0. It therefore has no fixed point. This
contradicts the fixed rational curve of the extended real circle action: a zero of the generating
field is fixed by its entire complex flow. Equivalently, the resulting nowhere-zero real vector field
would give χ(X0 ) = 0, whereas X0 is diffeomorphic to S 6 . The same argument applies to an
ordinary constant-image torus if its δ line has a second independent period.

Remark 16.17 (What the elliptic-action argument does not assume). The argument uses the
global one-dimensional space of vector fields on the known punctured members and the actual
marked period comparison on a central regular bidisc. It does not assume that all translations
of an ordinary central torus extend over the singular fibre. For an ordinary torus the δ line
may have only the one specified real period; such a case is not excluded by the elliptic-action
argument alone.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the argument and qualifications
immediately following.

Remark 16.19 (Scope of the volume argument). The proof uses the equality of line bundles
in (E.2.15.1), not just the topological vanishing of c1 (KX ). It also uses constancy of the torus
periods, which makes the fibre volume in (E.2.15.2) constant. It does not assert a general
good-reduction or comparison theorem for non-Kähler torus degenerations. Together with the
separate elliptic-action exclusion in 16.16, it removes the two types of collapsed target permitted
by 16.12. Identification of a noncollapsed interior completion, and the behaviour on arbitrary
new deformation branches, remain distinct questions.

Proposition 16.20 (the central cusp is reduced and irreducible). In the one-sided smooth

Proposition 16.21 (persistence of the normal-crossing cusp). In the smooth fixed-pair
specialization of 16.9, the cusp divisor is a relative normal-crossing divisor over the parameter
disc. More precisely, after shrinking that disc, at every point of the total cusp divisor there are
holomorphic coordinates (z1 , z2 , z3 , s), with s the original parameter, in which the cusp coordinate
of the intrinsic map is one of

                                q = z1 ,        q = z1 z 2 ,       q = z 1 z2 z3 .            (E.2.17.1)

There are exactly two relative triple-point sections. Both lie on the fixed rational curve of 16.16.
In particular the normalization of the total cusp divisor is smooth and proper over the parameter
disc, and its central fibre is the normalization of the central cusp.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.9; proposition 16.16;
proposition 16.20; Lazzeri (1973, Theorem 2 and its corollary, pp. 274–275).

Proof. By 16.16–16.20 the three labelled critical values remain distinct, the cusp has multiplicity
one, and its reduced central fibre is irreducible. We normalize its target section to q = 0. On
a sufficiently small target disc, zero is the only critical value on every parameter fibre. The
extended field δ is zero precisely on the relative fixed rational curve C, and the two normal
characters there are +1, −1. For s 6= 0 the two triple points of the prescribed cusp belong to Cs ;
outside that curve the cusp is smooth or has an ordinary double crossing.
     We first record exactly the local singularity result we use. If hs (a, b) is a holomorphic family
and h0 = 0 is a reduced plane-curve germ with an isolated critical point, choose a sufficiently
small representative of that germ. The sum of the multiplicities of all nearby critical points of
hs , regardless of their critical values, is µ(h0 ). One can see this directly from the analytic critical
scheme
                                         C{a, b, s}/((hs )a , (hs )b ).




                                                      523
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


After taking a sufficiently small representative, it is finite over the parameter disc. Its two
equations are a regular sequence, and its central fibre is zero-dimensional. It is thus Cohen–
Macaulay of dimension one, with s a nonzerodivisor, and is finite flat over the disc. Its degree is
the central Jacobian-algebra dimension, namely µ(h0 ).
     The non-splitting theorem of Lazzeri (1973, Theorem 2 and its corollary, pp. 274–275) says
that if a deformation of an isolated hypersurface singularity has more than one singular point
in a single deformed fibre, their summed Milnor numbers are strictly smaller than the original
Milnor number. The strict numerical inequality is the conclusion of the cited corollary’s proof.
Consequently, if all the critical points just counted have critical value zero, there can be only
one such point. This application uses a flat deformation of plane hypersurfaces: the map
(a, b, s) 7→ (hs (a, b), s) is flat near the central germ because its two base parameters form a regular
sequence in the smooth source. No assertion of separatedness of compact threefolds enters this
local argument.
     Let p be a central cusp point outside C0 . A relative holomorphic flow box for the nonzero
field δ gives coordinates (a, b, v, s) in which δ = ∂v . Invariance of the intrinsic map gives

                                             q = hs (a, b).

The central equation is reduced, by 16.20. A reduced plane-curve germ is either smooth or has
an isolated critical point. In the smooth case the implicit function theorem already gives the
first form in (E.2.17.1).
     In the singular case every critical point of hs in a small representative lifts to a critical
point of the actual map on Xs . All its critical values are therefore zero. For s 6= 0 each such
point is a node, since the flow box is disjoint from the fixed curve and hence from the two
triple points. Conservation and non-splitting give one node and µ(h0 ) = 1. Thus the central
Hessian is nondegenerate. The implicit function theorem gives its unique critical-point section,
whose critical value is zero. The holomorphic Morse lemma with parameters then gives q = ab
throughout this neighbourhood, with s unchanged.
     It remains to treat the fixed curve. Holomorphic coordinates obtained by averaging over
the extended compact circle may be chosen in the form (z, x, y, s), with C defined by x = y = 0
and with circle weights 0, +1, −1, 0. The original parameter s is retained by this averaging. The
holomorphic invariant function q vanishes on C, so its convergent power series has the form

                               q = Fs (T, z) = T gs (T, z),    T = xy.                       (E.2.17.2)

The coefficient Qs (z) = gs (0, z) is intrinsically a section of the dual of the product of the two
normal weight lines along Cs . By 16.16 this is OP1 (2).
    The central section Q0 is not identically zero. Otherwise the central equation in every such
chart would be divisible by x2 y 2 , contradicting reducedness of the central cusp. Its zero divisor
therefore has degree two. Suppose that both zeros coincide at a point z = 0. The plane equation
F0 (T, z) = T g0 (T, z) is reduced: a repeated factor of g0 would remain repeated after T = xy, and
T does not divide g0 because Q0 is not identically zero. Thus F0 has an isolated plane critical
point there.
    For s 6= 0 the two zeros of Qs are the two distinct triple points of the prescribed cusp.
Under the supposed collision they both lie in the chosen small plane representative. They are
distinct critical points of Fs with value zero. Every other critical point of Fs also has value zero:
this is automatic at T = 0, and at T 6= 0 it follows by lifting to xy = T , where the quotient
map (x, y, z) 7→ (T, z) is a submersion. All sufficiently small T have such a lift in the original
coordinate chart. A nonzero critical value would contradict the actual critical-value set of the
intrinsic map.
    Conservation of all critical multiplicities and Lazzeri’s non-splitting theorem now give a
contradiction to the two distinct critical points. Hence Q0 has two simple zeros. They extend as

                                                  524
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


two disjoint holomorphic sections over the parameter disc. Where Q0 6= 0, the factor gs (xy, z) is
a unit and can be absorbed into y, giving q = xy. At a simple zero, ∂g0 /∂z 6= 0; replace z by
gs (xy, z) to obtain q = xyz, again keeping s unchanged. This proves all local forms in (E.2.17.1).
    Properness makes the central cusp compact, so finitely many such neighbourhoods cover it and
a single shrinking of the parameter disc suffices. The normalization of a relative normal-crossing
divisor separates its local branches. In the coordinates above every normalized branch is smooth
over s, and these descriptions agree on overlaps. Normalization is finite for complex analytic
spaces; its composition with the proper cusp map is therefore proper. Its fibres are precisely the
normalizations of the cusp fibres in these local charts. This proves the final assertions.

Remark 16.22 (Literature and remaining identification). Non-splitting is a known theorem
of Lazzeri, not a new singularity-theoretic claim. We opened the original paper and use its
strict numerical corollary. The application combines that theorem with the actual extended
circle action, reducedness, and the absence of extra critical values proved above. Searches for
non-splitting, Milnor-number conservation and degenerations of torus-fibred complex six-spheres
did not locate this application. The proposition supplies relative normal-crossing charts and a
simultaneous normalization. It does not by itself identify the entire analytic cusp neighbourhood.
The prescribed marked Mumford completion is recovered by 16.23–16.25.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.23; proposition 16.25.

Proposition 16.23 (the normalized cusp and its marked hexagon). Let ν : S → W be the
simultaneous normalization of the relative cusp in 16.21, and let D ⊂ S be its reduced conductor.
After shrinking the parameter disc, each fibre pair is the standard toric pair

                                (Ss , Ds ) ≃ (dP6 , its toric hexagon).

The six conductor components may be labelled over the disc so that their incidence, self-intersections
−1, opposite-pair involution, and endpoint identifications are those of the punctured family. The
relative logarithmic tangent bundle has a global holomorphic frame:

                                       TS/∆ (− log D) ≃ OS⊕2 .

This assertion identifies the normalized pair and supplies a relative frame; it does not by itself
identify the analytic smoothing neighbourhood.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.21; Grauert (1962, §4,
no. 8(a), pp. 364–365); (Barth et al., 2004, Chapter VI, Theorem 1.1 and Table 10).

Proof. In the relative charts of 16.21, the normalized branches are smooth over the original
parameter. Their conductor branches and their intersections are also smooth over that parameter.
The normalization of the conductor is consequently a proper smooth family of curves, and the
normalized intersection strata are finite etale over the disc. Their connected components and
incidence are constant. Since the disc is simply connected, label the six curve families D1 , . . . , D6
and the six vertex sections by continuation from a punctured fibre. Each curve fibre is a smooth
curve of genus zero. Its two distinct vertex sections remain distinct; the same relative local
charts exclude a new self-intersection or an additional incidence at the centre. Thus the central
conductor is a hexagon of six embedded rational curves. The degree of each relative normal line
is constant in its proper curve family, so all six central self-intersections equal −1.
    Write S = S0 and Di = Di,0 . Ehresmann transport gives b1 (S) = 0 and b2 (S) = 4. Contract
the three disjoint curves D1 , D3 , D5 . The analytic Castelnuovo contraction gives a smooth
compact complex surface Y ; the needed analytic statement, including smoothness of the resulting


                                                 525
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


point, is Grauert (1962, §4, no. 8(a), pp. 364–365). Only these three contractions on the central
surface are used; no relative contraction theorem is assumed.
    The images C2 , C4 , C6 of the remaining curves are smooth rational curves. Each meets two
contracted curves transversely once, so has self-intersection −1 + 1 + 1 = 1. Each pair meets once,
at the image of their intervening contracted curve; these three intersection points are distinct
and the intersections are transverse. Thus they form a triangle. Also b1 (Y ) = 0 and b2 (Y ) = 1.
    Any one of these curves, say C = C2 , has nonnegative intersection with every effective
divisor: distinct irreducible curves have nonnegative local intersection multiplicities and C 2 = 1.
Adjunction gives KY · C = −3. A nonzero section of KY⊗r for r > 0 would give an effective divisor
of intersection −3r with C, impossible. Hence κ(Y ) = −∞. The compact-surface classification
(Barth et al., 2004, Chapter VI, Theorem 1.1 and Table 10) together with b1 (Y ) = 0 makes Y
rational: class VII has first Betti number one, and a ruled surface has the first Betti number
of its base curve. A rational surface with b2 = 1 is P2 . The curves C2 , C4 , C6 are lines, since
their self-intersections are one. Their three pairwise intersection points are distinct, so they
form a projective triangle. Blowing up its three vertices recovers exactly the toric degree-six del
Pezzo surface and its hexagonal boundary. This proves the assertion about the central pair; the
punctured pairs were already the prescribed ones.
    The conductor involution is holomorphic over the disc. Its permutation of the six labelled
curve families, and its permutation of the vertex sections, are locally constant. They are therefore
the same opposite-pair and endpoint identifications as on a punctured fibre. The remaining
scalar gluing parameters are not claimed to be determined by this discrete observation.
    Finally put E = TS/∆ (− log D). For every fibre pair just identified, the two toric infinitesimal
actions trivialize its logarithmic tangent bundle. Thus

                                  E|Ss ≃ OS⊕2
                                            s
                                              ,       h0 (Ss , Es ) = 2.

Constant-cohomology base change, in the form used in Paper I, Proposition 23.7, makes the
direct image a rank-two holomorphic vector bundle on the disc and identifies its fibres with these
section spaces. Choose a frame after shrinking the disc. The evaluation map from its pullback to
E is an isomorphism on every fibre, hence is an isomorphism everywhere by Nakayama’s lemma.
This gives the claimed relative frame without choosing a potentially singular family of projective
coordinate changes on the punctured disc.

Proposition 16.24 (extension of the marked cusp torus action). Let

                                      f : N −→ B = ∆q × ∆s

be the proper cusp neighbourhood of the smooth specialization in 16.21, and put W = f −1 (q = 0).
After shrinking the bidisc, the rank-two vertical logarithmic tangent bundle is trivial and is
generated by two commuting complete holomorphic vector fields. Their action factors through a
holomorphic action of (C∗ )2 over B, with the integral marking given by the periods w, δ. On the
normalization of every Ws this is its usual toric action.
    The marked rank-two lattice is primitive in the period lattice of each ordinary torus fibre
and equals the full invariant lattice of the cusp monodromy. At the two relative triple-point
sections, the three nonzero tangent characters are constant in s and equal to those of the prescribed
Mumford cusp. In the toric chart lattice coordinates, transported from that punctured model by
their fixed integral change of basis from the period marking, they are respectively

                      {(1, 0), (0, 1), (−1, −1)},         {(−1, 0), (0, −1), (1, 1)}.     (E.2.19.1)

The assertion constructs the action on the actual neighbourhood. It does not assert that an
arbitrary equivariant quotient is smooth or that the entire completion has already been identified
with a prescribed toric quotient.

and the identity theorem gives Gj (0) = I as well.

Proposition 16.25 (identification of the actual analytic cusp). In the smooth specialization of

regular torus Jacobians and their integral markings. Its affine origin may be fixed by choosing a
holomorphic section through a smooth point of the reduced cusp.

Proof. Write f : N → ∆q × ∆s for the proper actual cusp neighbourhood and W = f −1 (q = 0).

     The topology and the exact covering. The relative coordinates q = x, xy, xyz give smooth real

stratum. Away from the cusp such lifts exist because f is a submersion. A smooth partition
of unity preserves both these linear requirements. On the inverse image of a smaller closed
q-disc the lifts integrate along a sufficiently short parameter path: q remains constant, and
properness prevents escape. Thus their flows identify the cusp neighbourhoods, all strata, and
the regular-fibre inclusion maps by q-preserving diffeomorphisms.

                                    {(x, y, z) ∈ C3 : |xyz| < },

meet that dense set, so the intersection is connected. The same holds for the intersection with a
finite union of preceding charts. Van Kampen proves simple connectedness of each finite union;
a loop lies in such a union by compactness. The full toric cover is therefore simply connected.
The known free, properly discontinuous period action has deck group

                                          Λ = Λ/Λtor ≃ Z2 .

preceding argument verifies the step we use. The q-preserving transport transfers this exact

holomorphic base section av (q, s) through its dense H orbit. Its orbit map is an open holomorphic

                                      H × (∆q × ∆s ) −→ N  e.

It is injective on the central open orbit and on each regular fibre, and its differential is invertible
