by a holomorphic translation hvw (q, s) in H. We must prove that this function has no essential
singularity at q = 0.
     If both origins lie in the same central component, their ratio extends as a holomorphic
H-valued unit. The central open orbit is free and transitive, so this follows from the holomorphic
inverse-function theorem for the orbit map, with both parameters retained.
     For two adjacent components, use a crossing chart with q = ab and an orbit coordinate z 6= 0.
The stabilizer of a general conductor point is a primitive connected one-dimensional subtorus
of H. Its two normal characters are +1, −1: on each normalized toric component these are
the primitive boundary characters, and invariance of q makes them opposite. Compact-circle
averaging gives these exact local linear coordinates. A complementary torus direction provides
the orbit coordinate; an invariant unit in q can be absorbed while preserving the weights.
     Fix small nonzero constants a0 , b0 , z0 in this chart and take the two special origins

                       (a, b, z) = (q/b0 , b0 , z0 ),         (a, b, z) = (a0 , q/a0 , z0 ).   (E.2.20.4)

The stabilizer cocharacter evaluated at a0 b0 /q sends the first to the second. This equality is
justified by the local action itself: a path in that subgroup can increase the modulus of a and
decrease that of b, with ab = q fixed, staying inside the crossing chart; the phase can be varied
without changing either modulus. Thus the possibly large group parameter causes no unjustified
use of a local coordinate outside its domain.
    Comparing (E.2.20.4) with arbitrary chosen origins adds only holomorphic H-valued units,
by the same-component argument. The adjacent comparison therefore has the form

                              hvw (q, s) = q nvw uvw (q, s),            nvw ∈ Z2 ,             (E.2.20.5)

where uvw is holomorphic with values in H on the whole bidisc. Every central component is
reached by a finite adjacent path. Multiplying these expressions proves the same assertion for its

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


comparison with the initial origin. Different paths agree on the regular cover, and hence define
identical meromorphic characters. The exponents are locally constant in s, since (E.2.20.5) holds
with a nonvanishing unit on the full bidisc.
    The fan and the analytic coordinate maps. At either triple-point section the whole H fixes
the point. Compact-torus averaging gives three eigen-coordinates with the constant integer
characters of 16.24. Their only primitive positive invariant relation is their product. The reduced
normal-crossing equation therefore writes q as that product times a holomorphic invariant unit.
The unit is a function of the product and s; absorb it into one eigen-coordinate to obtain exactly
q = xyz.
    The orders of the two global characters along Dv , together with ordDv q = 1, give a ray (v, 1).
At a triple point the three incident rays form a unimodular cone. Indeed all adjacent orders and
tangent characters are constant in s and coincide with the known ones for s 6= 0. The entire
resulting fan is consequently the prescribed A2 triangulation, with its fixed labels. No additional
refinement is being introduced.
    In a triple chart a global character is a Laurent monomial in x, y, z times a function of q, s.
Evaluate it on a section keeping two nonzero coordinates fixed and solving the third from q. The
origin comparisons above show that the remaining function is a power of q times a holomorphic
unit. Thus the dual monomial coordinates of the unimodular fan cone pull back to x, y, z times
holomorphic units in q, s. They extend holomorphically and give a local biholomorphism through
the triple point. The crossing and open-orbit charts give the same conclusion on the other strata.
The maps agree on the dense regular cover and therefore glue.
    We finally check the common neighbourhood and the deck action. We do not take an infimum
of infinitely many chart radii. Choose finitely many charts covering one compact normalized
central del Pezzo component and finitely many overlaps for the two deck generators. Shrink
the bidisc once for this finite data. On the regular cover the character map intertwines the
actual deck action with the reference multipliers Pi (q, s) in (E.2.20.3). Both maps extend in the
charts just constructed, so their equality extends to the central strata. The reference multipliers
preserve the prescribed invariant fan. Deck translates of the finite chart collection cover the
entire central unfolding and use the same base bidisc.
    We have obtained local biholomorphisms at all central strata, bijections on their labelled
torus orbits, and the original isomorphism on the whole regular cover. The inverse coordinate
maps are the same unimodular monomial charts with the inverse units. Quotienting by the
identical free properly discontinuous deck actions gives the claimed biholomorphism of actual
analytic cusp neighbourhoods.

Remark 16.26 (Scope and source comparison). The toric covering and its period action are
the known Mumford construction. The point here is to recover that construction from the
actual smooth limit, using the action proved in 16.24. In particular the absence of an essential
singularity in the character comparison is proved in (E.2.20.4)–(E.2.20.5); it is not an assumed
meromorphic comparison. The local identification does not alone identify the global threefold or
settle arbitrary deformation chains. 16.27 supplies the finite affine and global collar comparison;
16.29–16.31 provide the additional propagation and closure arguments for general bases and
continuous structures.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.24; proposition 16.27;
proposition 16.29; corollary 16.31.

Every deck map is affine on the compact torus fibres. Its linear part is the fixed marked finite

are discrete. Changing the lift changes it by precisely the integral coboundary allowed in E.1.
    Consequently the finite affine cocycle has the same integral class at s = 0 as at s 6= 0. After
matching these classes, the remaining difference is a cocycle in the complex vector sheaf. The
explicit finite averaging in E.1 removes it, since division by the finite group order is allowed
in that sheaf. This constructs the finite-root comparisons with holomorphic dependence on s.
Equivalently one may use a finite chart cover and its deck translates; the same averaging solves
the equivariant comparison. The reduced finite fibres are the resulting free quotients; they have
not been assumed to be tori.
    The integral collar classes. Use the two finite-root neighbourhoods, the cusp neighbourhood,
ordinary simply connected charts, and fixed annular collars to cover the target. Choose local
holomorphic origins on the ordinary torus charts. A transition between two such descriptions is
fibrewise affine. The common integral marking makes its linear part the prescribed one, leaving
a translation section.
    Lift these sections to the Lie bundles on simply connected refinements of the collars. Differences
on deck translates and sums on triple overlaps are integral periods. Every resulting integral vector
is constant in s. This comparison takes place on fixed collars away from the singular centres; it
does not evaluate a logarithm at a singular fibre. The finite and cusp chart identifications specify
exactly which integral changes of origins are allowed.
    For s 6= 0 these classes are those of the prescribed logarithmic-transform data, modulo the
integral changes of origins in E.1. They are therefore the same at s = 0. One can normalize

them once on the connected parameter disc. This includes the cusp winding class, since 16.25
identifies the actual marked period action there. Thus there is no additional central integral
translation or fan datum.

comparison is the additive cocycle in the extension sheaf V of E.1. Its finite extension conditions

                   0 −→ OP1 δ −→ V −→ OP1 (−∞) −→ 0,              H 1 (P1 , V) = 0.

Remark 16.28 (Scope of 16.27). The known-pair locus is open by Paper I, Proposition 23.5
and is now stable under full punctured-disc smooth specializations. These two facts alone do not
prove that an arbitrary open known locus in a reduced analytic base is topologically closed. A
holomorphic disc through its boundary need not have its entire punctured image in that locus.
The needed generic propagation argument is proved in 16.29. 16.30–16.31 then establish the
arbitrary-base and continuous-family conclusions asserted in 16.1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 16.27; proposition 16.29;
theorem 16.30; corollary 16.31; corollary 16.1.

Proposition 16.29 (propagation from a known open subset of a disc). Let π : X → ∆ be a
proper holomorphic submersion with fibres diffeomorphic to S 6 . Suppose there is a nonempty
open subset U ⊂ ∆ such that every Xs , s ∈ U , is a member of the fixed coprime multiplicity

Table 10); (Demailly, 2012, Chapter II, Definition 7.9 and Theorem 7.12); proposition 16.23;
proposition 16.24; proposition 16.25.

Proof. Local miniversality in Paper I, Theorem 23.4 supplies actual holomorphic comparisons
with the prescribed family locally over U , with locally constant integral markings. Thus the
known open set has the relative root and normal-crossing charts used below; only pointwise
isomorphisms are not being substituted for these relative comparisons.
    The proof first propagates the actual geometric data outside finitely many successive discrete
analytic exceptional sets. It then fills these sets in reverse order by 16.27. Later exceptional sets
are only claimed to be discrete on the domain then under consideration; they may accumulate at
points removed at an earlier stage.
    The intrinsic line and the relative pencil. Put A = 12kl and D = kl − 3k − 4l 6= 0. The

Indeed Ehresmann transport over the contractible disc gives H 1 (X , Z) = H 2 (X , Z) = 0, so the

    Proper coherence makes V = π∗ L a torsion-free, hence locally free, sheaf on the disc. Its rank
is two because it has that rank on U . At every parameter its fibre injects into H 0 (Xs , Ls ) by

zero locus of its two evaluated sections is closed analytic in X . Its image is closed analytic by

is a discrete analytic subset. Remove it temporarily.
    On the remaining connected parameter curve S the sections define a proper holomorphic map

                                g : XS −→ P1 × S,           L = g ∗ O(1).                   (E.2.22.1)

Each gs is nonconstant because its two sections are independent. Its fibres have pure dimension
two; the smooth total space and smooth target then give flatness. The fibres are connected: the
finite Stein factor is generically of degree one, as it is so above U , and a finite birational map to
the normal target is an isomorphism. Its source is irreducible, so there is no additional vertical
component in the Stein factor. We retain

                                            KXAS /S = g ∗ O(D).                             (E.2.22.2)

    Critical values and ordinary tori. The relative critical locus of g is analytic and proper over
the target. Its image has finite intersection with each target fibre: the nonconstant proper map
gs to a curve has finitely many critical values. Thus the reduced critical image is finite over S. Its
one-dimensional part has degree three, as can be read over U ; every such component dominates
S. Remove the images of its zero-dimensional components and its branch and singular points.
These are further proper analytic discrete subsets, absent over the known open set.
    A finite etale parameter cover now labels the three critical sections. Pointwise classification
after this cover descends; images of later discrete exceptional sets remain discrete because this
cover is finite. One may work on each connected component, each of which meets the inverse
image of U . Send the labelled sections to 0, 1, ∞. There are exactly these three critical values on
the current parameter domain.
    The ordinary family over B ◦ × S, where B ◦ = P1 \ {0, 1, ∞}, is smooth and proper. Its
compact surface fibres have the topology of the known two-tori by Ehresmann’s theorem and
connectedness. Adjunction gives integral c1 (KF ) = 0, since F is a smooth fibre in a complex six-
sphere and its normal line is trivial. These surfaces are complex tori. To spell out the classification
step, b1 (F ) = 4 is even, so F is Kähler. The zero canonical class excludes exceptional curves
and ruled surfaces. On a Kähler surface, a nonzero effective divisor cannot have zero real Chern
class; hence a nonzero pluricanonical section has no zeros and cannot give positive Kodaira
dimension. The compact-surface classification leaves the Kodaira-dimension-zero list, in which
b1 = 4 identifies a two-torus (Barth et al., 2004, Chapter VI, Theorem 1.1 and Table 10).
    The finite root charts. For any labelled critical section Γj , every component of the Cartier

there is exactly one such component, and its multiplicity is the known one. In particular

                        g ∗ Γ1 = (3k)D1 ,       g ∗ Γ2 = (4l)D2 ,    g ∗ Γ0 = W,            (E.2.22.3)

with reduced total hypersurfaces on the right. For clarity, two distinct dominating components
could not both restrict to the known irreducible reduced fibre. Each is a Cartier prime in the
smooth total space, is torsion-free and hence flat over the smooth parameter curve, and has
pure two-dimensional fibres. Thus its fibre over any parameter in U contains the whole known

irreducible reduced surface. At a general smooth point of that fibre the known local equation

product of W f over XS . Its partial diagonals are both open and closed: a finite immersion is

There are only finitely many such deletions.

and submersive over S, with independent vertical normal covectors. Since the total W is a reduced

after absorbing a unit. These are actual relative normal-crossing charts; in particular the

base change before obtaining the charts.
    The normalized toric pair and its action. The smooth proper normalization and its conductor
strata have the same topology, incidence and normal degrees as over U . A further finite etale

conductor curves are a hexagon of (−1)-curves, three alternate contractions give a triangle in P2 ,
and the normalized pair is (dP6 , D). Its relative logarithmic tangent bundle is the evaluation
pullback of a rank-two bundle on the parameter curve.

    In this evaluation description the conductor descent maps are holomorphic endomorphisms of
that rank-two bundle. They are constant along the compact conductor curves. They equal the
identity over U , where both toric logarithmic fields descend. The holomorphic identity theorem
on the connected parameter curve makes them the identity everywhere. This is the descent proof
of 16.24; it requires a nonempty known open set, not specifically a punctured disc. Grauert
evaluation, commutation on the ordinary tori, completeness and the implicit extension of the
two primitive toric periods then give the actual marked cusp torus action locally on the current
parameter curve. The integral monodromy and triple-point characters are constant by transport
and are the prescribed ones.

cusp multipliers are the corresponding marked reference multipliers. The proof of 16.25 now
reconstructs the actual cusp at each parameter: relative normal-crossing transport gives its
known cover and incidence, the action gives the same characters, and adjacent-origin comparison
gives the monomial times unit extensions. The proof works along any path from U and locally
in the current parameter; it does not need an already known punctured neighbourhood at the
point being classified.

domain, hence remain those over U . The additive comparison in E.1 and 16.27 identifies every
remaining actual threefold with the reference member at c(s). The pointwise conclusion descends
from every finite parameter cover used to label the critical or conductor strata.

     Filling the exceptional layers. We have made only finitely many successive deletions. At each
stage the deleted subset was closed analytic and discrete on the parameter domain then present.
Finite covers do not change that property after taking their proper images. On the final domain
all fibres are known members of the fixed pair. At a point of the last deleted set, choose a small
disc containing no other point of that set and avoiding all earlier deleted sets. Its punctured disc
consists of known members. 16.27 identifies the central fibre as well. Fill the entire last layer in
this way, then the preceding one, and continue in reverse order. This is valid even when a later
layer accumulates at an earlier deleted point. Finally every fibre over the original disc is known.
No analytic curve selection for an arbitrary open locus has been assumed.

Theorem 16.30 (separation under arbitrary deformation chains). In a proper smooth holomorphic
family of compact complex manifolds over a connected reduced complex analytic base, if one fibre
is a sphere member of Paper I, Theorem 23.4 with coprime multiplicities (3k, 4l), then every fibre
is a constructed member with that same pair.
    Consequently two of the constructed sphere members are deformation equivalent, allowing
chains of proper smooth families over connected complex analytic bases, if and only if their
ordered multiplicity pairs agree. In particular the distinct coprime pairs give distinct deformation
classes, and 16.1 is resolved by this theorem.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; corollary 16.1; proposition 16.29;
Demailly (2012, Chapter II, Theorem 4.19, pp. 95–96); (Demailly, 2012, Chapter II,
Theorems 7.6 and 7.12).

Proof. Fix the pair and let U be the locus of its constructed members in the base B. It is open
by the actual local miniversality of Paper I, Theorem 23.4 and Paper I, Proposition 23.5. We
prove that it is closed without assuming a punctured analytic disc can be selected inside an
arbitrary open subset.
    First consider any proper smooth family over a connected Riemann surface. If its known-pair
locus is nonempty, Ehresmann’s theorem makes all its fibres diffeomorphic to S 6 , and that locus
is open. At any point of its closure choose a coordinate disc meeting that locus. The intersection
contains a nonempty open subset of the disc, so 16.29 makes the entire disc known. Thus the
known-pair locus is closed and equals the connected Riemann surface. Only this disc propagation,
not a special choice of punctured disc, is used below.
    Let b ∈ U ⊂ B. If b ∈ U there is nothing to prove. Otherwise choose a small local
representative and an irreducible branch T through b which meets U arbitrarily near b. There
are only finitely many such local branches. Its dimension is positive. The local parametrization
theorem gives a finite proper projection

                                 ρ : T −→ ∆d ,         ρ−1 (0) = {b},                    (E.2.23.1)

after shrinking the representative and translating b to the origin. This is the finite projection
of Demailly (2012, Chapter II, Theorem 4.19, pp. 95–96). The isolated central fibre is part of
choosing the generic projection for the germ; the Weierstrass representative is then taken small
enough to contain no other point over zero.
    Choose a ∈ U ∩ T in this representative, with ρ(a) 6= 0. Let L be the complex line through 0
and ρ(a), restricted to the polydisc. An irreducible component C of the reduced analytic set
ρ−1 (L) which contains a has dimension one. Indeed d − 1 linear equations give local dimension
at least one, while finiteness of ρ gives dimension at most one. Its finite proper image in L is
one-dimensional, so is all of L. Therefore C contains the unique point b over zero.
    Normalize C. Its normalization C   e is a connected Riemann surface, finite over C; analytic
normalization exists and a normal curve is smooth by (Demailly, 2012, Chapter II, Theorems 7.6
and 7.12). It has points above both a and b. Pull back the given proper smooth family to C.     e

                                                 537
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


Its known-pair locus contains the inverse image of the open set U ∩ C near a. The preceding
Riemann-surface argument makes every fibre on C     e known, in particular the fibre above b. Thus
b ∈ U.
    We have proved that U is open and closed. Since B is connected and U is nonempty, U = B.
A nonreduced base does not add fibre isomorphism classes: restriction to its reduction preserves
both the fibres and smoothness of the family. Thus the same conclusion also applies to such a
base when it is admitted in the definition of deformation equivalence.
    Applying this result to each link in a finite deformation chain preserves the pair. Conversely,
E.1 identifies all admissible sphere data with a fixed pair with the connected period family,
using its holomorphic comparisons and its period lattice 2klZ. The admissible half-plane and
its punctured-disc quotient are connected. Thus all members with that pair are deformation
equivalent. This proves both directions.

Corollary 16.31 (separation for continuous complex structures). Let I(S 6 ) be the space of
smooth integrable almost-complex structures on the fixed smooth sphere, with its C ∞ topology.
For a fixed coprime pair (3k, 4l), let Ik,l consist of the structures whose complex manifolds are
biholomorphic to constructed members with that pair. Then Ik,l is open and closed in I(S 6 ).
    Consequently a continuous family of such structures over any connected topological parameter
space cannot contain constructed members with two different pairs. The same separation holds
in the quotient spaces by Diff0 (S 6 ) or by all orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, with their
quotient topologies. This statement does not identify the number of marked connected components
belonging to a single pair.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Meersseman (2019, Section 3.2,
Theorem 3.4 and Remark 3.6, pp. 898–899); (Meersseman, 2019, Section 2.1, pp. 883–884);
theorem 16.30.

Proof. We use the classical Kuranishi local-completeness theorem at an arbitrary J0 ∈ I(S 6 ),
including an initially unconstructed structure. The complex orientation is locally constant, so
the oriented formulation applies on each such neighbourhood. The precise C ∞ version used
here is Meersseman (2019, Section 3.2, Theorem 3.4 and Remark 3.6, pp. 898–899). It supplies
a connected open neighbourhood U of J0 , a finite-dimensional Kuranishi analytic space K
containing J0 , and a continuous retraction Ξ : U → K such that every J ∈ U is obtained from
Ξ(J) by a diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity. In that theorem the local product map is
first constructed in Sobolev completions; elliptic regularity gives precisely this restriction to
smooth operators. The topology on these operators is the C ∞ topology of (Meersseman, 2019,
Section 2.1, pp. 883–884).
    The Kuranishi space carries its proper smooth holomorphic deformation family. We can
take K connected: in the stated local theorem it is the continuous retract of the connected
U. If necessary replace K by its reduction, which changes neither its points nor the complex
manifolds in its fibres. Suppose U contains some J ∈ Ik,l . Its Kuranishi representative Ξ(J) has
the same complex manifold up to biholomorphism. 16.30 applied to the connected Kuranishi
family therefore makes every point of K a member of the same pair. Since all points of U are
biholomorphic to their Kuranishi representatives, it follows that U ⊂ Ik,l .
    Thus at every J0 the neighbourhood U is either contained in Ik,l or disjoint from it. This
proves both openness and closedness. The inverse image of this set under a continuous map from
a connected parameter space is then empty or the whole space, proving the continuous-family
assertion. Finally Ik,l is saturated under the indicated diffeomorphism groups, because its
definition uses only the biholomorphism class. Its image in either quotient is open and closed by
the definition of the quotient topology. No assertion that the saturated set itself is connected is
needed.

the hexagonal point the same description uses two toric windings in K3 , and integer translation
of the fan extends over its three double curves and both triple points. This criterion includes
regularity of the remainder; membership of the defect in Kj alone would not exclude an essential
singularity of a preassigned punctured translation.

Proposition 17.3 (Counterexample: The universal two-vector-field bound). The assertion that
every complex structure on S 6 has h0 (T ) ≤ 2, printed in Huckleberry et al. (2000, Corollary 1.3;
verified preprint p. 2) and repeated in Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Remarks 1.2 and 9.26), is false
for the comb members.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Huckleberry et al. (2000, Corollary
1.3; verified preprint p. 2); Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Remarks 1.2 and 9.26); proposition 17.2.

Proof. 17.2 gives h0 (TXm ) = 2m + 1 ≥ 25 for m ≥ 12. The source proof expresses a third field
as a meromorphic linear combination of two fields and invokes the Campana–Demailly–Peternell
claim that all meromorphic functions on a complex six-sphere are constant. That implication is
unavailable here: fm supplies nonconstant meromorphic functions. The independently computed
2m + 1 sections above give the counterexample, so this is a refutation of the bound as well as
a location of the failed step. It does not refute a statement restricted to algebraic dimension
zero.


A    Known source results re-derived
Complete re-derivation of standard-pencil stability
This is the full expanded proof of Proposition 17.1. The stability conclusion follows from
the actual-family miniversality and intrinsic pencil of Du et al. (2026, Proposition 6.16 and
Theorem 7.1), together with the algebraic-reduction calculation of Claude and Alpöge (2026a,
Theorem 9.1(i),(iii)). The following complete proof retains the relative root-divisor calculation
and the meromorphic descent argument.

Proof. Paper I, Theorem 3.9 identifies the semiuniversal germ with the actual c-parameter germ.
Thus every sufficiently small deformation is isomorphic to a member Xc0 with Im c0 < −M . The
bundle identity KX = f¯∗ OB (−6) = OX (−2S2 ) in Paper I, Proposition Q.2 holds relatively in this
family: all root divisors and every determinant transition used in its proof vary holomorphically,
and their characters are constant. Consequently −2K = f¯∗ O(12) = f ∗ OB (1) on every member,
with a relative line-bundle isomorphism. Connected fibres imply f∗ OX = OB , so the two base
sections pull back to the entire two-dimensional section space. They have no common zero. The
resulting map is the constructed f followed by a projective coordinate change. Its general fibre is
a torus by the same local quotient construction.
    We spell out the algebraic-dimension reduction used here. On a manifold with H 2 (X, R) = 0,
a divisor restricts to a topologically trivial line bundle on any regular torus fibre. A nonzero


                                               546
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                                Paper II


effective divisor on a compact torus has positive degree against a Kahler form, whereas a
topologically trivial class has degree zero. Hence an effective divisor on X cannot meet a regular
fibre in a proper nonempty divisor: its restriction is either the whole fibre or empty. The zero
and pole divisors of a meromorphic function are therefore vertical. On a regular fibre where
neither contains the fibre, the restricted function has no pole and is constant. The function hence
descends meromorphically to the base on a dense open set, and the proper connected-fibre map
extends the descent across the finitely many special values. Thus the meromorphic field is C(t)
and a(X) = 1. This argument applies to each small member and does not appeal to an invalid
vanishing theorem.
    The conclusion is stronger than what semicontinuity alone gives. For the original member,
projection formula gives h• (f ∗ O(1)) = (2, 3, 1, 0); the nonzero degree-one group means that a
generic line-bundle extension argument would not establish stability of its two sections. Here
stability follows from the computed semiuniversal family and its relative root divisors.

Proposition A.1 (Credited re-derivation). For an action ρ : Q → Aut(K) and the corresponding
semidirect product G = K oρ Q, put

                             (K ab )Q = K ab /hρ(q)k̄ − k̄ : q ∈ Q, k̄ ∈ K ab i.

There is an isomorphism

                           Gab −→ Qab ⊕ (K ab )Q ,           [(k, q)] 7−→ ([q], [k]).

For a split extension without a specified splitting, the associated short exact sequence is canonical
and its splitting need not be.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.
   This semidirect-product abelianization is Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Lemma 10.7, p. 90).
We retain the complete re-derivation below, including the dependence of the direct-sum splitting
on the chosen splitting of the extension.

Proof. The product is (k, q)(k 0 , q 0 ) = (kρ(q)(k 0 ), qq 0 ). In the displayed quotient [ρ(q)(k 0 )] = [k 0 ],
so the displayed map is a surjective homomorphism to an abelian group. Its kernel contains
[K, K], [Q, Q] and all elements ρ(q)(k)k −1 . These elements are themselves commutators in G.
Conversely their normal closure makes the images of K and Q abelian and makes those images
commute, so the quotient by that normal closure is abelian. The kernel is exactly [G, G]. The
inverse homomorphism sends the two summands to the images of (1, q) and (k, 1). The induced
maps in 0 → (K ab )Q → Gab → Qab → 0 come from inclusion and projection; choosing the
original group section supplies its splitting.
    For a concrete failure of the uncorrected direct sum, take K = Q = Z and let the generator
of Q act on K by k 7→ −k. Then the coinvariant quotient is Z/2Z, and the displayed map gives
Gab = Z ⊕ Z/2Z, whereas Qab ⊕ K ab = Z2 .

Proposition A.2 (Credited re-derivation: The precise range of the normalization formula). The
canonical inclusion η∗ η ∗ N ∗ ,→ K is an isomorphism exactly when S has normal crossings outside
an analytic subset of codimension at least two in S.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Granger and Schulze, 2014,
Proposition 3.4).




                                                      547
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                        Paper II


Proof. Locally a logarithmic one-form can be written as α/F , with α holomorphic and α ∧ dF
divisible by F . Restriction to S is uniquely q dF at its generic points; the holomorphic coefficients
of α give q ∈ J −1 . Conversely, for q ∈ J −1 choose holomorphic lifts of the coefficients qFxi .
Their exterior product with dF vanishes modulo F , so they define a logarithmic form with
residue q. The kernel consists exactly of holomorphic forms. Thus the logarithmic residue
module in (Granger and Schulze, 2014, Proposition 3.4) is exactly our J −1 , with no change of
fractional-ideal embedding. Weakly holomorphic functions are exactly B. Theorems 1.1 and 1.3
there say that all logarithmic residues lie in B exactly when the stated normal-crossings condition
holds. Combining this with B ⊂ J −1 and (A.2) proves the result.

locally trivial bundle. Additivity over the cells and multiplicativity of compactly supported Euler
characteristic give zero for every multiple-branch stratum. On the one-branch stratum of Si the
fibre has mi points. Normalization identifies that stratum with Ti \ Di , giving (C.NC.1). This
also proves directly which local contributions enter the global formula.

Proof. We first check that the finite normal-form list is exhaustive. The delta formula under a
point blowup shows that a plane germ of multiplicity at least four has delta at least six. For an
irreducible branch of multiplicity two, Weierstrass preparation, completion of the square and a
root of a unit give y 2 − x2k+1 , of delta k ≤ 5. For an irreducible branch of multiplicity three,
the Puiseux conductor formula gives delta at least six unless its first characteristic exponent
is four or five. A term with exponent divisible by three is removed by subtracting a power of
the first coordinate. The remaining two possibilities have relatively prime exponents (3, 4) or
(3, 5), and no later characteristic pair. Their analytic normal forms are E6 and E8 . This last
analytic comparison is also the zero-parameter case of the semiquasihomogeneous normal-form
theorem: the bases of the two gradient algebras are respectively xi y j with i ≤ 2, j ≤ 1, and with
i ≤ 3, j ≤ 1, after interchanging variables if necessary. Every basis monomial has weight less
than one, so there is no higher-weight term left in the normal form; see (Arnol’d, 1976, §1, I.1.0,
and §2).

Four branches already contribute at least six. With three branches, a singular branch would
contribute at least 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6. Thus all three are smooth. They are either pairwise
transverse, or exactly one pair is tangent with contact two or three: if all three had a common
tangent, the sum would again be at least six. Straightening the transverse branch, subtracting the
mean of the other two graph functions and taking a root of their unit difference gives D4 , D6 , D8
respectively.
    With two smooth branches, subtracting their mean graph and rescaling the transverse
coordinate gives A2k−1 with contact k ≤ 5. With two singular branches the two delta contributions
and their intersection multiplicity give at least 1 + 1 + 4 = 6. The remaining possibility is one
smooth branch and one cusp. A multiplicity-three cusp would already give 3 + 3 = 6. A
multiplicity-two cusp of delta k has parameterization (t2 , t2k+1 ). Its intersection with a smooth
branch is either two, or, for the common tangent, one of 4, 6, . . . , 2k, 2k + 1. The inequality
k + I ≤ 5 leaves a transverse smooth branch with k = 1, 2, 3, giving D5 , D7 , D9 , or the ordinary
cusp with its tangent smooth branch, giving E7 . The actual analytic forms are again those

Proposition A.7 (Credited re-derivation: The non-holomorphic reduction theorem). Let Y
be a compact connected complex threefold with b2 (Y ) = 0 and let g : Y 99K C be a nonconstant
meromorphic map to a compact nonsingular curve which does not extend holomorphically. For
every holomorphic vector bundle V on Y , there is a dense open subset of each component of
Pic(Y ) on which
                              H q (Y, V ⊗ L) = 0 (0 ≤ q ≤ 3).
Consequently χ(Y, V ⊗ L) = 0 for every L ∈ Pic(Y ), and Y c3 (Y ) = 0.
                                                         R


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 15.12; Lehn et al. (2019,
Theorem 3.1, p. 9); equation (16); equation (15).
   The vanishing, Euler-index and third-Chern-number conclusions are Lehn et al. (2019,
Theorem 3.1, p. 9); its sphere consequence is Corollary 3.2 there. The extension from Pic0 to
each component follows by tensoring the arbitrary vector bundle with a fixed representative of
that component. We retain the complete graph proof below as a credited re-derivation, with the
multiplicity filtration made explicit.

Proof. We give the graph proof, including the comparison needed at the exceptional locus.
The corresponding resolution comparison in the printed proof of CDP20, Theorem 2.1, is
justified separately in the audit following 15.12. The graph method is that of Lehn et al. (2019,
Theorem 3.1, p. 9); the multiplicity filtration below specifies its use on a full scheme-theoretic
fibre.


                                                      552
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                   Paper II


    The curve C is rational. Indeed resolve the map by successive blowups with smooth centres.
A map from a projective space to a positive-genus curve is constant, so a holomorphic map from
the last blowup to such a curve is constant on its exceptional projective-space fibres. Its graph
then descends to the preceding smooth space: a proper bimeromorphic graph with singleton
fibres over a normal space is an isomorphism. Descending at each stage would extend g on Y ,
contrary to its definition. Take the Stein factor of a smooth resolution of the map and replace g
by the induced meromorphic map to that factor. It is still non-holomorphic, since otherwise the
original map would be holomorphic. The same descent argument makes its target P1 . Its general
fibre is irreducible and reduced; its image in the graph below need not be smooth.
    Let Z ⊂ Y × P1 be the closure of its graph and write

                                   π : Z → Y,         h : Z → P1

for the holomorphic projections. Locally the map is [a : b], where a, b are holomorphic germs
with no common prime factor. The graph has equation av − bu = 0 in coordinates [u : v] on P1 ;
this hypersurface is integral. On this local product the exact hypersurface sequence is
                                             av−bu
                               0 → O(−1) −−−−−→ O → OZ → 0,

with the harmless line bundle from Y included in the first term when the local equations are
changed. The cohomology of O and O(−1) on P1 gives Rπ∗ OZ = OY . Moreover Rq π∗ F = 0
for q ≥ 2 and every coherent F, since every fibre of π has dimension at most one. For every
closed subspace T ⊂ Z, the ideal sequence and these two facts imply R1 π∗ OT = 0. These are
statements about this graph projection, with their explicitly given local equations.
    The two sections defining the meromorphic map are sections of a line bundle P on Y with no
common divisorial component. Their pullbacks generate an invertible ideal on Z. It defines an
effective Cartier divisor Σ with

                                   h∗ OP1 (1) = π ∗ P ⊗ OZ (−Σ).                              (15)

The local ideal is generated by a/u or b/v on the corresponding graph chart, proving both the
asserted invertibility and the displayed comparison. Every component of Σ dominates P1 : its
support lies over the codimension-two common-zero locus of a, b, and the fibre over each such
point is the entire projective line. In particular Σ meets every fibre. A fibre Zc is identified
by π with the Cartier divisor (avc − buc = 0) in Y , including its multiplicities. It is therefore
Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein.
    We recall the elementary vanishing used below. On a compact reduced irreducible space D, for
a locally free sheaf W and a nonzero effective Cartier divisor A, the descending finite-dimensional
spaces H 0 (D, W (−kA)) stabilize. A section in their stable value vanishes to every order along
A, hence vanishes by the Krull intersection theorem and the identity theorem. The stable value
is zero. On a Cartier divisor with multiplicities, successively remove one prime component at a
time. The corresponding exact sequences have graded factors OD (−Dprevious ) on reduced prime
components; tensoring by an invertible sheaf and a vector bundle preserves exactness. Thus it
suffices to apply the preceding vanishing to the finitely many reduced-component factors.
    We now choose M ∈ Pic(Y ) and k > 0 such that

                   H 0 Zc , π ∗ (V ∗ ⊗ M −1 ) ⊗ ωZc ⊗ OZc (−kΣ) = 0 for every c.               (16)
                                                               

Here is a simultaneous construction. There are only finitely many reducible or nonreduced fibres.
Form the graph of their reduced prime components, joining two which intersect in Y . Give a
component weight equal to its shortest distance from a component meeting Σ on Z. Every weight
is finite because the fibres are connected and meet Σ. Let Di be the sum, with coefficient one, of
the components of weight i. The inclusion Di ,→ Y is a Cartier divisor since Y is smooth.

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


    Put M = OY ( i<d ni Di ), where d is the largest weight. Choose nd−1 first, then nd−2 , and
                    P
continue down to n0 . On each component of weight i > 0, Di−1 restricts to a nonzero effective
Cartier divisor; Dj with j < i − 1 is disjoint from it. After the higher-index coefficients have been
fixed, the preceding vanishing permits a choice of ni−1 which annihilates the sections on every
multiplicity-filtration factor belonging to weight i. Later choices do not affect those factors. The
remaining weight-zero factors are annihilated by increasing k, because Σ restricts to a nonzero
effective Cartier divisor on each. This proves (16) on the finitely many exceptional fibres.
    For clarity, uniformity on the other fibres does not presume local freeness of any higher direct
image. First choose a power of −Σ annihilating sections on one general irreducible reduced
fibre. Serre duality and top-degree base change show that R2 h∗ (π ∗ (V ⊗ P k )) then has finite
support. Increasing k can only decrease that support, because multiplication by the nonzero
divisor cutting out Σ injects the dual section spaces. At each of its finitely many irreducible
fibres the same vanishing lemma, with its multiplicity filtration, kills the remaining group. The
effective twist M cannot introduce a section on another fibre: each of its prime divisors restricts
there to an effective Cartier divisor. This completes the simultaneous construction.
    Restriction of (15) to Zc gives the actual line isomorphism π ∗ P |Zc = OZc (Σ). Serre duality
on the Gorenstein surface Zc turns (16) into

                                 H 2 (Zc , π ∗ (V ⊗ M ⊗ P k )|Zc ) = 0.

                            H 2 Z, π ∗ (V ⊗ M ⊗ P k ) ⊗ h∗ O(t) = 0.

By (15), this is H 2 (Z, π ∗ (V ⊗M ⊗P k+t )(−tΣ)) = 0. The sheaf on tΣ has zero second cohomology:
its pushforward to Y is supported on the at-most-one-dimensional exceptional image, and its
higher direct images vanish by the graph calculation above and the projection formula. The
divisor exact sequence therefore gives H 2 (Z, π ∗ (V ⊗ M ⊗ P k+t )) = 0. Finally Rπ∗ OZ = OY and
the projection formula give an isomorphism with H 2 (Y, V ⊗ M ⊗ P k+t ).
     Since H 2 (Y, Z) is finite, all exponents in this construction can be chosen divisible by its
exponent. The resulting twisting line lies in Pic0 (Y ). The same construction applied to V ⊗ L∗
reaches any fixed component L∗ Pic0 (Y ). For degree zero use the vanishing lemma directly with
any nonzero effective fibre divisor on Y and large negative multiples. For degrees three and
one use Serre duality, respectively with these degree-zero and degree-two arguments applied to
V ∗ ⊗ KY . Semicontinuity in the holomorphic exponential family of line bundles over H 1 (Y, OY )
gives proper analytic jumping loci; their finite union has dense open complement. The exponential
family is constructed by exponentiating a basis of additive Cech one-cocycles, so it includes every
line in Pic0 (Y ) and the semicontinuity assertion needs no compactness of that group.
    All line bundles have rationally zero first Chern class. Hence Riemann–Roch makes χ(V ⊗ L)
independent of L, and the just-proved vanishing  R makes it zero. For V = TY , the terms involving
c1 (Y ) vanish in the index, leaving χ(TY ) = 12 Y c3 (Y ). This proves the last assertion.

Proposition A.8 (Credited re-derivation: Excluded algebraic dimensions). A positive-
dimensional compact Moishezon manifold has b2 > 0. A compact complex manifold
homeomorphic to S 6 has algebraic dimension 0 or 1; in the latter case its algebraic reduction is
holomorphic onto P1 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition A.7.
    The Moishezon assertion is Campana et al. (1998, Lemma 1.4). The sphere assertions follow
from Lehn et al. (2019, Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.2, p. 9). We retain the complete deduction
as a known consequence.

                                                  554
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


Proof. For the first assertion take a projective modification π : Yb → Y . Choose a general very
ample divisor Db and a general complete-intersection curve Cb in the smooth projective manifold
Y so that they meet outside the exceptional locus and their intersection is finite. Their images
b
D, C meet properly and nontrivially. Since Y is smooth, D is Cartier and its effective restriction
to the normalization of C has positive degree. Thus hc1 (OY (D)), [C]i > 0, proving b2 (Y ) > 0.
This is the proof of CDP98, Lemma 1.4 in the opened arXiv source.
    On a six-sphere the Euler number is 2. Statement A.7 consequently excludes every
meromorphic function with an indeterminate map to P1 . If two meromorphic functions were
algebraically independent, both would extend to holomorphic maps to P1 . Their product map
to P1 × P1 has rank two at some point. In local target coordinates u, v centred there, the
meromorphic function u/v pulled back to Y has an indeterminacy: its restrictions to the local
curves u = 0 and v = 0 have distinct limits. This contradicts A.7. Thus a(Y ) ≤ 1. For a(Y ) = 1,
the algebraic reduction cannot be non-holomorphic by A.7, and its base has genus zero because
pullback injects H 1 (C, Q) into H 1 (Y, Q) = 0.

Proposition A.11 (Credited re-derivation: The structure sheaves of the comb members). Let
Xm be any sufficiently small smooth period section obtained by the m-tooth construction of
Viaclovsky (2026b, Theorem 1.1), with m ≥ 12, fixed limiting data at the three distinguished
values, and the standard logarithmic-transformation data. Write fm : Xm → B. Then

               R1 fm∗ OXm = O(am ) ⊕ O(bm ),      am , bm ≥ 0,     am + bm = 2m − 1,

            R2 fm∗ OXm = O(2m − 1),         (h0,0 , h0,1 , h0,2 , h0,3 ) = (1, 2m + 1, 2m, 0).     (E.1)
The individual summands are not specified by m in the construction.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Viaclovsky (2026b, Theorem 1.1).

Proof. The paper’s equation (7.5) proves that attaching and smoothing one twistor conic increases
the determinant degree of its quotient bundle by two. Its Proposition 9.1 identifies the initial
degree as −1, so the smoothed quotient has degree 2m − 1. The geometric gluing comparison
in its Section 6.3 identifies that quotient with R1 fm∗ OXm ; the fixed limiting periods preserve
the same cyclic representations at the finite points and the same normalization complex at the
cusp. Thus its Theorem 2.3 applies to these actual full scheme-theoretic fibres and gives the
cup-product isomorphism det R1 fm∗ O = R2 fm∗ O. Its Proposition 3.2, whose hypotheses are
connected fibres, torus general fibre and the topology of S 6 , gives the two possible splitting
alternatives: both degrees nonnegative, or (−1, 0). The positive determinant degree excludes
the latter. We have now derived the stated sheaves from the source comparisons in precisely
the form needed here. Leray on B gives h0,1 = am + bm + 2, h0,2 = am + bm + 1 and h0,3 = 0,
proving (E.1). The theorem is used for the smoothed section, not for the singular comb, which is
not a small deformation of X0 .

Lemma B.1 (identification of the torsion subsheaf). If S is a reduced effective Cartier divisor
in a smooth complex manifold, then

                              ker Ω1S −→ j∗ Ω1Sreg = Tor(Ω1S ).
                                                  


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Every irreducible component of a reduced hypersurface is generically smooth, so Sreg is
dense and its complement is a proper analytic subset. If a local section of Ω1S vanishes on Sreg ,
its support avoids all minimal primes of the reduced local ring. Prime avoidance therefore gives
an element of its annihilator outside every minimal prime; that element is a nonzerodivisor, so
the section is torsion. Conversely, Ω1S |Sreg is locally free, hence has no torsion, and every torsion
section restricts to zero there.

Local proof of the conormal filtration

Let S be a reduced effective Cartier divisor in a smooth complex threefold X. There are natural
short exact sequences
                                       ∗
                              0 −→ NS/X     −→ KS −→ TS −→ 0,

                                0 −→ KS −→ Ω1X |S −→ Ω
                                                     e 1S −→ 0.

Proof. The conormal sequence is right exact. It is also left exact here. Locally write S = (g = 0)
with g reduced. If h dg|S = 0, then h vanishes at the generic smooth point of every irreducible
component, because dg is nonzero there. The ring OS is reduced, so the intersection of its
minimal primes is zero; hence h = 0. Thus
                                       ∗
                                  0 → NS/X → Ω1X |S → Ω1S → 0

                                                561
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                    Paper II


is exact. By definition, KS is the inverse image of TS under the last surjection. Restriction to
that inverse image is onto TS and has kernel NS/X
                                               ∗   , proving the first sequence. Composing with
the quotient by TS proves the second.

The minimal-prime formulation of conormal injectivity. Right exactness is the conormal
sequence for a closed immersion. We check the left end. Work at a point of S and let R be the
regular local ring of X, with reduced local equation g for S. The map at the left is

                              R/(g) −→ (Ω1R /gΩ1R ),            h̄ 7−→ h dg.               (W.145)

Let p be a minimal prime of (g). Since R is regular and has characteristic zero, the height-one
local ring Rp is a discrete valuation ring. Reducedness of (g) gives ordp (g) = 1, so g is a unit
times a uniformizer there; in characteristic zero the differential of that uniformizer is nonzero
modulo p. Hence dg is nonzero in Ω1Rp ⊗ k(p), so (W.145) sends h̄ to zero only if h ∈ p. This
holds for every minimal prime. Because R/(g) is reduced, the intersection of its minimal primes
is zero; therefore h̄ = 0. Thus the conormal sequence in proposition 5.1 is exact.

between the three sheaf-cohomology groups for a non-torsion line bundle. The explicit extending
choice of A is constructed in the next subsection, which also treats the total-space line-bundle
condition on p. 692. The family (W.8) also does not satisfy all hypotheses of CDP Theorem 2.2,
so this is not a counterexample to that theorem.

Continue with

           C = {y 2 z = x2 (x + z) + tz 3 } ⊂ P2 × ∆,      X = C × P1 ,     S = C0 × P 1 .

Explicit normalization and crossing coordinates

The projection g is proper, X is a smooth complex threefold, and S is a reduced irreducible
normal-crossing (self-crossing) surface whose normalization is P1 × P1 . Its singular locus is
D = {[0 : 0 : 1]} × P1 , and locally along D the pair (X , S) has the model t = uv; away from D
the fibre is smooth and has the usual local model (C3 , {u = 0}).

Proof. Properness follows because C is closed in the projective projection P2 × ∆ → ∆. Write
the defining equation as
                                 F = y 2 z − x2 (x + z) − tz 3 .
On the chart z 6= 0, ∂F /∂t = −z 3 6= 0, so C is smooth there. On z = 0, the equation forces x = 0
and y 6= 0; at such points ∂F /∂z = y 2 6= 0. Hence C, and therefore X , is smooth. The only finite

Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                         Paper II


discriminant values of the fibres are t = 0 and t = −4/27; after shrinking ∆ to |t| < 4/27, every
noncentral fibre is smooth.
    The central curve is C0 : y 2 z = x2 (x + z). Its only singular point is n = [0 : 0 : 1]: on z = 1
the equations F = Fx = Fy = 0 give (x, y) = (0, 0), and the point at infinity [0 : 1 : 0] is smooth
because Fz = 1 there (Euler’s identity also gives the remaining projective singularity equation).
The parametrization

                    ν : P1 −→ C0 ,        [u : v] 7−→ [(u2 − v 2 )v : u(u2 − v 2 ) : v 3 ]     (W.160)

maps the two points p = [1 : 1], q = [−1 : 1] to n. On the chart v 6= 0, set r = u/v; after

is the node (0, 0), hit by [1 : 1] and [−1 : 1], and the point at infinity [0 : 1 : 0] is hit by [1 : 0].
Thus ν(P1 ) = C0 ; as a nonconstant morphism to a projective curve it is finite and generically

normalization is η = ν × idP1 : P1 × P1 → S.
    At n the affine equation is t = y√ 2 − x2 − x3 . On a sufficiently small neighbourhood choose

the holomorphic square root h(x) = 1 + x and set u = y − xh(x), v = y + xh(x). Then uv = t,
and the map (x, y) 7→ (u, v) has invertible 2 × 2 Jacobian at (0, 0), so u, v are local coordinates
on the surface C. If s is a local coordinate on P1 , then (u, v, s) are coordinates on X and t = uv.
Hence the pair has the asserted normal-crossing (self-crossing) local model, with singular locus
D as stated.

Lemma B.4 (the non-torsion gluing bundle). Fix λ ∈ C∗ that is not a root of unity. Gluing the

                  ν ∗ Aλ ≃ O P 1 ,   H 0 (C0 , Aλ ) = 0,        A⊗m

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and

Proof. For a nodal curve, a line bundle with trivial pullback to the normalization is obtained by
identifying the two fibres over the branches of the node. Use the identification whose scalar is λ.
A global section pulls back to a constant c on the projective line and must satisfy c = λc; since
λ 6= 1, c = 0. The mth tensor power has gluing scalar λm , which is never 1 because λ is not a
root of unity. This proves (W.161).

B.5    Cartier-divisor duality without a normality hypothesis
The next two results are explicit re-derivations of classical analytic Cartier duality. The
trace duality and complete-intersection identification are supplied by Ramis and Ruget (1970,
Theorem 2, pp. 82–84, and Proposition 2, p. 91). The proofs retain the full scheme structure of
the fibre and state separately where compactness is needed.

Theorem B.7 (complete Cartier-fibre duality). Let X be a compact smooth complex threefold,
i : W ,→ X an effective Cartier divisor, and E a holomorphic vector bundle. Put F = E|W and

                                    ωW = (ωX ⊗ OX (W ))|W .

For q = 0, 1, 2 there are natural perfect pairings

                                H q (W, F )∨ ≃ H 2−q (W, F ∨ ⊗ ωW ).                        (W.11)

Moreover H q (W, F ) = 0 for q > 2. No normality or reducedness hypothesis on W is used.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Ramis and Ruget, 1970,
Proposition 2 and pp. 90–91); (Ramis and Ruget, 1970, Theorem 2, pp. 82–83).

Proof. Let i : W ,→ X be the given Cartier inclusion. The length-one locally free resolution
                                               ·g
                            0 −→ OX (−W ) −−→ OX −→ i∗ OW −→ 0

is locally defined by a nonzerodivisor g; changing g by a unit gives the usual transition functions
for OX (W ). Applying sheaf Hom into ωX , the degree-zero map is injective and its cokernel is

                        Ext1X (i∗ OW , ωX ) = i∗ (ωX ⊗ OX (W ))|W = i∗ ωW .
                                                                 


The other sheaf Ext groups vanish. Equivalently, W is a two-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay
Gorenstein complex space and its analytic dualizing complex is
                                            •
                                           KW ≃ ωW [2].

This is the hypersurface calculation in (Ramis and Ruget, 1970, Proposition 2 and pp. 90–91);
no normality or reducedness of the Cartier divisor is used.
   For the locally free sheaf F = E|W , the analytic duality trace of (Ramis and Ruget, 1970,
Theorem 2, pp. 82–83) supplies the actual functorial pairing, and identifies the dual of Hcq (W, F )
with
                    Ext−q
                        W (F, KW ) = ExtW (F, ωW ) = H
                                •        2−q              2−q
                                                              (W, F ∨ ⊗ ωW ).
The last equality follows because the positive sheaf Ext groups of a locally free first argument
vanish. Since W is compact, Hcq (W, F ) = H q (W, F ); coherent cohomology is finite-dimensional,
so this pairing is perfect in the ordinary algebraic sense. It is this trace pairing, rather than an
unspecified arrow between two matching five-term sequences, that constructs the isomorphism
(W.11). Its contravariance in F is precomposition in the Ext argument.
    For q > 2, the displayed Ext degree 2 − q is negative. The derived Hom of the locally free
sheaf F , concentrated in degree zero, into the sheaf ωW , concentrated in degree zero, has no
negative cohomology. Hence the duality theorem gives H q (W, F ) = 0. This also follows directly
from coherent cohomological dimension on the compact surface W .

Proposition B.8 (absolute duality on a compact Cartier fibre). Let X be a smooth complex

is the full scheme-theoretic fibre of a holomorphic map f : X → B to a smooth curve. For every
vector bundle E on X there is a functorial perfect pairing

                          H 2 (W, E|W ) × H 0 (W, E ∨ |W ⊗ ωX |W ) −→ C.

Equivalently,
                             H 2 (W, E|W )∨ ≃ H 0 (W, E ∨ |W ⊗ ωX |W ).                       (W.12)
Neither normality of W nor compactness of the ambient threefold is required.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Ramis and Ruget, 1970,
Proposition 2 and the complete-intersection calculation, pp. 90–91); (Ramis and Ruget, 1970,
Theorem 2, pp. 82–83); Grauert (1960).

Proof. An effective Cartier divisor in a smooth threefold is locally a two-dimensional hypersurface
quotient of a regular local ring. Hence W is Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein. If KW     • denotes its

analytic dualizing complex, the complete-intersection calculation of Ramis–Ruget gives
                                            •
                                           KW ≃ ωW [2]

with ωW invertible (Ramis and Ruget, 1970, Proposition 2 and the complete-intersection
calculation, pp. 90–91). Cartier adjunction gives

                                     ωW ≃ (ωX ⊗ OX (W ))|W .

Because W is the full fibre over b ∈ B, one has OX (W ) ≃ f ∗ OB (b) locally along W ; its restriction
to W is the pullback of a one-dimensional vector space. Choosing a nonzero vector identifies
OX (W )|W ≃ OW and ωW ≃ ωX |W . A different choice rescales the final trace pairing by a
nonzero scalar.
    Ramis–Ruget duality pairs Hcp (W, G) with Ext−p
                                                  W (G, KW ) (Ramis and Ruget, 1970, Theorem 2,

                                 •                        0        ∨


Grauert finiteness makes both coherent cohomology spaces finite-dimensional Grauert (1960); the
strong analytic duality is therefore the ordinary algebraic perfect pairing (W.12). Its variance is
contravariant in E|W by precomposition on the Hom term. This proves the assertion.

B.6    Flatness and top-degree analytic base change
Lemma B.9 (automatic properness, flatness, and Cartier fibres). Let f : X → B be a
nonconstant holomorphic map from a connected complex manifold to a Riemann surface. Then f
is flat, every holomorphic vector bundle on X is f -flat, and every full scheme-theoretic fibre is
an effective Cartier divisor of pure codimension one. If X is compact, then f is proper.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026,
Tag 0AUW).

Proof. Fix x ∈ X, c = f (x), and put R = OB,c , S = OX,x . The ring R is a discrete valuation
ring and S is a regular local domain. The homomorphism R → S is injective. Indeed, if a
nonzero germ h ∈ R mapped to zero, h ◦ f would vanish on a neighbourhood of x. The zero


                                                569
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                     Paper II


set of a nonzero one-variable holomorphic germ is isolated, so f would be constant on that
neighbourhood and therefore, by the identity theorem on connected X, constant everywhere.
    Thus every nonzero element of R acts on the domain S as a nonzero element and hence as a
nonzerodivisor. Therefore S is torsion-free as an R-module. A module over a discrete valuation
ring is flat if and only if it is torsion-free (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0AUW);
hence S is R-flat. This holds at every point, so f is flat. A vector bundle is locally a finite free
OX -module, and a finite direct sum of R-flat modules is flat; hence it is f -flat. If t is a local
parameter at c, then f ∗ t is a nonzero element of the domain S and thus a nonzerodivisor. The
full scheme-theoretic fibre is therefore locally cut out by one nonzerodivisor, so it is an effective
Cartier divisor of pure codimension one. Finally, when X is compact, the underlying continuous
map to the Hausdorff surface B is proper.

Proposition B.10 (the exact analytic base-change input). Let f : X → B be proper between
complex spaces, let F be coherent and f -flat, and fix c ∈ B. If

                                          H 3 (Xc , F|Xc ) = 0,                              (W.13)

then the canonical fibre map

                           βc2 : (R2 f∗ F)c ⊗OB,c C(c) −→ H 2 (Xc , F|Xc )                   (W.14)

is an isomorphism.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Bănică and Stănăşilă, 1976,
pp. 120–121); (Campana et al., 1998, Lemma 1.5).

Proof. Apply Bănică–Stănăşilă, Chapter III, §3, Corollary 3.5, with q = 3 (Bănică and Stănăşilă,
1976, pp. 120–121). Its hypotheses are precisely properness, coherence, and flatness. Condition
(W.13) first forces the degree-three direct image to vanish near c. The corollary then applies the
equivalent base-change conditions of its preceding Theorem 3.4 in degree q − 1 = 2 and states
that the canonical map (W.14) is bijective. This is the top-degree argument used in (Campana
et al., 1998, Lemma 1.5); it does not require the stronger, false assertion that all direct images
are locally free.

B.8    A topology-independent Pic0 route and three all-Pic routes
The vanishing of the normalized restriction of every global line bundle for this threefold is already

Remark B.20 (the exact obstruction to the purely analytic route). The proposition proves that
the local homomorphism

                            Pic(N0 ) −→ Pic(E0 ),            L 7−→ ν ∗ (L|W ),

is not zero. Thus the toric cusp geometry, conductor descent on W , or local relative-Picard
representability cannot alone prove the desired global vanishing

                                    ν ∗ i∗ : Pic(X) −→ Pic(E0 ).

There is no contradiction with propositions B.14 and B.18: the local bundle above has nonzero
generic class −2q, whereas the two global proofs use the order-three and order-four fillings and
their common boundary relation to exclude every nonzero multiple of q.
     More generally, Bingener proves that if a holomorphic map is proper, flat, and cohomologically
flat in dimension zero, then its relative Picard functor is represented by a not necessarily
separated complex space (Bingener, 1980, Introduction, p. 318; Satz 6.2, pp. 336–337). The same
introduction explains that the exponential-sequence quotient works directly under topological
local triviality and cohomological flatness in dimension one, but that passage to the quotient
fails in general. The cusp map of Paper I, Theorem B.6 is not topologically locally trivial across
0. Bingener’s theorem therefore supplies representability but neither separatedness nor the
component-specialization assertion needed here.
     Consequently a purely analytic completion must add global compatibility with both finite
fillings and must control the boundary support function; neither relative-Picard representability
nor conductor descent supplies those statements. The later calculation in proposition B.21,
lemma B.22, and theorem B.23 now supplies them: it first forces the generic Appell–Humbert
form to vanish using the two finite fillings, and then proves that its mixed block is the polarization
of the three normalized central degrees. Thus this proposition remains the sharp cusp-local
obstruction, while the global purely analytic route is complete.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; propositions B.14 and B.18;
(Bingener, 1980, Introduction, p. 318; Satz 6.2, pp. 336–337); proposition B.21, lemma B.22,
and theorem B.23.


B.10    An analytic completion of the all-Picard certificate
The local example in proposition B.19 shows that the cusp neighbourhood alone cannot annihilate
normalized central restrictions. We now close the stronger analytic route by retaining the order-
three and order-four fillings. The proof has two independent parts. First, logarithms of the
actual O∗ -factors give the boundary cocycle and its two finite-filling norm identities. Second, a
standard-family support-function calculation reads every possible central restriction directly from
the mixed Appell–Humbert block on a nearby torus. No global Leray differential, nearby-cycle
specialization, or Chern-class evaluation on a cusp bounding chain occurs.

Lemma B.22 (the toric support function detects central restriction). Let M ∈ Pic(N0 ), let
π : Y → N0 be the cusp covering, and let ν : E0 → W be the normalization. If the Appell–

Remark B.25 (reconciliation of the three restriction routes). The Pic0 argument proves (W.44)
without global homology, Mayer–Vietoris, or Leray. The all-Pic statement proposition B.14 avoids
citing the packaged theorem H 2 (X; Z) = 0, but it reuses the same verified global integral Leray
and specialization machinery from which that theorem is deduced. By contrast, proposition B.18
supplies a second all-Pic proof without any global Leray differential: it recovers the primitive
4 − 3 = 1 obstruction directly from the finite logarithmic gluing and the cusp boundary. It still
uses the local integral cusp-specialization theorem. The third proof in theorem B.23 replaces
both that specialization and the cusp Chern-class bounding-chain evaluation by logarithmic O∗
factors, the argument principle, and the exact Ψ-equivariant support function. Thus the purely
analytic strengthening is now complete; the three proofs have different dependency sets.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (W.44); proposition B.14;
proposition B.18; theorem B.23.


B.11    Abstract conductor theorem for the standard fibre
The conductor mechanism below is the argument of Claude and Alpöge (2026a, Lemma 10.3 and
Theorem 10.5(a), pp. 87–89), with its sufficient hypotheses separated explicitly. In particular
the constructed-family conclusion of corollary B.27 is the known nonvanishing assertion of that
theorem. The complete proof is retained so that its normalization, duality and base-change
inputs can be checked individually.
Theorem B.26 (the conductor mechanism for the standard family). Assume:

(H1) X is a connected compact smooth complex threefold and f : X → B is a nonconstant
     holomorphic map to a smooth compact curve;

(H2) W = f −1 (p0 ) is the full scheme-theoretic fibre, is reduced, and has the normal-crossings
     local models (W.3);
                           f → W is the degree-six del Pezzo surface dP6 ;
(H3) the normalization η : W

                       H 2 (W, (TX ⊗ L)|W ) 6= 0    and R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ L) 6= 0.               (W.45)

Theorem 9.2.3, author preprint p. 410); (Serre, 1956, §12, Theorem 1, p. 19); theorem B.2;
theorem B.7; equation (W.47); lemma B.9; proposition B.10.

Proof. Fix L and put
                             FL = TX ⊗ L,          AL = (L∨ ⊗ ωX )|W .

dP6 is the blow-up of P2 at three noncollinear points. A projective change of coordinates moves
these points to the three coordinate points, so this is the smooth complete toric surface obtained
by subdividing the three two-dimensional cones of the fan of P2 . Its fan has support R2 , and
the zero Cartier divisor is nef. Demazure vanishing therefore gives H 1 (dP6 , O) = 0 in algebraic
cohomology (Cox et al., 2011, Theorem 9.2.3, author preprint p. 410). Since this surface is
projective and O is coherent, Serre’s comparison theorem identifies that group with analytic
cohomology (Serre, 1956, §12, Theorem 1, p. 19). In the exponential sequence, the kernel of

                                  c1 : Pic(dP6 ) −→ H 2 (dP6 ; Z)

   Because W = f ∗ (p0 ), one has OX (W ) = f ∗ OB (p0 ), whose restriction to the fibre is trivial.

B.12    The corrected theorem that survives both defects
The original hypotheses do not force the CDP conclusion: the constructed threefold above is a
counterexample. There is nevertheless a sharp useful replacement. It isolates the exact extra
global vanishing needed by the intact part of the argument, and the following fibrewise criterion
replaces the invalid p. 692 reduction.
Lemma B.28 (generic endpoint vanishing). Let Y be a connected compact complex manifold of
dimension n, let D be a nonzero effective Cartier divisor with OY (D) ∈ Pic0 (Y ), and let B be a
holomorphic vector bundle. Let P ⊂ Pic0 (Y ) be a connected irreducible reduced complex analytic
parameter space carrying a Poincaré line bundle on Y × P. Assume that dualization preserves
P, and suppose it contains points P0 = OY (−mD) and Q0 = OY (−`D) for some m, ` ≥ 1 with
H 0 (Y, B ⊗ P0 ) = 0 and H 0 (Y, B ∨ ⊗ ωY ⊗ Q0 ) = 0 (the stabilization argument supplies such
exponents whenever the corresponding twists lie in P). Then there is a dense open subset U ⊂ P
such that, for every P 0 ∈ U ,
                              H 0 (Y, B ⊗ P 0 ) = H n (Y, B ⊗ P 0 ) = 0.                   (W.169)

                                                 595
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                       Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Grauert (1960); Bănică and Stănăşilă
(1976).

Proof. Put Vk = H 0 (Y, B ⊗ OY (−kD)), viewed inside H 0 (Y, B), and note that Vk+1 ⊆ Vk . The
descending chain stabilizes. If s is in its stable value, then at a point of D choose a local defining
nonzerodivisor gD for the Cartier divisor and a local frame of B. Every coefficient of the germ of
s is divisible by gD  k for every k. The Krull-intersection theorem in the regular local ring O
                                                                                                    Y,y
gives k≥1 gD  kO
                   Y,y = 0, so the germ is zero at every point of D. Hence s vanishes on a nonempty
      T
open set and, by connectedness, on Y . Thus Vk = 0 for all sufficiently large k.
    The chosen point P0 satisfies H 0 (Y, B ⊗ P0 ) = 0. The Poincaré bundle gives, locally on P,
a family to which Grauert’s theorem applies; the local jump loci {P 0 : h0 (Y, B ⊗ P 0 ) ≥ 1} glue
to a closed analytic subset of P (Grauert’s theorem; see Grauert (1960); Bănică and Stănăşilă
(1976)). It is proper because it misses P0 , and irreducibility of P makes its complement dense
open. Applying the same stabilization argument to B ∨ ⊗ ωY and using the chosen point Q0
gives H 0 (Y, B ∨ ⊗ ωY ⊗ Q0 ) = 0; dualization stability puts Q∨    0 in P. Serre duality then gives
H n (Y, B ⊗ Q∨ 0 )  =  0. The   corresponding  top-degree  jump   locus is therefore also proper with
dense open complement. Intersecting the two dense open complements proves the claim.

    The following endpoint argument is a re-derivation of Campana et al. (1998, Proposition 1.1
and Corollaries 1.2–1.3), with Serre duality for the top degree. Its formulation makes the
effective-divisor Pic0 hypothesis explicit in arbitrary dimension.

Lemma B.29 (generic endpoint vanishing). Let Y be a connected compact complex manifold, let
D be a nonzero effective Cartier divisor, and suppose OY (D) ∈ Pic0 (Y ). For every holomorphic
vector bundle B, a general P ∈ Pic0 (Y ) satisfies

                          H 0 (Y, B ⊗ P ) = 0,      H dim Y (Y, B ⊗ P ) = 0.                   (W.50)

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The inclusions OY (−(k + 1)D) ,→ OY (−kD) give a descending chain

                             Vk = H 0 (Y, B ⊗ OY (−kD)) ⊆ H 0 (Y, B).

It stabilizes because the last vector space is finite-dimensional. A section in the stable value
belongs to every Vk . In a local equation z = 0 for D, every coefficient of that section is divisible
by z k for all k, and hence is zero. The section vanishes on a neighbourhood of D, and therefore
on connected Y by analytic continuation. Thus Vk = 0 for some k. Since OY (−kD) ∈ Pic0 (Y ),
upper semicontinuity in a local universal family of topologically trivial line bundles shows that

                                       {P : h0 (Y, B ⊗ P ) > 0}

is a proper analytic subset of Pic0 (Y ). This proves the first vanishing for general P . Serre duality
identifies the dual of the second group in (W.50) with

                                       H 0 (Y, B ∨ ⊗ ωY ⊗ P ∨ ).

Apply the first part to B ∨ ⊗ ωY and use that inversion is an automorphism of Pic0 (Y ).

    The cohomology-jump locus

                               {M ∈ Pic(X) : h2 (X, TX ⊗ M ) ≥ 1}

is analytic by upper semicontinuity. It is proper because (W.51) gives a point outside it. Its
complement therefore meets the two endpoint vanishing loci in a dense open set. This proves
(W.52), and on that set

                             χ(X, TX ⊗ M ) = −h1 (X, TX ⊗ M ) ≤ 0.                          (W.55)

    Every M ∈ Pic(X) has rationally trivial first Chern class. The hypotheses also give c1 (TX ) = 0
in rational cohomology and, by Poincaré duality, H 4 (X; Q) = 0, so c2 (TX ) = 0 rationally. The
degree-six term of ch(TX ⊗ M ) td(X) is consequently 12 c3 (TX ). Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch turns
(W.55) into
                                                 1
                            χ(X, TX ⊗ M ) = hc3 (TX ), [X]i ≤ 0,
                                                 2
which proves (W.53).

Corollary B.31 (intact relative criterion). In the setting of theorem B.30, it is enough that
one line bundle L ∈ Pic(X) satisfy

                                          R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ L) = 0.                               (W.56)

This is the valid content of the sufficient criterion printed as (Campana et al., 2020a,
Proposition 2.4, p. 680).



                                                 597
Torus-fibred compact complex threefolds                                                      Paper II


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem B.30; (Campana et al.,
2020a, Proposition 2.4, p. 680); equation (W.51).

Proof. Let A be a positive-degree line bundle on the compact Riemann surface C, and put
E = TX ⊗ L. Projection formula gives

                               R2 f∗ (E ⊗ f ∗ Am ) = R2 f∗ E ⊗ Am = 0.

For m  0, Serre vanishing on C gives

                                     H 1 (C, R1 f∗ E ⊗ Am ) = 0.

The Leray spectral sequence has only columns zero and one, so its total-degree-two terms yield

                                       H 2 (X, E ⊗ f ∗ Am ) = 0.

Thus L0 = L ⊗ f ∗ Am satisfies (W.51), and theorem B.30 applies.

Theorem B.32 (exact reduced-fibre repair of the p. 692 step). Retain the setting of theorem B.30,
assume every full scheme-theoretic fibre Wc = f −1 (c) is reduced, and fix L ∈ Pic(X). Put

Proof. Apply proposition 5.1 to the whole reduced Cartier fibre Wc , not separately to its

The map f is flat: a local parameter at c pulls back to a non-zero-divisor in every regular local

Remark B.33 (scope and sharpness of the repair). Under the two endpoint vanishings in
(W.58), injectivity of δc is equivalent to the desired ambient vanishing (W.59); it is the exact
lifting condition. For a reducible reduced fibre the map must be computed on the whole Cartier
fibre. A nonreduced fibre requires additional nilpotent-thickening layers and is not covered by
theorem B.32. The global criterion theorem B.30 and the relative criterion corollary B.31 do
allow nonreduced fibres.
     The restandard family violates both added conditions rather than being silently excluded by
terminology. Since c3 (X) = 2, the contrapositive of theorem B.30 proves

                          H 2 (X, TX ⊗ L0 ) 6= 0    for every L0 ∈ Pic(X).

Independently, corollary B.27 proves

                            R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ L) 6= 0     for every L ∈ Pic(X),

and its cusp conductor supplies a nonzero element of the relevant ker δc . The first conclusion
rules out the global hypothesis; the second independently rules out the stronger relative sufficient
condition. Thus the corrected theorem is compatible with, and precisely separates, the verified
counterexample to CDP20 Theorem 2.2 as stated.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (W.58); equation (W.59);
theorem B.32; theorem B.30; corollary B.31; corollary B.27; equation (W.60).

Corollary B.34 (Positive Euler number obstructs the added vanishings). For the standard

Proof. Paper I proves that the standard compact threefold has H 1 (X; Z) = H 2 (X; Z) = 0,
